en: The Sūtra on the Bodhisattva’s Ten Stages of Removing Defilements and Severing Bonds through the Most Excellent Inquiry, Scroll One;
also known as the Samādhi of Ten Thousand Sunbeams.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Chapter One: On Guiding the Way (Dàoyǐn Pǐn). Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Amra Grove in the city of Vaiśālī, together with a great assembly of eighty-four thousand bhikṣus and one hundred four thousand bodhisattvas—all of whom were great sages whose profound insight was all-pervasive.
Having attained mastery, they achieve total retention (*dhāraṇī*) and eloquence free from obstruction; they are constantly settled in samādhi, possessing wisdom that is fearless and invincible.

They thoroughly understand the twelve links of dependent origination at their root, thereby reaching the profound and essential patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Circulating through the five realms of existence, they observe and instruct beings, covering all sentient beings with the Buddha’s vast wisdom according to their respective origins.
They rescue and provide succor for others, maintaining majestic deportment and never losing proper etiquette—
namely: the Bodhisattva Constant Purity, the Bodhisattva Jewel Accumulation, the Bodhisattva Jewel Master, the Bodhisattva Jewel-Seal Head,
the Bodhisattva Jewel Treasury, the Bodhisattva Intent on the Goal, the Bodhisattva Turning the Wheel of Dharma, and the Bodhisattva Removing the Veils of the Skandhas.
...the Bodhisattva Padmadāna, the Bodhisattva Siṃha, the Bodhisattva Sūryaprabha,
the Bodhisattva Dṛṣṭiviparyāsa-vinivartaka, the Bodhisattva Anutsarga, the Bodhisattva Akṣīṇāśaya, the Bodhisattva Dharaṇīdhara,
the Bodhisattva Māradhara, the Bodhisattva Nirmāṇa, the Bodhisattva Jala-prabha, and the Bodhisattva Lakṣaṇadāna...
Together with them were the Bodhisattva Saṃgha, the Bodhisattva Suvarṇamāla, the Bodhisattva Maitreya, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, and others, numbering one hundred and four thousand.

At that time, the Earth Lord, the Four Great Heavenly Kings, and Śakra Devānām Indra, leading the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, the Yāma Heaven, the Tuṣita Heaven, the Nirmāṇarati Heaven, and the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven; the First Brahmā King, leading the assembly of Brahmās; as well as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans—all came together to the place where the Buddha was.
At that time, the Tathāgata was surrounded by a retinue of countless billions of followers as he preached the Dharma.

Māra Pāpīyān, feeling uneasy in his own domain, led his officials and subordinates, who surrounded him from front and back, to the place where the Buddha was; there he prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet and stood to one side.
All the great sages and noble beings of this Bhadrakalpa have gathered like clouds.
At that time, the Tathāgata again used the radiance of his tongue-mark to universally illuminate the trichiliocosm. Those who beheld the light said to one another:

"Today, Śākyamuni Buddha in the Sahā world-system emits a great radiance to summon the Bodhisattvas of lofty conduct from the ten directions. Within this light, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Kāśyapa utters these sounds: 'The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni is in the Sahā world-system, emitting subtle and wondrous light, and expounding ten thousand samādhis and right concentrations for the sake of these great beings—concentrations that are not within the sphere of activity of pratyekabuddhas or śrāvakas.'"
"Each of us shall take our own offerings and go to that Land of Endurance (Sahā) to pay homage, receive [the teachings], and behold [the Buddha].

At that time, ninety-two thousand Buddha-worlds to the east of here was a land named Śrīmat, where the Buddha was named Viśeṣa Tathāgata. To the left and right of that Buddha was a bodhisattva named Dṛḍhamati, a mahāsattva of penetrating wisdom who dwelt in the stage of non-retrogression. His radiance pervaded that realm, and he exhorted the bodhisattvas; thereupon, he himself went to the presence of the Śrīmat Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, prostrated himself, knelt for a long time, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"O Great Sage, I wish to go to the Land of Endurance to behold the Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, prostrate myself, inquire after his well-being, and receive instruction on what I have not yet heard."
That Buddha told him:
"You should know that now is the time; go without hesitation.
He then addressed Adhyāśaya:
"Even upon arriving in the Sahā world, you must immediately practice fifty-five matters, keeping them firmly in mind so that none are lost.
What are these fifty-five matters?..."
Giving and non-giving are equal; regarding precepts and their violation, patience and the absence of anger, diligence and indolence, strong will and weakness,
a distracted mind and meditative concentration, profound wisdom and shallow folly, enemies and one’s own kin,
seeing insults as empty space, and the three vehicles— there is no high or low among these, nor is there any thought of diversity.
They neither perceive the good nor the unwholesome; they neither perceive the purity of a buddha-field nor the impurity of a buddha-field.
If they see beings being born in the evil destinies, they harbor no fear.
They view all noble beings as if they were the Protectors (the Buddhas), maintaining a state of non-duality and always remaining single-minded. Even if they witness an act of killing...
Regarding theft, lewdness, frivolous speech, and flowery talk; indulgence in alcohol, folly, and confusion; jealousy, anger, delusion, and mutual litigation;
and the mind’s adherence to false views—such as claiming the impermanent is permanent—one should regard all these with equanimity, maintaining a mind free from increase or decrease.
Do not think that by observing the precepts one receives superior karmic rewards, or that by practicing giving one receives great merit; nor should you say:
"By now protecting against killing, I shall extend my life for immeasurable eons."

"Furthermore, do not disparage one another; my appearance and marks are superior, and my instructions are extraordinary. Those people are base, defiled, and partisans of the ordinary worldlings. By eliminating the seven types of pride and the twelve indeterminate states, these constitute the fifty-five matters."
"You should contemplate and practice this.
The Buddha said to Cchih-chih:

"If there are sons or daughters of good family whose minds are upright and who dwell in meditative concentration, they may travel to that land. Even if one were to establish pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) in my land for hundreds of thousands of kalpas, it would not equal the merit of maintaining a mind free from pride or inferiority in the Sahā world for the duration of a finger-snap; the latter is superior by billions of times."
At that time, fifty thousand bodhisattvas from that land each made a vow, saying:
"We shall fully perfect the purity of our minds and serve the Bodhisattva Who Holds His Resolve, so that we may go to pay homage to the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Śākyamuni."

The Bodhisattva Dṛḍhamati, together with fifty thousand bodhisattvas, vanished from that buddha-field in the brief interval it takes a strong man to flex and extend his arm; in an instant, he appeared in this Sahā world to pay homage to the Buddha Śākyamuni, prostrated himself, and withdrew to stand to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One, observing that the assembled congregation had taken their seats, addressed the fourfold assembly:
"Do you see this Bodhisattva Dṛḍhādhyāśaya? They replied:
“I have seen them,” he replied.

The Buddha said, “O sons of noble family, this Great Being has transcended the profound distinctions of the three realms of existence; his eloquence is thorough and his compassion is moving. Through his supernormal powers and transformations, he guides and encourages others, bringing great benefit to all those in whose path he dwells.”

At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Most Victorious (Jiāngshèng). Empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, he rose from his seat, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the World-Honored One:
“Indeed, though my disposition is free from attachment, it is dull and ignorant. I wish to ask a question; if I am granted permission, I would venture to present it.”
The Buddha told Sujaya: "Ask whatever you wish; the Tathāgata shall explain it for you.
At that time, having received permission to inquire, the Bodhisattva Sujaya addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Indeed, World-Honored One, in what samādhi does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Perfectly Enlightened One, enter to emit a great radiance surpassing that of the sun and moon? If there are sentient beings who behold the light of the Tathāgata, they will surely attain their aspirations without losing their human faculties. What kind of transformation is so wondrous and miraculous?”
The Buddha told Most Victorious:
"Excellent indeed is your question!

It is truly as I have said regarding the power of my radiance: it receives and delivers sentient beings, bringing about great transformation and edification. The Tathāgata enters hundreds of thousands of millions of various samādhis as appropriate, traveling through immeasurable buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Regarding the inclinations and conducts of beings, which are as vast as the atoms of a world-system—whether there are those who possess lust, anger, and ignorance, or those who are arrogant, self-willed, conceited, and dissolute—the Tathāgata observes them all and discerns them completely."
At that time, Varaprabha again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"What is meant by a bodhisattva, from the first setting forth until the attainment of Buddhahood—from the first ground and the second ground up to the tenth ground—severing how many fetters and eliminating how many defilements?"
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s thorough understanding that their own body is without arising internally or externally?
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s self-proclamation of extensive giving without cessation or annihilation?
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s practice of the precepts being complete so as to never commit an offense, nor violate the precepts and fall from their original station?
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s patience that does not arise, and their retreating from patience to engage in the conduct of an ordinary person?
What is meant by a bodhisattva’s diligent and tireless effort, yet still possessing arrogance and indolence as they accumulate karma from the beginning?
What is meant by a bodhisattva entering the dharma of concentrated mind such that their heart is not disturbed even when the heavens thunder and shake?
How is it that a bodhisattva’s initial resolve and practice cannot be severed by anyone?
How is it that a bodhisattva’s mental consciousness is secure and cannot be abandoned?
What is meant by a bodhisattva whose mind is uniquely exalted and transcends all others?
How is it that the destination of a bodhisattva’s mind is such that its intent cannot be known?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ajita:
"Excellent, excellent!
That you ask about this meaning will bring great benefit and accomplish much; I shall now expound its significance for you."

The conduct of Bodhisattvas is inconceivable; their wisdom is boundless and has no equal. They are thus able to arouse their minds before the Tathāgata and let out the lion’s roar. Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon this well.
Jiaye replied, "I shall receive your instructions and listen.
The Buddha said:

“When a Bodhisattva resolves their mind to seek the Unsurpassed Way, they first sever false views, attachment to the body, and the misconception of precepts; they cultivate the wisdom that discerns suffering and establish their vows by fulfilling the prohibitions and precepts. They constantly reflect: ‘In all my actions, I vow to joyfully distance myself from mundane dharmas, for the nature of the five aggregates is ungraspable.’”

"The Path itself cannot be apprehended, much less those who stand outside the Path, who rely upon form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness to seek the deliverance of sentient beings.
The Buddha again addressed Ajita:

"The five aggregates have no contemplative practice, and sentient beings likewise have no contemplative practice; furthermore, one does not perceive anyone who can be delivered. This teaching of the ineffable Dharma is beyond the reach of Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Most Victorious addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

One does not attain the Way through non-contemplation of the five aggregates, nor does one attain the Way through non-contemplation of sentient beings; might it be possible to attain it through the four prohibitive dharmas?”
The Buddha said, "No.
Varasūra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If it cannot be obtained through these four matters, can it then be obtained through emptiness?
The Buddha said, "No."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Most Victorious again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If it is not obtained from emptiness, nor obtained from the four requisites, then would the Tathāgata and those in this assembly today not have accomplished the Unsurpassed Way, nor would they have attained its fruit and retribution?"
The Buddha said:
"One merely accomplishes the unsurpassed way; however, one does not accomplish equal and perfect enlightenment by abiding in existence, nor by abiding in non-existence.
Most Victorious addressed the Buddha, saying:

"What are form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, as well as internal and external phenomena, wholesome and unwholesome phenomena, outflowing and non-outflowing phenomena, and conditioned and unconditioned phenomena?
Regarding the phenomena designated by names spoken by the Tathāgata, how does he teach all beings through names, concepts, and the substance of syllables?"
The Buddha said:

"In practice there is neither name nor conceptualization; one does not perceive the duality of entering and exiting, nor the coming and going or circling about. Therefore, it is called 'All-Knowledge' (Sarvajña)."
A bodhisattva should always understand the matters of the ten stages by means of ten dharmas.
What are these ten dharmas for understanding the matters of the ten stages?

They are: the meaning of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path; the meaning of the cessation of all things and non-arising that is universally pervasive; the meaning of self-cognition regarding one's own body and that of others; and the meaning of knowing that the six roots of error and the sixty-two views are all empty and non-existent.
When a bodhisattva practices in this way, they should eliminate both the trace of existence and the trace of non-existence.
How does one eliminate the trace of existence and the trace of non-existence?
The path is a trace, while that which is not the path is no trace; coming and going are traces, whereas for one who neither comes nor goes, there is no trace.
A bodhisattva should mindfully cultivate the various stages (bhūmis) and practice the meaning of suffering to sever the fire of lust, the poison of hatred, and the thorns of ignorance.
With a heart of compassion and loving-kindness pervading the four quarters, though they possess a mind of pity, they remain free from conceptualization;
whatever they bestow as a gift is never for their own sake, but is extended universally to all beings.
One should be without stinginess even regarding one's life; when giving, one does not perceive the act of giving, nor the recipient, nor the material object.

One should contemplate associating with those who are virtuous, always maintaining a humble mind and remaining free from arrogance. When preaching the Dharma, one does not perceive the existence of dharmas;
one emerges from the nest of conceptualization, free from the notion of "dharmas. On the day of renouncing the household life, one abandons attachment...

Desiring to depart, one should sever all lingering attachment through the realization that phenomena are empty and non-existent. When seeking the Buddha’s attainment of the Way, do not cling to the marks and signs of physical excellence;
nor should you think, "I shall attain the Way first, while such-and-such a person follows behind me.

Even if you wish to disseminate the teachings of the Dharma, never allow them to be defeated or destroyed. As you advance toward the realization of the fruit, do not be led astray by worldly desires; let your mind [remain steadfast].
Constantly maintaining mindfulness to extinguish arrogance, one does not seek the rewards of the Dharma or material wealth through self-will;
regarding the true teachings received as being beyond verbal instruction, one sustains the body like empty space, free from all conceptualization—
this is how a bodhisattva accomplishes the purification of the traces of the first stage through the wisdom of suffering.

"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva again practices one hundred thousand concentrations through the meaning of suffering and the meaning of cultivation. If he wishes to attain the Buddha’s mental concentration and samādhi, he does not do so by means of perceptions of form, nor by means of the marks of physical excellence, nor does he reach this single abiding by means of his past habitual practices. He neither hopes to achieve this by doing this, nor fails to achieve this by not doing this. He constantly establishes this resolve without dwelling on the past or the future, nor does he dwell on the destinations of birth and death in the present world. He does not derive this Dharma from the five aggregates or the six sense-bases, yet he is not separate from the five aggregates and the six sense-bases."
Furthermore, one should contemplate the six bases that lack a fundamental essence.
These six bases that lack a fundamental essence are the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind; they arise from their conditions of origination and cease from their conditions of origination.

Furthermore, one should distinguish the arising of the six sense-decadays (*ṣaḍāyatana*) and thoroughly examine and understand the phenomena of form, sound, odor, taste, and touch; moreover, by not employing the functions of seeing, hearing, remembering, knowing, mind, or consciousness, one attains the purity of the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*).
By means of neither artifice nor the phenomena of arising and ceasing, nor the notion of permanence, one purifies this ground.

There is neither right nor wrong; one does not form an equanimous mind nor harbor any expectations. One neither affirms what is right nor denies what is wrong, yet dwells purely in the ground. Furthermore, one does not proceed from one, two, three, or four up to a hundred thousand concentrations, nor does one depart from the mind of a hundred thousand concentrations to dwell purely in the ground.

One does not, by means of mind or intention, comprehend the internal and external manifold thoughts, expectations, or matters of right and wrong; nor does one purify the stages through form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. Nor does one rely on morality, learning, concentration, wisdom, liberation, or the knowledge and vision of liberation; nor on the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, or the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha which are the treasures of all Buddhas. One cannot know or see this through conceptual thought, nor through the notion of self or the notion of non-self. It is not by way of the five aggregates or the six sense-fields—the locus of arising and ceasing—that one dwells, nor is there a place where one does not dwell. This is called the Bodhisattva’s purification of the first stage (*bhūmi*).

Furthermore, there is no dwelling of form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness; nor is there any locus of the eye and forms, the ear and sounds, the nose and odors, the tongue and tastes, or the body and tactile objects. Why is this so?

One cannot see it with the eye, yet one understands the manifold conceptions; it is the dharma that neither arises nor ceases, having no end and no beginning. This is called the Bodhisattva purifying his tracks within the first stage (*bhūmi*), fully accomplishing them all, and bringing the wisdom of the Way (*mārgajñatā*) to perfection. There is no difference from what the Tathāgata has proclaimed; he is able to understand and expound various thoughts, and can also instruct others to receive, recite, and chant them, universally and completely mastering the profound treasury of all Buddhas.
The Buddha again addressed Ajita:

"Furthermore, a bodhisattva should fulfill the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā). To mindfully relinquish physical form and appearance without harboring any expectations, and not to give rise to the three types of thoughts that involve defiled attachment—this is called the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramitā)."

If one wishes to know the root source, one must realize that the Buddha-body is fundamentally non-existent through the practice of mindfulness; thus, one should know that this constitutes the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).

Not conceiving the thought that "I have achieved the thirty-two marks," and reckoning all dharmas as mere provisional names, phrases, and designations—wherein appearances are inexhaustible yet abide in the state of non-arising—is therefore called the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).

All dharmas are universally without the practice of contemplation, nor is there the practice of hearing or seeing the Dharma of the Path-seeker; seeing good, one does not rejoice, and encountering evil, one does not grieve; the mind has neither attachment nor aversion—therefore, it is called the Perfection of Vigor (Vīrya-pāramitā).

When the mind does not give rise to thoughts or stir up distracted imaginings, but remains in tranquil stillness, guarding itself so that consciousness is permanently settled, it is therefore called the Perfection of Dhyāna (Dhyanapāramitā).

Understanding that the characteristics of form are empty and that form is subject to decay and destruction, and neither exalting oneself nor harboring arrogance, one realizes that the characteristics of all phenomena are one and the same, yet even this oneness does not exist; it is therefore called the Perfection of Prajñā (Prajñāpāramitā).
Furthermore, by employing skillful means (*upāya*) to respond appropriately to sentient beings, one delivers them according to their conditions so that none are lost.
Therefore, O Most Victorious One!

A bodhisattva who has resolved upon enlightenment uses the noble wisdom of suffering (*duḥkha-āryajñāna*) to cultivate the practices of the first stage (*bhūmi*), whereby they are able to fully perfect the various gates of samādhi, the gates of dhāraṇī, and mastery over wisdom.

"Furthermore, when a bodhisattva attains these ten thousand samādhis and dwells in the desire realm, they should, by means of the fruit of the knowledge of suffering and the knowledge of equality, discern ten dharmas—namely, desire, ill will, pride, delusion, doubt, the view of a self-identity, extreme views, views regarding one's own perspective, adherence to precepts and rituals, and the grasping of views—and having known and understood them, neither eliminate nor exhaust them, nor allow them to arise."

Furthermore, by means of the knowledge of suffering (*duḥkha-jñāna*) and the knowledge of equality (*samatā-jñāna*), one thoroughly understands the eighteen root-afflictions (*saṃyojana-mātṛkā*) regarding both the conditioned and the unconditioned. Although one discriminates these afflictions, they are neither exhausted nor bestowed.

Most Excellent One, you should know that when a beginner first resolves their mind, they further employ the meaning of practice (*abhyāsa-artha*) and the meaning of equality (*samatā-artha*) to abide in the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) within the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm. Therein, they contemplate the calamities of the nineteen adversaries and the afflictions of wounds and sores, as well as the meanings of leakage without beginning and total extinction.
Furthermore, one observes nineteen modes of delusion within the three realms; there are twenty-two [factors] pertaining to the Path across the three stages.

One should also contemplate the thirty-four untainted noble mental states that possess all virtues and bring them to full accomplishment. By contemplating impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self, and by understanding the non-duality [of these truths], one purifies one's traces upon the first stage.
2. Chapter on Remaining in Transformation (Nirmāṇasthiti-parivarta). Second. At that time, the Bodhisattva Most Victorious (Varajaya) came before the Buddha and addressed him, saying:
"How does a bodhisattva fulfill their practice within the two stages of dwelling, so that they will surely realize their vows without any error?"
The Buddha told Ajita:

"A bodhisattva, while in the second stage, should constantly contemplate and purify their precepts, remain mindful of the gravity of [the Buddha’s] kindness, diligently practice patience, humility, and self-effacement, always maintain a joyful heart, smile before speaking, practice great compassion, be filial toward teachers and elders, have deep faith in the Triple Gem, cultivate sublime wisdom, and refrain from generating attachments or conceptualizing things as permanent."

Now, those who calculate based on permanence claim that within the cycle of birth and death and the karma of liberation there is a permanent Way; yet this permanent Way is not truly supreme. It is only that which emerges from the non-permanent that is called supreme.
Since the supreme itself has no supremacy, how can one speak of the supremacy of the Way?

Therefore, O Most Victorious One, the Bodhisattva realizes that the Way is neither noble nor base, and possesses no form or likeness; while space is conventionally said to have a physical substance, the true Way cannot be seen through names or designations.
His mind is serene and free from all fetters or attachments; the virtuous deeds he cultivates never depart from the Buddhas, and none can sever his progress midway.

All evils are completely exhausted without remainder; their minds are permanently settled and cannot be moved or turned back. Their resolve is like a diamond, having no peer; they know the root of all dharmas. Having removed all defilements and extinguished darkness, their Dharma shines radiantly, illuminating everything. Their hearts are sincere and upright, free from flattery; their nature and conduct are impartial, without thoughts of self or other. Since first generating the aspiration for enlightenment, they have always maintained purity; because they are pure from the beginning, they are able to remove all stains. They bathe in the clear depths of the profound pool to wash away all filth; their faith is firm and steadfast, with nothing abandoned or discarded. Their intent to give is vast and expansive, without boundaries; their mind is like space, inexhaustible. They embrace those who are inferior and lowly, nurturing them until they cross over to liberation.
The reason for this is that their wisdom is pure and refined, free from all obstructions; what the mind intends to encompass admits nothing it cannot contain.
Possessing the inexhaustible treasury of great compassion, they attain eloquence through discernment and always maintain a sense of shame.
Their firm conduct cannot be discouraged, and the power of their awakening penetrates everywhere. Their eloquence...
As soon as he appeared before the assembly, all were filled with thirsting admiration; he attained all *dhāraṇīs* and never forgot them.

From the beginning, he never discoursed on matters that were not urgent; amidst hundreds of thousands of samādhis, he never harbored doubt. Hearing of good or evil dharmas, he felt neither sorrow nor joy;
he was neither conceited nor self-depreciating, proceeding with composure and never losing his majestic dignity.
As for the ritual observances, he fundamentally understood the arising of the five aggregates and the six decays through twelve modes of practice;

furthermore, by means of the truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, he analytically discerned the twelve links of dependent origination, penetrating all aspects of birth and death within the cycle of ignorance.

Observing that the five faculties were fully perfected and his mindfulness complete, he no longer returned to the defiled attachments of birth and death; instead, by means of eighty-four types of knowledge, he extinguished all outflows (*āsrava*) and vowed to remain as a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) for one *kalpa* to instruct sentient beings.

Just as my present body shall certainly enter into *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, yet without entering final extinction, I shall likewise remain as a transformation-body (*nirmāṇakāya*), surrounded before and behind by countless multitudes in the Land of the Wise and Virtuous, preaching the subtle and wondrous Dharma.
“Most Excellent One, you should know that to the north of here, beyond as many Buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in thirteen hundred million Ganges Rivers,
there is a world named Acala. There dwells a Buddha named Ālokamanas Tathāgata,
Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, who currently teaches the Dharma in that realm of Acala.”
There were no names of śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; it was exclusively composed of Mahāyāna practitioners who had ascended to the stages.
They delighted themselves in the perfections of giving, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, and meditative concentration, employing supernatural powers and wisdom for their own enjoyment.

Boundless knowledge enveloped their bodies, and they distinguished the profound and subtle meanings of the sūtra passages at all times, while their compassion, joy, and equanimity were as vast as space.
Embracing emptiness, he contemplates the sentient beings before him, knowing their dispositions and natures, and rains down the boundless flavor of the Dharma as ambrosia.

Those who partake of it are freed from the fetters of anger and resentment; they practice the three samādhis of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, rescue others from birth and death, and establish them on the shore of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), subduing the dust of demonic afflictions and the poison of malevolence.

That Buddha, through his supernormal powers, moved and manifested transformations, traveling back and forth across immeasurable buddha-fields; those who received his instruction did not know it was a manifestation and took him for the true Buddha.

All the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the past, have each left behind transformation-buddhas to receive sentient beings according to their conditions and enable them to attain the unconditioned; therefore, the Tathāgata’s concealment of his form and his timely transformations are inconceivable.
In the future, Maitreya and other such Buddhas will likewise each manifest transformed images of Tathāgatas to guide sentient beings.
Although I shall enter parinirvāṇa, those transformed bodies of the Buddha will not themselves enter parinirvāṇa.

Therefore, the Most Victorious One (the Buddha) is neither a transformation nor a non-transformation, and likewise neither a Buddha nor a non-Buddha; he understands emptiness and stillness, and perceives no marks of duality, plurality, or variety.

Bodhisattvas of the second stage should constantly practice the dharma of illusion and transformation, observing and comprehending the stages of wisdom, the stage of sincere faith, the stage of vision, the stage of refinement, the stage of final accomplishment, and the stages inhabited by Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas. Although they treat the illnesses [of sentient beings], they do not take up their [respective] realizations; yet if a Bodhisattva dwelling in the second stage were to wish to take up the realization of a Śrāvaka or a Pratyekabuddha, it would be extremely easy for him to do so.

It is, for example, like a person who takes a flower garland and a bright moon-jewel in their hand and hurls them upward into the void; before they have fallen to the ground, one cuts off the fetters, removes defilements, and extinguishes all outflows within that interval, such that there is no longer the suffering of birth, old age, death, or affliction. Yet, although the Bodhisattva knows how to sever these fetters, he ultimately does not realize [nirvana] himself.
The reason for this is that, without yet having examined the superior, middling, or inferior intentions of sentient beings, one steadies their minds so they may dwell forever in the ultimate state;
one raises clouds of boundless compassion, strikes the thunder of wisdom, rains down the medicine of ambrosia, and proclaims the treasure of the True Dharma.
Without severing the three karmas, one’s thoughts remain as pure and transparent as clear water, constantly employing the prohibitive precepts.
Self-adorned, they further embellish their physical forms with manifold virtues and reverently follow the sublime path of awakening of the worthy sages.
Reaching the final stage of existence in a womb as a Bodhisattva in his last birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*), they awaken to the fundamental karmic deeds performed by all Buddhas;

their awakened mind and *dhāraṇī* are entirely without fixed location. First, through recollection, they give rise to the intention to purify the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) according to the occasion.
In his comings and goings, he practices *ānāpānasmṛti* (mindfulness of breathing); among the assembly, he maintains a resolute will and controls himself without fear;
his mind is thus courageous and attains mastery. He resolves to achieve the most lovable and venerable state, preaching the Dharma of joy and bliss for all sentient beings;
his mind is exceptionally noble, transcending and excelling the multitude.
"If one can maintain the mark of emptiness and non-existence, the wondrous arts of the heterodox cannot prevail against them;
they are constantly revered by Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Varaprabha:

"A Bodhisattva of the Second Stage understands fundamental non-existence and remains far removed from bodily actions; he eliminates verbal calamities and removes mental distractions. He extinguishes the three defilements, restrains the three disasters, and blocks off the five corruptions. He investigates the root of the twelve deluded practices; as for the five upper fetters scattered throughout the triple world, he gradually eliminates them so that they do not increase."

Contemplate the eleven types of suffering as sores; abandon the disease of attachment to the four great elements; discern the impure nature of all things; one should avoid worldly affairs and cease mundane customs; sever craving, hatred, and the defilement of greed; and thoroughly uproot the source so that it no longer flows forth.

Constantly reflecting upon and contemplating the notion of non-self, firmly establishing the four kinds of faith, abiding in the four foundations of mindfulness, accomplishing the four right efforts, extolling the five faculties, manifesting the five powers with an unflagging resolve, understanding the seven treasures of the factors of enlightenment, practicing the noble eightfold path, and never abandoning the eight thoughts of a great person.
Thus it is, O Most Victorious One!

A Bodhisattva of the second stage holds their mind and disciplines their thoughts so that they do not harbor manifold notions; understanding that all things are empty and lack true reality, they then attain the higher station and receive the Bodhisattva’s prediction of enlightenment. They neither remain fixed in arduous practice nor abandon practice, as they train in supreme wisdom.

Though possessing noble status, his mind is free from arrogance; he contemplates and knows all dharmas as being neither one nor two, nor does he conceive of them as three. Furthermore, he does not give rise to useless thoughts, nor thoughts of limits, existence, or non-existence. He realizes that thought has no locus and does not dwell even in the absence of a locus. Only the perfect enlightenment is pure, and the Buddhas are likewise pure. Skillfully governing the mind, he abides correctly and not erroneously. Equalizing good and evil, he discerns that both are empty; this emptiness is free from doubt and obstruction. Moreover, he perceives neither contention nor non-contention, neither contemplation nor non-contemplation.

Fundamentally, there is neither oneness nor does one perceive oneness; knowing oneness and eliminating oneness, one does not dwell in oneness, nor does one give rise to manifold conceptions from oneness, but practices with equanimity toward superior intention.

There is no cultivation of limits; one does not perceive limits, nor victory or defeat. One does not allow the mind to be distracted by internal or external phenomena, but skillfully restrains consciousness so that it remains concentrated and unswerving.

Although they dwell within the three realms of existence, they do not cling to them; they profoundly examine all natures and realize they have no root. To know that there is no root is what is called the "Pure Ground.

A Bodhisattva at the second stage disciplines their own mind and contemplates the source of all phenomena as entirely impermanent. Being eternally without entry, they see no arising; there are no names of good or evil, beauty or ugliness, profit or loss, defamation or praise, censure or commendation, nor suffering or pleasure.

He harmonizes and rectifies his mind so that it is free from sorrow or distress; wherever he enters, he reveals the great treasury; he enters the ocean of the Great Dharma and seeks the seven types of wisdom; he sears away the three cravings and skillfully restrains the four torrents; he cultivates the six dharmas of respect and realizes the practice of fruition.
Thus it is, O Most Excellent One!
When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is endowed with all dharmas, he knows them to be formless and invisible; this is called training in the purification of the second stage.
Chapter Three: The Contemplation of Emptiness (Śūnyatā-darśana-parivarta). At that time, the Bodhisattva Most Victorious (Varasūra) again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How should a bodhisattva purify their conduct within the third stage?"

The World-Honored One said: "A Bodhisattva who advances in learning has no thoughts of entering or exiting. Though he studies extensively, he never tires of the meaning; he does not dwell on the origins or endings of words, phrases, or characters. He distributes the gift of Dharma with humility toward others. He cultivates and purifies buddha-lands without the notion of a 'land. He establishes wholesome deeds without arrogance. From the first arousal of the mind, his practice is never interrupted; his vows for merit and virtue are as steadfast as Mount Sumeru. Observing all sentient beings, he preaches the Dharma of joy and bliss. Taking the initial aspiration as the root of the Way, he thereby attains the fruit of the eternally quiescent Path."

With a mind intent on universal giving that extends to all beings, they establish their vows and fulfill the precepts; with an open mind and diligent practice free from indolence, they find no worldly delight but take only the Path as their task; for those who have no refuge, they act as guides by means of discerning the Dharma of great wisdom.

From the first moment of generating the resolve, one is forever without abiding; because the ultimate great compassion is invisible, one seeks to uproot the source and establish the traces of the Mahāyāna. One should practice sorrowful pity for those not yet liberated, and should harbor joy whenever one sees those who have been liberated.
Maintaining an impartial mind toward all sentient beings, one remains unmoved even when encountering suffering or joy; protecting and guiding them all, one leads them into the gateway of the Way.

Supported by the Tathāgatas and mindful of the exhortations of the Buddhas of the ten directions, one shall deliver all from the perils of the five destinies, cause the transformation of the Way to flourish, and ensure that the Three Jewels suffer no harm. Without transgression or loss, one shall thus attain the fruit of the Way.

He shall follow and uphold the prohibitions and precepts as an example for all people, extensively expounding the treasure of inexhaustible wisdom; just as space cannot be exhausted, so too his omniscience is inexhaustible.

The mind-consciousness of the Tathāgata is also like this: it is devoid of the two extremes of arising-and-ceasing or attachment-and-interruption; within the body of concentration, samādhi, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge-and-vision of deliverance, there is neither near nor far, and it cannot be seen.

"O Most Victorious One, you should know that the essential core of the profound Dharma of all Buddhas is likewise inexhaustible and without beginning; throughout the convergence and dispersal of the three periods of past, future, and present, there is nothing that exists, nor is any accumulation seen. That which is accomplished has no further scattering; its transformations are not singular, yet it is not created by the four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—and being without opposition, it is invisible."

Using wisdom, one discerns the mental activities of sentient beings; their original vows are uninterrupted and inconceivable, all being without arising and without even a semblance. All dharmas cannot be known upon investigation; for this reason, there is no arising, nor is there any dharma that can arise. Since what has arisen is non-arising, what is it that arises?
Therefore, O Most Victorious One!

One should give rise to the bodhicitta so that it is inexhaustible; one should not establish the mind, intentions, forms, or characteristics of any phenomena, nor harbor flattery or expectations regarding any phenomena.

His mind is upright and straightforward, preeminent among the assembly; he cultivates the dharma of calming the mind and observes the dharmas of his own body. He observes the bodies of others as entirely empty and quiescent, giving rise to no conceptualizations; he observes that the body is undefiled and ungraspable, and that there is no giver, nor any distinction between them as a single entity.

In walking, stopping, advancing, or retreating, one observes that all beings who take form within the three realms encounter various sufferings and afflictions due to ignorance and craving; yet, one realizes they are non-dual and invisible, and that the phenomena of painful mental formations are empty both internally and externally, devoid of arising or ceasing.
"Furthermore, Most Excellent One!

A bodhisattva who advances in training observes the inhalation and exhalation of breath—its length and brevity, its slowness and rapidity—and thoroughly penetrates and understands everything through which the breath passes within the pores of the body. He knows that the exhaled breath is warm and the returning breath is cool, and he realizes that it is ultimately quiescent, devoid of any form or substance."

The Bodhisattva contemplates the body as being devoid of any locus for the discerning consciousness; because it is pure, it is level and upright without deviation. He makes his mind supple and does not harbor coarseness or ferocity; he has profound faith in the true essence that never changes, and his will is always firm and unshakable, such that no one can harbor malice or jealousy to afflict or harm him.

Why is this so? Because the limits of their practice cannot be reached, and as for what they have established, none can revile it; how then would anyone dare to create [false accusations]? Being rootless and faultless, the defilements of the mind are extinguished.

They vow that the Wheel of Dharma shall constantly turn in the world, causing all people to swiftly attain wondrous wisdom. Its light illuminates the dark and obscure like the sun piercing through clouds. They establish the wholesome roots of the Path and personally contemplate non-self; birth has no location. This is likewise true for both internal and external phenomena. Furthermore, they do not perceive any place where birth and death proceed, nor any point of arising and ceasing; even regarding Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and Buddhas, there is nothing to be seen or heard.

To have a perception of seeing is not to see; when there is no perception of anything seen, all is pure. Not to dwell even on the perception of purity is non-perception; this is the view of emptiness, which is to have nothing seen.

"Furthermore, Most Victorious One! The mind is not within, nor does it abide without; it does not dwell in the dharmas of the Path, nor does it abide in the mundane; it abides neither in existence nor in non-existence. It perceives no place of arising, ceasing, or movement; the mind has no boundaries, being vast, universal, and bottomless, and it is devoid of sound, its beginning and end being utterly exhausted."

Thus it is, O Most Victorious One! You should contemplate in this way, contemplating that which is not to be contemplated; you should see in this way, seeing that which is not to be seen. For a Bodhisattva who practices, emptiness, cessation, and non-existence are the goal.

A Bodhisattva established in the third stage stabilizes all dharmas, causing the mind to be single-mindedly focused and pure through reflection. One who reflects in this manner accords with Nirvāṇa and accords with non-arising. These dharmas are neither existent nor non-existent, yet even "non-existence" is absent. It is by force of convention that names are created for them as "dharma-nature. One clearly understands that dharma-nature has no coming or going and is without conditions; one cultivates the mind to sever all dharmas, yet out of compassion for the world, manifests names.

One exerts diligence to restrain and suppress unwholesome states that have not yet arisen so that they do not arise; one restrains the mind to sever those unwholesome states already produced; one applies diligent effort to bring about wholesome states that have not yet arisen; and once they have arisen, one increases them so that they are not lost.

The Bodhisattva in the third stage practices the concentration of the divine feet (*ṛddhipāda-samādhi*). Having attained the concentration of joy and bliss, he brings to rest all conditioned activities; he unifies his divine feet to sustain body, speech, and mind, and through the concentration of diligent effort, he eliminates all that is evil. Again, unifying the divine feet, he gathers and sustains body and mind; again, through the concentration of mental intention, he eliminates what has been done. Governing the divine feet, he sustains body and mind, and through the concentration of wisdom, he eliminates all conditioned activities. Governing these divine feet and likewise sustaining body and mind, he gradually cultivates the faculties of faith and diligence; through the faculties of mental intention and wisdom, he then enters the essential core.

The Buddha-dharma is empty and exhausted, devoid of self and devoid of "that"; there are no causes and conditions, nor are there any fetters. Craving for existence and the calculation of permanence sever the suffering of birth and death; yet all things leave no trace, while people mostly rely upon signs, becoming attached to natures and names throughout countless lifetimes.

One should further practice with diligence; for anxiety and affliction follow one another like a shadow follows a form, coming and going without ceasing, like a wheel in its ruts, such that no beginning or end can be known. Through the practice of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) without dependence, one attains right contemplation (*samyag-darśana*) and non-attachment. When craving is exhausted and conceptualization extinguished, the fetters are untied and one becomes pure. One is no longer deluded regarding conduct and the mind is free from anxiety and affliction. Birth, old age, and sickness are severed, and there is no further coming and going. With the great brilliance of the eye of wisdom, one universally illumines the world of men, uprooting the twelve links of dependent origination and the delusions of unwise intelligence.
"Furthermore, Most Victorious One!
A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should further cultivate the virtue of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*).

As for these supernormal powers, they cannot be thwarted or destroyed; neither the celestial Māras nor the powerful deities of external paths can commit violence against them. The power of faith, diligence, concentration of mind, and wisdom—these are what the Bodhisattva cultivates at every stage."

Thereupon, one should gradually advance toward the blossoms of the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*). By practicing with the blossoms of mental awakening through the fifteen moments of mind, one severs the mind of stinginess and treads the path of the bodhisattva; accomplishing profound and wondrous wisdom, one does not regress.
The blossom of the factor of dharma-awakening is unconditioned and effortless, removing defiled, evil, and unwholesome conduct.
The blossom of the factor of diligence-awakening joins with the pride of receiving precepts, suppressing and preventing those who are negligent from arising.
The flower of the awakening of joy corresponds to the stage of the third dhyāna; it gathers all distracted thoughts into tranquil, non-active stillness.
The flower of the awakening of pliancy is free from attachment; it contemplates and understands all dharmas without further cultivation.
With the flower of the awakening of faith, one’s resolve is firm; one eloquently expounds the subtle and wondrous, free from regret.
Furthermore, one should contemplate the flower of awakening that is free from attachment, thereby severing the mind stained by the hundred and eight defects.

One should also cultivate the Eightfold Noble Path: equanimity in mindfulness, equanimity in concentration, equanimity in speech, equanimity in conduct, equanimity in action, equanimity in training, equanimity in thought, and equanimity in concentration; thereby transcending the eight difficulties and crossing beyond the six decays.
Furthermore, one discriminates the dharmas of the three samādhis; having perfected these practices, one may then be called one who has attained the purity of the third stage.
"Thus it is, Most Victorious One!"

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the gateway of wisdom, they calculate that emptiness is non-existent and cannot be perceived; it has no form, no conceptualization, and even no characteristic. When teaching the Dharma to others, they always employ the mean and the right; their words are sincere and ultimately never change. Even when giving, they harbor no expectations and do not seek renown; thus they are praised by others, who all together revere them and offer worship. Whatever they undertake is not for their own sake; they first seek the peace of others and only afterwards attend to themselves. The reason they personally attain peace and security is that they never harbor weariness regarding the merit they bestow; in whatever they perform, they find no satiety in their toil, because they take pity on all sentient beings.

Using boundless compassion, one rescues others from old age and death; for those who are weary, one arouses diligence. The reason for arousing such courageous diligence is the desire to nurture and sustain the various classes of sentient beings. One should constantly reflect: "It is because of sentient beings that I have attained the fruit of the Way, and my various meritorious deeds are likewise complete; thus, I shall exert my strength without hoping for any recompense."
The reason for this is that because the mind is pure, one receives the moistening nourishment of the Dharma; therefore, there is no seeking.

Worldly people seek in order to eliminate their own interests; by means of this power of wisdom, one protects all dharmas, vowing to cause all sentient beings to each find peace in their respective places, so that those of high, middle, and low station shall all be free from resentment, and their undertakings shall be secure and certain.
For this reason, no one is able to restrain the Bodhisattva, nor is anyone able to suppress or sever him.
"Thus it is, O Most Victorious One!
The Bodhisattva’s former vows are vast and universal, immeasurable; his wisdom is boundless and inexhaustible, like celestial gold that is free from any stain."

The reason for this is that by employing a state free from blemish and defilement, one washes away the veil of dust so that greed and desire are forever eliminated; thus, various evil thoughts can no longer cause disturbance. Furthermore, because one’s will is fierce and not to be cowed by evil, one guards against perverse thoughts and does not allow anger, delusion, or any form of attachment to arise. One also eliminates all that is improper, such as the frantic pursuit of the five desires, arrogance, and self-importance. All such things are completely eradicated.

A Bodhisattva dwelling in the third stage constantly protects this mind, clearly understanding that internal phenomena are invisible and without form; for if they were to possess form, they would destroy the nature of reality (*dharmatā*). Having cast off the heavy burden and all defilements, he should establish this mind so as not to become indolent. He investigates the consciousness of the mind and finds it has no location; it is invisible and free from manifold conceptualizations. For those who are distracted, he protects them so that their minds may become concentrated; for those lacking wisdom, he nurtures and brings them to completion. Regarding all beings who have taken form—whether they possess merit or lack it—he desires to deliver them all to the Great Vehicle.

Even the contemplation of the Mahāyāna leaves no trace; yet, by instructing all who practice the Dharma, one’s resolve becomes firm and steadfast, purifying the third stage and realizing the fruit of the Path.

All those in distress and hardship are caused to establish boundless merit; yet though they receive its retribution, they know it is non-existent, and their minds likewise remain forever unobservable.
The reason for this is that through the observation of wisdom, one knows there is no past, future, or present.
"Thus it is, O Most Victorious One!

A bodhisattva constantly trains in and cultivates great loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*). If there are those who, facing hardship and suffering, cast themselves upon him seeking refuge, desiring rescue and protection for their very lives, he would rather lose his own body and endure affliction than first deliver those in immediate peril, thereby not failing his solemn vow."

One who practices loving-kindness does so with impartiality like a scale: if there is gain, they feel no joy; if they are slandered, they harbor no sorrow. This is the bodhisattva’s practice of loving-kindness according to the occasion.

Now, one who practices compassion always purifies body, speech, and mind through three matters; they never transmit evil nor harbor perverse thoughts. Although they dwell amidst the dust and toil of ignorance, they walk alone without fear and yet remain free from arrogance. They do not abandon universal wisdom regarding the Dharma they study, and they grasp all Buddha-dharmas through their various supernormal powers and insights. According to what others seek, they do not oppose their hearts' desires.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Varaprabha:

"In the past, when I was traveling and studying to purify the bonds of the three dwellings, those whose merit was equal and whose virtue was orderly, with whom I shared companionship, were beyond counting; among them, those who regressed and remained behind me are beyond description."

From my first stage of dwelling up to the third, I established a heart of great vows that did not waver; the merits I performed during that interval were likewise immeasurable. I gave away rare treasures, extraordinary and wonderful objects, national wealth, and even my wife and children—none of these were comparable to my practice. Thinking only of the wish to give, I bestowed [my body] nine thousand nine hundred and ninety-nine times upon others. Finally, I encountered a tiger, emaciated by hunger and in desperate straits, who had been watching for prey but failed to capture any. It then sought to devour its own cubs to preserve its own life, spreading its body, baring its claws, and lunging forward to seize them.
I was accompanied by Maitreya and Nandiyashas; looking back at the two of them, I said:
"Now is the very time; who among you can resolve with such exceptional courage as to cast this body away to be given to that starving beast?"
The two men each turned to look at one another; though they did not speak, their hearts harbored a sense of retreat.
I immediately perceived through observation that they felt regret, and so I cast myself from the mountain peak down into the deep valley.

The Śuddhāvāsa devas immediately descended to receive and support him; they then transformed into nectar resembling my own form to feed that starving tigress until she was fully satisfied, so that both mother and child were preserved and I myself remained uninjured.
He reflected that his body would suffice for ten thousand heads.
Therefore, Most Excellent One!
Even when a bodhisattva who has advanced in study attains the third stage, there may still be a mind of regret and retreat, as their resolve is not yet firm.
Even if my body were to enter the jaws of a tiger, the tiger would neither devour me nor even draw near to me.

This is because, by establishing the roots of virtue and attaining supernatural powers, I have gained mastery over all phenomena; I shall practice repentance without ever concealing my faults, and employ immeasurable giving to encourage and assist in meritorious deeds.

The Bodhisattva cultivates and studies, proclaiming and disseminating the meaning of the Way; he diligently practices the Dharma of the Mahāsattva with a firm resolve, never abandoning his great vow, and girds himself with the armor of infinite virtue.
The Buddha again addressed Ajita:
"When a Bodhisattva who has advanced in study cultivates the third stage, he should always concentrate his mind and not allow it to fluctuate.
He should not let what he perceives disturb the minds of others; he should constantly know how to remain far removed from all afflictions and abide within himself."
His feet possess no element of chance; his mind does not flow toward attachments or conceptualizations, nor does he seek glory, hope, or positions of high honor and nobility.
He causes all people to practice the Dharma according to the Dharma, proclaiming and opening up supreme wisdom so that they may share in its source.
He regards self and others as one, without distinction, manifesting himself in accordance with causes and conditions.
One should not regard arising as non-arising; when there is neither arising nor non-arising, and no birth or non-birth, one then purifies that ground.

Thus, one does not become deluded and never acts out of delusion. To think that delusion emerges from worldly toil is itself called delusion. When delusion does not perceive delusion, there is neither delusion nor non-delusion.
Only by deeply understanding this optical illusion of delusion does one accord with true emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Thus it is, Most Victorious One!
The practice of a bodhisattva distinguishes emptiness and non-existence to lead others into the Dharma; being fully present amidst suffering, they cause all to be universally at peace.
This is what is meant, Most Victorious One!
"The Bodhisattva who advances in learning purifies his conduct within the third stage.
Chapter Four: The Entry into Form (*Rūpāyatana*). At that time, the Bodhisattva Most Victorious (*Jin-jie*) came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is meant by the Bodhisattva of Noble Birth (*Janmaja*) purifying his conduct within the fourth stage?"

The Buddha told Ajita: "A Bodhisattva of Noble Birth within the fourth stage should always never abandon the practice of the True Man's Dharma; his mindfulness should dwell in seclusion and he must not depart from *pratisaṃlayanā* (solitary meditation). Regarding lust, anger, and delusion, he should always maintain few desires, finding contentment in his aspirations and remaining free from greed and attachment. He does not abandon the twelve essential requirements of ascetic practice, upholding the prohibitive precepts as if guarding against venomous snakes. He views sensual desires as loathsome as if they were being consumed by fire, eliminating the intent for craving so that it does not arise again. He directs his mind toward all beings with the thought of *nirvāṇa*. He practices generous giving of all he possesses, not sparing even his own body or life. He harbors no pride or indolence, nor does he exalt himself before the assembly; he does not long for possessions, nor does he possess the three obstructions."

The Bodhisattva practices the methods of mental consciousness; amidst the great assembly, he contemplates and practices the gift of Dharma, instructing and transforming sentient beings so that their aspirations are fulfilled, accumulating merit and virtue for the sake of the Unsurpassed Way.

He habitually dwells in seclusion, alone in mountain caves; taking only as much as he requires for his needs, he practices all virtuous deeds without weariness. He is extensively learned and possesses great knowledge, consulting and receiving instruction without ever growing weary, and he does not consider it a labor to expound wisdom.

By calculating and deliberating upon the body, one contemplates its beginning and end; with wisdom and discernment penetrating all things and mindfulness fully perfected, one leaves behind all evils and practices the gates of liberation. This liberation is the teaching of the Bodhisattva.

Having thoroughly understood the root of all phenomena and contemplated their subtlety, one should discern the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates (*skandha*). One observes and knows the four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—and beholds the fundamental source from which the six sense-fields (*āyatana*) arise. The twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) are profound and boundless; the transformations of birth and death are inexhaustible. One speaks of suffering with sincerity and offers earnest admonition, maintaining mindfulness without forgetting. Without reckoning self, person, or the duration of one's lifespan, one dwells in tranquil non-action and practices the karma of impermanence, understanding that all things are empty and unreal.

"Furthermore, Most Victorious One! A Bodhisattva dwelling in the fourth stage should protect the Buddha-field; he discerns the distinction between the secular and the monastic, yet neither is ultimately perceivable. The wisdom of the Bodhisattva’s practice is inexhaustible; he accomplishes all virtues and cultivates the purification of the land, achieving its various locations in their proper sequence. His ocean of wisdom is boundless, and he never tires of what he receives, delivering and saving many sentient beings."

In all that they practice, they are always foremost; most honored and supreme, none can equal them. In their reflections, they possess *dhāraṇī* and a powerful memory, never forgetting, so that each attains the roots of goodness without deficiency or omission.

The reason for this is that by means of the noble and honored Dharma, one attains liberation from distant karmic bonds; through this, one receives the prediction of enlightenment and enters the chamber of the true sages. Furthermore, by virtue of diligent application and an undeterred mind, one spontaneously achieves the fulfillment of unsurpassed holy deeds. Whatever one aspires to is immediately accomplished, yet there is no perception of accomplishment; if one were to perceive accomplishment, it would not be true accomplishment.

In their practice, they forever perceive nothing; they cultivate meditative concentration to encompass all dharmas, ensuring that their actions are never deficient. To subdue the mind and its thoughts is the work of the Path; practicing self-restraint, they remain free from manifold conceptualizations.
Why is this so? It is because they distance themselves from all evils and do not engage in them, but instead single-mindedly practice giving as a field of merit for blessings.

When a Bodhisattva resolves their mind upon all sentient beings, they harbor no greed or attachment regarding body or mind; rather, they further increase their supreme, wondrous, and boundless compassion. They single-mindedly uphold the precepts as if protecting their own two eyes, and they instruct those who violate the precepts to refrain from evil.

One should also practice patience with single-minded diligence; indeed, the practice of patience is extremely difficult, for even when one holds a position of honor, possesses great wealth, and enjoys extreme pleasure, one must not look down upon those who are poor, lowly, emaciated, or weak.
Thus it is, O Most Victorious One! Forbearance is difficult; yet even diligent and ardent exertion is not easily attained.

Sitting beneath the Bodhi tree with body upright and mind focused, one sits in the full lotus posture without wavering. If someone should come and say, "Make way for me; I wish to sit here," one should establish a firm resolve, thinking, "I shall not be overcome by him. First, one must attain the requisites of Buddhahood and all the marks and signs of excellence; only after subduing Māra will one relinquish the place to him. This is what is meant by the difficulty of attaining such ardent exertion.

His single-minded concentration is likewise difficult to surpass; when the Bodhisattva Jātyabhibhū enters this state of meditative absorption, even if celestial thunder and lightning roar with ten thousand simultaneous crashes, those wishing to disturb the Bodhisattva’s mind cannot unsettle it by so much as a hair’s breadth.
"O Most Victorious One! This is called the meditative concentration of a bodhisattva; therefore, it is said to be difficult.

A bodhisattva cultivates all merits through wisdom and does not harbor weariness toward sentient beings. Whether entering or exiting, walking or standing, they are harmonious, peaceful, and composed; their deportment is fully perfected and their dharma robes are neatly arranged. This is called a bodhisattva cultivating the merit of wisdom with such fortitude that no one can endanger them."
Knowing clearly that all things are fundamentally non-existent, he grasps the profound mysteries and reaches far, extensively surveying the subtle and wondrous.
His brilliance shines with ultimate clarity, reaching everywhere without obstruction; his mind is single-mindedly focused, free from wandering or distraction.

He constantly contemplates all those who have no support and establishes skillful means for them to find support; for those in darkness, he causes them to behold the Great Light. There is none... [who is not so aided].
To those who seek refuge, he provides that refuge; among the lowly and humble, he acts as a virtuous friend;

to those who practice deceit and hypocrisy, he teaches the cultivation of sincerity and simplicity; upon seeing the violent and overbearing, he practices patience for their sake; amidst finery and adornment, he does not pursue elegance;
seeing those who lack gratitude, he teaches them to repay kindness; and when dwelling in celestial palaces, he causes them to practice the ten [virtues].
It is well; while dwelling in a state of indolence or regression, one cultivates and honors meritorious virtues. Even if one encounters those who are arrogant, one harbors no self-conceit;
if others seek an opportunity to find fault, one cannot be found lacking. One does not contemplate evil nor speak of others' defects.
If one encounters those engaged in wrong actions, one immediately stays with them to protect and guide them, leading them into tranquility and truth.

When beings of various kinds come to his presence, they receive him with joy and without malice; those who offer counsel or admonition are shown the principles of advancement and retreat—what should be done and what should not be done—and whether something is appropriate or inappropriate, his mind remains without increase or decrease.
He has profound faith in the retribution of sin and merit, knowing that there are corresponding consequences for one's actions.

Whether he dwells within city walls among the populace or resides in the wilderness among the crags, he remains no different. He does not covet gainful occupations nor does he spare his own life; his mind is pure and free from thoughts of right or wrong. He constantly guards against verbal transgressions, speaking without distinction between self and others. He does not seek offerings or hope for veneration, but clearly understands moderation and contentment alone.

The mind is always gentle and never follows what is corrupt or evil; it crosses over birth and death and brings rest to all afflictions and sufferings. By means of this, one forever attains the path of the Great Vehicle.

The wisdom-mind of a bodhisattva is likewise invisible; coming and going within birth and death is also non-existent. Through skillful means, they provide clear instruction and guidance, transforming beings according to the time and circumstances to sever the cycle of beginning and end. Since there is no coming or going in the cycle of beginning and end, they understand that all things are empty and have no fixed location.

If a bodhisattva conceives of existence, they are attached to existence; yet within the practice of giving, they also conceive of non-existence, which is likewise nothingness and invisible. Why is this so?
"The six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā) are likewise invisible and non-existent.
Thus it is, O Most Victorious One!
A bodhisattva’s giving is entirely without limitation; that which has limitations is not true giving."

If one discriminates between those who should receive a gift and those who should not, giving rise to thoughts of superiority and inferiority or right and wrong, then the giving will not be universal, and such giving should not be considered true generosity.

If one can practice giving without generating attachment and without various discursive thoughts, this is called true giving. The recipient of the gift is able to preserve their life, whereby they can sit and rise in peace and stability, engage in recitation and study, attain concentration of body and mind, and possess vigorous strength.

They will never suffer from thirst or exhaustion throughout the cycle of birth and death; wherever they are born, they will travel with supernormal power and be revered by others. They will attain the divine eye to see the lands of the ten directions, and the divine ear to hear distant and infinite sounds. They will attain a body of wondrous fragrance, consisting of precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. They will be renowned for their manifold virtues and meritorious deeds; their bodies will be pure and fragrant such that all find joy in them. They will always obtain delicious and sweet delicacies, and through the planting of past merit, they will manifest extraordinary marks, remaining pure and stainless while being protected by others.

They bestow gifts according to whatever is lacking; their bodies are forever free from illness, neither born nor dying, and devoid of all afflictions. They constantly attain peace and security with everything fully provided, completely perfecting the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and attaining the eighty minor signs of excellence. They open wide the treasury of the Dharma without giving rise to greed, and they are fully endowed with the wisdom of the Path, lacking nothing.

When there are those who come seeking, they do not begrudge anything but are able to give everything away until they reach all-knowledge; through their various supernormal powers and noble wisdom, they extensively save others without end, attaining the profound sutras and the joy of the Dharma.

Sitting beneath the Bodhi tree at the site of enlightenment, he subdued the demonic armies and their various officials and subordinates. He did not engage in any conditioned activity for the sake of form; knowing that form is empty and that form is itself empty, he realized that form does not know itself, and thus he knew the emptiness of form.
"Thus it is, Most Excellent One!

When a bodhisattva understands that the nature of form is empty, they become the foremost of all dharmas of the path. Having accomplished the Dharma-eye for the sake of all paths, they are uniquely honored throughout the three periods of time, walking alone without peer; this is because they are fully endowed with the various supernormal knowledges and wisdoms."
The Buddha again addressed Ajita:

“The Bodhisattva Jātyabhirūpa never believes in false or perverted dharmas. If he sees sentient beings each making offerings to those they revere, seeking blessings through sacrifice, his mind remains unmoved; he simply takes food toward his mouth.”
Seeing sentient beings who have correctly established themselves in the unsurpassed and peerless practice, never wavering or turning back to abandon it for the Lesser Vehicle;
knowing that this profound Dharma has no equal, they apply themselves with diligent hearts and advance in their deeds without any other thoughts.

Although there may be other dharmas with diverse and differing rituals, one always uses the contemplation of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) to discern and understand them; thus, even while interacting with them, the mind never turns toward other paths.

Even if one encounters a world where a Buddha has appeared and entered parinirvāṇa, and his bequeathed teachings and instructions have further vanished; even if the noble assembly’s travels and transformations have met with interruption—the mind remains constantly fixed and undergoes no change. Although the Three Jewels are absent, one does not follow deviant thoughts, but constantly practices the profound and wondrous immeasurable scriptures. Using the twelve divisions of the canon, one perceives all things; through skillful means and expedient methods, there is nothing into which one does not enter. One does not crave fame or reputation, and while manifesting bodily transformations, one does not praise oneself.
"Thus it is, Most Excellent One!

When the Bodhisattva Jātyabhirūpa practices right view, he knows that emptiness is not real; there is neither right nor wrong, for even right itself is non-existent. To clearly understand this is called the Right Path."

"Furthermore, Most Victorious One! When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva cultivates wisdom and discriminates between existence and non-existence, he understands true emptiness and remains unattached to it. He should further practice the meanings of all wisdom-terms, yet find them to be non-existent. Having exhausted the truth of suffering and extinguished the fetters of the accumulation of suffering, he completely severs the habituation to craving and realizes the fruit of the Path. With equalizing wisdom (*samatājñāna*), he illuminates and examines to still lust, anger, and delusion; with the wisdom of phenomena (*dharmajñāna*), he removes defilements and penetrates the superior, middling, and inferior [faculties]; and with the wisdom of distant reflection (*dūradarśanajñāna*), he surveys the two realms above."

The knowledge of others' minds universally comprehends what is being thought within the hearts of sentient beings. The knowledge of non-arising does not undergo the defilement of the womb-portion of birth and death.

The knowledge of the extinction of formations understands the source of the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates; it contemplates the fundamental basis of what should be practiced through the three faculties: the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown," the faculty of "knowing," and the faculty of "one who has known. One should study these faculties until the ultimate attainment of the Way: from the stage of the three white-robed lay practitioners up to the *srotāpanna*, one cultivates the faculty of "I shall come to know the unknown"; from the *sakṛdāgāmin* up to the *anāgāmin*, one studies the faculty of "knowing"; and from the *arhat* up to the attainment of Buddhahood, one studies the faculty of "one who has known."

Furthermore, one should practice meditative concentration to fully comprehend the wisdom of the dhyānas: the first dhyāna encompasses both applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*); in the intermediate state of the second dhyāna, there is no applied thought but sustained thought remains; from the subsequent second dhyāna up to the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*), there is neither applied nor sustained thought, and the mind is tranquil, extinguished, and unmoving. One should constantly maintain mindful recollection and firm faith to enter into right concentration.
"In this way, Most Excellent One!

Day and night, the Bodhisattva does not form such thoughts as: 'I know the dwelling place of the true person who upholds the precepts,' nor does he think, 'I know the person who lacks the precepts and commits evil. He has no mind of dualistic discrimination; he knows all things to be empty and quiescent, without any notions of one or two, before or after, or intermediate confusion of thought."

The bodhisattva diligently maintains mindfulness, never being separated from the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Noble Sangha; he practices mindfulness of ethical discipline, generosity, and the devas, as well as mindfulness of breathing and the cessation of activity; and regarding the suffering of the body and the thought of death, he also knows them to be without fixed location.

He contemplated the severing of the five fetters and revered the sixfold dharma of respect; he practiced the four bases of psychic power to nurture the great assembly, maintaining an upright mind and correct intention with courageous and fearless resolve.
Even if there were śramaṇas, followers of external paths, or heterodox teachers—whether gods, Brahmās, Māras, or any other such beings—none would dare to challenge or interrogate him.
