One with non-retrogressive wisdom abides in all phenomena, fully endowed with manifold wonders; the six perfections are pervasive throughout space without deficiency or diminution.

The one who is non-regressive in patience, though amidst all phenomena there is neither coming nor going, remains without either responding or not responding while standing, sitting, reclining, or sleeping.
The one who is non-regressive in wisdom dwells in the eternally abiding nature of phenomena (dharmatā) yet dwells nowhere; furthermore, they have no nest or dwelling place.
The one who possesses non-retrogressive patience perceives that among all phenomena there is neither superior nor inferior, neither high nor low;
the one who possesses non-retrogressive wisdom abandons and eliminates from all phenomena the mind that calculates permanence.
Those who possess the patience of non-retrogression all give rise to fear due to manifold sufferings; one should know that these are fundamentally empty and have no locus.
Those who possess non-retrogressive wisdom remove all veils regarding all phenomena, being as universal as space and relinquishing the six matters.
The one who is non-regressive in patience further digests the defilements regarding all phenomena, neither thinking of them nor forgetting them;

the one who is non-regressive in wisdom perceives that among all phenomena there is neither what is appropriate nor inappropriate, nor any joining or dispersing. Although they traverse all phenomena, they eliminate worldly toil so that nothing remains.
The non-regressing patience consists in following that wisdom such that there is no practice, no one who knows, and no one who does not know; it is without thought and without vision.
The non-regressing knowledge is that all phenomena are unmoving and cannot be shaken; they are tranquil and still, and free from conceptualization.
The one who possesses non-retrogressive patience is such that all phenomena are worn away and extinguished, without any turning back; they are entirely exhausted and cannot be grasped.
The one who possesses non-retrogressive wisdom is such that regarding all phenomena, from beginning to end, there is no abiding nature, being as it is like space.
The one who is non-retrogressive in patience perceives that all dharmas abide in a realm of profound seclusion and tranquility; wherever they go, there is no obstruction and no suffering.
The one who is non-retrogressive in wisdom understands that the nature of the dharma-realm dwells eternally, manifesting all dharmas according to the occasion.
The one who is non-regressive in patience regards all dharmas as entirely empty and quiescent; they do not think of them nor abandon them, being neither attached nor unattached.

The one who is non-regressive in wisdom carries all dharmas to cross to the other shore, yet perceives neither "this side" nor "that side," nor does he perceive anyone who has crossed or has not crossed.
The one who is non-regressive in patience does not dwell upon the birth, old age, sickness, death, sense-bases, or the sorrows and afflictions of all phenomena;
the one who is non-regressive in wisdom grasps all phenomena yet finds them unobtainable, their resolve set upon the profound and subtle attainment of the six perfections.
The one who possesses non-retrogressive patience calculates all dharmas as being free from defilement, without flaw from beginning to end;
the one who possesses non-retrogressive wisdom reverently cultivates equanimity toward all dharmas and does not undergo any turning back.
One who possesses non-retrogressive patience does not perceive the lineages or natures of phenomena as being produced by causes, but understands them as one.
One who possesses non-retrogressive wisdom seeks nothing among all phenomena and harbors no sorrow or distress.
The one who possesses non-retrogressive patience also arises through the common characteristics of all dharmas; there is no cessation therein, nor does he harbor indolence or fall into extremes.
The one who possesses non-retrogressive wisdom clearly understands that from the beginning there is nothingness—neither progress nor retrogression, and no plurality whatsoever.

The one who is non-retrogressive in patience severs the sounds to which all phenomena return; seeing them all as empty and devoid of characteristics, they do not abandon the fundamental nature of phenomena, which is naturally so.
The one who is non-retrogressive in wisdom encounters no obstruction regarding any phenomenon; there is no going and no coming, no attachment and no liberation, nor is there anything that arises.
The one who is non-regressive in patience eliminates all defiled and evil conduct and becomes exceedingly pure;

the one who is non-regressive in wisdom proclaims and elucidates all dharmas, harmonizes and stabilizes the various forms of knowledge, subdues bondage and attachment, and inspires the aspiration for the Way.

Those who possess non-retrogressive patience completely transcend all those who are arrogant regarding the various dharmas, as well as the conditions of karmic retribution arising from affection and love;
those who possess non-retrogressive wisdom regard all dharmas as being free from names and phrases, for such names are fundamentally non-existent, being neither gained nor lost.
The one who possesses non-retrogressive patience causes all phenomena to be without relinquishing or grasping, neither sinking nor arising;
the one who possesses non-retrogressive wisdom removes mental attachment, reaching the ultimate end of both the beginning and the end, such that there is neither increase nor decrease;
the one who possesses non-retrogressive wisdom is the root of the Dharma, giving birth to the extraordinary and surpassing all within the three realms.
One who is non-regressive in patience contemplates the root of suffering, withdrawing from it and discerning where it originates;
one who is non-regressive in wisdom discerns the causal conditions of the sense bases and mental consciousness.
One who possesses non-retrogressive patience is one whose essential vows as a bodhisattva never deviate;
one who possesses non-retrogressive wisdom is one who shall not undergo further rebirth in a womb in this body, but shall always be born through transformation.
The non-regressive patience consists in contemplating the arising and decaying of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*), as well as the nature of the aggregates;
the non-regressive wisdom consists in discerning within the body the practice of impurity-contemplation (*aśubha-bhāvanā*), seeing that from head to foot there is nothing worthy of attachment.
"O Most Excellent One!

A bodhisattva should always contemplate, discern, and fully understand that one who first initiates the aspiration for bodhicitta should, through non-retrogressive patience, observe and realize the seven fundamentals, without giving rise to the names of arising and ceasing, attachment, or cessation."

A Bodhisattva in the seventh stage should further contemplate the eight fundamental principles of the noble ones (*ārya-aṣṭamūla*), perceiving them all as devoid of arising, ceasing, attachment, or annihilation.
O Most Victorious One!

According to the place of birth one receives, one calculates therein: if born in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), whether in the five stages, the sixteen, the four, the three, the two, or the one, for those in the lower positions, there are precisely seven fundamental principles.
One should also contemplate that within the formless realm there are further eleven [stages], realizing their emptiness and stillness.

Because the Avaivartika (Non-retrogressive) Bodhisattva can accomplish the patience regarding suffering and the knowledge of suffering, as well as the patience regarding the origin, cessation, and path, and the wisdom of the noble ones, they should also discern the eight profound penetrations and patiences, thereby eliminating the fifty-two outflows of ignorance.

A Bodhisattva in the seventh stage constantly maintains mindfulness and, relying on the first dhyāna, practices the six noble knowledges (*ṣaḍ-āryajñāna*). He cultivates the two samādhis and the three Brahma-abodes, taking the faculty of joy as their object. Even if he relies on the middle dhyānas, he does not realize [the fruit]; rather, he should cultivate the seven knowledges characterized by non-discursive thought and sustained reflection (*avitarko vicāramātra*), guarding the mental activities within emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

Suppose a bodhisattva, by means of that second dhyāna, contemplates the eight knowledges (*jñāna*), yet does not realize the cessation of applied thought (*vitarka*) and sustained thought (*vicāra*), joy (*prīti*), emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).

Furthermore, if the bodhisattva again reflects upon the third dhyāna, he discerns the ten knowledges without attending to applied and sustained thought, and delights in the bliss of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.

At that time, within the four dhyānas, the bodhisattva should further distinguish the sixteen noble wisdoms; moreover, being free from the activities of vitarka and vicāra, he dwells in the three Brahma-abodes, guarding his mind so that it does not leak or lose its focus.

Those who are able to enter this Bodhisattva Treasury, practicing the patience of wisdom and understanding it to be free from affliction, will not be bound or attached by the fifty-two outflows; they will discern the various dharmas and their successive stages of progression, attaining noble wisdom and the dharma of non-retrogression.
If a bodhisattva practices these sixteen superior wisdoms, they will never harbor doubt or false views;
thus, they can eliminate all fetters, their mind becoming firm and not timid,
their intention steadfast and not deluded, walking alone through the three realms without fear or hindrance, their resolve like—
The Vajra is ultimately never weak or inferior; his mind is always filled with a sense of shame and remorse for falling short;
his intellect can reflect and discern everything without fail; his wisdom is as profound and luminous as the dark void, such that none are not illuminated by its radiance;
his eloquence and speech are never obstructed; he has attained dhāraṇī and never forgets it; and in all that he does, he is decisive and resolute, harboring no lingering hesitation.
Wherever they dwell or travel, they constantly perform the deeds of a Buddha; their cultivated equanimity remains without increase or decrease.
Their speech is always gentle and never harms others; by nature they are not impulsive or violent, but are instead discerning, profound, and serene.

Knowing the inclinations of others, they immediately preach the Dharma for them, analyzing the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and dissecting the sense bases (*āyatana*), clearly understanding all phenomena without fail.

Without needing to rely on exhaustive investigation, they perceive from afar the causes and conditions of retribution throughout the three periods of time; knowing the thoughts within the minds of others, they preach the Dharma for them.
Regarding what is possible and what is impossible, as well as the karmic fruits of good and evil, their wisdom-mind is profoundly deep and boundless.

They clearly understand skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) to transform beings according to the times, and they know when to advance or withdraw, how to enter or exit, and how to walk, discerning what is appropriate.

"No, his deportment and ritual decorum were from the outset never out of accord with what is appropriate; wherever he traveled or resided, he gave rise to the unsurpassed, true, and right intention for the Way.
It is thus, O Most Victorious One!"

Wherever the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva may be, he expounds the Dharma to deliver sentient beings and cause them to attain the fruit of the Way. He causes them to cast off all hardships and obtain eternal peace; he never again takes birth in the eight states of non-leisure. In whatever realm he travels, he attains mastery; those who hear what he teaches immediately attain liberation. Those who receive and uphold his instructions will, in that very moment, reach the stage of non-retrogression. Having clearly realized the wisdom of emptiness and the state of non-arising, they shall then achieve the unsurpassed, true, and correct path.

A bodhisattva should always employ skillful means and never think to himself, "I have now been able to subdue perceptions of form; my original aspiration has today borne fruit. He does not give rise to a limited mind to prematurely realize the fruit for himself; this is called the non-retrogression of a bodhisattva.

To discern the dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination: all arise from ignorance and thus lead to birth and death; yet when one seeks their place of origin, it cannot be seen nor can it be observed. It is neither characterized by marks nor devoid of marks; it is neither not characterized by marks nor not devoid of marks.

To thoroughly understand the root of such causal conditions, and not perceive in one's practice anything that is correct or incorrect, superior, middling, or inferior; furthermore, not perceiving the retribution of sin or merit, nor the commission of unwholesome deeds; to comprehend that all phenomena are entirely without arising, and in cultivating the root of all phenomena, not perceiving their conjunction or dispersion—this is what is called "that which arises from causes and conditions."

If there were no conditions, there would be no suffering; as for what is called "no suffering," it means that when ignorance and volitional formations cease, then aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair cease.
One thoroughly understands and discerns these twelve factors, realizing that everything has a cause.

The names and designations of all phenomena arise from the conjunction and dispersal of causes and conditions; they are neither self nor non-self, neither that nor non-that. Furthermore, one does not perceive a self, a person, a life-span, birth, aging, or impermanence.

One does not see that which enters, nor is there any entering; one realizes that the entry into consciousness is entirely without entry. One who enters in this manner fully understands all dharmas of falling back and not falling back.
"Thus it is said, O Most Victorious One!

If a non-regressing Mahāsattva wishes to be fully endowed with all dharmas, he should thoroughly understand impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self; yet, although he knows them to be void and tranquil, he does not realize [nirvana] for the sake of sentient beings."

The Bodhisattva’s practice is pure and does not cling to the conditioned; yet because the faculties of sentient beings are deep-rooted, they cannot exhaust the conditioned. Understanding that these twelve links of dependent origination are conditioned phenomena, the Bodhisattva guides them so that they may realize the unconditioned.

Although the Bodhisattva dwells within the realm of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and practices the dharmas of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*), he does not abide in the unconditioned to take its realization as a final goal.

Understanding that impermanence is a law of decay, he cultivates meritorious virtues without succumbing to weariness; observing that birth is the source of all suffering, he protects sentient beings while engaging in self-examination.

He contemplates the cessation of all phenomena, yet does not regard it as ultimate; he contemplates sensation, mind, and dharmas, finding them to have no fixed location; he contemplates non-arising and sees nothing that arises; he contemplates sentient beings as his great responsibility; he contemplates outflows and the absence of outflows, yet does not extinguish himself within the three realms; he practices the four immeasurable minds to take pity on those who follow later; and his intent remains unattached, yet he does not abandon the path of the disciples and pratyekabuddhas.
"Thus it is, Most Victorious One!

The Bodhisattva’s pure intention is profound and discerning; he manifests according to the inclinations of others, adapting to sentient beings so that they are never harmed, and he fulfills all their aspirations."

With the wisdom of merit, his mind is pure and bright; when he looks upon forms with his eyes, he searches for them and finds nothing at all. He practices patience and does not give rise to distracted thoughts; even when others revile him or direct anger toward him, he thinks only of the Dharma.
One understands internal and external emptiness as being without anything at all, yet one does not give rise to doubt or become limited by emptiness.
One does not perceive oneself or others. Why is this so?

An avaivartika bodhisattva, when asked for his hands or feet, joyfully gives them; even if his head is sought, his mind is all the more delighted. He does not oppose the seeker and has no sense of greed or stinginess; if someone asks for his wife or children, he immediately bestows them as a gift, his mind remaining unchanged.
The chapters and verses he expounds are dedicated solely to the unsurpassed, true, and correct Way, rather than being overly earnest in exhorting others.

He becomes a Golden Wheel-turning King, Śakra, or Brahmā, preaching the subtle and wondrous Dharma to all people; he resolves his mind and begins his training for the path of a Bodhisattva, traveling by means of supernatural powers to behold the Buddhas of the ten directions, paying homage, serving, and making offerings to all those Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.

Even if the three thousand great thousandfold world-systems were filled with jewels, his mind would never give rise to thoughts of attachment; he regards all that exists as non-existent, nor does he think of anything as "mine," for his mind is entirely pure and free from seeking after form.

Because the single Dharma-body is invisible, one regards all people as abiding within the Dharma-realm; thus, one attains the divine eye and becomes fully endowed with the power of the feet. Having attained the wisdom-eye, one knows that all that exists is ultimately non-existent;

gradually understanding suchness, the limit of reality, and the nature of phenomena, one then obtains the Buddha-eye and the eighteen fundamental dharmas. Discerning with the Dharma-eye, one penetrates all things without obstruction; fully possessing the ten powers and upholding great vows, one reaches the unconditioned realm of deathlessness.
"O Most Excellent One!

You should know that their practice is like that of omniscience; because they habitually practice abiding, they abide nowhere. Understanding this abiding as abiding nowhere, their training is both with training and without training."

The Bodhisattva constantly contemplates the dharma of emptiness and quiescence; all dharmas accord with this without opposition. He does not abide in equanimity because of such accord, nor does he follow extreme views because of opposition. Furthermore, he does not practice what is deviant as to fall into the realm of Māra, nor does he study what is correct merely out of a desire for the Great Vehicle.

The reason for this is that by not abandoning the essential tenet of the Dharma, one does not commit transgressions through such non-abandonment; and because one knows for oneself that there is nothing further to be done, one is able to single-mindedly restrain and maintain the five aggregates so that they do not wander, thereby crossing beyond the realm of Māra, such that no one can midway corrupt the bodhisattva mind.
At that time, Ajita addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"How is it that a non-retrogressive bodhisattva dwells in non-dwelling, such that they have neither training nor no-more-training?
The Buddha told Ajita:
“The Bodhisattva of the seventh stage dwells within the triple world, yet is unstained by it and has no further training to undergo.
That which is not practiced or learned is called ‘internal’; that which is not sought after through practice is called ‘external.’”
Although one practices externally, one does not follow disciples; observing that there is nothing to be learned, one does not even conditionally learn.

What is called "practice" (śikṣā) refers to that which is studied within birth and death, and that which is cultivated by Bodhisattvas. It means studying non-knowing; practicing that which is not practiced; studying that which is not studied. Practice is name-and-form; practice is dependent origination. Practice is the view of self; practice is craving. Practice is the notion of "mine" as well as "not mine. Practice is the cultivation of giving despite being greedy; practice is the cultivation of guarding the precepts despite having violated them, yet without becoming conceited on account of those precepts. Practice is the cultivation of patience despite the appearance of anger; practice is the cultivation of diligence despite being indolent; practice is the cultivation of single-mindedness despite distracted thoughts. Practice is the cultivation of wisdom despite ignorance; practice is the cultivation of merit despite the absence of karmic retribution. Practice is the cultivation of the Path despite worldly activities; practice is the cultivation of attaining liberation despite the absence of release.
Thus it is, O Most Victorious One!

A Bodhisattva in the seventh stage practices that which is practiced-less and learns that which is learning-less, reaching the ultimate wisdom wherein one perceives neither gain nor loss in any phenomena (*dharma*). There is neither entry nor non-entry; one cannot reckon an entry by means of form (*rūpa*), and the same applies to sensation (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
One does not reach the ultimate through the enumeration of dharmas, nor does one reach the ultimate through the enumeration of non-dharmas.

In seeking all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), one should abide as wisdom itself; one should not think of dharmas, saying "I am the doer," for it is the one who attains clear understanding that becomes all-knowing.
A bodhisattva who seeks omniscience should seek it within the derived matter of the four great elements. Why is this?
If one calculates the body, there is obstruction and one undergoes the four modes of birth; if one does not calculate the body, one is free from craving and desire.

The dwelling of a Bodhisattva is like the dwelling of wisdom; by transcending all realms, they dwell in non-dwelling. They do not calculate that there is birth, nor do they act as a mother to birth. If they perceive birth, they see it as entirely non-birth. Because they know non-birth, it is called the wisdom of non-birth. To practice in this manner is what is called the equality of the peerless, limitless Great Vehicle.

When the Buddha had spoken these words, one hundred and ten *nayuta* koṭis of devaputras all attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), and seventy-two thousand people all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, equal Way.

At that time, the venerable great śrāvakas seated there—the Elder Kāśyapa, Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Aniruddha, Revata, Nandupāla, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, and Subhūti the Empty—along with five hundred arhats, immediately rose from their seats. They adjusted their saṃghāṭī robes, placed their right knees upon the ground, and touched their heads to the Buddha’s feet. Simultaneously, they raised their voices in mournful wailing; choked with grief and moved by sorrow, they wiped away their tears with their hands and stepped forward to address the Buddha, saying:
“Our vision is shallow and we have forever severed the lineage of the sages; the Way of the Buddha is profound, yet we have not received its cleansing.”

If there are men or women, down to ordinary worldlings, who, while within the three miserable realms, desire to seek the Way, they should give rise to the noble resolve to attain Buddhahood. Why is this so?

Just as the Buddha has today expounded hundreds of thousands of dharmas for us, we have been unable to achieve the arousal of the bodhicitta; we privately harbor regret that it will forever be beyond our reach.

Although one has now attained the Way and is called an Arhat, with the six supernormal powers clear and penetrating and virtue surpassing the three realms of existence, this is not as good as having, in the past, committed the five heinous crimes over hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas and entered the Avīci Hell, hoping that once the retribution for those sins was extinguished, there would be a time of release; gradually receiving liberation and reaching nirvana, thereby attaining the resolve to become a Bodhisattva and perfect the Bodhisattva path.
Now that their faculties are ruined, they have no opportunity for benefit.
This is because they have scorched the seeds of the Bodhisattvas; as vessels that are cracked and leaking, they can no longer contain or sustain the path to becoming a Bodhisattva.

All classes of beings with form—whether flying or crawling, from those with one foot or two up to those with a hundred thousand feet—all depend upon the earth for their livelihood; they eat what is sweet and delicious and wear what is soft and fine. Though flocks of birds fly through the air, their lives are tethered to the ground. Although I have attained the Way, I still nourish the four great elements; how then am I any different from birds and beasts?

Although they were mixed with defilements, they gradually escaped the forms of beasts; by planting roots of virtue without ceasing, they established the traces of the Mahāyāna. Both devas and humans received their deliverance, yet they all lamented their own baseness and inferiority compared to the Exalted Ones, harboring sorrow and regret for what they had previously cultivated.

At that time, there were seventeen hundred people in the assembly who had not yet entered the [noble] paths; having previously practiced the dharmas of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, they now resolved with firm intent to give rise to the unsurpassed mind. Immediately upon their seats, they attained the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (the forbearance that all phenomena are unarisen). Because he expounded the Great Dharma of the Six Perfections and proclaimed the Four Noble Truths—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—as well as the four debts of gratitude and the four immeasurables, he instructed all beings and caused them to resolve upon the Bodhi-mind.
At that time, Śāriputra, receiving the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, proclaimed to the assembly of bodhisattvas who had gathered:

"Listen to me as I recount how, in the past when I was like an unbaked clay vessel, I progressed from the first stage to the fifth stage, only to fall back again to the first stage; then, starting once more from the first stage, I reached the fifth and sixth stages. Thus I passed through sixty kalpas, yet in the end I could not reach the stage of non-retrogression. Whatever I undertook, I immediately regretted, and I never attained completion.

Had I maintained my mind as I do my pure precepts, my vows would surely have been fulfilled without transgressing the mundane, and there would have been nothing that the light of the Dharma of wisdom did not illuminate."

The Bodhisattva, abiding in the stage of non-retrogression, likewise does not calculate whether there is giving or no giving; nor does he perceive morality, patience, diligence, concentration, or wisdom. Furthermore, he does not follow the dharmas of the desire, form, or formless realms, nor does he follow the activities of body, speech, or mind. Regarding all dharmas, he is entirely without attachment, seeing them all as like illusions, transformations, mirages, shadows, or echoes. That which he abides in is pure from beginning to end, devoid of self, life, or the duration of existence. He does not perceive the distinctions between the sacred and the secular, nor the names of right and wrong. He does not think to himself, "I shall seek this," or "I shall not seek this. He is without thoughts of sorrow or joy, without conditions, and without volitional action. There is nothing produced, nothing seen, and no location.

One who trains in this manner trains without desire, anger, or delusion, and without increase or decrease; such a person does not fall into the evil realms nor harbor a regressive mind. Desiring to achieve the state of a Buddha, one should practice in this way.

They neither commit transgressions nor cultivate merit; they neither achieve realization nor fail to achieve it; they conceive neither of thought nor of non-thought; all dharmas are entirely equal and without distinction.
When Śāriputra had spoken these words, there were again countless hundreds of thousands of sentient beings who all resolved to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment.
At that time, Sujaya came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In what way are all dharmas like illusions, transformations, and mirages?"
The Buddha told Ajita: "It is like a magical transformation (*nirmāṇa*):

when it comes, its coming is not perceived; when it departs, there is no place to which it goes. Understanding all phenomena (*dharma*) in this same way, one sees that they come from nowhere and go nowhere; their nature abides spontaneously without being seen to change. All phenomena are without action, nor is there any creator."
The body of the Tathāgata is twofold: first, the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya); second, the dharma-body (dharmakāya).
Now, as for the dharma-body, it cannot be seen and possesses no form or image.
The transformation body is likewise like empty space, without form.

"O Most Victorious One! This is called the fundamental practice of an *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive) bodhisattva: being able to roar the lion’s roar amidst the great assemblies; practicing the wisdom of emptiness such that none can equal it; with meritorious virtues fully matured and all dharmas purified; infinite, profound, subtle, inconceivable, majestic, and immeasurable."
"In this way, Most Victorious One!
the non-retrogressive Mahāsattva purifies his conduct within the seventh dwelling.
*The Scripture on the Ten Dwellings and the Severing of Bonds*, Fascicle Two.
*The Scripture on the Ten Abodes and the Severing of Bonds*, Scroll Three, translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Chapter Eight: The Chapter on the Youthful Truth (*Kumārabhūta*). Chapter Eight: The Youthful Truth.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Most Victorious addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
How does the eighth bodhisattva purify their practice within the eight stages of abiding?"

The Buddha told Ajita: "The eighth-stage bodhisattva must always be fully endowed with supernatural powers and wisdom to understand the faculties of sentient beings; observing their inclinations, he manifests accordingly. Furthermore, by means of supernatural powers, he travels to the various buddha-fields to observe their extraordinary and sublime practices, returning to adorn his own buddha-field. He goes in person to visit, pay homage to, and honor the various Buddhas, yet observes that the physical marks of the Buddhas' bodies are empty and non-existent. He trains in the knowledge of patience and the discernment of the various faculties, constantly entering the *māyopama-samādhi* (illusion-like samādhi) to know that all things are without origin. Whatever merits he performs accord with the capacities of those before him, each being brought to fulfillment according to its respective need."

By transcending emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, one is without form or image; having crossed beyond the triple world, one is forever free from bondage and attachment. Wisdom is without recollection and is devoid of arising or ceasing; because it is without that which arises, it is called wisdom.
To act without seeing action and without an agent—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
It has no boundaries, no intermediate space, and no location; it abides nowhere and has no nest. Wisdom is pure, and consciousness has nothing upon which to rely.
The reason for this is that they are free from conceptualization. Their wisdom is limitless;

through the application of skillful means, they do not cease their efforts regarding desire, nor do they dwell in the realm of form or the formless realm. Although they share in the same defilements, they are not stained by them. This, O Most Excellent One, is what is called [true practice].
This is called Great Wisdom. It is free from lust, anger, and delusion; it does not dwell in ignorance or darkness. It is eternally liberated, without obstruction, neither clinging nor severing.

It eliminates the root of ignorance within the twelve links of dependent origination. It perceives no self or person, yet is neither without self nor possesses a self. It does not abide in craving, realizing all as one. It seeks no conceptualization of form, nor does it dwell upon the presence of forms in all things. This is called the eighth wisdom-activity of a bodhisattva.

Ultimately, they do not follow conditions and are free from the affliction of defilements; they are not joined with doubt, nor are they conditioned, yet they are not unconditioned; they do not seek worldly fortune, yet they are not devoid of merit, for they have transcended all evil and unrighteous matters.

The reason for this is that the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is eternally present; one does not see the fool practicing what is contrary to the Dharma, nor does one see him agitating his body, mind, or consciousness, such that his intent is not distracted by discursive thoughts or wandering toward heterodox notions.
"O Most Victorious One! This is called wisdom (*prajñā*). It is the discernment of the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) and the thorough knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda*).

It cuts off and extinguishes the notions of annihilationism and eternalism so that they do not arise again; it restrains the six sense-gates so that one never looks askance toward the wrong. Its vow lies in vastness and distance, not in calculating limits or boundaries. One cultivates the prohibitions of the youthful truth (*kumāra-brahmacarya*) without transgressing the proper order. If one sees those who have fallen back and remain in lower stations, one immediately exhorts and encourages them, striving to lead them upward. Those who reverently follow the Dharma do not sever the fundamental precepts (*vinaya-mūla*) practiced by all Buddhas. Body and mind are serene and joyful beyond measure; they promote the joy of the Path (*mārga-sukha*) without discarding the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), and they do not sever the assembly of the noble ones (*āryasaṃgha*), nor do they harbor [dualistic notions of] bondage or liberation."

Furthermore, one should cultivate both the methods of the monastic and the lay; by means of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), one does not sever any of the trainings, ensuring that the observance of the precepts remains fundamentally pure and inexhaustible.

All those who dwell within birth and death must eventually come to an end; they circulate through the five realms of existence, moving back and forth without rest, and as they abide in this impermanent state, they too shall perish.

Although non-Buddhist heterodox practitioners may attain the five supernatural powers, they do not transcend worldly wisdom; even if they aspire for longevity and subsequently lose their spiritual faculties, they will still face the cycle of birth and death upon the end of their lives.

There are sentient beings who, by diligently practicing the dharmas of the five precepts and the ten wholesome paths, attain birth among humans or devas; those who are diligent in the five precepts abide among the heavens of the desire realm, where they receive natural rewards and are fully endowed with merit.

There are some sentient beings who practice the concentration on emptiness while dwelling among the gods of the form realm; taking joy as their sustenance, they do not contemplate the root of suffering.

There are other sentient beings whose consciousness is tranquil and who aspire to the unconditioned, claiming that non-conception is eternal stillness and *nirvāṇa*. These are all those who discipline themselves but do not reach the ultimate place of extinction.
The eighth bodhisattva contemplates this state and remains unstained by it; he constantly expounds the Dharma, exhorting and encouraging students to distance themselves from it.
"O Most Victorious One, you should know!

The karma of the state of pure youth likewise remains far removed from the paths of the two vehicles; from the stage of Srotāpanna up to that of Pratyekabuddha, there are all manner of faults and blemishes, and the Bodhisattva never entertains thoughts of the dharma of Arhats.

The reason for this is that they apply their minds toward the path of *nirvāṇa*, which is what Pratyekabuddhas cultivate but Bodhisattvas do not study; because they have resolved their intentions without great compassion (*mahāmaitrīkaruṇā*), those who study in such a manner are all incorrect.

If there are bodhisattvas who wish to study the ocean of wisdom to its ultimate conclusion, exhausting its very source so that it remains inexhaustible; who vow never to abandon any sentient being; who cultivate the Dharma of the Tathāgata as an indestructible nature; whose wisdom is so boundless that it cannot be perceived; and who cause the fruits of the Way to blossom so that they may achieve fulfillment.

Regarding the "seeds and fruits," they refer to the Bodhisattva’s resolve and the heart of great vows, as well as the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities—extraordinary dharmas that are both inconceivable and inexhaustible.

The eighth-stage Bodhisattva wanders and transforms beings wherever they may be; he maintains his resolve and practices patience beyond the reach of thought. His mind does not harbor what is improper, nor does it give rise to any evils. He harbors no resentment toward sentient beings, nor does he stir his intent to compete or contend with others. Furthermore, he does not incite others to destruction or ruin. He carefully guards his body and speech so as not to commit transgressions at random. Protecting sentient beings, he is cautious regarding the root of his own conduct; he does not dwell among the heterodox factions but contemplates wholesome karma. Free from the mind of craving and desire, he is able to adorn his body like the physical form of a Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Jyotiprabha:
"A bodhisattva in the stage of youthful innocence (kumārabhūta) should constantly practice the sounds, phrases, and meanings.
How does a bodhisattva study the meaning of sounds and phrases?"

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva knows that all phenomena are empty and is not defiled by various views; contemplating signlessness, he does not give rise to distracted thoughts; discerning wishlessness, he is forever detached from the three realms of existence; knowing that phenomena are free from lust and their intrinsic nature is inherently pure, he does not arouse anger so that it may never arise again; and clearly perceiving ignorance, he does not remain in delusion.

Furthermore, one should contemplate the phenomena of the future, the past, and the present: that all things are ultimately without arising and are naturally so; that one perceives neither emergence nor extinction, neither birth nor death, nor retribution; yet, one maintains faith in the performance of good and evil, knowing that there are fruits and results.
He cultivates purity of speech and refrains from false speech; his mind is clear and understanding, and his conduct is untainted.

His undertakings are superior and he does not abandon anything; he constantly reflects upon the dream-like and illusionary nature of all phenomena. Should any wrong thoughts arise, he immediately recognizes them; his disposition is gentle and supple as he guards his mind, ensuring that evil does not arise and that purity is ever-present.

The truly real land, even if situated within the human realm, is fully endowed with manifold virtues; its inhabitants possess the eighty marks of excellence and voices like those of the kalaviṅka bird.
Their speech is as subtle and refined as that of Brahmā, free from ornate embellishment. Having abandoned lust, anger, and delusion, they no longer harbor sorrow or grief;
they never show a frowning face or harbor resentment toward others, and the merit they cultivate is never... [incomplete].
To eliminate loss and, according to its root, lead one to eternal peace; to constantly exhort all beings with the words of the Dharma;
to subdue those of external paths, heterodox studies, and strange arts; to be free from suffering and affliction so that there are no further calamities;
to fully comprehend the complete dharmas of all Buddhas; and for a person to always practice patience with body and mind so perfectly secret that they can endure being reviled in the present life.

When reviled, he remains silent and does not retaliate; even if sentient beings were to seize and beat him, he would harbor no thoughts of enmity, just as the great earth broadly receives all things, never having a conscious perception of increase or decrease.
The reason for this is that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is fundamentally empty.

Even if one should become angry, one ultimately harbors no resentment; one regards the expression of anger in others as like an illusion or a magical transformation, and when they approach with such intent, one does not harbor a contrary mind.
If someone harbors ill will toward you, do not pretend not to know; rather, reflect privately to yourself:
"I now clearly understand that this is empty. I shall seek to remain detached and refrain from giving rise to such conditions. Since the other person harbors resentment, I ought to be cautious."
"Even if someone were to come and praise him, he would not feel joy; nor would he feel distress or sorrow if he were seen being beaten.
This is because he perceives neither his own body nor the pain of the staff, as he has subdued his mind through the accumulation of practice."
In a secluded place, one examines within the body the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death, as well as the constant afflictions of sorrow, anxiety, fear, hunger, thirst, cold, and heat.

One further observes that this body is subject to decay and impermanence; this body is a vessel of suffering where all manner of diseases gather; this body is empty, for the four great elements return to their source; and this body is without self, without arising, and without ceasing.

Sentient beings in the three realms are drifted by currents; those swept by the current of craving and desire sink and transmigrate without rest. Therefore, one should first restrain the mind so that it does not proliferate.
Furthermore, one should contemplate the root of the outflows (*āsrava*), which resides within the three realms, where the cycle of birth and death continues without end as bodies are received.

One should also contemplate the stream of false views, wherein sentient beings, in their ignorance, give rise to inverted perceptions and become lost in the wild paths of the sixty-two dust-like delusions.

Regarding the flood of ignorance (*avidyā-ogha*): sentient beings of the three realms are shrouded in darkness by delusion and do not know the true Path. Taking the impure for the pure, they enter back into the flood of desire; taking suffering for pleasure, the impermanent for permanent, and what is not-self for self. Furthermore, they do not contemplate the removal of greedy turbidity, but instead deceive themselves; throughout the long night they do not practice, they do not cease from lust, they do not give away their wealth, and they do not accept the Buddha’s words. These are called the four corruptions, through which the root of craving increases, and mental intention and bodily action mutually enter into one another.

"In this way, Most Victorious One! The Bodhisattva enters meditative concentration in silence and observes; he abandons evil, eliminates desire and unwholesome thoughts, and internally contemplates his own body while recollecting the Three Jewels. He reflects upon and examines impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self. Following the teachings of the noble ones, he maintains a mind free from both suffering and pleasure. He practices the Fourfold Realization to fully master its meaning: that birth is the realization of suffering, craving is the realization of the origin, purification is the realization of cessation, and the path is the realization of the way. He grows weary of and detests this physical form, finding nothing in it worth desiring, and deeply contemplates its root: from what does it arise?"

By observing according to their nature, one comes to know the root source: suffering arises from the body, and its accumulation arises from craving; when craving is extinguished, it reaches cessation, and through the absence of desire, one attains the Way.

Always adhering to compassion and kindness without any harmful intent, one nurtures the transformation of the Way by taking pity on sentient beings. One strives to deliver them from the hardships of birth and death, approaching all living beings with a harmonious countenance and pleasant expression, exhorting and instructing them to resolve upon the aspiration for the Way, such that what is spoken is fluent and free from obstruction.

He understands the meaning of the ultimate truth regarding the characteristics of all phenomena; he penetrates and masters how all phenomena enter according to the occasion; when questioned, he responds immediately and without difficulty according to the capacities of those present; and his teachings are timely, with words that are never confused or disordered.

The Bodhisattva, with a heart of loving-kindness, takes pity on all beings; he universally contemplates the various classes of sentient beings who possess form and see that they cannot escape the pains of illness, decay, and death, and thus establishes skillful means to bring them liberation.

Again, he gives rise to a heart of compassion that takes pity on all beings suffering from hunger, thirst, cold, heat, gain, loss, transgression, and hardship; contemplating skillful means, he desires to bring them to a state of tranquility.

Furthermore, with a mind of joy, he reflects that all in the world are beset by the hardships of sorrow, suffering, and fear, and thinks: "I must ensure they are forever secure and at peace. With a heart of constant protection, he vows to deliver those born within the three realms and the eight difficulties—those who are foolish and ignorant, failing to see the Right Path—and seeks to bring them to liberation so they may attain the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). Thus, his compassion for sentient beings remains steadfast and unshakable.

Although they practice this dharma, their minds remain unstained by attachment; they do not give rise to retreat through hardship and toil, but thirst for and yearn after the unsurpassed, right, and true path, never feeling satiated in their pursuit of all-encompassing wisdom and insight.

Even when amidst the five types of music, song, and dance, he does not give rise to a mind of delight; for he clearly understands that these worldly things are all illusory transformations and that all phenomena ultimately return to impermanence. He is not swayed by the eight worldly winds, and his mind is always detached from them as if avoiding the conflagration at the end of an eon, never dwelling within their midst.

If one is troubled by others, and those who harbor anger or resentment come toward them, they will never retaliate even to the extent of a hair’s breadth; thus they are respected by others, and none dare to offend them.

Suppose there were someone who wished to harm a bodhisattva by dismembering their body, limb by limb, each placed in a different location; [the bodhisattva] would be able to endure all of this without giving rise to distracted thoughts, desiring thereby to fulfill the conduct of a *kumārabhūta*.
The Bodhisattva further contemplates that the phenomena of body and mind are but a composite that disperses and perishes; what is there to be greedily attached to, or what is worth treasuring?

Through these causal practices, one will inevitably attain the Buddha-body, fully perfecting the secret treasury of the Tathāgata, and establishing great vows to investigate the very source of the Way.

The Bodhisattva’s practice of skillful means and transformations is inexhaustible; should he be among those of external paths or heterodox studies, he manifests his body entering fire, sitting or lying within it with ease, and then emerges from the flames unharmed. He thereby causes those people to know that there is the True Way, so that their minds may spontaneously repent and they cultivate pure conduct. Thus he transforms the deluded and confused intentions, leading them back to the truth.
Because he followed [the gods] when they were born in heaven to lecture on the Dharma for them, they came to understand that even their celestial status is subject to decay and loss.

The expedient path of the Bodhisattva enters everywhere; there are none among Śakra, Brahmā, or the Four Heavenly Kings who do not take refuge in him and prostrate themselves. This is due to his accumulation of merit and the extraordinary excellence of his virtue and wisdom, which is beyond the reach of those of the Two Vehicles.
His divine wisdom as a youth is likewise boundless; his mind is vast and shoreless, beyond measure. What he speaks is beneficial and never diminishes; for this reason, his wisdom is inexhaustible.

One analyzes each of the dharmas of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind individually; realizing that they are all empty and non-existent, one attains the wisdom of transcendence through patience and thereby acquires manifold knowledges. Without conceiving of anything as either permanent or impermanent, one immediately enters into infinite wisdom.
If one engages in vocal exchange with others and contemplates their teachings as being like echoes in the mountains, one who understands this is said to possess expedient wisdom (*upāya-prajñā*).
Furthermore, one observes that all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena are empty by nature; they are fundamentally void and still, existing only as provisional designations.
He does not think of his own body as having attained the fruit of the Way, nor does he consider others who are inferior to have reached it.

Furthermore, he does not harbor self-conscious thoughts; he practices the precepts and reveres the sublime teachings of the Dharma, never giving rise to the intention to produce manifold discursive thoughts. This is called the boundless provisional wisdom of the Childlike Innocence (Kumārabhūta).

There may be bodhisattvas who practice the patience of the middle way, the patience of emptiness, the patience of the summit, and the patience of non-retrogression; they observe reality as it is without falsehood, cultivate the three Brahma-abodes, abide in emptiness without clinging to a basis or conceiving of solidity, maintain a state of non-conceptualization without dwelling on the notion of having thoughts, and neither seek nor give rise to the conceptualization of making vows.

The single mark of the Dharma-realm is likewise formless; contemplating birth and death, there is neither end nor beginning. There is no purposeful action, yet it is not without purposeful action. One does not perceive the past, the future, or the present; circulating through coming and going, there is ultimately nothing real. The past has been extinguished, the present does not abide, and the future is unborn. Those with virtue do not see those without virtue, and those without virtue do not see those with virtue. One does not act for the sake of having virtue, nor for the sake of lacking virtue; one is neither non-virtuous nor non-avirtuous. Fully understanding virtue and lack of virtue, one is profoundly tranquil and empty.

There are no such designations as arising and ceasing, attachment and severance; furthermore, one contemplates non-arising such that there is nothing arisen and no non-arising seen. To differentiate between arising and non-arising is empty and without reality; they are one and not two.

One does not perceive the realization of the fruits of the path that transcends the world, nor does one perceive before, after, or in between; one does not perceive the dissolution of written words or verbal teachings, nor their conformity with the world, nor their aggregation into a common flow.
“In this way, Most Excellent One!

That which is cultivated by the Youthful (kumārabhūta) is profound and far-reaching, difficult to reach, inconceivable, and beyond compare. One does not see the patience of the path (mārga-kṣānti) conjoined with the patience of wisdom (jñāna-kṣānti), nor does one see the patience of wisdom conjoined with the patience of the path, nor is there a lack of conjunction. One does not see the absence of the path conjoined with the absence of wisdom, nor does one see the absence of wisdom conjoined with the absence of the path. The patience of the path and the path itself do not conjoin with one another; yet it is not that they do not conjoin, nor is it that they are not conjoined.”
The reason for this is that their nature is inherently empty.
Most Excellent One!
You should know that there are two dharmas in the world that cause those who are newly learning to harbor doubts.
What are the two dharmas that give rise to doubt?
In this regard, a bodhisattva practices hundreds of thousands of dharmas, yet clings to nirvāṇa, believing himself to be liberated; for one who acts in such a way, there is diminution.

There may be a bodhisattva who knows that the nature of nirvāṇa is eternally liberation; they do not give rise to defiled attachment by establishing the convention of birth and death. Being neither from nor departing, they deeply know it to be one, without the names of various divisions. The bodhisattva’s wisdom-patience never gives rise to a dualistic mind, yet possesses the Great Vehicle of equality between self and other.

To understand and enter the wisdom of emptiness—being without attachment and without interruption, and being unstained—is called equanimity. To contemplate and realize this nature of equality as being neither bound nor liberated, and because there is nothing created, there is nothing produced; not seeing anything that arises or ceases spontaneously—this liberation from such [views] is what is called "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*).
Not seeing existence, not seeing non-existence, one thoroughly understands that all things are naturally non-existent; this is called purity, this is called cessation.
Thus it is, O Most Victorious One!

The Bodhisattva’s accumulation of practice brings wisdom to infinite heights; practicing the wisdom of non-arising, it is inexhaustible. From the initial accumulation of study until reaching the site of enlightenment, sitting beneath the Bodhi tree to subdue demonic adversaries and achieve the Unsurpassed Way, one must first enter this samādhi of patient wisdom and mental concentration; only thereafter does one roam in the Lion’s Vigorous Stride, the Peerless Samādhi, emitting great radiance that universally illumines the three thousandfold world system.

Those who behold this light all do so because they are enveloped by the vision of patience and wisdom; their mental consciousness is supple and free from arrogance. They constantly restrain body, speech, and mind with compassion;

their words and teachings are pure, remaining unimpaired from beginning to end. They devote themselves freely to the sublime path of the Buddha, roaming in samādhi with minds free from distracted thoughts. They are humble toward others and do not treat them with pride or contempt. Thus, the fruits of merit and the Way flourish day and night; the fetters of enmity and evil are forever without root or sprout, making them capable of traveling to the buddha-fields of other directions.

One knows that this is the response to the spiritual resonance of radiant light, through which all sentient beings are transformed and none fail to be delivered; yet upon investigating that radiance, it is found to be utterly non-existent, and even the discernment of its characteristics lacks any reality.
Furthermore, one should distinguish the characteristics arising from form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
How does one contemplate and penetrate the characteristics of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*)?

That which is seen as light is called form; that which possesses physical substance is also form; that which receives, accepts, and bestows is also form; the protection and maintenance of one’s own body is also form; and giving it to others is likewise form.
Next, one should thoroughly understand the arising and ceasing of sensation (*vedanā*). By what cause does this sensation exist?

Whether it be painful sensation, pleasant sensation, or neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation, if one constantly maintains mindfulness and discernment such that there is neither suffering nor pleasure, how could there be sensation? This is not the case; for one who possesses full understanding, this is the characteristic of sensation.

To deeply record the constant flow and movement of the mind as it rushes on without ceasing—recalling the past, future, and present, whether concerning men or women, and all other countless and limitless thoughts—is called "ideation" (vitarka).

One understands that this perception has no coming and no going, nor does it have a location; it is empty and not real, and lacks even a name or designation, and is therefore called "thought-perception" (*saṃjñā*).

Furthermore, when one perceives the phenomena of good and evil conduct—whether they are determinate or indeterminate, with outflows or without outflows, conditioned or unconditioned—one does not regard their active manifestation as an obstruction.

At that time, the Bodhisattva sees those who practice good as not being non-good, and sees those who practice evil as not being non-evil; furthermore, when there is a time when one neither practices good nor practices evil, one should contemplate and discern so as not to perceive the absence of good or the absence of evil. This, O Most Victorious One, is called [the Bodhisattva’s practice].
This is called "action" (*saṃskāra*). Furthermore, one should clearly understand by what cause there is consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Consciousness is not of a single characteristic: the phenomena of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are also called consciousness; the phenomena of form, sound, odor, taste, and tangibility are also called consciousness; the phenomena of contact, arising, and decay are also called consciousness; that which exists within thought is also called consciousness; that which is free from thought is also called consciousness; that which is wholesome is also called consciousness; that which is unwholesome is also called consciousness; and that which is neither wholesome nor unwholesome is also called consciousness.

To understand from what this consciousness arises and from what it ceases, and to understand that it is without arising and without birth or cessation—to realize this is what is called "consciousness."
“Thus it is, Most Victorious One!

When a Bodhisattva in the state of a youth (kumārabhūta) casts off one body and receives another, his faculty of the body and his mental consciousness are not initially disturbed, and he does not encounter obstacles while remaining in the intermediate state (antarābhava).
When the spirits of sentient beings depart and dwell in the intermediate state, they encounter obstacles according to the gravity of the root causes of their calamities.”
At the very moment a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva resolves his mind [upon enlightenment], he proceeds wherever his will leads, assuming form without hindrance.
Most Excellent One!

You should know that a Bodhisattva in the stage of Youth (kumārabhūta) is always a companion to a Bodhisattva who is in his last birth before Buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha). Attending upon him, they travel together to observe the purity of Buddha-fields; they select the most exquisite and supreme Buddha-fields, their aspirations fixed upon the magnificent and beautiful, performing the works of a Buddha.

The eighth-stage bodhisattva attains mastery; their transformative manifestations through conditions are all-pervasive, and the Dharma they proclaim is inexhaustible, always gladdening sentient beings with virtuous teachings.
At that time, there were bodhisattvas in the assembly who each thought to themselves:

"Today the Tathāgata proclaims the work of wisdom and extols the practice of the state of a youthful seeker (kumārabhūta); its meritorious fruit and retribution are likewise peerless. Now, observing the cultivation of the most excellent Mahāsattva, his practice of the youthful path is also without deviation."
If you, Most Victorious One, should attain the unsurpassed path of perfect enlightenment, what will be your name when you achieve Buddhahood?
And of what kind will the meritorious adornments and purity of that Buddha-land be?
"What is the accomplishment of the assembly of bodhisattvas?
Is there any distinction in their practice of the Dharma and Vinaya?

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the assembly, immediately smiled upon his seat. Countless hundreds of thousands of millions of rays of light issued from the Buddha’s mouth, illuminating infinite worlds in the ten directions, eclipsing the brilliance of the sun and moon and overshadowing the palaces of Māra. The light returned, circling the Buddha countless times before entering through the crown of his head.
At that time, the bodhisattvas in the assembly rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, joined their palms in homage to the Buddha, and asked about the meaning of his smile:
"The Buddha does not smile without cause; we pray that you will explain its significance."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the assembly, saying:
"Do you see this Bodhisattva Most Victorious? They replied:
“Yes, we have indeed seen them.
The Buddha then addressed the bodhisattvas assembled there:

“In this Bhadrakalpa, after one hundred buddhas have passed away, there shall appear a buddha named Siṃhavikrāntagāmin Tathāgata, arising in the world—a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, called Buddha, the World-Honored One. His land and its name shall be no different from those of the present.”

At that time, the territory and boundaries of that land were wondrous and sublime; even the five grains, though once base and lowly, were naturally priceless. The population was flourishing and the city walls were majestic and orderly, composed of the seven treasures: gold, silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, musaragalva, agate, coral, amber, and maṇi jewels.

At that time, that Buddha-land was level and even, with eight-way intersections composed entirely of jewels. Its ground was as soft as celestial fine cloth; its garments, food and drink, palaces, and dwellings were like those of the Tuṣita Heaven. Its gardens, groves, bathing pools, intersecting roads, and tiered pavilions were towering, exquisite, and wondrous. Such was the divine virtue of that Buddha-land.

The devas and humans spontaneously manifested themselves, performing music and dance, hanging silk banners, erecting victory banners and canopies, burning various famous incenses, and raining down precious, exquisite flowers; they protected the True Dharma so that it would not be deficient or lost, guiding and benefiting immeasurable sentient beings.
Now this most excellent Bodhisattva, passing away from this world, shall be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, the Buddha-field of Aśoka.

When he has been born in that land, the Buddha Aśoka will proclaim eight thousand four hundred marvelous Dharma-gates for the sake of the Bodhisattvas; he will expound the Way and its teachings so they may return to their essential meaning, circulating and revolving through them without interruption, ensuring that the Triple Gem remains unbroken and causing all sentient beings to establish themselves in the stage of non-retrogression.
When these words were spoken, all those present in the assembly sighed in admiration, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
O Most Victorious Mahāsattva!"

"Why is it that the attainment of Buddhahood is so swift? I vow that in a future life I shall be born in this land, and when the Tathāgata Siṃhavikrama appears in the world, may I encounter his teachings and cultivate the practice of a *kumārabhūta* (pure youth) just as the Most Victorious One did."
At that time, the bodhisattvas in the assembly thought again to themselves:

"May all sentient beings universally attain the dharma of wisdom, patience, and knowledge, no different from what we have now; upon hearing this sound, may they have no fear and harbor no hesitation."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Sujaya, saying:

"The Bodhisattva, having fully perfected all virtues in his practice, manifests extraordinary and immeasurable teachings; appearing at the appropriate times, there is nowhere he does not enter—whether taking the form of an ordinary person, a widower, or an elderly man, or appearing as the likeness of a youth or an infant."

Furthermore, employing skillful means, he enters the four paths and becomes a friend to those who have already attained the stage of *srotāpanna*, preaching the supreme essentials so that they do not slacken. He then employs further expedients to enter the stage of *sakṛdāgāmin*, exhorting them to sever the five calamities and difficulties, enabling them to attain entry without undergoing seven more returns.
Sometimes he spreads the nectar of immortality in the heavens for practitioners of pure maturity who will no longer return to this world;

sometimes he meets with stainless *arhats* and speaks to them of the sixty-eight dharmas concerning bodily suffering, lamenting his own meanness and lack of the unsurpassed path, and how he has merely wasted his wisdom and brought disgrace upon the Dharma scriptures.

In some cases, he manifests the path of the Buddhas and Pratyekabuddhas, proclaiming his supernormal powers and displaying the eighteen transformations; he teaches through silence, bringing about liberation, while inwardly harboring skillful means and wisdom to respond appropriately to the minds of others, administering the medicine according to conditions so that it neither exceeds nor falls short.

Or, together with those newly trained and first resolved in mind, he enters the pure samādhi, causing all sentient beings to universally behold his form-body; he then causes the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world-system of Buddha-lands to rest within the palm of his hand for them to mutually offer worship, coming and going therein without increase or decrease, thereby causing them to give rise to the aspiration for the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva named Jiuchang, who rose from his seat, knelt with palms joined, and stepped forward to address the Buddha, saying:
"So be it, World-Honored One!"

What is the name of this samādhi concentration that causes the three thousand great thousandfold world systems and the realms of the ten directions to appear universally within the palm of one's hand, such that the sentient beings therein offer respectful worship without increase or decrease?
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Jiuchang, saying:

"That samādhi is named 'Pure. It universally perceives the manifestation of physical bodies and their transformations, encompassing all without exception; yet the realms of the lands remain as they were, neither different nor subject to increase or decrease."

Even if the three thousandfold great chiliocosm, as well as immeasurable Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, were all contained within his palm, and he performed acts of merit by honoring and serving them together, sitting, lying down, walking, or enjoying himself as he pleased, the sentient beings therein would not know one another, nor would they be disturbed or troubled by his presence.

Jiuchang, you should know that all these are the manifestations of the majestic spiritual power of the *kumārabhūta* Bodhisattvas; though they manifest transformations wherever they may be, no body is perceived, and ultimately, they ensure that sentient beings harbor no thoughts of increase or decrease.

At that time, all those assembled in the hall—the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans—each conceived this thought: they wished for the Most Excellent Great Being, the Bodhisattva, to manifest supernatural transformations and the purity of meditative concentration.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that each member of the assembly had various thoughts in their minds, addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Most Victorious (Jinsheng), saying:
"Most Victorious, you now..."
"For the sake of all sentient beings and those gathered here, you should manifest this samādhi of pure meditative concentration, so that all those in the assembly may develop firm faith.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Most Victorious (Varasena), receiving the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power and reverently upholding the holy teaching, immediately entered right-mindfulness samādhi while seated upon his throne. He caused all the lands of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—including devas, nāgas, humans, and the kings of ghosts and spirits, as well as other honored deities, the bodhisattvas in the assembly, and all beings with form—to appear within his palm. Among them were those practicing dhyāna-concentration, those practicing the recitation of sutras, and those cultivating merit and performing the works of a Buddha; what was manifested was extraordinary, sublime, and beyond comparison, such that no analogy could suffice.

Having manifested these supernatural powers, all those who had gathered from the ten directions returned to their original seats, remaining exactly as they were before without change; the Bodhisattva Most Victorious (Varabodhisattva) likewise remained on his seat, his robes properly adjusted and his dignified demeanor unimpaired.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Juchang addressed Zhisheng, saying:

"The majestic power of the samādhi manifested by you, O Benevolent One, surpasses immeasurable and limitless virtue; its divine resonance and manifest majesty are truly peerless, for it is able to contain the worlds of the ten directions within your right palm without any increase or decrease."

"We shall diligently apply ourselves to performing meritorious deeds and establishing virtue, advancing in the practice of the Dharma of pure meditative concentration, striving to reach the conduct of a Great Being in the stage of the Youthful (Kumārabhūta).
At that time, Bhadra-pratibhāna said: "So it is, so it is!"
As you have said:

if there are those who are newly trained and have resolved to practice, and who are intent on cultivating the dharma of the youthful (kumāra), they should mindfully apply themselves with diligence to achieve the fruit of the Way, so that they do not regress midway.
When a bodhisattva exerts diligence, there are twenty matters that ought to be practiced, which nurture and protect [the bodhisattva path] so that it does not diminish.
What are these twenty faultless dharmas?

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva cultivates the conduct of a youthful seeker, giving rise to a great, far-reaching vow and an unobstructed mind, intending to rescue others from perilous calamities; this is what it means to be diligent and without retreat.

"Furthermore, when a bodhisattva gathers a multitude of followers and instructs them in the Way through the formless Dharma, constantly proclaiming the sounds of emptiness, non-existence, and profound stillness—this is called the practice of the stage of youthful innocence (kumārabhūta) without regression."

"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva extensively distributes his merits so that even those of inferior capacity may receive their entanglement [of benefit]; first, he eliminates their greedy intentions so they are free from conceptualization, and only thereafter does he instruct them in the Perfection of Giving (Dānapāramitā)."

"Furthermore, when a bodhisattva sees sentient beings before him who are in distress or hardship, he immediately goes in person to transform them, comforting those people so that they do not suffer pain, always mindful of nurturing them with a mind that never wavers."

"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva undertakes ascetic practices and, after enduring countless hardships, seeks out a sublime teacher. Having received instruction on the precepts and laws from him, he reverently practices the True Dharma, constantly mindful of obstructing the six rootless [afflictions]."

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva seeks the unsurpassed path, their mind is free from worldly ambition and defilement; they constantly apply themselves with diligence to the various supernormal powers and wisdom, practicing tranquility and insight to eliminate the mind of craving and attachment.

"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva, being timely and adaptable, clearly understands skillful means and transformations such that no one perceives his conscious deliberation; he first ensures that the person receiving the teaching has their deluded mind thoroughly penetrated, and only then does he instruct them on what is appropriate regarding skillful means."

"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva arouses the mind of aspiration and vows to fully perfect the primary and secondary marks to adorn his body, to purify his own land so that it becomes the color of gold, and to ensure that his retinue shares the same characteristics as himself."

"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva vows to deliver those who are vast and remote; he harbors no timidity or weakness that would cause obstruction. Though dwelling within birth and death, he does not shrink from toil and suffering; his resolve is steadfast and firm as he subdues the heterodox."

Furthermore, the bodhisattva establishes countless karmas of merit and virtue; he constantly keeps sentient beings in mind without regarding them as his own, remaining free from attachment, and contemplates the Four Noble Truths with clear awakening and penetrative insight.

"Furthermore, a bodhisattva donning the armor of the great vow seeks the unsurpassed path for incalculable eons, yet never gives rise to the thought, 'I am practicing the truth,' for if one harbors such a thought, there will be decline and diminution."

"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva embraces ordinary beings; to those who come for refuge, he briefly explains the teachings of the Way, pointing out the path so they may know where to go, and observing the capacity of the person before him, he then bestows the nectar of immortality."

"Furthermore, when a bodhisattva observes the customs of the land, he shall not give rise to rebellion against what is established by the royal law; he should follow what is good and secretly avoid what is evil, never being self-conceited as to ruin the social customs."

"Furthermore, a bodhisattva should train in entering assemblies—whether an assembly of brahmins or an assembly of householders—observing and adopting their etiquette: knowing when to walk, knowing when to sit, and knowing when to lie down; adapting one's deportment appropriately without error. This is called a bodhisattva in the stage of youthful innocence (kumārabhūta) who knows how to enter assemblies."

"Furthermore, a bodhisattva should constantly cultivate and study the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), and by possessing the wisdom that is neither arising nor ceasing, they shall fully complete all Buddha-dharmas. Wandering to transform beings throughout the infinite Buddha-lands of the ten directions, and desiring to master all doors of dhāraṇī and all doors of various knowledges, with a wisdom that is clear, penetrating, and inexhaustible, they should mindfully practice the conduct of the youthful (kumāra-bhūta)."

"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva upholds what is correct and restrains what is chaotic, remaining aloof from heterodox factions. He is fully endowed with generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. His mind is neither lax nor weary; he never neglects or forgets his heart of great vows. This is called the firm mind of the stage of youthful innocence."

"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva gathers the multitude of merits that are the root of all wholesome deeds; he entwines his own body, cultivating the various marks and signs (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana) to adorn himself. He eliminates arrogance, ignorance, and false views; as a *kumārabhūta* Bodhisattva, he is pure in a single aspect and thus remains unstained by attachment. He perceives no realms as either pure or impure. Only then does he fully perfect the merits of the marks and signs, becoming completely endowed with immeasurable karmic blessings, never succumbing to indolence or a mind of regression."

Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva in the state of youthful purity (kumārabhūta) gives rise to great, far-reaching vows, does not abandon his original aspiration, extensively disseminates the work of wisdom, and practices with diligence without weariness; this is called the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the practice of youthful purity.

"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva discriminates the illusory and deceptive nature of phenomena, perceiving them as empty and quiescent, ultimately non-existent, and devoid of any form or substance that can be seen. He nurtures his vigor and devotes himself to cultivating his fundamental practice, not neglecting it for even a sixteenth part of a moment. The Bodhisattva practicing compassion constantly reflects: 'For the sake of my birth, from where does it arise?'"

Reflecting deeply within myself, I find no nest from which I have emerged; this is merely the worldly person’s own arising of conscious conceptions and the intent of defiled attachment that stirs the fire of desire. This burns away the roots of goodness and causes one to fall into the five realms of existence, all because of the fetters of craving, ignorance, and delusion.
