If there is a bodhisattva who discerns that the five desires are all unreal, and diligently contemplates them so as never again to dwell with them; and if they hear of people in the wilderness of other regions who practice asceticism to sever desire, they are able to skillfully guide sentient beings to those lands. Upon seeing those practitioners of asceticism who have severed desire, their own minds become cool and clear, free from the feverish affliction of passion. They cause those sentient beings to all resolve upon the Bodhi-mind, leading them away gradually by removing the five desires. They then travel through various Buddha-lands to pay homage to and make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones. Furthermore, they lead them into the profound depths of the Dharma, and only then do they fully perfect the virtue of giving, as well as the establishment of the will for precept, patience, kindness, harmony, and diligence. With single-mindedness they enter meditative concentration so that mindfulness does not wander, and they extensively cultivate the boundless karma of wisdom.
This is what is meant, O Jiuchang!

It is the path practiced by the *kumārabhūta* (Ever-Youthful) Bodhisattva, whose vast benefit is all-encompassing and exhaustive. If there is a Bodhisattva who first begins to train in, recite, and discourse upon the twenty practices, they shall thereafter set out to tread the tracks of the *kumārabhūta*.

When the Most Victorious One preached this Dharma, seventeen thousand people all conceived the vast and inexhaustible aspiration, and yearned to cultivate the twenty practices of the state of youthful purity (*kumārabhūta*).
Ten thousand devas and humans all attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Furthermore, there were countless classes of sentient beings who increased their merit and no longer harbored any thoughts of regression.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Most Victorious, saying:
"Excellent, O Bodhisattva!
You bring great benefit and deliver many beings."

If there is a bodhisattva who, having donned the mind of great vows, accumulates meritorious deeds without harboring weariness or indolence, and further applies diligent effort to provide assistance while practicing the gift of Dharma, desiring thereby to transform and enlighten the various classes of sentient beings, so that they may be gathered together for deliverance and enter the realm of Nirvana, forever free from coming and going.
"Thus it is said, O Most Victorious One!
The virtues cultivated by a youth in his state of purity are immeasurable.

If there are bodhisattvas who resolve their minds and begin their training, they should constantly practice twenty dharmas; only then will they gradually enter the profound treasury of the Dharma-jewels."
"So it is, Most Excellent One!
You should train yourself in this way; one who trains in this way accords with the path of the eighth-stage bodhisattva."
Chapter Nine: On Meditative Concentration (Samādhi) At that time, the Bodhisattva Most Victorious (Varabodhisattva) again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What is meant by the Bodhisattva Constantly Pure (Sadāśuddha) purifying his dwelling in the ninth stage?”

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Varaprabha, saying: "The Bodhisattva of the Ninth Stage cultivates the gate of single-minded liberation through the practice of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). He enters into right reception (*samāpatti*) without depletion; whether amidst the pure or the impure, he remains constantly as one-pointed in mind. Though dwelling amidst the dust and toil of afflictions and resentment, he does not give rise to distracted thoughts or manifold notions. He observes and knows how the minds, consciousnesses, and perceptions of sentient beings are attached, and how they are bound by the fetters of causal conditions and suffering. He understands the retributions and responses that lead to these calamities, and further seeks skillful means and provisional methods: by what clever expedient can he reach eternal cessation and attain deliverance?"

At that time, the ninth Bodhisattva Mahāsattva further reflected upon these various attachments and perceptions: they all arise from failing to accord with the characteristics of the True Dharma; through ignorance and volitional formations, one incurs such conditioned retributions. One should therefore single-mindedly give rise to the mindfulness of the Path—mindfulness of the Buddha, the Dharma, the Saṅgha, morality, generosity, and the heavens; mindfulness of ānāpāna, the withdrawal of the body, and death; guarding all things so they do not become disordered, practicing with diligence as if extinguishing a fire. May the merits attained fill all things; harboring aspirations within for the fruits of the Path, one practices all supernormal knowledges and wisdoms without exception.

Constantly reflecting with compassion for all beings, he pondered: "By what cause do sentient beings suffer from the afflictions of *kleśa*? He observed himself with discernment to seek their origin and found that they all result from ignorance (*avidyā*), which leads to formative action (*saṃskāra*).

Because formative action arises, there is consciousness (*vijñāna*); once consciousness has its abode, it is called name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*). Once name-and-form have arisen, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are fully established. With the internal and external mutually dependent, contact (*sparśa*) arises; when the mind becomes stained by attachment, sensation (*vedanā*) subsequently arises. Discerning pleasure and pain, the intention of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is born. Once the root of craving has arisen, one undergoes mutual reception and entry, whereby birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and despair gradually increase, resulting in the retribution of desire and love.

The ninth bodhisattva contemplates this retribution with profound reflection, considering that the bonds of affliction are empty and not real; seeing that they truly have no substance, he observes his own conditioned retribution.
Furthermore, he knows that the conceptualized fruits of sentient beings have no location whatsoever; thus, there is nothing to be responded to, and no response to be given.

Moreover, by means of the method of pure true contemplation, he causes those sentient beings to attain purity. He constantly encourages them to diligently cultivate a concentrated mind, first employing skillful means to contemplate a single Buddha-field: how many sentient beings therein establish firm vows and perform meritorious deeds to collectively cultivate the unsurpassed path to the tree of enlightenment?
How many sentient beings are there who, through meditative stillness and entry into samādhi, manifest supernatural powers and transformations with unimpeded skillful means?

Furthermore, how many sentient beings are there who shoulder heavy burdens as a great responsibility for others, acting on their behalf to uproot suffering so that they do not have to endure affliction?
How many sentient beings have severed the three fetters and fully realized the fruit of stream-entry?
How many sentient beings, having thinned the three stains, have attained the stage of once-returning and are forever separated from suffering?
How many sentient beings are free from the affliction of the five lower fetters, such that they no longer return to this world?
How many sentient beings have severed the five higher fetters, dwelling in various liberations and finding joy therein?

Furthermore, using his supernormal powers and five eyes, he observes those places where the Dharma has vanished into obscurity; there are pratyekabuddhas dwelling in mountain forests who appear from time to time among humans to teach and transform them, and the bodhisattva likewise contemplates whether those locations are suitable for him to approach or not.

How does a son of noble family, with single-minded contemplation, observe the classes of sentient beings within the realm of a single Buddha, establishing firm resolve and performing meritorious deeds, so as to advance in the cultivation of the unsurpassed path to the tree of enlightenment?

Thereupon, a son of good family, a Bodhisattva established in the ninth stage, if he perceives that sentient beings possess a firm and resolute mind, immediately employs skillful means to act as their spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
He nurtures them according to the occasion, increasing their diligence, protecting and bringing them to fulfillment, so that their ultimate resolve becomes steadfast and indestructible.
He guides and inspires them, revealing and instructing them so that they may come to know the profound Dharma.
Without regarding distance, nearness, or perilous difficulties— even if there were a blazing fire ahead, so fiercely burning that a single Buddha-field were fused into a single mass—
one would pass through its midst to reach another world-system. Hearing that in that place a Buddha was expounding the Dharma—
the teaching of non-arising and non-ceasing, free from old age and death— one would then press forward, casting away one's very body.
Taking refuge, they shall reach that place in safety; their bodies will not be burned, nor will they suffer any feverish affliction.

They shall obtain the opportunity to behold that Buddha, to pay homage, serve, and make offerings to him. By accumulating the merit of these extraordinary dharmas, they shall swiftly achieve accomplishment and never regress.
Even if they should encounter the deep waters of a great ocean, extending as far as a single Buddha-field above and below, and all around...
Yet there is no difference [in his resolve]; therein he makes a vow, able to cast himself back into it, nor does he shrink from the difficulty of the merit he has established.

His aspiration is firm and unshakable; this is called the ninth dwelling of a Bodhisattva, who abides in great loving-kindness and compassion because he does not abandon any means of gathering in sentient beings.

"What is it that a bodhisattva in the ninth stage observes regarding those sentient beings who dwell in meditative stillness and enter concentration, manifesting supernatural transformations (ṛddhi-vikurvaṇa) with unimpeded adaptability?

In this regard, if a bodhisattva sees sentient beings dwelling far away in deep mountains or uninhabited places, they focus their minds in contemplation and enter the first dhyāna, the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna."
At that time, the Bodhisattva, seeing those sentient beings, again arose from the fourth dhyāna of the fourfold dhyānas and entered the third, second, and first dhyānas of the fourfold dhyānas.

At that time, the Bodhisattva further observed sentient beings who entered only the first dhyāna but not the second, third, or fourth; or entered the second dhyāna but not the first, third, or fourth; or entered the third dhyāna but not the first, second, or fourth; or entered the fourth dhyāna but not the first, second, or third.
At that time, the Bodhisattva also sees sentient beings entering the sphere of infinite space, the sphere of infinite consciousness, and the sphere of nothingness;
or at times the Bodhisattva observes sentient beings abiding only in the sphere of infinite space but not in the sphere of infinite consciousness or the sphere of nothingness;
or at times they abide alone in the sphere of infinite consciousness but not in the sphere of infinite space or the sphere of nothingness.
At times he dwells alone, not entering the sphere of infinite space, nor the sphere of infinite consciousness;
at times he dwells in the fourth dhyāna, but not in the three lower or higher dhyānas.

When a Bodhisattva at the ninth stage proceeds to those beings and acts as their virtuous benefactor, enabling them to accomplish meritorious virtues without weariness, and being able to cause sentient beings to surely reach a state of firmness, one may then designate this stage by the name "the Ninth Stage."

What is meant by the ninth stage of the Bodhisattva, who bears the heavy burden for others and takes on their heavy responsibilities, constantly acting as their substitute to extract them from suffering so that they do not experience affliction?

In this regard, the Bodhisattva, through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), enters the five realms of existence (*pañca-gati*) to provide, as the occasion requires, clothing, food and drink, bedding, seats, and medicines for the sick and emaciated. If there are those in the three miserable paths or the eight difficult conditions, he immediately goes there in person to deliver them, ensuring that the people before him do not suffer. Or, entering among the denizens of hell and the hungry ghosts (*preta*), he is able to bestow vast bounty so that each may be fully satisfied. This is called the ninth Bodhisattva being capable of bearing the heavy burden for sentient beings.
"How does a bodhisattva exhort others to sever the three fetters and attain the stage of the path, gradually realizing the fruits of realization and forever parting from suffering?

To this end, the bodhisattva employs skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) and manifests various transformations, preaching the teachings of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, and describing the bliss of Nirvāṇa as tranquil and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)."

At times, he teaches the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas the dharma of non-arising, non-ceasing, and emptiness; having discerned the thoughts of those sentient beings, he first discusses the essentials of the Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras: generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom; great kindness and great compassion; the four dhyānas and the four immeasurables; the faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, and the three Brahma-abodes. Upon hearing this, their minds become solemn and the hair on their bodies stands on end; according to their capacities, he encourages them to advance so that they may realize the Way.

At times, when a Bodhisattva observes that a certain sentient being originally aspired to the bodhicitta but now, out of weariness and fatigue, is unable to attain it and wishes to retreat into the path of the śrāvakas, the Bodhisattva then goes to that person and says:

"Since you have accumulated merit until now, your accomplishment is nearly complete; the radiant marks and secondary signs shall adorn your body, and you shall extensively deliver sentient beings while cultivating and purifying a Buddha-field. Why then do you retreat to follow the Lesser Vehicle?"
Upon hearing this, the man redoubled his self-reproach, saying:
"Alas! My conduct was improper and truly shameful, that I should cause the Bodhisattva who has attained spiritual penetration to be rebuked by me.

From now on, I shall exert myself with courage and vigor; I will accumulate merit, resolve my will, and uphold the spirit of the great vow, so that for the sake of all beings, I shall never abandon my original aspiration."

When the Bodhisattva who has resolved his mind gave rise to this thought, at that moment the heavens and earth shook in six ways, and the palaces of Māra trembled so that they could not remain in their original positions.
At that time, the evil Māra conceived this thought:
"What kind of auspicious omen is this that has manifested, causing the heavens and earth to shake in six ways just now?"

Could it not be that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has appeared in the world? If it were otherwise, it must be that some person free from desire who has attained arhatship has caused such a miraculous response to reach this point.

If this were not the case, it must be that a bodhisattva who has resolved his mind has established firm vows and generated the aspiration for the Mahāyāna, desiring to seek Buddhahood and walk alone through the triple world; out of compassion for those in peril and distress, he seeks to deliver beings throughout the ten directions, emptying my realm so that no attendants remain.

If it were not so, he must be a king of the one hundred and twenty-eight *kalāpa* hells who has been born into this hell; because he governs and transforms through principle with a mind that neither increases nor decreases, he may well have been moved by such a divine transformation.

"If it were not so, I have ten thousand sons, valiant, robust, and possessed of extraordinary talents, who stand by my side governing the six heavens. My youngest son is named Evil Son; he is by nature fierce and violent, his conduct lacking in compassion and benevolence. I have dispatched him to oversee the affairs of the King of Hell, to deliberate between good and evil and distinguish the worthy from the foolish. He also possesses supernormal powers that move heaven and earth, and is now titled the King Who Governs Punishment and Governs the Law, treating all without distinction of high or low. Could this not be a manifestation of divine response?"
The Māra further reflected:

"I have a servant named Ābāng, who can also manifest transformations and possesses immeasurable majesty and virtue. On the day he was born, heaven and earth shook violently; when his life comes to an end, the earth likewise shakes violently. It may well be that he is now manifesting such an auspicious and strange omen."

Thus Māra the King gave rise to various thoughts; he then used his divine eye to survey the trichiliocosm and saw that a person who had severed desire and was destined for the stage of *srotāpanna* had now instead resolved upon the mind of the Mahāyāna.
"This is precisely that person who wishes to empty my realm; I must seek skillful means to destroy this son's wholesome mind.

At that time, the evil Māra led his host of soldiers to the place where the good man was, but upon seeing the Bodhisattva of Constant Purity in the Ninth Stage, his heart was filled with fear and his hair stood on end; he then retreated immediately, unable to advance further.

This is called the spiritual power and responsive resonance of the Bodhisattva Changjing (Constant Purity), which causes the traces of the Path to become tranquil and perfect the Unsurpassed Way, establishing vows that never bend or retreat.

What is meant by the Bodhisattva Jiuzhu (Nine Abodes) observing the various classes of sentient beings, knowing those whose three fetters have been attenuated as having attained the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin, and being forever separated from suffering through the eternal absence of desire, anger, and delusion?

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva observes those sentient beings and the merits they have accumulated over a long period of time—whether they possess sharp faculties or dull faculties. Even if he sees that a sentient being’s mind is fully matured and on the verge of attaining the fruit of the Way, such that their intent cannot be turned back from reaching the Great Way;
or if he sees one with dull faculties, he exhorts them to be diligent so that they may be endowed with the various roots of virtue and the retribution of the fruit of the Way.

The Bodhisattva guides them so that their minds do not become indolent, enabling them to soon achieve the realization of the four paths; some may even transcend [the lower stages] to attain the fourth fruit, ensuring they do not stagnate at the stage of Anāgāmin.

All of these are the ninth virtue of eternal purity: never having forsaken the mind of great vows. This is called the bodhisattva’s cultivation of diligent vigor, which is beyond measure, and which does not calculate karmic retribution or the twelve links of dependent origination.

The Bodhisattva in the ninth stage cultivates constant purity and thereby attains purification. Whether hearing the Dharma of gentleness and compliance from others or reflecting inwardly upon his own person in accordance with that Dharma-recollection, he applies himself with single-minded devotion, setting his will upon study. He always dwells in seclusion and tranquility, never remaining in the midst of clamor and confusion. Knowing those skillful means and maintaining a tranquil, concentrated mind, he observes the faculties of others and never errs; this is called the Bodhisattva’s further advancement toward the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin.

"How does a bodhisattva assist sentient beings, severing the afflictions of the five fetters and entanglements, and then exhort them toward parinirvāṇa in those very heavens, without returning again to this world?"

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva went to that celestial realm and taught them the Dharma of non-arising and non-cessation; he then entered the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) right before them, manifesting his parinirvāṇa. All the Anāgāmin devas in that realm each conceived this thought and exhorted one another to enter parinirvāṇa within the realm of nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*).

Although a bodhisattva manifests extraordinary phenomena, his mind does not undergo change or give rise to manifold perceptions. He recognizes events from countless kalpas in the distant past and fully understands all movements and destinations; yet he perceives no one who goes, nor is there any returning, nor does he perceive any place of dwelling. Observing that nothing is produced and that there is fundamentally no location, he personally attains purity, tranquility, and non-action. This is called the bodhisattva’s further advancement within the stage of Anāgāmin.
"How does a bodhisattva further observe sentient beings so as to nurture those in training until they attain non-attachment?

In this regard, a bodhisattva mahāsattva in the ninth stage uses the divine eye to observe the trichiliocosm, [asking]: 'Who is destined for the exhaustion of outflows and is about to attain the fruit of the Path?'"

Having made this contemplation, he may see ten, a hundred, a thousand, or even an incalculable and immeasurable number of people who sever their fetters and, on the same day and at the same time, shall become stainless Arhats.

At that time, by means of his supernormal powers, the Bodhisattva traverses the entire trichiliocosm in a single day; through skillful means, he protects those people, causing each to fulfill their aspirations and attain non-attachment, forever departing from birth and death to abide in tranquil non-action. This is called the Bodhisattva’s enhancement of the Arhat.
"How does a bodhisattva exhort those of the pratyekabuddha vehicle so that they attain non-attachment?

In this regard, the bodhisattva further uses the divine eye to observe the high mountains, level plains, and secluded places throughout all worlds, where [pratyekabuddhas] dwell in solitary tranquility, contemplating with profound focus the forty-three methods of meditative concentration."

At that time, the Bodhisattva likewise went there; not far away, he spread grass upon the ground, sat down cross-legged, and fixed his mind before him. Without looking about distractedly, he reflected within himself, wishing to manifest skillful transformations: sometimes manifesting the sounds of thunder and lightning, or trees rubbing against one another so that flames issued from them more brilliant than fire, or the mournful cries of birds and beasts.

At that time, the Bodhisattva stood before the assembly and suddenly transformed his form, soaring into the void. He performed the eighteen transformations with mastery over both existence and non-existence; he was endowed with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics, and though water and fire issued from his body, he remained unharmed.
Those pratyekabuddhas immediately beheld extraordinary and marvelous transformations, and each conceived this thought:

"We shall surely attain the Buddha-way at an early date; we too shall likewise have our bodies adorned with the various marks. We ought to cultivate diligence together with vigor, never allowing ourselves to become lax."
At another time, those people left that mountain forest and went to human villages and settlements, begging from house to house to sustain their lives.

At that time, they might hear the sound of bells, drums, and music, or encounter the sounds of lamentation, weeping, and sighing; their hearts were moved with such compassion as if they were being consumed by fire, and they suddenly awakened as if from sleep, exhausting their outflows and attaining liberation of mind. Therefore, he was named the Pratyekabuddha Asaṅga.
"In this way, the practices of the Bodhisattvas in the nine stages are understood through wisdom that is inexhaustible;
although Pratyekabuddhas possess the merit of radiant marks, they do not equal the merit of even a single pore on a Tathāgata’s body.

Furthermore, even if one were to calculate the merit produced by every single hair pore throughout the limbs and joints of their entire bodies, it would still not equal the merit of the *ūrṇā* mark between the Tathāgata’s eyebrows."
If one were to calculate it again, it would not equal the merit of the Tathāgata’s uṣṇīṣa.

Even if all the sentient beings within the trichiliocosm were to possess profound faith in the Buddha, faith in the Dharma, and faith in the Saṅgha of bhikṣus—were their faith to be multiplied a hundred thousand million times—it would still not equal the merit of a person who upholds the faith and reveres the Dharma, even by a hundred thousand million times.

Furthermore, even if one were to fill the three thousandfold world system with people who uphold faith and honor the Dharma, and were to combine all their merit from wisdom, learning, and generosity, it would still not equal the root of virtue produced by one who has attained the stage of Stream-enterer (srotāpanna).

Furthermore, if one calculates each stage from the path of the stream-enterer up to the stainless state and its wisdom, even multiplied by hundreds, thousands, or tens of millions of times, it would not equal a single portion of the wisdom and merit of a pratyekabuddha.

Even if the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system were filled with pratyekabuddhas, they would still not equal the wisdom and merit of a single bodhisattva who has first resolved their mind [for enlightenment].

Furthermore, even if the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system were filled with such bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds, and their wisdom and learning were a hundred, a thousand, or ten million times greater, it would still not equal the merit produced by a single *avaivartika* (non-retrogressive) bodhisattva.

Furthermore, if one were to take all the *avaivartika* bodhisattvas who fill a great trichiliocosm and multiply their wisdom a hundred thousand million times, it would still not equal even a hundred thousand millionth part of the merit produced by a bodhisattva in his final birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*).
Furthermore, even if the entire trichiliocosm were filled with Bodhisattvas in their last birth before Buddhahood, they would still not equal the power of wisdom and merit of a single Tathāgata.
"So it is, Most Victorious One!

The mind of a Bodhisattva dwelling in the ninth stage is luminous, penetratingly knowing the mentalities of sentient beings throughout the three periods of time. According to their ailments, he provides healing and rescue, such that there are none whom he does not deliver. I myself recall that while in the ninth stage, the number of common folk he liberated and delivered is beyond measure."
From the first generation of the resolve for enlightenment up to the ninth stage, the number of those he has delivered who have attained arhatship is one asaṃkhyeya;
to remove the defilements of the mind so that there is forever not even a trace of obscuration, from the stage of srotāpanna up to anāgāmin, there is another asaṃkhyeya;
he universally practices the four truths, cultivating the perception of the knowledge of cessation, and further exhorts sentient beings to generate [the resolve].
The Bodhisattvas’ intentions and resolves were each firm and established in non-retrogression for one asaṃkhyeya;

at the very end, when they descended from spirit to be about to ascend to birth in Tuṣita Heaven, they vowed to eliminate the nineteen types of unaccomplished thoughts and the afflictions of sensual desire.
With eloquence and valor, they were without fear, and they cleansed away all abodes of the conscious spirit.
Having exhausted all outflows and deceptive dharmas, they cultivate various liberations with an outflow-free mind;
grasping the sharp sword of wisdom, they reap away worldly desires, attain supernormal powers and realization, and reverently follow that practice.
Birth and death have been severed, the holy life has been established, what was to be done has been accomplished, and they know as it truly is: "I shall not undergo further existence."

The Bodhisattva’s practice of the dharma of great compassion (mahākaruṇā) is such that his deportment and ritual decorum are likewise without deficiency. Abiding within firm merit and wisdom, no Māras or externalists can fully fathom the Bodhisattva’s activities. For the sake of sentient beings subject to the outflows of desire, he preaches the untainted (anāsrava) dharma of non-arising and non-ceasing, eliminating all conceptual attachments and becoming free from limitations and obstructions.

“O Most Excellent One, you should know! At that time, I contemplated entering inexhaustible wisdom and observed the dharmas of birth received by past Buddhas; their conduct was impartial and without partiality. Regarding the dharmas of ordinary beings and the path of the noble ones, the dharmas practiced by those in training (*śaikṣa*), those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones—all were entirely equal. Whether mundane or supramundane, numbered or unnumbered, conditioned or unconditioned, outflowing or non-outflowing—among all these dharmas they were entirely equal. Therefore, they are titled ‘Equally and Perfectly Awakened’ (*samyaksaṃbuddha*).”
Regarding the Dharma of equality: one should treat self and others as equal, for they are identical to the natural state (*dharmatā*), wherein neither arising nor ceasing is perceived.
One should reflect that what one has cultivated contains many omissions and lapses, and thus one ought to exercise restraint and broaden the Dharma of equality.

If the mind is distracted and cannot be focused with single-minded diligence, one should be mindful of governing the will so that it does not wander; having realized that both distraction and concentration are ultimately non-existent, all things are universally equal and identical to the natural state.
Furthermore, when one harbors shamelessness and lack of remorse, one should employ skillful means to induce a sense of dread.

Moreover, whenever there are unwholesome dharmas consisting of misconduct of body, speech, or mind, one should further reflect upon them so as to eliminate and extinguish them, ensuring they do not increase.

Furthermore, if the mind conceives thoughts of envy, jealousy, delusion, doubt, or the dharma of leakage, one should again seek skillful means to ensure these are forever eliminated without remainder.
If one again gives rise to thoughts of killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, false speech, or drinking intoxicants, one should further contemplate the source of such calamity and ruin.

Furthermore, if one’s mind is intent on craving and attachment to the noble and honored, lacking a spirit of reverence; if one, when requested by others, begrudges the secret Dharma and teachings; if one treats the prohibitions and precepts with contempt and does not accord with the Vinaya; if one teaches entry into dhyāna and tranquility but does not follow the methods of meditative concentration; and if one never gives rise to thoughts of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, harboring instead a heart of arrogance and pride toward the Dharma Master—should such persons exist, they all obstruct the Noble Path; one must not draw near to them or practice under their guidance.

If one should again give rise to thoughts that produce various forms of conceit—namely, first, arrogance; second, extreme conceit; third, the conceit of being superior to the superior; fourth, self-conceit; fifth, false conceit; sixth, equal conceit; and seventh, the conceit of being equal to the unequaled—one should instead maintain a mind of wisdom so that these never arise. Understanding that nothing exists and that nothing can be produced, one realizes they are all equal and non-dual, without distinction. These are all spontaneous and have no fixed location; this is called the Bodhisattva’s Equal Perfect Enlightenment.

If thoughts arise in the mind that give rise to distracted conceptions—namely, first, wrong view; second, wrong thought; third, wrong speech; fourth, wrong action; fifth, wrong livelihood; sixth, wrong effort; seventh, wrong intention; and eighth, wrong concentration—one must always calm the mind so that it does not suffer depletion.
Furthermore, there may be times when a thought arises crosswise in the mind:

"He whom I have always respected now treats me with contempt; as he does so now, he may well treat me with further insult in the future. He whom I have always loathed you now respect, and before my very eyes you continue to revere him; surely you shall continue to revere him in the future as well."
He further reflected again:
"In the past, they have deceived me; now, appearing before me, they deceive me once more. Who knows whether they will not deceive me again in the future?"

If one sets the mind and forms such a conception, it will destroy the very root of the Noble Path; one will fall into perversity, give rise to the hindrances (*āvaraṇa*), and rely upon the filth of false views and worldly attachment, thereby losing oneself forever and being eternally severed from the human realm.

Furthermore, if at any time the mind conceives of the ten unwholesome and non-virtuous actions—the path of heedlessness—namely: first, killing; second, stealing; third, sexual misconduct; fourth, false speech; fifth, divisive speech; sixth, harsh speech; seventh, frivolous chatter; eighth, anger and resentment; ninth, jealousy; and tenth, wrong views—if such factors of body, speech, and mind arise, one should distance oneself from them all and refrain from creating those conditions; one should eliminate these states so that they do not become obstacles.

Furthermore, one should contemplate: by what cause does evil cease, and by what means does goodness arise? One must realize that both good and evil are entirely non-existent, being empty and not real; they are all equal and without duality.

Although a bodhisattva attains the state of the nine stages of abiding, they should constantly contemplate these various defilements: "The reason I have now realized the Unsurpassed Way and received the prediction of a bodhisattva is entirely due to the ten evil deeds committed out of ignorance; yet, through this, I have attained the fulfillment of the fivefold Dharma-body, proceeding directly to the Single Way without any duality, distinguishing each and every aspect as empty, signless, and wishless."
Furthermore, one should diligently practice the cultivation of the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*). What are these four?

They are the body, feelings, mind, and dharmas. One should thoroughly master the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) and direct the mind toward the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*), the four formless attainments (*catasra ārūpya-samāpattayaḥ*), the eight liberations (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*), and the nine successive meditative concentrations (*navānupūrva-samāpattayaḥ*).
Furthermore, seeking skillful means, one departs from that which is born to enter into the unborn; this is called the equal path of the noble ones (*ārya*).
All things are both finite and infinite; by thoroughly understanding finitude and infinity, one accords with the unborn. All worldly afflictions (*kleśa*) are the "exhaustion" of a bodhisattva;
even if they do not arise again, this so-called "inexhaustibility" is the "exhaustion" of a bodhisattva regarding the bonds and fetters of desire.
That which does not arise is called inexhaustible; anger, stinginess, and greed are the exhaustion of the bodhisattva.
If these do not exist, it is called inexhaustible; the path of delusion and confusion is the exhaustion of the bodhisattva.

If there is no delusion or confusion, it is called inexhaustible; for the mind to possess gates of liberation is the exhaustion of the bodhisattva, while the absence of such gates of liberation is called inexhaustible. For the mind to dwell upon and sever dharmas is the exhaustion of the bodhisattva.
That which is called "inexhaustible" refers to the absence of intentional abandonment; the faculties, powers, factors of enlightenment, and the path—these are the exhaustion of the bodhisattva.
That which is called "inexhaustible" refers to the absence of these [faculties and so forth]; the four fruits of the śramaṇa—these are the exhaustion of the bodhisattva.
That which is called "inexhaustible" refers to the absence of the four fruits; the existence of the path of the pratyekabuddha—this is the exhaustion of the bodhisattva.
To understand that there is no pratyekabuddha is what is called inexhaustible; that there is the bodhisattva path is what is the exhaustion of the bodhisattva.
If there were no such thing, it would be called inexhaustible; that there is equal and perfect awakening is the exhaustion of the bodhisattva.
That there is no equal and perfect awakening is what is called inexhaustible; that one attains the way of buddhahood is the exhaustion of the bodhisattva.
Not perceiving the existence of accomplishment is what is called inexhaustibility; yet to proceed to the bodhi-trees of all Buddhas is the exhaustion of the bodhisattva.
Having no lingering attachment is what is called inexhaustibility; yet to cultivate the primary and secondary marks and to purify the Buddha-lands is the exhaustion of the bodhisattva.
To teach and transform sentient beings and to proclaim the essentials of the Dharma is the exhaustion of the bodhisattva.
To practice the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness is the exhaustion of a bodhisattva;
to have expectations while single-mindedly practicing the roots of virtue is the exhaustion of a bodhisattva;
to create various merits and distribute them throughout the Great Way is the exhaustion of a bodhisattva.
The dwelling place of a bodhisattva is likewise without high or low, nor does he perceive internal, external, or intermediate; this is the exhaustion of the bodhisattva.
He does not perceive the practices cultivated by ordinary beings, nor does he perceive the practices of sages and saints; this is the exhaustion of the bodhisattva.
Although remaining within birth and death, he perceives no defilement or attachment toward defiled phenomena; this is the exhaustion of the bodhisattva.
When a bodhisattva speaks of cessation, they contemplate cessation as non-arising, yet they do not take final nirvāṇa within that cessation; this is the bodhisattva’s exhaustion.
When they thoroughly realize the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) yet do not conform to it, this is the bodhisattva’s exhaustion.
When they do not seek to distance themselves from the realms of Māra, this is the bodhisattva’s exhaustion.
To not consider one's vast wisdom and karma inferior is the exhaustion of a bodhisattva;
to constantly practice the knowledge of acting at the proper time is the exhaustion of a bodhisattva;
to not depart from or distance oneself from all dependent origination is the exhaustion of a bodhisattva.
Not regarding the ultimate truth as non-existent, yet not regarding it as not being truth—this is the bodhisattva’s exhaustion;
not perceiving concentration or distraction within the gates of liberation—this is the bodhisattva’s exhaustion;
though dwelling among people, remaining no different from one in seclusion—this is the bodhisattva’s exhaustion.
To enter into worldly clamor according to custom without maintaining dignified deportment is the exhaustion of a bodhisattva;
if, while in meditative stillness, one does not extinguish body and mind, this is the exhaustion of a bodhisattva;

not seeing that there is giving, yet not seeing that there is no giving—and likewise for morality, patience, diligence, upholding precepts, endurance, single-mindedness, and wisdom—not seeing that there is practice, yet not seeing that there is no practice, is the exhaustion of a bodhisattva.

To personally realize the three knowledges, for the eye of wisdom to arise, and for insight to flourish; to roam through the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) without perceiving the arising or ceasing of afflictions (*kleśa*); to dwell constantly amidst sensual desires without ever becoming weary—this is the exhaustion of the bodhisattva.
To abide in the stage of the stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*) while cultivating the tracks of the path, yet without extinguishing the practice of the Great Way—this is the exhaustion of the bodhisattva.
To see the extinction of the Buddha-dharma without giving rise to fear, and likewise not perceiving the length or brevity of kalpas—this is the exhaustion of the bodhisattva.
Not perceiving the essence of phrases, the essence of syllables, or the essence of flavors—this is the exhaustion of the bodhisattva;
that the roots of lust, anger, and delusion do not constitute the practice of the truths—this is the exhaustion of the bodhisattva;
from the patience of the non-arising of dharmas up to the wisdom of non-birth—this is the exhaustion of the bodhisattva.
The desire realm and the nine abodes of sentient beings devoid of thought—these are the limits of the bodhisattva.

Roaming among human settlements, districts, kingdoms, and cities, as well as the palaces of devas, nāgas, and various divine spirits, he practices there the proper deportment and etiquette, including what is approachable and what is not approachable; these too are the limits of the bodhisattva.
This is called the supreme dharma-gate of the ninth stage bodhisattva regarding the finite and the infinite.

"The practices of Bodhisattvas encompass all that is complete and perfect, containing the essential methods for liberation regarding both the finite and the infinite. Sentient beings habituate themselves to suffering, and Bodhisattvas likewise habituate themselves to it; they then expound for them the nature of the Noble Truth of Suffering. Whether the eye perceives forms as painful or pleasant, they contemplate that the visual consciousness is entirely empty and quiescent, cultivating equanimity to eliminate all afflictions and harms."

The Bodhisattva constantly transforms sentient beings through the True Dharma, remaining tranquil and non-active; this is called the Bodhisattva expounding the wisdom of suffering for the sake of suffering beings. [He teaches that] there is the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, and the suffering of death; the suffering of grief, lamentation, affliction, and despair; the suffering of association with the hated and the suffering of separation from the loved; furthermore, not obtaining what one desires is also suffering. To speak in brief, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering. To realize and know that this suffering neither arises nor ceases—this is called the Bodhisattva’s dharma-gate of the finite and the infinite.

Furthermore, if a bodhisattva sees sentient beings who habitually practice [attachment], he then expounds for them the root of craving and attachment. He explains that this heart of craving is deep-seated and firmly rooted, so difficult to uproot. "I have previously made a vow to ensure its total eradication; as long as it is not extinguished, I shall never realize final enlightenment."

At that time, the Bodhisattva gradually entered the contemplation of observing countenances (*ānanadarśana-dharmavipaśyanā*), manifesting his physical appearance before the assembly. Those who saw him marveled at him, and there was none who did not respectfully follow him. In an instant, he transformed his form into one that was hideous; those who saw him were moved in heart, giving rise to the perception of impermanence (*anityasaṃjñā*). [They realized: "This body is not real and lacks solidity. Our own countenances are far superior to those of the world, yet even these will soon fall into ruin. We ought to cultivate ourselves, eliminate attachment, and no longer dwell in the bonds of affection."
In this way, the bodhisattva brings benefit to sentient beings through his practice.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva perceives that all sentient beings are subject to exhaustion, he teaches the Dharma through skillful means: "That which is born must come to an end; that which is formed must also perish. Even if one’s lifespan were as many as the sands of ten billion *gaṅgā* rivers, it would all be extinguished and could not endure for long. Sons of good family, you should know that the nature of phenomena is impermanent and subject to change; they are like illusions and transformations, devoid of any reality."

The Bodhisattva understands that there is no reality; thus, he should be pure and free from defilement. Although he practices by accumulating [merit], he does not abandon it; yet, through the contemplation of the dharma of total extinction, he perceives nothing existent, nor does he see any place where arising or ceasing occurs.

If the mind gives rise to arrogance and delusion regarding what is permanent or impermanent, one should further analyze it through the wisdom of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).

At times, the Bodhisattva explains the ultimate single path to the sons of noble family, instructing them to contemplate and reflect upon the seven stations of mindfulness (*saptasmṛtyupasthāna*). If one analyzes the arising and ceasing within the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), one sees that sentient beings thereby incur the afflictions of the aggregates. One should reflect individually on how form (*rūpa*) arises: first there is the appearance of form, and I give rise to consciousness (*vijñāna*) with attachment; because of consciousness, sensation (*vedanā*) arises, which is mutually experienced and entered; then volition (*saṃskāra*) arises, followed by perception (*saṃjñā*), which in turn transforms into karmic action (*karma*). Thus, from a single form, these five dharmas are successively established; sensation, perception, volition, and consciousness are likewise so.

Furthermore, if a bodhisattva sees sentient beings before him giving rise to the poison of the eighteen decays of the aggregates (*skandha*), which afflict and obstruct the human mind, causing hindrances so that they fail to reach the further shore; [the bodhisattva] shall gradually protect them through skillful means (*upāya*) and harmonious compliance, necessarily employing expedient devices to ensure their ultimate accomplishment and prevent them from falling.

Furthermore, if a bodhisattva sees these sentient beings, their mind constantly dwells within the mindfulness of the exhaustion of craving; they see neither that which is to be detached from nor that which is detached. This is called being fully endowed with the sevenfold observation of dharmas. They do not falsely abandon the methods of contemplative practice, but examine their slowness or speed and distinguish their warmth or coldness. Having themselves become fully endowed, they further teach others to practice so that they may achieve accomplishment.
“In this way, Most Victorious One!

When a Bodhisattva in the ninth stage practices the dharma of śamatha and vipaśyanā, they are likewise without fear. Neither Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Heavenly Kings, devas, nāgas, śramaṇas, brahmins, nor the sons of Māra can obstruct or block their practice of śamatha and vipaśyanā, nor cause any hindrance to the dharma of perfect enlightenment.”

The reason for this is that the Bodhisattva clearly understands and realizes that all phenomena are entirely equal; regarding both the dharmas of ordinary beings and the path of the noble ones, their mind is like space, without partiality. Whether it be the dharmas of those in training (*śaikṣa*) or those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), or the dharmas of Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, or Buddhas—all are likewise equal.

Furthermore, when one perceives both contaminated and uncontaminated phenomena, and discriminates between mundane and supramundane dharmas, completely eliminating all attachments and burdens, one thereby accomplishes the path of a bodhisattva.
The reason for this is that because they are observed through emptiness, they are called "spontaneous" (*svabhāva*).

That which comes forth spontaneously extinguishes spontaneously; emptiness and reality are equal, signlessness is equal to signlessness, and wishlessness is equal to wishlessness; within the three realms, they are identical to spontaneity.

Furthermore, one should contemplate that non-arising is equal to arising, and that the contemplation of the dharma of non-activity is equal to the contemplation of dharmas; that reliance is equal to non-reliance, and equality is equal to non-equality; that arising is equal to non-arising—all these are spontaneous (*svabhāva*). There is no spontaneity within the three realms, and one does not perceive the realm of desire, the realm of form, or the formless realm.

The Bodhisattva should further contemplate and deliberate that the paths of lust, anger, and delusion, as well as clear wisdom, are all inherently spontaneous (*svabhāva*). The bondage and liberation of craving and desire constitute the Way; entering the realm of *nirvāṇa*, one fully realizes that they are non-dual, equal, and spontaneously natural.

This is called the Bodhisattva practicing great loving-kindness and compassion for the sake of sentient beings; by establishing various and manifold causes and conditions, he guides sentient beings according to their respective roots, explaining the Dharma to each one as appropriate, universally causing them to be harmonious and compliant as they abide in the Mahāyāna, and leading them all to utterly extinguish the root of suffering and affliction.
At that time, the Bodhisattva stood alone among the great assembly, fearless and peerless, without equal or rival; the root of all virtues naturally adorned his body.

If a bodhisattva is among a great assembly of mahāsattvas, they are able to eloquently expound the sublime path of the Buddha. Out of compassion for śrāvakas who have not attained superior wisdom—though they have exhausted their outflows, they do not leave their place of abiding, being liberated only from their own bonds and lacking a vast mind—and further considering that pratyekabuddhas lack the intent for great benefit, [the bodhisattva] possesses holy wisdom and eloquence that are pure and flawless. They can also know the roots and destinies of others, yet [the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas] merely abide in and guard their own impure lands.

Therefore, the Bodhisattva stands out preeminently therein, being able to discern all things and attain the supreme path of the Buddha. He causes the ten directions to tremble and brings salvation to an infinite number of beings. His mind is ever compassionate toward those who have not yet reached the Way; with the power of his valor, he subdues the followers of external paths, constantly turning the Wheel of Dharma so that it never ceases, and causing the sublime and wondrous Great Dharma to flow through the world.

"Thus it is, Most Victorious One! The Bodhisattva in the ninth stage manifests through skillful means and adapts to transform beings, entering everywhere without exception. He understands Nirvana as being like the characteristic of Nirvana: he knows that while there is a True Dharma, it is not a truly existent dharma; its wisdom of emptiness has no master and no place of abiding. Therefore, it is called the unconditioned, spontaneous bliss. It is neither there nor here, having no location whatsoever; it is formless, without counterpart, and invisible. Abiding in non-abiding, this is called 'abiding,' namely abiding in the Dharma-realm. This is called 'exhaustion,' and 'non-arising. This is called Nirvana, quiescent extinction, and the unconditioned."
Only thirty-four subtle fetters remain; all other afflictions are no longer an obstruction.

When a Bodhisattva in the ninth stage attains perfect enlightenment, he extinguishes four [fetters] in the present, four in the future, and four in the past. Having sat beneath the Bodhi tree and subdued Māra, he maintains patience and enters the formless concentration of the mind, surveying the entire trichiliocosm: "I shall now become a Buddha in this world of five turbidities. What I sought has been accomplished; there is no further doubt or difficulty. I should now personally employ skillful means to proclaim the principles of the Way for the sake of sentient beings, exhausting all outflows and fetters, just as I do today, without any difference."
At that time, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the ten directions each praised him from afar in their respective quarters, saying:

"Today, in such-and-such a direction and such-and-such a land, a Buddha has appeared, endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and adorned with the eighty minor characteristics. His light illuminates the darkness, and his voice is like the cry of a sorrowful phoenix. Excellent! The lineage of Buddhas shall not be severed."
"When the Buddhas of the ten directions spoke these words, at that moment the trichiliocosm shook in six ways;
and the devas, nāgas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans and non-humans, as well as Māras and the celestial Māras,"

Each was struck with amazement and found no peace in their own place; they all gathered together like clouds and went to the presence of that Buddha, prostrating themselves in worship and taking refuge.
They attended upon the Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, protecting him with complete purity and without any resentment.
All paid him the highest respect and reached the City of Ambrosia, where the Dharma of the Path is fully endowed with all virtues.

Being untainted, their minds give rise to valor as they traverse various liberations; observing the thoughts appropriate for sentient beings, they manifest accordingly at all times so that each may find their place.

To extinguish defilements and attain eternal quiescence in the unconditioned, they cause all classes of beings to eliminate the notion of self, to abandon distinctions between self and other, and to be free from manifold characteristics, seeing nothing upon which to rely.
The Dharma does not rely on what is non-Dharma; it is neither that there is no reliance, nor that there is no non-reliance.
One realizes that all phenomena are equal, elusive, like space, like echoes, and like magical illusions, devoid of reality.
Such a person attains the crossing to the shore beyond birth and death, no longer wandering back and forth within the cycle of existence.

This is called the meritorious legacy of the bodhisattva dwelling in the ninth stage. He causes the work of the Way to flourish without end; what he cultivates is true and correct, free from doubt. Regarding all outflows (*āsrava*), he remains untainted; amidst all defilements, he does not perceive anything to be grasped. He forever transcends the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm, fully returning to this wisdom of non-arising, which he further expounds extensively so that all may hear and know it.

"Thus it is, Most Victorious One! The practices cultivated by a Bodhisattva in the ninth stage possess a majestic power so sublime that they transcend all in the world. When entering a multitude, he maintains dignified deportment without losing propriety; his every movement and gaze accord with the True Dharma. His clothing and attire are likewise not ostentatious or ornate. Should he wish to enter a kingdom, province, district, or town, his dharma-robe and alms bowl are always carried with a composed and relaxed mind. Whether walking, stopping, coming, going, turning, sitting, lying down, rising, or standing, his mind is always discerning and attentive. His speech is gentle and never coarse or harsh; what he expounds is like space, free from conceptual attachment. He brings his ascetic practices to ultimate completion without creating the conditions for karmic retribution, for all that he ordains is directed solely toward the Buddha-way."
“Thus it is said, Most Victorious One!

A Bodhisattva dwelling in the ninth stage is called one who dwells in the ‘one’ stage, not the ninth; nor do they dwell in the eighth, seventh, sixth, fifth, or even the first stage. As the Bodhisattva advances to cultivate the dharma of the tenth stage—namely, the stage of sincerity, the stage of truth, the stage of fearlessness, and likewise the stage of the Tathāgata, the stage of the path, the stage of concentration, the stage of fearlessness, the stage of contemplation, the stage of wisdom, and the stage of natural nature.”

When a bodhisattva attains this dharma of the tenth stage, they no longer bear the title of "bodhisattva," but shall be named Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, and Bhagavat. They are without equal, fully endowed with the eighteen unique qualities, and their speech is always eloquent and timely. With all practices perfected, they manifest birth in the Tuṣita heaven, pure and without blemish; or they manifest the descent of their spirit to deliver sentient beings. This is called the purification of one's conduct by a bodhisattva in the ninth stage.
*The Scripture on the Severing of Bonds in the Ten Abodes*, Fascicle Three.
*The Scripture on the Severing of Bonds in the Ten Abodes*, Fascicle Four.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Chapter Ten: Attaining Enlightenment.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Most Victorious again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"How does a Bodhisattva in the ten stages purify their conduct within the ten grounds?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Most Victorious (Ajita):

"It is said that a Bodhisattva cultivates the wondrous path to extensively deliver sentient beings; they expound upon written words through the dharma of the emptiness of nature, and advance in the cultivation of prohibitive precepts. Their virtue is immeasurable, inconceivable, and without limit; it cannot be matched by any worldly person, nor can it be equaled or restricted by devas, nāgas, spirits, or divine venerables, who all praise their virtue."
The noble sages remained silent from the beginning and spoke nothing; yet whatever they might expound would all be composed in perfect verses.
They manifested supernatural powers to travel to the lands of the ten directions, where they personally visited, beheld, and paid homage to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
Furthermore, they entered into meditative concentration, liberation, and right reception, pervading Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Beholding all the Perfectly Enlightened Ones and hearing their wondrous and essential teachings, they completely transcend the karma of the heterodox factions;
their resolve is as stable and luminous as Mount Sumeru and remains unshakable, while their mind is like space, free from all conceptualization;
they discern and clearly understand the arising and ceasing of the Dharma-realm, and all the teachings they proclaim accord with the Seal of the Sages.
They roam through various meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) from the very beginning without any deviation;
the verbal teachings spoken by the Buddhas of the ten directions do not contradict the noble Dharma and Vinaya, and the sounds they produce are subtle and sublime;
they contemplate all worlds as being equal to empty space.
Their mental intentions are filled with the gates of liberation;
the Bodhisattvas in their final birth possess eloquence that penetrates the meaning and accords with the capacities of beings, their minds being in perfect resonance with the wisdom of the Path.
What is meant by "mind"?
What is meant by "wisdom of the Way"?
To circulate through worldly scriptures and manifest entry into deviant practices—this is what is meant by "mind."
To concentrate one’s intent single-mindedly on the Dharma for transcending the world is called the wisdom of the Way (*mārga-prajñā*).

To relinquish stinginess through giving so as to be free from the retribution of conceptualization, to harmonize and subdue the mind, and to be discerning and tranquil—this is called the mind (*citta*).
To enter correctly into stillness without giving rise to various conceptions, to maintain oneself in detachment, and not to depart from the sacred scriptures—this is called the wisdom of the Way.
If one diligently cultivates the Dharma while within the cycle of birth and death, remaining free from revulsion even while dwelling therein, this is the mind of a bodhisattva.

Furthermore, if a bodhisattva, while amidst the eight difficulties and places of inaccessibility, does not give rise to inverted views or dualistic perceptions, and is able to fully transcend the maladies of beginning and end, this is called the wisdom of the Path.
To praise the unconditioned path of Nirvana amidst worldly dharmas, such that the merit one creates never goes to waste—this is called the mind.
For a bodhisattva to roam within the emptiness of all dharmas, realizing their purity and non-existence—this is called the wisdom of the Path.
To observe the preceding individuals according to their original intentions and thereby differentiate the dharmas that correspond to them is called "mind-wisdom" (citta-jñāna).

When a Bodhisattva enters meditative concentration and contemplates the wisdom of a single dharma as being identical to the characteristics of hundreds of thousands of dharmas, this is called "path-wisdom" (mārga-jñāna).
To resolutely resolve upon giving away all that one possesses without begrudging anything—neither national wealth, nor wife, nor children—is what is called "mind.
To abide in equanimity where there are no three vehicles, purifying the site of enlightenment so that all return to the Buddha-way, is what is called "wisdom of the path."

This is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva of the tenth stage, whose entry into the mind of the Way is all-pervasive and complete; who guards body and speech so as not to be negligent; who praises the fulfillment of the eight thoughts of a great man; who should contemplate the practice of few desires and contentment; who reverently cultivates the prohibitive precepts without defilement; and who is able to purify sentient beings of their dust and grime.

If he sees sentient beings who constantly disparage themselves while insulting others, who are conceited, arrogant, haughty, and proud, and who harbor unwholesome states such as lust, anger, and ignorance—for those of such a kind, he is able to preach the virtue of patience, causing all these sentient beings to attain, at that very moment, the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (the forbearance that all phenomena are unborn) and to abide therein.

Diligently pitying those who are in distress and have not yet attained the Way, his will is fierce and his vigor is such that his mind never regresses. He discerns the karma of all roots of virtue, seeing neither their accumulation nor their combination, nor does he see them as dispersed into various distinctions. The meritorious karma he initiates has no place of abiding, yet it is not that there is no abiding; it is entirely in accord with reality, yet there is nothing to which it corresponds. He sees neither correspondence nor non-correspondence; this absence of both correspondence and non-correspondence is called thorough discernment.
The mind constantly delights in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and the gates of liberation (*vimokṣa*); contemplating the four nutriments (*āhāra*), it eliminates defiled attachment.
Observing their exhaustion and cessation, it does not give rise to fixed mental states; what it hears it remembers firmly and is able to recite at will.
Its wisdom is undisturbed, discerning the fundamental source as having no location; even if one seeks its origin, it cannot be found. For the sake of the multitude...
They give birth to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and understand the practices of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness;
they are always able to uphold and revere the Buddha-way, attaining the fruits of the path according to various karmic responses.
That which is proclaimed by all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, is likewise without variation; that from which it arises is the True Dharma, extending even unto Nirvana.
It is likewise so; being free from any other thoughts or distracted minds, this is called the supreme skillful means of a Bodhisattva in the tenth stage, which is unobstructed and unrestrained.

By means of the path of non-obstruction, they cultivate equal enlightenment and turn the wheel of Dharma for sentient beings, causing them to reach the stage of steadfastness from which there is no regression.

Bodhisattvas of the tenth dwelling establish firm vows to receive and deliver sentient beings without difficulty; it is like a skilled artisan who carves seals: knowing the names and surnames of people, he engraves them accordingly, recording each according to its kind without error.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is likewise: using the seal of the noble ones (ārya-mudrā) to seal birth and death, he accomplishes according to the capacity [of beings] and never errs.
Furthermore, one should carefully contemplate this meaning: the seal is not the clay, nor is the clay the origin of the seal; yet it is able to manifest names, titles, and surnames.

The noble wisdom of the Bodhisattva is likewise: grasping the seal of the jewel of wisdom, they authenticate sentient beings, manifesting according to their capacities to establish their names and titles, and are thus able to give birth to the teachings of the Three Vehicles.

It is like sowing grain seeds in a fertile field: the stalks, nodes, and sprouts grow and develop in succession until the grain decays and the sprout emerges; though the original substance no longer exists, one should reflect deeply that the sprout is neither the original seed nor is it separate from it.

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is also like this: when causes and conditions converge, he accords with the Dharma and Vinaya. Observing the defilements, the three afflictions, the six hindrances, and the twelve links of dependent origination that arise within sentient beings, as well as their false doubts, views of self, and inverted perceptions, he then expounds for them the teachings of suffering, emptiness, non-self, and impermanence. Only thereafter does he explain the suchness of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), distinguishing the truths of suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, so that they may cast off their heavy burden and eternally attain nirvana.

Furthermore, one should contemplate and investigate the root and the branch, for it is because of their arising that these afflictions exist; all result from ignorance and the absence of the dharma of wisdom, leading to the suffering and distress of old age, sickness, birth, and death.

I shall employ skillful means to dissolve and eliminate this illness, gradually causing them to enter the law and discipline of the noble ones, so as to extinguish ignorance, birth, old age, sickness, and death, leaving nothing remaining.

He preached the dharma of the tranquil contemplation of emptiness, causing all to find a refuge and have something upon which to rely; he expanded their wisdom and clarity until they reached liberation. Together, they all venerated and practiced subtle wisdom, realizing that lust, anger, and delusion are without distinction, and that when their original source is sought, they likewise cannot be differentiated. Thus they attained the extinction of all conceptual thoughts, never harboring resentment or giving rise to a mind of increase or decrease. They became free from all kinds of hindrances, coverings, fetters, and latent tendencies, and were no longer subject to any obstruction.

The mind constantly dwells upon the gates of liberation, extols the meritorious deeds of the Triple Gem, and perpetually reflects upon remaining far removed from the afflictions of greed; such a one is capable of proclaiming their glorious achievements for the sake of sentient beings.

The Bodhisattva applies diligence toward this without doubt, manifesting the wisdom of emptiness to guide others; regarding all dharmas they study, they remain entirely unattached, thereby successively achieving the stage of non-retrogression.

Proclaiming the path of the sutras and purely cultivating the Buddha-seat, they attract sentient beings to enter the realm of the Buddha, enabling them to attain nirvana where there is forever no arising or ceasing.
This is called the essential scripture of the unsurpassed benefactor for bodhisattvas; thus should a bodhisattva practice such contemplation.

"The ten abodes of entry are inconceivable; one cultivates the gate of equality and non-duality, attains the uninterrupted Three Jewels throughout the three periods of time, removes the three impurities, and accomplishes the three gates of liberation."

The Bodhisattva manifests the inconceivable therein; from the first aspiration up to the tenth stage, he constantly extols the prohibitions and precepts practiced by the *kai-shi* (bodhisattvas). The fragrance of his virtue pervades everywhere without exception. In the space of a finger-snap, he fully comprehends the meaning of sounds and achieves perfection in all supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*). He is able to expound upon immeasurable essential teachings of the Dharma. Regarding all written characters, he understands them as being without attachment and free from conceptualization; when seeking their source, he finds no nest or dwelling place whatsoever.

If there are practitioners whose consciousness is bound to form and whose minds do not oppose it, who constantly harbor hopes and remain fettered by attachment without relinquishing them, they wander through birth and death, circling and coming and going; their minds are perpetually deluded and desolate, unable to extricate themselves. Possessing such a web of fetters, they fall into birth and death, transmigrating through the five realms of existence without rest.

The Bodhisattva maintains correct mastery over all disordered thoughts, so as not to be carried away by the five aggregates (*skandha*). He severs the veils of the aggregates and does not allow form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness to undergo arising or ceasing;

he contemplates *ānāpāna*, the mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation. Furthermore, he should discern the four great elements and the derived matter: earth, water, fire, and wind each have their own nature. If he can cause that consciousness not to abide in these five locations, he is then able to accomplish the indestructible Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). His consciousness does not flow toward the twelve objects of affliction: eye and form, ear and sound, nose and fragrance, tongue and flavor, body and touch, mind and phenomena. This is called the consciousness of the untainted faculty of wisdom (*anāsrava-prajñendriya*); it is not the consciousness defiled by birth and death.

If one can eliminate external distractions and does not race toward them, then there will be no longing for any phenomena. Should there be anything upon which one leans, consciousness and perception arise; even having something to hope for is likewise termed consciousness.

The Bodhisattva gives rise to training that is without grasping and enters therein; his mind does not give rise to thoughts of longing or delight. He does not expect retribution for the merit he exerts; conditioned and out-flowing states are the seeds of consciousness, whereas practicing the unconditioned is called non-consciousness.

The Bodhisattva proclaims the lamp of the light of wisdom, erects the torch of the unconditioned to radiate great brilliance, and reveals the supreme, peerless teaching; he seeks straightforwardness rather than literary embellishment.

Abiding in the practices of the Path, his person is naturally such that none can equal him; he is able to manifest all Buddha-lands, therein displaying solitary prowess and fearlessness. Furthermore, regarding all dharmas, he ultimately attains nothing, nor does he discriminate by perceiving them as superior or inferior. His mind is sovereign and free from timidity, teaching and transforming beings according to their voices and sounds.

If, for the sake of sentient beings, one expounds the essential points of the profound Dharma, one abandons all causes and conditions that have arisen, fully comprehending the thoughts in the minds of sentient beings and the inclinations of their natures toward wholesome or unwholesome dharmas.

They are all able to pervade all Buddha-lands; that which the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, cultivate is equanimity. They do not perceive sentient beings or the purity of Buddha-lands; if they were to see any conditioned activity, they would be destroying the Dharma-realm. Therefore, the Bodhisattva’s mind dwells nowhere.

If they were to observe sentient beings abiding in the realm of arising, they would naturally give rise to the defilement of consciousness within the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). When there is neither arising nor ceasing, consciousness has no place to dwell; this is called the pure wisdom of the unconditioned path (*anabhisaṃskāra-mārga-prajñā*).
If there were no Dharma of the equality of the wisdom of the Way, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, would never out of compassion arise in the world.

The bodhisattva’s great vows and practices have no fundamental basis, yet they do not abide in a basis, attaining spontaneity; they do not achieve anything through strenuous effort, nor do they perceive weariness or indolence. Within the contemplation of equality, there is neither arising nor ceasing; with courageous diligence, they receive the prediction of bodhisattvahood, being able to discern the beginning and end of all scriptures, extracting essential wisdom to eliminate worldly afflictions, and observing both birth-and-death and nirvana as not being different.

He constantly cherishes the profound meaning of the sutras within his breast; he explores both the distant and the near in silent stillness, leaving no trace. Although he delivers sentient beings, he harbors no conceptualization or consciousness; he associates with virtuous friends with a mind free from attachment, reckoning neither self nor life-span. He discerns and contemplates emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness as being neither arising nor ceasing.

If one contemplates the foulness, stench, and impurity of desire within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), one realizes that even the places where forms are received in the realms of form (*rūpadhātu*) and formlessness (*ārūpyadhātu*) are impure.
Because they wish to transform and enlighten those who are deluded, they expound this meaning of the True Dharma (*satya*):

they discern that all is empty and non-existent, with no fixed location; they see nothing created with substantial form, neither action nor non-action, and perceive no basis for reliance. They abide in non-abiding and possess no root; furthermore, they do not perceive the undergoing of the three evil destinies, nor do they perceive birth in heaven or the spontaneous enjoyment of natural rewards. They reveal the path so that beings may enter the meaning of the Way, remaining without expectation and without any practice whatsoever.
Regarding all phenomena, one observes that they are spontaneously self-arisen; the characteristics of all phenomena cannot be fully exhausted, being like empty space without limit or boundary.

A Bodhisattva of the tenth stage teaches others to practice giving without giving rise to conceptual obstructions, and to maintain precepts, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and to proclaim wisdom along with skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*). Through kindness, compassion, joy, and equanimity, they rescue and gather in the impoverished, establishing them in the Great Way.

"Although Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes have not yet ascended the Tathāgata’s true throne, they are already able to exhaustively fathom the source of the ocean of wisdom; they adorn the lands and cultivate pure realms, radiate great light to reach all sentient beings, instruct them with the True Dharma so that they all return to the Way, establish the karmic deeds of wisdom, and attain the Mahāyāna."

The Buddhas of the ten directions will constantly protect them, always using their majestic spiritual power to assist and promote their virtue, until they attain Buddhahood and achieve all-encompassing wisdom as the unsurpassed path, never allowing the hosts of Māra to find an opportunity to harm them.

When a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage, through self-awakening, realizes that his merits are fully perfected and desires to achieve Buddhahood by sitting beneath the King of Trees, he must first practice and cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*). He discerns that body and mind each have their own distinct nature; he then observes for himself the arising and ceasing, the flourishing and decline of the body. His heart rejoices at being forever freed from suffering and affliction. By contemplating the causal conditions of the body, he achieves the concentration of diligence (*vīrya-samādhi*); he reflects upon this body as a correspondence of karmic retribution, seeing that it is formed through the combination of causes and conditions and perishes when they disperse. Knowing that the body has no master and is not to be craved, why would one give rise to thoughts of attachment toward this physical form?
Do not be deluded by the five aggregates, the four great elements, or the various sense bases. This body is empty; do not perceive the four elements as having the nature of a self.
Having accumulated practices over many kalpas, you have only now attained this realization. Why then do you cling to this body, which is without solidity and is a fragile, brittle thing?

I shall now receive both the Tathāgata’s form-body (*rūpakāya*) and his Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). As for the form-body, it is a mass of merit, indestructible like a diamond; even if the worlds of the ten directions were filled with mundane, outflow-tainted bodies as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they would not equal the virtue of a single hair-pore of the Tathāgata’s form-body.
