The Bodhisattva reflects to himself: "By means of immeasurable virtues, I have accomplished this physical body; now, through this form, I shall receive the body of the Tathāgata’s Buddha-dharma. Although I may traverse birth and death, coming and going through the five realms of existence and undergoing immeasurable, incalculable suffering, now that I have received the substance of the Tathāgata’s physical body, I do not dwell upon my former afflictions and distresses. From this day forth, I am forever separated from all worldly defilements and no longer crave or cling to the midst of the five desires. Having observed my own body, I observe the bodies of others and find them to be entirely without fixed location. Thus I cultivate pure conduct free from blemish or impurity. This is called the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the method of mindfulness directed toward the body.
"How should a bodhisattva further contemplate the dharma of the stationing of mindfulness on sensation (*vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna*)?

In this regard, from the first generation of the thought of enlightenment until the attainment of Buddhahood, the sufferings experienced by the bodhisattva in the interim are immeasurable; yet, with single-minded resolve and aspiration for the Buddha-way, they do not allow such suffering to occupy their minds.

If they see those who suffer or those heading toward evil destinies, they are able to rescue and deliver them so that they no longer undergo suffering. They constantly reflect that sentient beings are unable to awaken on their own, and thus never follow their desires or become attached to them."

The sensations I have experienced since the past are neither real nor existent, and are entirely unarisen; if one encounters a sensation that is neither painful nor pleasant, this is termed "indeterminate" (avyākṛta) and cannot be designated by words.

O Lady, one who habitually dwells in and clings to the sensation of pleasure immediately distances themselves from the seat of the Tathāgata and fails to accord with the noble and holy precepts of the Tathāgata. From this day forward, let such sensations be forever stilled so that they no longer arise, and cause all sentient beings to contemplate that sensation has no master.

If those sentient beings give rise to sensations regarding forms—whether beautiful or ugly, pleasant or unpleasant, or the derivative forms composed of the four great elements of earth, water, fire, and wind—they thoroughly understand them to be empty, quiescent, and non-existent.

There are sentient beings for whom suffering comes first and pleasure later, and there are those for whom pleasure comes first and suffering later; one should preach the profound sutras so that they may protect themselves from these sensations.

Regarding the phenomena of forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects associated with the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—these arise from causes and conditions and cease through causes and conditions. When one contemplates suffering and pleasure, both are found to be ultimately neither suffering nor pleasure.

Furthermore, one should discern internal and external sensations (*vedanā*): there may be pleasant sensations arising in the present life, or those that have already passed, or those yet to arise in future lives;
there may be pleasant sensations born from the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*), which further increase conscious attachment and cannot be relinquished;
or there may be pleasant sensations born from delusion and craving, which are extinguished only through correct contemplation and insight.

There may be pleasant sensations that grow ever more intense due to wrong views and doubt; these should be eliminated so they do not arise by means of the profound wisdom regarding the four marks of impermanence.
There may be pleasant sensations arising from the four types of feeling; these should be eliminated through the attainment of the meditative absorption of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).

There may be pleasant sensations arising from the five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*); one should then contemplate the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) so that they are forever left without remainder.
There may be pleasant sensations arising from the six bases of consciousness, which one should discern as empty, signless, and wishless;
there may be pleasant sensations arising from the seven types of consciousness, for which one should establish diligence and refrain from creating their conditions;
there may be pleasant sensations arising from the eight worldly dharmas, for which one should always humble the mind and not be conceited.
There may be pleasant sensations arising from the nine afflictions; one should exert oneself to forever leave these nine states behind.
There may be pleasant sensations arising from the ten calamities; one should eliminate longing and craving, and not think of illicit wealth.
There may be pleasant sensations arising from the seven floods and four yokes; one should then contemplate the great brilliance of wisdom.

There may be pleasant sensations arising from the nine abodes of sentient beings and the three contemplations, whereby one immediately fixes the mind and enters the samādhi of emptiness and stillness.

There may be pleasant sensations that do not have the past or present as their cause but depend on future craving; nor do they have the future or present as their cause but depend on past craving; nor do they have the past or future as their cause but depend on present craving; or those that do not have the past as their cause but depend on future and present craving; or those that do not have the future as their cause but depend on past and present craving; or those that do not have the present as their cause but depend on future and past craving. Regarding these, the Bodhisattva contemplates the dharma of the seven bases and the three contemplations to extinguish these thirteen poisons of intense affliction.

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva further contemplates the arising of pleasant sensations (*sukha-vedanā*). There may be pleasant sensations that arise through the mutual engagement of the eight wrong views and the six groups of consciousness; these subsequently increase the seeds of the aggregates (*skandha*), the sense-fields (*āyatana*), and the elements (*dhātu*). This is what is meant by the Bodhisattva, through the contemplation of liberation, discerning these sensations so that they are forever rendered without remainder.

Alternatively, there may be pleasant sensations that share causal conditions with the ten unwholesome, defiled, and base dharmas. These are severed by the karma of wisdom (*prajñā-karma*) and the net of five doubts. They are extinguished in the present moment even as they arise in the present life; they are extinguished in the present moment even as they would arise in the future; and they are extinguished in the present moment even as they arose in the past. This is what is meant by the Bodhisattva, through the contemplation of liberation, being able to eliminate the fifteen nets of doubt.

"How does a bodhisattva further constantly contemplate the dharma of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*)? In this regard, the bodhisattva maintains his intent and restrains a distracted mind so that it does not wander;

whatever he performs necessarily has an object of focus (*ālambana*). He observes his own mind and observes the minds of others; his mind is perfectly equanimous, harboring neither increase nor decrease. In whatever direction he goes, whether walking, entering or exiting, or moving about, he is composed and serene. He always remains single-mindedly diligent in guarding his mind. Regarding sentient beings with conditions and those without conditions, there is the arising and ceasing of those without conditions, and the arising and ceasing of those with conditions. As for the arising of one's own conditions, one causes them to cease through one's own conditions; as for the arising and ceasing due to the conditions of others, they cease because of the conditions of others.

Furthermore, the arising and ceasing of conditions is neither within nor without, nor does it abide in between the two; yet from within this [state], there arises the arising and ceasing of conditions and the non-arising and non-ceasing of conditions."

Whether it be due to greed, lust, anger, or delusion; the seven latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), the seven types of pride (*māna*), the seven stations of consciousness (*vijñānasthiti*), the seven liberations (*vimokṣa*), the seven contemplations (*vipaśyanā*), or the karmic activities of the seven patiences (*kṣānti*); if through these conditions there is the arising and ceasing of that which is dependently originated, or the arising and ceasing of that which is not dependently originated—all of these arise from the mind and are produced by the mind. These forty-five dharmas of blinding darkness are created by the mental consciousness, yet one does not self-awaken to them. If the mind does not know the mind, who is the root of the mind? Since there is no fundamental basis, how can there be a mind?

The Bodhisattva discriminates the dharmas of mind, thought, and consciousness, penetrating their coming and going without any fixed location; this is called the Bodhisattva’s contemplation of liberation, through which he knows that the root of mental conditions is unobtainable.
Furthermore, one does not perceive the mind as conjoining with good or evil; being without conjunction or non-conjunction, one should contemplate liberation.
Again, one reflects upon the twelve links of dependent origination, which are exceedingly profound and far-reaching, impossible to exhaustively fathom;
the fruits that are sown do not fail to yield their retribution, and within all dharma-realms, the mind remains unstained by attachment. Even when contemplating the dharma-realm...
Arising from causes and conditions, one thoroughly understands that all phenomena lack any ultimate truth; naturally quiescent and pure, one sustains and guards oneself.
That which is produced by the mind has no form or substance and cannot be seen; even when seeking its characteristics, it possesses no color or image.
Through the penetration of noble wisdom, one enters the state where things do not arise and nothing is produced. Not...
Abiding in the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, one constantly maintains one's own intent while traversing the various Buddha-dharmas;
inwardly reflecting with immeasurable joy, one thinks: "I have now attained mastery over the mind, having abandoned attachment to birth and death and entered the ocean of wisdom;
this is because my mind has attained the unsurpassed, right, and true path, achieving supreme perfect enlightenment."

This is called the Bodhisattva attaining mastery over the dharma of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). How does the Bodhisattva analytically contemplate the dharma of the foundations of mindfulness?

In this regard, the Bodhisattva practices the dharma of tranquility (*śamatha*) from the very beginning without ever forgetting it, never abandoning it until the attainment of the Buddha-way. Internally he contemplates his own dharmas, and externally he contemplates the dharmas of others. The Bodhisattva thoroughly knows that the characteristics of all dharmas are one and not two, nor are they manifold; they all converge in emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. He remains far removed from false views and regards all dharmas as equal. He analytically discerns the root of the twelve links of dependent origination, constantly mindful of the arising and ceasing, the flourishing and decline within the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), whether they be with outflows or without outflows, conditioned or unconditioned, wholesome or unwholesome, determinate or indeterminate.

At that time, the Bodhisattva contemplated and observed, not giving rise to perceptions of consciousness in accordance with the dharma-realm; he did not perceive non-dharmas as having a self, nor did he give rise to thoughts calculating the lifespan of persons.

There may be bodhisattvas who give rise to the notion of a dharma and become habitually attached to a self; they nurture their own lives while contemplating annihilation, perceiving the impermanent as permanent, and believing that all categories of things in the world are eternally constant, reckoning within the midst of impermanence that there is no joining or dispersing.

Or one may give rise to inverted conceptions regarding phenomena: that what is non-existent is eternal and what exists is impermanent; that non-existence does not arise from existence and existence does not arise from non-existence; that non-existence arises spontaneously and perishes spontaneously, and existence arises spontaneously and perishes spontaneously; or that non-existence cannot see that "I" am spontaneously existent, and existence cannot see that "I" am spontaneously non-existent.

The Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes possess clear wisdom and penetrating insight that distinguishes existence from non-existence. They sever the notions of annihilationism and eternalism, as well as those of self, person, and life-span. All is equal, empty, and non-existent; they observe with the most wondrous and supreme emptiness. This primary nature of emptiness does not give rise to existence; existence is eternally existent, yet one does not know the non-existence of non-existence.

Non-existence is eternally non-existent, yet one does not know the existence of existence. The Bodhisattva contemplates and discriminates through wisdom that the nature of existence is itself empty and non-existence is also itself empty. Non-existence does not create existence, nor does existence create non-existence. To cling to existence and non-existence is the dharma of birth and death; it is not the essential path to the supreme Nirvana.

Non-existence is empty of non-existence; one does not know non-existence as being empty of the self-nature of non-existence. Existence is empty of existence; one does not know existence as being empty of the self-nature of existence. Existence is non-existence, and non-existence is existence. This is called the Bodhisattva’s thorough discernment of the nature of all phenomena, one by one.

Contemplating and deliberating upon what is permanent and impermanent, arising and ceasing, attachment and severance, the conditioned and the unconditioned, the tainted and the untainted, wholesome dharmas and unwholesome dharmas, the determinate and the indeterminate—seeing that all dharmas, whether they possess names or lack names, are entirely empty and quiescent, without arising or ceasing—one observes one's own dharmas and the dharmas of others. Regarding all conceptualizations and attachments, one remains free from such thoughts. One understands the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. Within the dharma-realm, one seeks the Buddha-dharmas and the prohibitive precepts, yet finds them to have no location and no path. One does not see anyone who delivers others to liberation, nor does one see anyone submerged in birth and death; therein, one guides all sentient beings and is able to give rise to immeasurable great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), healing all afflictions and resolving all fetters.

Emptiness is non-existent; one distinguishes the five destinies and trains them in equanimity. Though dwelling amidst worldly desires, one harbors no timidity or weakness; having realized that the three poisons leave nothing to obstruct, one who attains this state is called a Mahāsattva. Abiding in the path of inconceivable expedient manifestations, suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path all universally return to spontaneity (*svabhāva*).

Within the natural state (*dharmatā*), one perceives neither arising nor ceasing; the mind is exhausted like space, being without anything whatsoever, and one does not dwell upon a place of abiding. One investigates the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) and the realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*); the dwelling places of sentient beings are entirely without any fixed location. All phenomena are equal to the realm of space; this is called the Bodhisattva guiding others at the appropriate time in accordance with the Dharma. Although they deliver sentient beings, they do not perceive any who are delivered.

If there is a bodhisattva who contemplates the dharmas of their own body and contemplates the dharmas of others, being able to restrain the mind and dwell within wisdom, understanding that all dharmas ultimately return to liberation, they are then able to guide all sentient beings, manifesting the unsurpassed, true, and correct path, enabling them to attain the unconditioned and spontaneous dharma. They do not perceive what is born, nor do they perceive what is unborn; though dwelling amidst what is born, they contemplate what is born, yet they do not abandon the dharma of non-arising and the absence of birth or cessation. This is called a bodhisattva attaining mastery through the application of mindfulness to dharmas.

The Buddha again addressed Varaprabha: "A Bodhisattva of the tenth stage should further contemplate the four right efforts (*catvāri samyakprahāṇāni*). He should constantly and discerningly attend to what is present before him: he shall prevent unarisen evil dharmas from arising; he shall employ skillful means to eliminate evil dharmas already arisen; he shall seek to bring about the arising of unarisen wholesome dharmas; and he shall cause wholesome dharmas already arisen to increase further. He should always cultivate diligent practice and exertion, restraining his own mind so that it does not wander. Regarding the merits accumulated since ancient times, he shall not lose the laws of dignified demeanor and ritual propriety; his conduct shall be impartial, and he shall be able to restrain his thoughts and contemplate the true reality."
Among calamities, the most grave are the three unwholesome roots, which cause one to fall into the evil destinies and transmigrate through the five realms of existence without rest;

therefore, the Bodhisattva diligently cultivates vigor, whereby he is able to extinguish the evil unwholesome roots so that they no longer arise again to incite distracted thoughts. He constantly observes for himself the retribution of unwholesome deeds, realizing that these are defiled practices and not the True Path. "I have now abandoned unlawful conduct and practice the Ultimate Truth, exhausting all afflictions and forever eliminating anger."

Discerning the root of the twelve links of dependent origination, he establishes merit through the yet-unarisen wholesome dharmas, causing their sprouts to grow so they do not wither or decay. His mind is pure and free from blemish; he does not rely upon the three realms nor cling to various obstructions. Detached from all attachments, he is forever without clinging, and is always able to lead others toward omniscience. Regarding profound wisdom, he never suffers diminution. Thus, that he attains the foundation of merit and achieves the fruit of the Path through diligent effort is called the Bodhisattva’s attainment of mastery over the four right efforts (*catur-samyak-prahāṇa*).

"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva should then contemplate and discern the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*). Although the Bodhisattva has attained the concentration of the bases of psychic power, when approaching the fulfillment of the Way in the tenth stage (*daśamī bhūmi*), he must necessarily practice meditative concentration."

Just as he had first trained, he focused his mind to enter meditative concentration (*samādhi*), contemplating the four immeasurables (*catvāry apramāṇāni*) with compassion for sentient beings. He addressed himself by name and called upon his own mind; he then entered the first dhyāna and subsequently the second dhyāna. Returning to collect his mind, he arose from the first dhyāna and entered the third dhyāna, wherein he contemplated with single-minded diligence. Arising from the third dhyāna, he re-entered the first dhyāna, manifesting transformations within that dhyāna and displaying supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*). Arising from the first dhyāna, he entered the fourth dhyāna.

At that time, while within the four dhyānas, the Bodhisattva tested his supernormal powers by lifting his body with his mind and lifting his mind with his body. Initially like a mustard seed, it grew to the size of a hemp seed or a bean; gradually increasing in height and breadth until it was as large as a walnut. Thus he applied himself diligently for twenty-one days, until his body and mind were light and agile, free from all obstruction.

Therefore, the Bodhisattva again entered meditative concentration to test his supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*); by means of these supernormal powers, he was able to transform one hundred million people, establishing them in non-retrogression and bringing them to the concentration of supernormal powers.

At that time, the Bodhisattva further manifested and extensively displayed his supernormal powers (ṛddhi) without limit; from Jambudvīpa he ascended to the first, second, third, and even up to the sixth heavens. When the various devas saw this, each gave rise to this thought:

"Now this Bodhisattva has personally manifested his supernormal powers, and the radiance he emits shines everywhere without exception. We devas shall each exhort one another to protect the Bodhisattva so that he may attain the Way of Buddhahood."

Some may offer celestial flowers, various incenses, heavenly robes and garments, and natural nectar as offerings. Among them, he transforms and enlightens the devas and humans; they will surely resolve upon spiritual powers (*ṛddhipāda*) and attain long-lasting benefit.

The bodhisattvas of the past, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who cultivated the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and purified their conduct, all tested their spiritual powers in this place. With single-minded observation, they sought skillful means (*upāya*) to manifest various transformations; through the power of diligence, they immediately accomplished the Way. Their actions were sovereign and could not be thwarted; those they intended to transform would submit upon his arrival. He brought their fundamental capacities to ultimate fulfillment, causing them to obtain the fruits of retribution, such that neither Māra nor the devas of Māra could shake them.

At that time, the Bodhisattva, using his divine eye, observed the three-thousandfold world system: those with lust, anger, and ignorance, and those without lust, anger, and ignorance; those with pure conduct, and those without pure conduct; those with concentrated minds, and those without concentrated minds; those with distracted minds, and those without distracted minds. The Bodhisattva knew them all and distinguished the various dispositions of their faculties.
Furthermore, with the divine ear, they hear the voices of sentient beings and are able to follow their respective capacities to understand their sounds and thereby transform them through teaching.

By means of the power of the divine feet, they enter the samādhi of meditative concentration, perceiving the inclinations and dispositions of all people and beholding for themselves the original source from which they have come; this is the bodhisattva’s practice of the divine feet.

"Thereupon, the Bodhisattva further contemplates and discriminates the faculties (*indriya*), powers (*bala*), the factors of the seven limbs of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga-dharma*), and the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*); namely, the faculties of faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom. With his profound and penetrating knowledge, the Bodhisattva constantly observes whether sentient beings have achieved the faculties, powers, the path of enlightenment, and various supernormal knowledges and wisdoms."

At that time, the Bodhisattva, using the wisdom of the knowledge of others' minds, observed the sentient beings before him. Some were fully endowed with the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) and constantly practiced the impartial Dharma of the Eightfold Path; their minds harbored right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) and did not dwell within the realm of Māra. They believed and knew that the suffering of birth and death is immeasurable, and they further knew that Nirvāṇa is blissful and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). They believed in the Three Honored Ones as the great illumination of the world, and did not believe in the ninety-six heterodox paths. They harbored no doubt regarding the various supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) and wisdoms, accumulating merit and virtue to kindle the True Dharma, establishing straightforward faith therein without difficulty.

Furthermore, by means of the profound, unimpeded wisdom of universal penetration, he observes those sentient beings who, day and night, exert themselves with diligence to cultivate the faculty of vigor; whether sitting, lying down, or walking, their minds are free from indolence. Because they have attained vigor, they are endowed with all the faculties, just as a celestial robe extends equally in all four directions, being perfectly uniform above and below without any discrepancy.
Suppose, at that time, someone were to come from one direction, grasp a corner of a garment and lift it up to move it; the other three corners would all follow along.

It is the same with the faculty of diligence (*vīryendriya*): if there is one who cultivates the faculty of diligence, you should know that they are fully endowed with all dharmas. Because there is diligence, the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*) is accomplished;
when the mind is not distracted, it is called the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*).
Constantly employing skillful means to gather the mind and maintain one-pointedness, discerning good and evil with a mind as vast as space—this is called the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*).

When a Bodhisattva of the tenth stage enters the Samādhi of Profound Penetration, they foreknow the signs of sentient beings’ conception in the womb, distinguishing male and female, the male organ and the female organ, and whether it be one birth, ten births, a hundred births, a thousand births, or even up to incalculable births—they are able to understand them all without limit. This is called the Bodhisattva’s fulfillment of the gateway to the Way.
Contemplating the wisdom that abides in all stages, one should be capable of responding to difficult challenges and bring forth a stirring influence throughout the lands of the ten directions;
furthermore, one should roam through the buddha-fields manifesting radiance, so that all who behold this light may attain liberation;
moreover, one should establish the laws and precepts within all lands, causing everyone everywhere to reverently follow the scriptures of the sages and saints.

Furthermore, one should bring benefit and peace to the lands and their inhabitants, guiding them toward the flavor of the Dharma so that they never tire of hearing it; one should always clearly understand the lineages and accomplishments of the people in the lands, as well as their non-separable kinships.
One should also observe and know the mentalities of sentient beings and then expound for them the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā).

Moreover, one should restrain the distracted thoughts of sentient beings and gradually lead all beings forward, acting as a guide to draw them into the wisdom of wholesome dharmas. One should constantly maintain mindfulness and enter meditative concentration without losing the supernormal powers (ṛddhi-pāda), cultivating one's own spiritual penetrations to discern the three periods of time and know the past, future, and present.
Furthermore, one should contemplate and study the Buddha’s profound treasury of boundless wisdom;

one should also train to be endowed with all Buddha-dharmas, study to understand all phenomena without attachment, study to expound the bottomless [truth] and open the treasury of the seven jewels, and study to perfect a buddha-field through divine intelligence. One should study the light that universally illumines the ten directions, attain the meditative concentration of a Buddha to move and transform lands, study skillful means to convert non-Buddhists, and study the precepts to achieve the fruits of the Way. One should study to convene assemblies and turn the wheel of Dharma, such that what one learns personally becomes all-encompassing wisdom; having perfected what is learned, there is nothing further to learn.

The Buddha told Ajita: "This is called the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the ten stages of practice (*daśabhūmi*). Advancing toward the attainment of Buddhahood, he purifies his buddha-field; he descends in spirit to Tuṣita Heaven to exercise skillful transformations among devas and humans, manifesting extraordinary and most excellent dharmas. He observes the lineage and the country into which he shall be born, descending from Tuṣita Heaven to the world thirty-six times, circulating and coming and going to transform devas and humans. Within those realms, he delivers and liberates countless sentient beings; through skillful means (*upāya*), he walks alone throughout the triple world without fear. Finally, he descends and practices austerities for six years, concentrating his mind until his body is emaciated, no different from a withered tree."

Although I manifest here in these ascetic practices, I am actually in the Buddha-field named Nameless; there I teach and transform eighty-four billion nayutas of devas and humans, causing them all to establish themselves on the stage of non-retrogression.

When the sentient beings of this land see my form, they think that my life has passed away and that the life-faculty is no longer present; yet as I pass through the world, these beings pile up wood to burn me, unable to set me ablaze. Through skillful means and single-minded application, I advance toward noble wisdom; I do not abandon the various inclinations and longings of sentient beings, removing what is unnecessary and showing compassion for those who have not yet reached it. For this reason, the Bodhisattva manifests ascetic practices.

When Bodhisattvas of the Ten Abodes transform and guide sentient beings within the Ten Grounds, they do not distinguish between birth and death; the people they deliver are equal to those who have attained Buddhahood. If a Bodhisattva desires to swiftly accomplish the Unsurpassed Way, in the time it takes to snap one's fingers, their body becomes the color of gold, and they become fully endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique and sublime dharmas.

When the retinue of a bodhisattva is established in a single day, he does not seek whether their lineage or status is superior or inferior; rather, he perceives that sentient beings harbor arrogance, disparage others while exalting themselves, and do not relinquish their conceit.
For this reason, the Bodhisattva manifests birth from a womb as a skillful means to conform to the world, bringing great benefit wherever he goes.

When a Bodhisattva of the Ten Abodes no longer bears the title of "Bodhisattva," he is then designated by these names: Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-sampanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām; he is called Buddha, the World-Honored One. He is surrounded by immeasurable assemblies of merit, protected by all Buddhas, and guarded by the devas. The essential principles of the Dharma he preaches have their causal origins; he adapts to the times and circumstances, never speaking in vain.

"O Most Victorious One, you should know! As for why it is called the Buddha-land Without Designation: seventy-seven hundred million Ganges-sands of Buddha-lands to the southeast of here, there is a world named Benevolent and Virtuous (Renxian). The Buddha there is named Good Eye (Shanyan). In that land, there is no path of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas; rather, they instruct one another through the nameless and the dharma of non-arising and non-ceasing. They understand liberation as emptiness and do not conceptualize liberation. Upon hearing of emptiness, they immediately comprehend it with ease and proficiency. Furthermore, they are free from the diseases of the three poisons—lust, anger, and delusion—and their power of dhāraṇī and retentive memory is inexhaustible."
In that land I perform the Buddha-work, yet the sentient beings there do not know that my body is their dwelling place.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s vast benefit; this is called the most excellent tenth-stage Bodhisattva purifying his practice within the ten stages.
Chapter Eleven: The Chapter on the Extinction of the Mind. At that time, the Bodhisattva Most Victorious (Varabodhisattva) came before the Buddha and addressed him, saying:
"How does a bodhisattva contemplate the meaning of impermanence, discern emptiness through the ultimate truth, and understand that his own body, both internally and externally, has no master?"
"Furthermore, how does one achieve the perfection of mastery over the mind?
At that time, the World-Honored One told Most Victorious: "The mind with which a bodhisattva dwells is free from attachment;

in expounding and discussing all dharmas, there is no obstruction. They penetrate and know the faculties of others as being like dreams and illusions. They fully comprehend the minds of all sentient beings—their thoughts of good and evil, the coming and going of causes, conditions, and retributions, whether pure or impure, suffering or pleasure, beautiful or ugly, favorable or adverse, bound or liberated, concentrated or distracted, and their various habitual tendencies. All of these they are able to know."

First, they clearly understand that things are empty and not substantial; then, through the path of supernormal knowledge of past lives, they teach the Dharma as appropriate to lead others to know emptiness and stillness. Their spiritual powers are unhindered, such that there is nothing they do not behold; this is called the Bodhisattva’s contemplative penetration of fundamental non-being.
Sometimes they manifest in the body of a Buddha and enter parinirvāṇa, yet through skillful means they manifest so as not to enter final extinction.
They fully know that the beginning and end of sentient beings are fundamentally pure;

or they manifest being separated and scattered to different places in order to preach the Dharma, knowing that [the body] is a foul-smelling place of impurity and excrement, so as to cause those who reckon things as permanent to eliminate their attachment;
furthermore, they praise the exhaustion of outflows and the gate of Nirvana, yet even if the outflows are not exhausted, they do not accept realization.

Furthermore, for the sake of sentient beings, he praises the untainted (*anāsrava*) state, so that all sprouts of life may attain inexhaustible wisdom. He practices great compassion and governs the *dhyāna-samādhis*, dwelling and abiding in the first through fourth dhyānas up to the four formless concentrations (*ārūpya-samāpatti*). Having attained the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, he cultivates the virtues of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*). Through skillful means and expedient methods, there are none whom he does not transform and guide. Observing those sentient beings within the eight difficult conditions (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*), he removes their defilements and toil so that they are forever free from stain.

Furthermore, by means of the unimpeded path of the worthy and noble ones (*ārya*), he enters into birth and death to lead them to *nirvāṇa*. Moreover, with the dharmas of skillful wisdom and great insight, he simultaneously transforms those of the *pratyekabuddha* and *śrāvaka* vehicles;

following and encouraging them, he causes them to reach the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*). If they are amidst the clamor and afflictions of the world, he teaches people to practice stillness and not give rise to manifold thoughts.

If there are sentient beings who conceive attachments to various things—whether they be finite or infinite, or manifest as non-existent—and yet cause others to attain non-attachment, so that even while dwelling within the sphere of sensory objects and moving to and fro, they do not give rise to conceptual attachment and remain free from all hindrances.

He constantly preaches the subtle and wondrous Dharma to sentient beings; he fully understands and is unimpeded regarding all phenomena—whether with outflows or without outflows, conditioned or unconditioned, wholesome or unwholesome.

Furthermore, by means of the foundation of unimpeded, outflow-free wisdom, he clearly comprehends the fundamental nature of the mental activities and behaviors of sentient beings. Adapting to their various forms and appearances, he establishes them in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); following conventional teachings, he causes them to understand and clarify the Dharma. He does not allow the mind, intellect, consciousness, or perceptions to arise or cease. Through skillful wisdom, he transforms others appropriately and always attains mastery; this is called the supreme Bodhisattva practice of contemplation.

One understands that the body is fundamentally without a master within or without; by constantly practicing with mindfulness and maintaining an insatiable resolve, one attains eternal peace for oneself.

Furthermore, one causes all sentient beings to receive its blessings and protection, practicing great compassion without harboring any cowardice or weakness; only then does one reach the understanding that the body has no master, and this applies equally to internal and external phenomena.

He regards all sentient beings as his own flesh and bone; when they have needs or seek anything, he places them before himself. His great compassion is steadfast and firm, and that which he brings to salvation is never in vain. He causes all to establish extraordinary virtues, while his mind remains tranquil and pure, unmoving and unswerving, observing that the body is fundamentally devoid of anything worth craving.

Furthermore, for the sake of sentient beings, he speaks of impurity: this body is like a city that never truly waxes or wanes; the body is like a ditch or a gully that overflows from time to time; the body is like a blazing fire that never tires of devouring fuel; it is also like rivers and lakes that never reach satiety even when pouring into the sea.
"Thus it is, Most Victorious One!

A bodhisattva instructs others by discerning and contemplating impurity, causing those before him to likewise give rise to the perception of impurity. Their eloquence is profound and without obstruction; they attain *dhāraṇī* and never forget; the words they teach do not lose their proper sequence; they constantly attain the samādhi of precise and correct reception; they perpetually enter the tranquility of the various *pāramitās*; and they subdue demonic enemies and eliminate deviant, distracted thoughts."

"O Most Victorious One! The Bodhisattva contemplates the body, realizing that there is no location for it, either internally or externally; it is like an illusion, a transformation, a shadow, an echo, or a mirage. Entering the Dharma of True Reality, he discerns the Dharma-realm, remaining far removed from the dust of craving while diligently cultivating Right Enlightenment through emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. He knows that all dharmas arise yet are non-arising, and that even this non-arising is itself non-arising; though situated within arising, there is no duality. Following wherever they are born, he guides and delivers them, maintaining a resolute will and never abandoning the aspiration for the Way.
Sitting beneath the King of Trees, he makes this vow: 'I now bind myself by oath: if I do not attain Equal and Perfect Enlightenment, I shall never rise from this seat.'"

Maintaining an equanimous mind, he does not abandon the Buddha-way; though constantly dwelling within the triple world, he remains unattached. He observes his own internal phenomena, and observes the things of others in the same way. He contemplates and seeks the pure wisdom of thorough discernment, fully realizing that all notions of permanence are in fact notions of impermanence.
"Furthermore, Most Victorious One!
The Bodhisattva reflects to himself:
'Just as I am today, by what cause have I obtained this tainted form?'"
"This is because, through accumulating merit over eternal kalpas without weariness and gathering the karmic work of wisdom, one has attained this body.
One does not think of the paths of the Pratyekabuddhas or Śrāvakas; even if someone were to come and incline toward them, the mind would feel neither fear nor doubt.
Practicing generosity, he eliminates all distracted thoughts and reflects within himself:
"When I attain the state of Equal and Perfect Enlightenment, may my body be adorned with the primary and secondary marks and be of golden hue."

Furthermore, they instruct sentient beings to establish themselves in the prohibitions and precepts so as not to fall into the evil destinies; they accord with patience so that the sense-faculties do not arise in disorder; they apply diligent vigor to abandon the mind of self-conceit; through the correct reception of samādhi, their minds do not wander; they cultivate and perfect great wisdom to remain far removed from the dust of desire; they use skillful means to instruct others so as to reach the boundless limit; the karma of their noble wisdom is never lost; their dwelling is firm like the dwelling of a Buddha; their analytical eloquence accords with and responds to the meaning; they let their minds roam within dhāraṇī without damaging the Way and its teachings; they fulfill all the wishes of sentient beings; they encourage those who advance and restrain those who regress so that none fall away; the verbal instructions they set forth correspond with the prohibitions; being themselves without fault, they do not speak of the shortcomings of others; practicing the bodhisattva path, they constantly examine their own faults; they would rather lose their very life-force than disparage either themselves or others.

If there are sentient beings who come of their own accord to take refuge, he does not consider this a cause for joy; even if they do not come, he does not feel sorrow or distress. Hearing of good, he is not delighted; hearing of evil, he is not angered. He accords with all beings, leading them to the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) so that they ultimately achieve the Buddha-way.

Without violating the prohibitions and precepts, they first rescue others from peril rather than seeking their own security; they bestow the seven treasures with such generosity that they never regret it; and having entered the profound essentials of the Dharma, their supernormal powers are unimpeded.

Furthermore, by means of supernormal power, he observes the depth or shallowness, the height or lowness of sentient beings' faculties, and having discerned their noble wisdom, he expounds it for them.

His practice is without attachment and is inexhaustible; though he exists within dependent origination, his mind is not defiled by or attached to any outflows (*āsrava*), nor does he take them as a realization. He contemplates the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) without a self; the True Dharma is tranquil, pure, and unattached. Regarding the rise and fall of the three periods of time, phenomena have no abiding place: he does not perceive the past as something eternally extinguished, he does not examine the future as having either opposition or non-opposition, and he does not dwell upon the present as something constantly existing.

"O Most Victorious One! The Bodhisattva universally contemplates billions of koṭis of worlds, seeing that dharmas neither arise nor cease. His physical conduct is pure and he commits no evil; his speech is pure and his mindfulness is always sincere; his mind is clear and white, refraining from the ten unwholesome deeds. This is called the Bodhisattva’s Perfection of Deliverance (Dāna-pāramitā). He is then granted a prophecy by all the Buddhas; his faculty of wisdom is towering and his merit is blazing. Abiding in the stage of the Ten Dwellings, he is fixed in non-retrogression. He reveres and follows the Dharma without deviation; his temperament is harmonious and compliant, and his practices are fully perfected. Having attained the Ten Powers of a Buddha, his will is like a diamond. He understands that the root of dharmas has both arising and ceasing, and he comprehends the lightness and gravity of the mental ailments of all people. Regarding the various dispositions and conducts of sentient beings, which differ from one another, he is able to clearly discern the retributions they receive."
"How does a bodhisattva receive the fruition?
Grasping the light of wisdom in hand, they dispel the great darkness and contemplate the realization of the fruit; O Most Excellent One, you should know this!
Wielding the sword of powerful memory, they cut away the mass of doubts; whatever they undertake is entirely the realization of the fruit."

Because he has realized the fruit of his practice through extensive giving, his observance of the precepts is as complete as an auspicious vase; his mind practices patience like the Great Being Piṇḍola; his diligence is transcendent like King Śūra; and his meditative concentration has entered the subtle, making him a Bodhisattva of wisdom.

The realization of the fruit of the wisdom-mind is immutable; the Bodhisattva’s giving is equal and non-dual. He perceives no notion of a self or of diversity; he is likewise equal toward all persons and things. Because persons and things are equal, they attain the equality of all dharmas. Understanding the equality of dharmas, his perfect awakening is also equal. Precepts, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom are all understood as equal and without distinction. He realizes that all beings are unborn—birth is non-birth and non-birth is also non-birth. To understand birth as non-birth is to accord with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
This is called, O Most Victorious One!

the Bodhisattva’s penetrating observation that truly exhausts all genuine and great dharmas; he does not give rise to worldly afflictions yet dwells together with them, relinquishing all births without perceiving any birth, and having already practiced giving himself, he does not perceive any act of giving.

There may be bodhisattvas who seek the Way through giving, yet still harbor attachments and desires for the attainment of nirvana; because they mix poison with their practice, they remain within the cycle of birth and death.

"I reckon that in the past, during incalculable kalpas, I once became a Wheel-Turning King, a Universal Monarch (Cakravartin) in this world. Whatever I thought of would naturally appear before me, and none dared to disobey. My descendants succeeded one another for sixty-nine intermediate kalpas (*antarakalpa*). During that time, I practiced giving, precepts, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom, erecting stupas made of the seven treasures as high as the Brahma Heaven, filling the entire world."

At that time, there was a Buddha in the world named Vīryaprabha (Brave Progress), who was attended by ninety billion hundred thousand nayutas of arhats and an incalculable number of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas. I personally provided him with the four types of offerings—robes, food and drink, bedding and seating, and medicines for the sick—and offered my national treasures, wife and children, elephants and horses, the seven precious gems, as well as my slaves, servants, and even down to the commoners and officials, giving them all to serve and honor that Blessed One, the Buddha.

At that time, my acts of giving were accompanied by a mind of attachment; because of this, I fell and remained within the cycle of birth and death. My efforts were in vain and I did not obtain their fruit. If one were to calculate even a hair’s breadth of the merit produced at that time, I do not see anything remaining today.

"Thus it is, Most Victorious One! When a bodhisattva practices giving, there is both giving and non-giving; one neither perceives giving nor perceives non-giving. Giving is neither giving, and non-giving is neither non-giving. One who attains equality regarding giving attains the equality of all dharmas; understanding that giving is non-giving is what accords with spontaneity (svabhāva). It is likewise for precepts, patience, diligence, single-mindedness, and wisdom."
When one realizes that wisdom is empty and quiescent, and yet there is no wisdom, being without wisdom within wisdom—this is what accords with true wisdom.
"Furthermore, Most Victorious One!
A bodhisattva should further contemplate the Jewel of the Dharma."
What is the Jewel of the Dharma?

It refers to the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, the supernormal powers and samādhis, and the various perfections (pāramitās).

Discerning each and every part without a sense of self, they eliminate darkness and bring about great illumination; establishing wisdom and insight to transform sentient beings, they cast off all heavy burdens without hesitation, cultivating and upholding the precepts with body and mind in tranquil stillness.

Furthermore, one should contemplate the establishment of the treasure of wisdom; yet, one should not give rise to a mind that relies upon anything. The mind is detached from the three periods of time and possesses neither interior nor exterior. One does not rely on the aggregates (*skandha*), the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*), the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), or the sense bases (*āyatana*). One realizes and attests to *nirvāṇa*, yet does not perceive a *nirvāṇa* to be attained. Taking the flowers of the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*) as a floral garland, and the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*) as the fruit of retribution, one adorns the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) as one’s dwelling. Guiding and advancing sentient beings, one leads them to the ultimate; being tranquil and serene, one is free from old age, sickness, and death, and likewise free from the afflictions of grief, joy, and all sufferings. One walks alone through the triple world without fear.
One contemplates that all persons and things are entirely pure; the self and persons are pure, and persons and things are likewise pure. One thoroughly realizes this purity such that nothing exists.

From the moment the Bodhisattva first resolves upon enlightenment, they should contemplate purity and give rise to a subtle and wondrous intention. Throughout this interval, they never again give rise to thoughts of lust, anger, or delusion, nor do they direct their minds toward harassing sentient beings. Furthermore, they do not give rise to the mind of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvaka and Pratyekabuddha). Standing as a leader among the great assembly, though dwelling in nobility and wealth, they remain free from arrogance. They protect sentient beings and do not abandon them. Since the mind of fundamental non-existence is individually devoid of reality, the mind has no mind and is free from the net of fetters. This is the diamond-like intention of a Bodhisattva, which cannot be thwarted.

They nurture wholesome dharmas so that they do not leak away or be lost; they contemplate profound, wondrous, vast, and great vows that are inconceivable; they examine all natures and do not see anything that arises, nor do they see anyone who achieves them.

One contemplates that all illusory phenomena of the world are not real; through pure contemplation, one recognizes these as inversions. One does not follow after dharmas—whether they are appropriate or inappropriate—and yet does not abandon them.

There are those who, amidst the entanglements of seeking, do not perceive anything currently accumulated in the present; they do not perceive any origin from which the past and future emerge. Departure has no beginning and arrival has no sequence; when analyzing the present, it is found to have no location whatsoever. Even when one investigates the True Dharma, it cannot be apprehended.

The Bodhisattva’s resolve must lie in perversion; the thought of non-attainment is the Bodhisattva’s essential requirement; the sixty-two false views are the Bodhisattva’s essential requirement; the perception of self and attachment to precepts and views are the Bodhisattva’s essential requirement; hesitation and indecision are the Bodhisattva’s essential requirement; seeking heavenly blessings through trade is the Bodhisattva’s essential requirement; entering hell without reckoning its suffering is the Bodhisattva’s essential requirement; and furthermore, transforming one's body to enter among the hungry ghosts and the realm of animals is the Bodhisattva’s essential requirement.

Although a bodhisattva may dwell amidst the five immediate retributions (*pañcānantarya*), they rescue suffering sentient beings therein, establishing them in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) for eternal and perpetual bliss; furthermore, they are free from the affliction of discursive thoughts regarding arising and ceasing, and even when contemplating the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), it is found to be ungraspable.

Why is this so? Humans arise from the Dharma, and the Dharma flourishes through humans; they arise and perish of themselves, yet there is no fundamental basis for death. Humans do not depart from their nature, nor does nature depart from humans; humans and things are spontaneous, leaving no trace behind.

My own life-span is likewise thus: the self is spontaneous and all dharmas are spontaneous; since dharmas are spontaneous, the Way is also spontaneous. One who understands and realizes this emptiness and attains such contemplation shall then obtain the Way of the spontaneous accumulation.
What is called the path of natural accumulation means that through sublime contemplation one perceives non-duality and does not even see duality.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva possesses the Samādhi of Swift Movement; entering this samādhi, in the mere twinkling of an eye, he travels to the Buddha-lands of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, where he pays homage, serves, and makes offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, before returning.

While no one at that place was aware of him, he immediately from his seat entered the *samādhi* of "Just as It Is" (*yathāvat*) and traveled toward the east to hundreds of millions of *nayuta* of Buddha-fields, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

There he paid homage to, served, and made offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; he inquired after their well-being and listened to the reception of the subtle and wondrous Dharma. Suddenly, having passed through the west...

Having traveled to Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of immeasurable Ganges Rivers to pay homage, serve, and make offerings to the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, he then immediately traveled south to immeasurable lands, and subsequently returned to immeasurable lands in the north;
the same was true for the four intermediate directions and the zenith and nadir. Throughout this, among the great assembly, there was not one who perceived him sitting down or rising up.
"O Most Victorious One!

When a bodhisattva enters this samādhi of right concentration, they travel to immeasurable lands in the ten directions in the mere twinkling of an eye, and suddenly return to their original position; yet among the sentient beings seated there at that time, none are aware of it."

Just as I now expound the meaning of the Dharma within this great assembly, there are twenty million bodhisattvas who do not rise from their seats; each has traveled to the lands of the ten directions and now returns here to sit once more. Among the sentient beings listening to the Dharma, none are able to perceive them, all because the conduct of these bodhisattvas is so pure and refined.
At that time, Varagāmin came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is the name of the samādhi entered by these noble beings, which enables the bodhisattvas to travel back and forth with such extreme swiftness?"

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Varaprabha, saying: "Set aside for a moment the samādhi entered by the Bodhisattva; there is another samādhi called 'Unimpeded Supernatural Power' (anāvaraṇa-abhijñā), which all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, constantly dwell within. Once the Tathāgata has entered this samādhi, in the interval between a single inhalation and exhalation, he travels to as many Buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in hundreds of thousands of koṭis of Ganges Rivers. He can also cause the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the ten directions to enter this realm without disturbing any sentient beings who possess consciousness. Or, he may take all the waters of the oceans of the ten directions and move them into space like suspended bright pearls, such that there is no one who does not see them, yet without causing any fear or alarm among those of the watery nature. This is called the Samādhi of Unimpeded Supernatural Wisdom."
At that time, among the two hundred million foremost great beings, there was a bodhisattva named Sāgaragarbha who, while seated upon his throne, reflected to himself:
"The Tathāgata surely intends for me to manifest the spiritual power of samādhi."

He immediately rose from his seat and went before the high seat where the assembly was gathered. He prostrated himself in homage to the Buddha and the various elders, then stood before the Buddha with palms joined and said:

"The Way of the Buddha is profound and far-reaching, beyond all analogy; the unsurpassed, true, and correct Way is truly difficult to attain. As I now observe all the bodhisattvas, the fourfold assembly, the honored devas and spirits, and all who have come to this gathering, I see this bodhisattva uttering a lion’s roar amidst the great multitude. Furthermore, these people have long been hungry and parched for the Dharma; such a time is difficult to encounter. I wish to ask a question, and if I am granted leave, I shall venture to speak."
The Buddha said to Sāgaragarbha:

“Ask whatever you wish according to the net of your doubts; the Tathāgata shall explain them all for you in detail, so as to bring joy to all the bodhisattvas and the entire assembly. With the great fire of the sword of wisdom, I shall burn away the forest of your ignorance.”
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sāgaragarbha again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"So be it, World-Honored One.
Previously, while seated upon his mat, he had been reflecting alone in his mind and thinking to himself:

"These two hundred million virtuous men have accumulated goodness for a very long time and are fully endowed with merit. Having subdued and harmonized their minds and wills, they abide in the Dharma; through the accumulation of various roots of goodness, they have attained this right concentration (*samādhi*). For incalculable kalpas, they have served, honored, and made offerings to various Buddhas. These bodhisattvas of supernatural powers, for the sake of sentient beings, have bestowed elephants, horses, and the seven treasures as gifts, causing all classes of living beings to attain the Buddha-way. Or, for those who might regress and lack firm resolve, they practice this meditative state of right concentration and *samādhi*."

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who, out of compassion for the afflictions, enter deeply into birth and death, desiring to bring about a state where sentient beings are forever free from suffering;
or there are bodhisattvas who enter the samādhi of loving-kindness, causing those sentient beings to be eternally separated from hatred and envy;
and there are further bodhisattvas who give rise to the mind of great compassion, enabling those sentient beings to understand the meaning of impermanence.
There are some bodhisattvas who, by dwelling in the meditative concentration of joy, cause those who behold them to understand emptiness and stillness;
there are others who, having resolved upon the adamantine mind, cause all sentient beings to give rise to the intention of great vows;
and there are yet others who broaden their aspirations so as to welcome and bring all beings into their own buddha-fields.
Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who, through the fundamental nature of body and dharmas, cause those sentient beings to be virtuous in the beginning, middle, and end;

furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who manifest in the eight unfavorable states to ensure that the Three Jewels are not interrupted; or there are bodhisattvas who, through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), adapt their transformations and teachings according to the needs of sentient beings before them;

furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who dwell in quietude and seclusion, contemplating conditioned phenomena as being like illusions or magical transformations; or there are bodhisattvas who delight in dwelling in the wisdom of emptiness, contemplating this physical form as being like a wall; or there are bodhisattvas whose minds and intentions are upright, whose conduct is pure, and who are free from defilement.
Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas whose nature is profoundly subtle and secret, such that in whatever direction they travel, there is no loss or error;
furthermore, there are bodhisattvas whose minds aspire to the Single Path, ensuring that sentient beings do not even hear the names of the Three Vehicles;
furthermore, there are bodhisattvas whose resolve and understanding delight in clarity and purity, bathing those before them so that they are forever free from defilement.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised that bodhisattva amidst the great assembly, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!
Bodhisattva Sāgaragarbha!"

You have been able, before me and in this great assembly, to let out a lion’s roar, extolling the meditative states entered by Bodhisattvas, so that all those gathered here may hear and know these samādhis and meditative attainments in which these true beings roam—samādhis that are inconceivable and beyond reach, which cannot be fathomed by those of the two vehicles.
A bodhisattva accumulates merit not for their own sake, but with the thought of uprooting sentient beings who suffer affliction;
even if a wind were to arise within a trichiliocosm, filling the world and circulating as swiftly as the Svalana wind,
and if there were someone following the tracks of the path, desiring to proceed single-mindedly through its midst—

Coming and going, he accomplishes his tasks with immediate success and without obstruction; how much more so for the inconceivable supernormal powers of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva in the meditative absorption of *samādhi*?

In the space of a single thought-moment, he traverses immeasurable lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and by means of the Dharma of the six perfections and the ten wholesome paths, he teaches and transforms sentient beings, instructing them in the Way of Goodness.
Their mind is eternally secure and cannot be moved; their resolve and conduct are tranquil and free from confusion. Even if one were to exert mental effort, none could equal them.
This is because in previous lives they were fully endowed with manifold virtues; their resolve and conduct were orderly and impartial toward all classes of beings.
Their great compassion is inexhaustible and without limit, and regarding all phenomena, they are ever self-...
Regarding existence, sentient beings fail to realize that it is subject to arising and decaying.

Phenomena arise from themselves and phenomena perish from themselves; phenomena do not give birth to phenomena, nor do phenomena perish through phenomena. The nature of the arising and perishing of phenomena does not undergo transmigration. This is the path of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, which is beyond the reach of ordinary worldly people.
Sentient beings, remaining within birth and death, do not penetrate the fundamental source of the Way; they claim that the dharma-nature undergoes change and transformation.
If this were indeed the case, it would not be so.

Since first generating the aspiration for enlightenment, the Bodhisattva has practiced giving and maintained the precepts, becoming fully endowed with all virtues. As for the attainment of the fruit of the path, it arises from understanding the contemplation of emptiness—its voidness and tranquility—and through proclaiming and perfecting the wondrous karmic deeds of the past and future, they enter the stages practiced by all Bodhisattvas. They roam through supreme and immeasurable Buddha-lands, exhorting and inspiring sentient beings to cross to the further shore of birth and death; having clearly understood the gates of their faculties, they transform them according to the times, leaving none unaided.

Sometimes he nurtures and sustains sentient beings through worldly decorum and etiquette; sometimes he does so through the supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), the paths of spiritual penetration (*abhijñā*), and the wisdom of the Way. He discerns the rise and fall of the six sense-faculties and their afflictions (*kleśa*): those arising from the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind. He realizes that the eye is impermanent and lacks any true reality; it has no place of departure and leaves no trace upon its arrival. The ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are likewise thus.

Regarding the dharmas of the past, future, and present, one perceives neither their arising nor their ceasing; yet sentient beings, deluded and confused, conceive the notion of permanence. Why is this?

"O Most Victorious One, you should know! The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is universally endowed with skillful means and wisdom; he practices the immeasurable *pāramitās*, establishes himself in the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*), and extensively cultivates all dharmas. He is praised by all Tathāgatas; having eliminated false conceptualizations, he attains immeasurable wisdom. His eloquence is unimpeded and he is ever mindful of shame and remorse; he contemplates that dharmas do not arise and perceives no movement or fluctuation.

Sometimes he adorns Buddha-lands with the primary and secondary marks; his conduct never deviates from or contradicts the Dharma. He enters into the profound wisdom of all paths, never tiring of listening to the Dharma with joyful admiration. With the singular stride of skillful means and wisdom, he subdues all Māras."

Whether they reach the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, or the palaces of Brahmā and Śakra, or travel through lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions—whichever regions they visit, the Buddha-dharma flourishes there; that which they establish is profound, remote, and inconceivable.
They eliminate arrogance and indolence, remaining free from both affirmation and negation.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed Varaprabha: "The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva cultivates the immeasurable Dharma-gates of perfect enlightenment:

the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*), the four right efforts (*samyakprahāṇa*), the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*), the five faculties (*indriya*), the five powers (*bala*), the seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhyaṅga*), and the eightfold right path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*). Possessing total retention and powerful memory without deficiency, he uses the foundation of mindfulness regarding phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) to contemplate the conditioned and the unconditioned, the determinate and the indeterminate, and the out-flowing and the non-out-flowing. He is fully endowed with the ten powers (*daśabala*) and the fearlessnesses regarding all dharmas; through the correct reception of samādhi, he eliminates the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) and clearly understands and discerns the stage of non-retrogression.
Furthermore, by the power of the correct reception of samādhi, he transcends the fifty-seven dharmas of the wisdom-karma; the Bodhisattva should maintain mindfulness so as not to forget them."

If a person practices giving in pursuit of blessings among the devas, or seeks rebirth within the palaces of ghosts, spirits, or nāgas, or gives with the intention of being born among the Four Heavenly Kings, or further desires to be born as one of the twenty-eight generals of the ghost-spirits—all such cases are not genuine and they shall not obtain their wishes.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses to Varaprabha:
"The body is pure and does not commit evil; The mouth acts without the four calamities;
The mind does not conceive of offenses regarding dharmas— This is the dhāraṇī of the bodhisattva."
Proclaiming immeasurable virtues, forever free from the mind of stinginess and greed,
using supernormal powers to dispel darkness— this is the bodhisattva’s dhāraṇī.
When teaching others to practice giving, do not allow them to harbor any seeking or expectations.
Failing in one's vows leads to falling into the three miserable realms, where all past labors are cast away in vain.
In the past, when I sought perfect enlightenment, my thoughts remained bound for the duration of kalpas;
through skillful means I traversed birth and death, taking the five paths of existence as my field of observation.
Furthermore, throughout incalculable eons, you cultivated and established the roots of virtue;
yet, because you did not attain mastery, you sported within the four profound pools.
Now, though you have attained Buddhahood and alone reign as king over the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system, [you still do not dwell in ease].
By means of these conditions, one casts off conceptual thoughts and gains entry to the gate of the profound path.
At the site of enlightenment, golden light is emitted; billions of spirits come to take refuge.
Following the virtuous deities of the śramaṇa, they all arrive and take refuge of their own accord.

"Therefore, Most Victorious One! You should maintain mindfulness with single-minded intent to eliminate conceptual seeking; understand that the Dharma-realm is of a single characteristic and formless; cultivate the Buddha-lands so that clear wisdom is never interrupted; do not encourage karmic deeds but universally bestow upon all; realize that there is no giving and no holy ones, understanding that nothing is produced; and perceive the equality of the One Vehicle without seeing any diversity."
"O Most Excellent One!
You should further discern the Four Noble Truths: from what does suffering arise, and by what is it extinguished?
This body of the five aggregates is the root of suffering; through careful and precise contemplation, you should seek its extinction."

The habitual tendencies arise from suffering; when they are extinguished without remainder, the sixty-two types of false doubt and inverted views are resolved through immeasurable wisdom as having no fixed location.
Furthermore, one contemplates the Four Noble Truths and the twelve links of dependent origination to discern from what they arise and into what they cease.

Gradually contemplating this, one comes to know its purity and stillness; the actions of body, speech, and mind likewise have no master, no recipient, no coming or going, and no place of abiding. From the stage of *srotāpanna* up to perfect enlightenment, it is also thus; one likewise analyzes the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm in this same way.
Furthermore, Most Excellent One!

A bodhisattva contemplates and knows the escape from suffering, the escape from the accumulation of suffering, the escape from the cessation of suffering, and the escape via the path to the cessation of suffering; he contemplates them according to reality.

Furthermore, one should distinguish the sixteen noble dharmas that are profound and difficult to fathom, as well as the thirty-six impure substances of foul secretions; proclaiming the wisdom of the unsurpassed fruit of the Path, he distributes instructions and guides them by gradual stages. There is no profound treasury of the Buddhas that he does not penetrate, and the teachings he utters never fail to be meaningful.
Sometimes I manifest as a wealthy and extraordinary elder, gathering in sentient beings through my giving, leading them back and forth until they achieve the Way;
or I use incense, flowers, light, banners, and canopies to extensively illuminate and pervade all places;

furthermore, using my supernormal powers, I move the various devas and proclaim the Buddha-way so that they may enter the One Vehicle—therefore, throughout kalpas upon kalpas, I have not been bound by these acts.
Furthermore, he manifests the paths of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, dwelling among mountains and marshes while not manifesting parinirvāṇa;
he also enters the palaces of the nāgas to transform the nāga sons, causing them to abide within the restraints of the Way.

Thus it is, O Most Victorious One! The meritorious deeds of a bodhisattva are beyond measure; they cannot be fully proclaimed by speech nor conceived by the mind. At times, a bodhisattva is born into the family of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*);

the entire heavenly world receives his guidance and further embraces the ten wholesome paths of action. If he sees sentient beings amidst famine and scarcity, he immediately provides them with ambrosia (*amṛta*) to satisfy their lack. He bears the burden of their manifold afflictions and leads them away from the midst of craving and desire. The likeness of such a bodhisattva is immeasurable.
"Furthermore, Most Excellent One!
A bodhisattva should contemplate the dharma-gate of one thousand seven hundred samādhis, so that all those free from attachment may attain perfect enlightenment.
There is also the dharma-gate of the samādhi of radiance, which enables a bodhisattva to master the essential dhāraṇīs."
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of the Samādhi of the Bodhi-tree’s Shading Canopy, by which the three thousandfold world-system receives its protection;

furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of the Samādhi of the Divine Jewel Rain upon the World, which emits hundreds of thousands of billions of countless rays of light, and from each ray of light issue various sounds of suffering, emptiness, non-self, and the absence of a person; those who hear these sounds all give rise to the unsurpassed mind of non-seeing;

furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of the Samādhi of the Formless Crystal, which causes the worlds of the ten directions to become a single radiant color and further produces the sounds of various music; those who hear these sounds recognize their own past lives and know the places and lairs from which they have come.
Furthermore, there is the light of the full moon, which shines uniquely among the multitude like the moon among the stars;
there is the light of solar essence, which appears before the eyes of sentient beings to enable them to know how to advance;
and there is the light of majestic spiritual power, which bestows the prediction of the Mahāyāna upon those who cannot otherwise be known.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of the Samādhi of Light from the Unseen-Crown-Mark, because one is uniquely honored among the assembly and inspires reverence;
furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of the Samādhi of Light from the Tongue-Mark, because one is trusted within the assembly and remains beyond reproach.
"O Most Victorious One!

This Dharma-gate of the Radiance of Seventeen Hundred Samādhis, which Bodhisattvas enter as a likeness, is immeasurably pure. At that very seat, countless members of the assembly who heard this Dharma gave rise to the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment—something they had never before heard or seen since time immemorial."

At that time, in the eastern direction, beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of countless Ganges Rivers, there was a bodhisattva named Ratnavīra. Surrounded by his retinue before and behind him, he arrived at this Sahā world and approached the Buddha’s presence. Bowing his head to the Buddha’s feet, he stood to one side and, with palms joined toward the Buddha, uttered this verse of praise:
“Your countenance is exceptionally serene; The foremost among the Honored Ones of Men.
Free from the defilement of worldly afflictions, You bestow immeasurable virtue.”
His brilliance illuminates ten billion worlds; his purity is known to be boundless.
With compassion for all people, he walks alone as king over the three thousandfold world.
We have come today desiring to hear the nectar-like wisdom.
We pray that you will manifest yourself so that we may find relief, like those parched with thirst rushing toward a flowing spring.
O Guide, may you appear even as rarely as the udumbara flower;
for us who are afflicted by the roots of disease, act as our savior and our protector.
"I have come from a place far removed from here, across countless lands;
having been afflicted by hunger and thirst for a very long time, I pray that you will explain this to me.
At that time, after the Bodhisattva Ratnavīra had praised the Buddha with these verses, he again prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and sat down in his proper place.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed those assembled:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon this well!
I shall now explain in detail the bodhisattva’s practice of non-arising and non-ceasing; let it be well-considered as excellent in its beginning, middle, and end, and held firmly within your hearts."
At that time, the bodhisattvas addressed the World-Honored One, saying,
"We wish and desire to hear it.
The World-Honored One told them:

“The Way is not that which gives rise to birth, nor is it birth itself; non-conceptualization is the Way, yet conceptualization is not the Way. Non-existence is the Way, while existence is not the Way. Non-attachment is the Way, while attachment is not the Way. To seek to accomplish the Way through desire is also not the Way; only when there is neither accomplishment nor desire is it called the Way. When the mind is bound to the gates of the senses, this is not the true Way; only when one eliminates the gates of the senses is it called the Way.”
At that time, the bodhisattvas in the assembly again had this thought:
"What is meant by 'practice without arising or ceasing,' and why is it further called the Way?
Now, is Nirvana not itself the Way?"
At that time, the World-Honored One, again knowing the thoughts in the minds of the great assembly, addressed the multitude of bodhisattvas, saying:
"In what way is nirvāṇa different from the Path?"
He replied, "No.
[The Buddha asked,] "If nirvana were not different from the Path, for what reason would one say, 'This is nirvana' and 'This is the Path'?"
"Is this the unconditioned? Is this cessation? Is this the place of bliss and tranquility?
