Or again, is it that which is called name-and-form and the six sense bases—wherein these arise when they arise and these cease when they cease—is this the path to Nirvana?"
He replied, “No, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha told him:
“Excellent, excellent!
It is just as you have said!”

The Path is not Nirvana, and Nirvana is not the Path; birth is the root of cessation, yet cessation is not birth. The Path is the root of Nirvana, yet Nirvana is also not the Path; name-and-form and the six sense bases are likewise so.

At that time, when the assembly heard this teaching on the practice of concentration through the contemplation of the mind regarding the absence of arising and ceasing, they all attained the mind of non-arising and non-ceasing and no longer regressed.
The Scripture on the Ten Abodes and the Severing of Bonds, Scroll Four.
The Scripture on the Ten Abodes and the Severing of Bonds, Scroll Five.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin Dynasty.
Chapter Twelve: The Chapter on the Divine Footings (Ṛddhipāda) At that time, the Bodhisattva Varaprabha came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How is it that a bodhisattva may advance or retreat in regard to generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom?

Furthermore, how is it that there are bodhisattvas who, from their first resolution until they attain Buddhahood, never dwell within the womb of a mother’s belly but always achieve miraculous birth, and moreover, travel through various Buddha-lands by means of their supernormal powers without any conceptualization of those lands?
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain each point in detail, so that those who study the bodhisattva path in future ages may know their destination.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ajita:
“Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well!”
"I shall explain this to you one by one.
Most Victorious addressed the Buddha, saying,
"I wish and desire to hear it."

The Buddha told Jiasheng: "If there is a bodhisattva who practices giving, precepts, and patience while maintaining conceptual thoughts; who exerts diligence, dhyāna, and wisdom while giving rise to attachments toward all dharmas; or who perceives worlds yet has no thought of worlds; sees sentient beings yet has no thought of sentient beings; sees coming and going yet has no mind of coming and going; sees the present yet has no intention of the present; and sees attachment and cessation yet has no mind of attachment and cessation—this is the accomplishment of the faculties and powers of the first stage, and one shall then be in correspondence with ten dharmas."

What are the ten? They are as follows: the Tathāgata’s divine virtues are immeasurable; his single mark is thus unimpeded; he perceives no defilement or attachment in the name of Perfect Enlightenment; he perceives no transcending or crossing over of any dharmas; he manifests the three vehicles equally yet perceives no destination and is not attached to worlds; and he understands that names have no past, future, or present.
Regarding what are called names and signs: all-knowledge is also called the Dharma-realm because it brings forth the Path; therefore, one should protect their resolve and not wound their mind.
It is thus, O Most Victorious One!
These dharmas likewise have no location; when they come, one does not know from where they come, and when they go, one does not know where they cease.

The Bodhisattva’s practice of precepts, patience, and diligence is also like this: the precepts are without precepts, and patience is without patience. Understanding diligence, one does not perceive any progress. If a person upholds the precepts, they constantly guard against others' shortcomings; even if they see someone violating the precepts, they do not harbor resentment; and seeing another's precepts complete, they do not feel joy. This is called the Bodhisattva’s accomplishment of the precepts.

When a Bodhisattva practices patience, the mind neither increases nor decreases. Even if someone comes to take his body, dismembering it limb by limb, he maintains a firm resolve that cannot be broken or destroyed. The Bodhisattva is fully endowed with generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; his conceptual attachments are severed and his mind harbors no duality. He gives rise to neither arising nor ceasing, nor does he produce manifold thoughts; regarding all transgressions and merits, he remains equanimous and non-dual.

Furthermore, one should contemplate the three gates to the Brahma-palace—emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)—and not perceive emptiness as being joined with signs or wishes; nor should signs or wishes be perceived as being joined with emptiness. Wishlessness is not perceived as being joined with emptiness or signs; emptiness and signs are not perceived as being joined with wishlessness, nor are they not joined. Signlessness is not perceived as being joined with emptiness or wishlessness; emptiness and wishlessness are not perceived as being joined with signlessness, nor are they not joined. This is likewise for the past, future, and present.

Furthermore, Most Victorious One! A bodhisattva’s supernormal power is neither thought nor deliberation; it is the inconceivable realm of the Dragon Lineage. It neither clings to the world nor is it detached from the world; its coming and going and its constant movement have no place of abiding. The characteristics of all phenomena are likewise thus.

The Bodhisattva advances forward to cultivate the fruits of the Way; the noble path is naturally such that its boundaries or shores cannot be seen. If anyone comes seeking its starting point or end, it will only result in self-injury within the Dharma of the Sages and Worthies.
"O Most Victorious One!
These six profound and pure dharmas—bodhisattva precepts, learning, wisdom, and giving—possess deep principles through which one may practice the Brahma-faring.

If a bodhisattva attains these roots of virtue and acquires this subtle and essential profound dharma, they will attain parinirvāṇa within the nirvana-without-remainder; yet, by teaching sentient beings throughout the bounds of neither coming nor going, this is what is called the Way."
The Bodhisattva manifests entry into the midst of sensual desires, observing their fundamental causes and expounding the Dharma for them;

at other times, he enters the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), where inhalation and exhalation are severed and nothing remains, his physical form becoming bloated and leaking impurities, so that sentient beings who behold him give rise to the perception of impermanence;
furthermore, observing whether sentient beings are settled or distracted, he manifests accordingly to enable them to attain liberation.
Whether it be through the dharmas of dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*) and the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), he instructs all beings to remove their heavy burdens.

Divine wisdom and the five dharmas are the bodhisattva’s work; the eighteen subtle refinements are the bodhisattva’s work; the sixteen adamantine [realizations] are the bodhisattva’s work; the twenty-one precepts cultivated by the noble ones are the bodhisattva’s work; contemplating the thirty-four dharmas beneath the King of Trees is the bodhisattva’s work; not perceiving a self in giving, morality, and so forth is the bodhisattva’s work; and non-abiding in the discrimination of the past, future, and present is the bodhisattva’s work.
"O Most Victorious One! The realm cultivated by a bodhisattva is immeasurable. One must understand and know the law of retribution in order to attain the Way.

When anything comes, it accords with the convergence of causes and conditions: sound comes from space and the ear-consciousness goes forth to hear it. Verbal teachings and written texts are neither true nor real; they assemble according to conditions and disperse according to conditions. When conditions converge, they converge; when conditions disperse, they disperse. In their dispersal, they do not know of themselves from where they disperse; in their gathering, they do not know of themselves from where they gather."
At that time, Ajita came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!

It is wonderful how you have so clearly explained this Dharma, analyzing it in its various aspects and explaining the beginning and end of its causal conditions. You have caused all bodhisattvas to don the great armor of virtue, led countless people to resolve upon the Great Way, and praised the goals of the bodhisattvas’ meritorious deeds, as well as the ten dharmas of the Tathāgata’s names, qualities, and meanings. All those gathered here have now heard and understood them; the Tathāgata’s wisdom and karma are entirely without obstruction.”
If there are bodhisattvas who hear this Dharma, their aggregates, decays, and hindrances will be forever eliminated, and they shall cause all sentient beings to attain thorough understanding.
We, World-Honored One!
From this day forward, I shall reverently uphold the teachings and the Way instructed by the World-Honored Tathāgata; I dare not be negligent in my practice of pure and mature conduct.

Through generosity, I shall harmonize my mind, constantly discerning the meanings and principles of all words, phrases, and chapters so that they are ever present before me. With a heart of equanimity as vast as space covering all, I shall extend my compassionate love universally to all beings, transforming them according to their individual roots and origins.

Constantly bestowing the four immeasurables upon sentient beings, he feeds them with ambrosia; he causes them to cast off all fetters of resentment and afflictions, relinquish the ten unwholesome dharmas, and depart from the three poisons. He uproots the nine afflictions and the dharmas of distracted thoughts, ensuring that the dust of the Mara of Death which harms the human heart shall forever be eliminated without remainder.

One discerns the root of the twelve links of dependent origination, from ignorance conditioned by volitional formations up to birth, old age, and death. Furthermore, one should contemplate the course of dependent origination: that with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease, and so on, until old age, sickness, and death likewise cease. Examining their origins according to their respective categories, one then applies the appropriate remedy and maintains a firm mind. Clearly discerning what the minds of sentient beings contemplate constitutes wholesome conduct; by repeatedly expounding the Dharma for them, one prevents them from wandering astray, ensuring that defiled and turbid thoughts do not arise again.

"Therefore, Most Victorious One! When a Bodhisattva proclaims the teachings he has established, they bring great benefit and achieve much fulfillment. He regards those sentient beings as a mother loves her child, nurturing them at all times with a mind free from increase or decrease. Constantly abiding in right view, he does not follow heterodox teachers; amidst the great assembly, he is like a lion king. He contemplates the earth, water, fire, and wind within his own body: when the earth moves, the water subsides; when the water moves, the fire subsides; when the fire moves, the wind subsides. When these four elements move, the various faculties decay and the spirit departs from the body. At that moment, what reliance can one's kinsmen provide? Only the wholesome Dharma can be depended upon."

Furthermore, one should contemplate and deeply observe the Dharma: the samādhi of right reception in which all Buddhas roam; following its fundamental principle so as not to lose dignified deportment; discerning the conduct that is free from outflows and errors; transcending the karma of the eight worldly dharmas; remaining unstained in mind by gain, loss, defamation, or praise; and realizing that the notions of self, person, life, and soul have no locus whatsoever.
"O Most Victorious One, you should know this!

If there are sentient beings who harbor perverted views and come to interrogate a bodhisattva regarding the principles of his practice, even if they do so for one kalpa up to a hundred thousand kalpas—receiving and retaining everything the bodhisattva in that state of abiding says—their speech shall be fluent and unimpeded."
Therefore, you should know that the conduct of a bodhisattva is beyond compare and cannot be illustrated by analogy. Why is this so?

It is because all these are manifestations produced through the miraculous powers (*ṛddhi*) of the bodhisattva; they travel to the ten directions to pay homage to, serve, and make offerings to the Buddhas, proceeding from one buddha-field to another. In every place they arrive, they manifest and proclaim the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings, eliminating all hardships from beginning to end, such that all those who harbor enmity or encounter suffering and affliction are naturally brought to extinction [of their distress].
What is the accomplishment of his retinue?

It is entirely due to his abandonment of arrogance and self-importance. Whether at times he is amidst a great assembly, his voice flows smoothly like the Brahma-voice, enabling the three classes of followers to attain their aspirations, leading them toward the ultimate state of the unconditioned and bringing them to parinirvāṇa.

It is also like a great dragon that raises an unobstructed cloud and rains upon the trichiliocosm, so that the hundred grains, grasses, and trees all receive its moisture and grow in abundance according to the seasons.

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is likewise: emitting a single sound, he distributes the water of the flavor of the Dharma of the eight liberations throughout the teachings of the Way, causing all within the three thousandfold world system to universally receive his deliverance. Those who attain liberation possess a will like diamond, pure both internally and externally; furthermore, by means of the divine feet, the prohibitions, and the laws and regulations, they adorn their own bodies with various marks so brilliantly manifest as a mountain of pure gold. Wherever they pass, they cause each being to find their proper place, and those who hear the Dharma believe it with firm conviction and without doubt.

Furthermore, they cause sentient beings to enter the *bodhyanga-samādhi*, so that all sentient beings within this trichiliocosm—whether possessing form or moving about, even the smallest insects and crawling creatures—may each recognize their own past lives. They cause all these beings to awaken to the traces of their original habits and to know the origins of suffering; thereby, they cause them all to give rise to the bodhicitta and to reverently practice the *samāpatti* of the Tathāgata.

At that time, the sentient beings who heard the Dharma applied themselves with diligent effort; sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, they recognized their destination and proceeded toward it. Whether far or near, they all arrived at the pure and wondrous place of practice. Those who reached the place of practice were firm in resolve and entered into fearlessness; no longer trembling, their will was brought to ultimate fulfillment. Sentient beings of sharp faculties—some after one day, two days, three days, or even seven days—cast off their physical forms and lives, passing away to be reborn in the heavens.

Those whose virtues are matured and whose conduct is flawless are born in the Buddha-fields of the ten directions. The sentient beings born in heaven take various kinds of celestial flowers, as well as diverse incenses and all manner of spontaneous offerings, and come to present them; they scatter these over the great assembly and those gathered there. The flowers remain suspended in mid-air without falling to the ground, transforming into natural jeweled pavilions with latticed canopies. With a great voice, they offer this self-praise:
"We have gained excellent benefit and joyfully received this merit, for we have been able to encounter this *bodhicitta-samādhi*, causing the trichiliocosm to attain its aspirations."
"So it is, World-Honored One!
We have swiftly attained a great and wholesome benefit!
They then further made offerings of incense and flowers specifically to the Most Excellent Bodhisattva.

"Now, by virtue of your benevolence, we have encountered this Bodhicitta-samādhi, causing our very bodies to partake in this auspicious assembly. We should know that any sentient beings who hear of this Bodhicitta-samādhi yet do not believe it with deep conviction are those whose failure to encounter this samādhi was the result of their past lives."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed those gathered there:

"In the past, throughout incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, I practiced this samādhi, which enabled me today to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. All the Buddhas of the past, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and those yet to come, shall all cultivate this *bodhyaṅga-samādhi*; the majestic power of this samādhi is beyond measure."
All who heard his name were inspired to awaken the great mind of a bodhisattva; it was impossible to calculate how many among the fourfold assembly had attained this samādhi of meditative intent.
Furthermore, hundreds of thousands of others who had gathered at the assembly immediately, while still upon their seats, resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment.

At that time, the World-Honored One again emitted the radiance of the *bodhikusuma-samādhi*, which illuminated the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals throughout this trichiliocosm; their manifold sufferings were extinguished, and they all attained rebirth within the human realm, where they could personally recall their past lives.
At that time, there were four hundred million beings in the assembly. Witnessing this auspicious omen, they each conceived a sense of weariness with worldly existence and reflected within themselves:

"Birth is followed by death; all things arise from causes and conditions. Dying here and being born there occurs in an unbroken succession. Lust is the source, and this stems from craving. We vow to be reborn in a land free of desire, so that we may cultivate this Samādhi of Awakening-Mind and attain the meditative absorption of Right Reception."
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of those assembled, addressed them, saying:

"To the west, beyond countless Buddha-lands, there is a Buddha named Amitāyus. His land is pure and free from lust, anger, and ignorance; all beings therein share a single mind. They are all born from within lotus flowers and are not born through the passions of parents. They consist purely of youths, with no female forms and no excrement or urine. They take the joy of dhyāna and the delight in the Dharma as their sustenance, having no conceptualization or consciousness of food. They regard one another with reverence and affection, as if toward a father or a mother. Those who wish to be born there should resolve to make a vow."
At that time, the assembly of four hundred million beings, while still upon their seats, made a unified vow to seek rebirth in that land.

Then the World-Honored One, manifesting the radiance of the *bodhicitta-samādhi* according to its form, shone upon that land, enabling the four hundred million people to behold the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, and the bodhisattvas born by transformation there. That land was vast and expansive, interspersed with various jewels such as pure gold, silver, and lapis lazuli; it was free from the three evil realms and the suffering of the eight difficulties.

Having seen that land, these four hundred million people, according to their respective forms and lifespans, were all born simultaneously in that realm and attained the cultivation of this Samādhi of the Awakening Mind (bodhicitta-samādhi). This was brought about by the power of their original vows and aspirations; such is the virtue manifested through the inspiration of the Samādhi of the Awakening Mind.
13. Chapter on Reverence. At that time, the Bodhisattva Most Victorious again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In what manner does a bodhisattva of such a kind constantly hear the Dharma from the Buddha, giving rise to a mind of reverence and such exuberant joy that he cannot restrain himself?"

The World-Honored One said: “This essential Dharma is like the divine elixir of the Nāgas. If a person consumes this divine elixir, their mind and spirit will be joyful and naturally filled with serenity; lust, anger, and delusion will be eliminated, and they will no longer suffer from various ailments. Should one hear even a single phrase of meaning from this Dharma that leads to the Mahāyāna, they will transcend delusive thoughts and escape the evil realms. Their aspirations will become sovereign, they shall obtain what they have not yet obtained, and their faculties will be complete without ever being deficient.”

If there is a person who focuses their mind with single-minded intent to diligently cultivate right practice, free from other distracting thoughts and remaining in accordance with the Dharma, all defilements and afflictions will naturally be eliminated.

If a son or daughter of good family attains faith through the resonance of the teachings and shows increased reverence for the True Dharma, they should sit upright at the foot of a tree and contemplate with single-minded focus. Should their thoughts become confused or inverted, they should begin again from the start; if the mind remains unsettled, they should reproach themselves, asking, "What is it that I have failed to do?"

If one does not eliminate the evil mind and remains subject to the cycles of suffering through kalpas without being restrained by the Way, on what day will one advance toward accomplishment and attain the state of no-outflows, thereby receiving liberation through the Dharma of equality?
Thus it is, O Most Victorious One!

One who accords with the Dharma neither dwells within the three realms nor is separate from them; furthermore, they guard themselves with the three contemplations and the seven purifications as clear prohibitions, constantly repenting past transgressions and ensuring they are not committed in the future. Such a person shall attain the eighteen unique qualities of the Buddhas, the four fearlessnesses, the five faculties, the five powers, and the gates of dhyāna, vimokṣa, and samādhi.

The Dharma he teaches is impartial and non-dual; his body is golden-hued, adorned with the primary and secondary marks; he is graced by various merits as his own ornaments; and his voice and instructions reach throughout the ten directions. This is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s attainment of the merit of the ten dharmas, which is most supreme.

What are these ten? They are: to single-mindedly contemplate the true teachings one has heard; not to oppose or be arrogant toward spiritual friends; to remain neither conceited nor self-deprecating, but always abiding in the middle way; to ensure that the actions one performs are never false or vain; to enter deeply into profound wisdom with an undistracted mind; to joyfully contemplate giving with a heart of gladness and without regret; to practice generosity before others without making distinctions; to reach the limit of suffering and proclaim the non-self; and to roam freely through supernormal powers without losing skillful means. These are called the ten dharmas by which one obtains ten merits.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
"Hear the teaching and listen with single-minded intent; Be cautious regarding the Path, free from conceptualization and aspiration.
Rely upon and receive the guidance of virtuous friends; Practice giving with mindfulness, without regret or stinginess."

"Love them as you would nourish yourself; follow their high and low status according to their character, and with a single mind, maintain mindfulness and respect. Thus one obtains the merit of ten virtues.
Most Excellent One, you should know this!"
Through the perfection of wisdom and skillful means in adapting to transformation, he attains the Vaipulya of the Bodhisattva Great Vehicle.
Because the Tathāgata appears in the world out of compassion for the mundane, he manifests various different modes of practice:
sometimes manifesting the vehicles of the Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas; sometimes remaining hidden in mountain precipices or deep caves; or again, practicing walking meditation by himself.
Reproach yourself and calculate that within your body there is not a single thing worth craving. For this reason, you should reflect:
"I have been transformed and enlightened by the Tathāgata. Those who believe my words should hold them in their hearts;
they will attain parinirvāṇa within this very life. Even if one remains among those of heterodox views and does not correct their conduct, for the sake of all such heterodox...
He studies and expounds the Dharma-drum; its method is without conceptualization and without discursive thoughts, causing all sentient beings to exhaust their outflows (*āsrava*).
All those gathered in the assembly attain subtle and wondrous wisdom. Their practices vary according to their diverse dispositions and natures;
such as these are beyond measure or calculation. Those who delight in and yearn to hear the sutras do not belong to a single category.
Those who abandon the true for the false are likewise beyond reckoning; their number at present before our eyes is difficult to measure.
There may be bodhisattvas who focus exclusively on the gates of liberation, and though they are fully equipped in their practice, they still harbor attachment to nirvana.
The reason for this is that, because they do not yet understand skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), they encounter obstacles.

The Tathāgata, through his supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-pāda*), guides them so that they may come to know; only then do they awaken to the realization that [their previous practice] was not the conduct of a bodhisattva. Yet, being again disturbed and constrained by Pāpīyān, they once more regress from this and return to the state of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).

"O Most Victorious One, you should know! The Tathāgata observes throughout the day and night with the threefold transcendental knowledge (*trividyā*): who has dull faculties and regresses rather than progressing; who advances forward to the rank of a Bodhisattva; how those who regress are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges while those who advance are like a single hair; and how they know this within their own minds yet lack supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). As for the original intention of a noble person, their mind is firm and steadfast; even if they were to attain [enlightenment], the faculties of sentient beings would be severed. The Dharma of non-action (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) is fixed and certainly without arising or ceasing, yet sentient beings harbor doubts and claim it is not the truth. Through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), one should apply oneself to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Wishing to hear and delight in the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one must first distinguish and understand the emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness of the profound essentials of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*). One must realize that impermanence is not the truth, and that there is no self, person, life-span, or soul—only voidness and quiescence."
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Most Victorious and the assembled multitude:

"Furthermore, reflect on how in the past, before I had attained Buddhahood, I was instructed by all the Tathāgatas and further guided by their majestic spiritual power. This was also attained through the mindfulness of my original vows and practices; thus I was able to receive purity and find peace in my aspirations. Now, having become a Tathāgata of equal and perfect enlightenment, fully endowed with all practices and appearing in the world, this is due to my resolute intention never retreating."
The assembly of bodhisattvas shall also be incalculable, and the transformations of their supernormal powers shall be immeasurable; they will subdue Māra without exception or chance.

When they arrive at cities, prefectures, counties, or market towns, those living beings who behold me will fix their intent upon listening to the sutras without other thoughts; they will cause the Three Jewels to flourish so that they are never severed, and all who seek the Dharma shall obtain fulfillment and attain peaceful conduct.
The Buddha again addressed the Bodhisattva Most Victorious:

"If there are sentient beings who have faith in and follow the teachings of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, they should practice thirty-six matters to ensure they do not fall into decline."
How does a bodhisattva practice thirty-six matters so as not to fall into decline?
In this regard, the bodhisattva discerns the three inclinations yet harbors no resentment; though dwelling amidst desire, he remains undefiled;
he contemplates impermanence yet maintains no conceptualization; his mental conduct is pure and he does not lose the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Seeking the dharmas of the various gates of liberation, the noble and holy ones embrace the Way to deliver sentient beings;

having severed false views, they fully know impermanence and practice the conduct of equanimity and perfect enlightenment without attachment. Following the arising and ceasing of conditions, they eliminate fetters and attachments;
whatever deeds they perform are not for their own sake, as they understand that the fundamental nature of persons is originally non-existent.
Birth occurs, yet this lifespan is subject to decay and does not endure for long; life passes away and changes like an illusion or a magical transformation.
That which has passed is forever exhausted, leaving no trace behind; that which comes has no form, yet one must again undergo existence.
The present flows on rapidly, with no known destination; through the clear wisdom of knowing karma, one realizes that the conscious spirit does not abide, but rests in the wisdom of emptiness.

Abiding in the liberation from bonds yet remaining unbound, one diligently cultivates the three matters and further practices the elimination of the three; without relying on the wisdom of emptiness, one realizes its fruit and verification.
One nurtures the physical form and life-force until reaching the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*); regarding desire, there is neither desire nor the abandoning of desire.

The right reception (*samāpatti*) of all Buddhas is ever present before them, and as they come and go and circulate through the world, they do not give rise to the state of non-conception (*asaṃjñika*).
Their resolve is always fixed upon the wisdom of the various supernormal powers; they enter deeply into the treasury of the Dharma yet perceive no point of entry.

They take the cessation of all things and non-arising as their dwelling place. It is suchness and thusness—formless and signless. Originally there is no limit, nor is there even the absence of a limit.
They never regard anything as permanent, yet they constantly contemplate impermanence. Although they perceive birth and death, they do not...
Seeing birth, one enters the five realms of existence while understanding that there are no five realms; though afflictions act as bonds, one has already abandoned them.
One maintains the state of non-action (*asaṃskṛta*), free from hope or expectation; in delivering others, it is like empty space, with nothing accomplished.
In the actions of body and speech, there is nothing to be diminished. This is called the most supreme!

The thirty-six supreme and wondrous dharmas practiced by Bodhisattvas are not within the reach of Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas; one should skillfully examine them and explain them clearly for others, ensuring that sentient beings harbor no contentious or disputatious thoughts.

The reason for this is that it is rare for sentient beings to be able to believe [this teaching]. To be able to eloquently expound the Dharma of conditions and karma is to accord with the mind of non-arising (*anutpāda*). If you observe that the minds of sentient beings are not yet firm, you should gradually open their understanding so they may attain liberation; though gain and loss differ, you must immediately set aside your own concerns and not boast of your own achievements.

Furthermore, if there should be doubt, one should contemplate through primordial non-existence (*mūla-abhāva*): the three periods of time are equal and without distinction; one perceives neither equality nor inequality. Since even perception is non-perception and there is no further seeing, how could there be any marks of form? Form itself is formless, for originally there was no form; where form-consciousness is non-consciousness, how could there be consciousness?

When the ear perceives sounds, consciousness arises to receive external tones; when the nose encounters fragrances, consciousness arises spontaneously to perceive odors, whether foul or pleasant; when the tongue encounters tastes, consciousness arises to distinguish between the beautiful and the ugly; when the body encounters the smooth or the coarse, consciousness arises because of those textures; and when the mind encounters mental objects (*dharma*), consciousness arises due to what was previously wholesome or unwholesome. Thus one thoroughly understands that all phenomena neither abide nor do not abide, and yet one does not even perceive abiding.

"O Most Victorious One, you should know that all dharmas belonging to the self and all dharmas belonging to existence are fundamentally pure, yet purity itself is not perceived; all dharmas and the self are fundamentally non-existent, yet non-existence is not perceived; even non-existence is itself non-existent, yet that non-existence is not perceived. To the wisdom and liberation of a Bodhisattva, all these are non-existent."

The Bodhisattva’s wisdom of liberation does not rely upon body or speech; neither does he exalt himself nor disparage others, for from the beginning until the end, he thoroughly realizes the state of spontaneity (*svabhāva*).
Thus, when a Bodhisattva understands the meaning of the wisdom of emptiness, he shall attain unexcelled, perfect, true, and equal enlightenment, establishing much and bringing great benefit to many.

At that time, all those gathered in the assembly—the fourfold community of disciples and the eight classes of spirits—were filled with such exultation that they could not contain themselves. Each paid homage and scattered celestial incense, flowers, *manojñā* (mind-pleasing) flowers, and *mahāmanojñā* (greatly mind-pleasing) flowers upon the Buddha and upon the bodhisattvas and great disciples. These remained suspended in the void, arrayed in rows, while musical instruments played spontaneously.
Furthermore, various devas filled the void, all emitting great sounds like natural thunderclaps, and they sighed to themselves, saying:

"The Dharma we have heard today is unprecedented since antiquity. For the sake of the bodhisattvas, the essential points of the Dharma—the teaching of emptiness and non-existence—have been expounded. The conduct, speech, and intentions thus cultivated are all firm and resolute. The turning of the wheel of Dharma previously in the Deer Park among devas and worldlings was not even worth mentioning; now we hear the Tathāgata speak of emptiness, the non-existence of dharmas, and neither arising nor ceasing. This is the supreme ultimate truth, peerless in the world and beyond measure. Never before have we heard the Dharma in such a manner."
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
May our minds be forever free from hesitation, and may the net of doubt be entirely removed so that no resentment remains.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed those assembled:

"The Bodhisattva who understands through wisdom, for the sake of all sentient beings, does not depart from the root of all dharmas; how much less would he ever distance himself from the dharma of emptiness and non-existence?"
This matter is not so. When a bodhisattva practices and studies, they should not give rise to thoughts of right and wrong.
If one remains mindful of all phenomena without attachment, one realizes that phenomena are truly profound and inconceivable.

Those whose practice of wisdom is shallow, because they lack discernment, fall into the four inversions and give rise to the hindrances of the aggregates (*skandha-āvaraṇa*); through the departure from and grasping at the sense bases (*āyatana*), they are born again.
The twelve links of dependent origination, once produced, mutually encompass the sixty-two views;
being thus encompassed, they further coincide with all the defilements and impurities of worldly toil.
A bodhisattva should always remain far removed from these, neither dwelling in their company nor abandoning them entirely, for from ignorance to death, the world is in turmoil.
Regarding perceptions and mental reflections, if one sees those who are diligent, the mind does not harbor envy toward them;

seeing those who are indolent, one likewise does not become arrogant or lazy. Toward those who uphold the precepts, one does not feel differently; seeing those who violate the precepts, the mind remains equal and non-dual.
The essence of patience is fully perfected, for anger leads to the evil realms. With a single, undistracted mind, no discursive thoughts arise.
With wisdom one delivers others from suffering so that it is forever exhausted without remainder; one should always remain far removed from all discursive thoughts and abandon worldly affairs.
What are worldly affairs?

That which is called the five aggregates, the six sense-spheres, the four great elements, the four afflictions, the eighteen bases, and the twelve links of dependent origination—those things that do not correspond with the mind—are termed worldly dharmas.
The Buddha told Jiǔshèng:

"If there is a bodhisattva who practices giving throughout the three periods of time, they should not contemplate receiving retribution in past lives; they should not think of the wealth and goods given in past lives, nor should they think of the person who received the gift in past lives. They should not think of the place where the gift was given, such as the house or dwelling, nor of the lineage, being born into such-and-such a family with such-and-such a name. Furthermore, they should not think that because they gave a gift at that time, they now receive its reward, or that by performing merit now, the future retribution will be many times greater."

Such a bodhisattva, being unaccomplished, having fallen into extremes, remaining within the realm of Māra, and severing the lineage of the Buddhas, shall ultimately never reach the unsurpassed, right, and true path to attain supreme perfect enlightenment.
The reason for this is that because there is conceptual attachment, giving with such attachment does not yield a true fruit.
Furthermore, if a bodhisattva contemplates both present and future giving, they should always maintain a firm mind free from all distracted thoughts.
At times, a bodhisattva provides whatever is lacking—clothing, food and drink, bedding and seating, and medicine for the sick—according to their needs without refusal.
One who wishes to achieve unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment understands that all phenomena are empty and realizes them as one;
they understand that empty phenomena are signless, that empty phenomena are unarisen, and that there is no creation.

There is no action and nothing to be performed; one neither perceives the time of coming nor the time of going. Through the contemplation of the emptiness of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), one realizes that there is no form.

This includes the aggregate of ethical discipline, the aggregate of wisdom, the aggregate of meditative concentration, the aggregate of liberation, and the aggregate of the vision and knowledge of liberation;

as well as the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics; and the suchness of the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-tathatā*), the stability of the dharma-realm, and the contemplation of the dharma-realm.
The non-attachment to the *dharmadhātu*, the Buddha-like state, the Buddha-concentration, the Buddha-contemplation, the Buddha’s non-attachment,
the Buddha who is without self and without that which is produced, the clarity of the mind of the path, the clarity of the mind of the Dharma, and the clarity of the mind of the assembly—
these thirteen modes of untainted wisdom-contemplation pertain to the thirteen [times] of the future, the past, and the present.

The Buddha, beholding all realms, discerns that these realms neither come nor go; he sees no arising, for phenomena are eternally abiding, neither moving nor returning. Yet all sentient beings spontaneously give rise to perceptions and conceptions; thus, for those who lack faith, he brings about transformation. He purifies the three spheres and cultivates the chamber of the Tathāgata. Although the various practices of all dharmas are not yet ultimate, his teachings differ according to the varying capacities of those who receive them.

One who wishes to purify the three fields and the five eyes should manifest the perception of unimpeded turning of the wheel of Dharma; first practicing the thirteen contemplations of the outflows-free state—this, O Most Victorious One, is called [the method].

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, possessing unimpeded wisdom and the faculty of unimpeded insight, manifests for the sake of sentient beings the Dharma-realm with its clans, surnames, and titles—immeasurable, limitless, and inconceivable—all of which are within the reach of the power of skillful means and wisdom.
At that time, Ajita again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How does a bodhisattva enter meditative concentration (samādhi), practice skillful means (upāya), and maintain the integration of wisdom without distraction?
The Buddha told Ajita:

"Thereupon, the Bodhisattva enters the concentration of non-attachment; his body, mind, and verbal teachings are free from all obstruction. He contemplates the Buddha-fields as clearly as one views beads in the palm of one's hand; he nurtures and transforms sentient beings without attachment, emitting great radiance to guide all beings and turning the Wheel of Dharma."

The Buddha’s power is unimpeded; he may take bodhisattvas as his retinue, and further, adorning his body with the wisdom of a buddha, he dwells as a buddha dwells. He travels through various lands as a buddha travels, purifying all buddha-fields and delivering beings through the liberation of a buddha. With a heart of solemn vow, he instructs people through his teachings and trains them with wisdom.
This is called the most supreme!

The concentration and samādhi into which all Buddhas enter, their sphere of activity and conduct, are inconceivable; they are without fear, without dread, and without hesitation; they listen without satiety, their minds do not turn back, nor do they grow weary; they do not abandon what they should attain by falling into other dharmas.

Why is this? Because the bodhisattva’s resolve among all phenomena is vast and expansive; their heart of great vows cannot be thwarted or destroyed. Having resolved to train and cultivate the inexhaustible source of the Buddha’s true Dharma, they empower sentient beings without ever abandoning them, understanding that sentient beings are empty and that all phenomena are likewise so.

The emptiness of all phenomena is likewise the nature of the Path; one skillfully observes the coming and going of sentient beings, pervades all things with a heart of great compassion, does not deviate from the dharmic principles practiced by the Buddhas of the three periods of time, and fully accomplishes the formless Dharma.

Why is this? It is like a man who hangs a wish-fulfilling jewel in the air; all who behold it are filled with joy. Its color is exceedingly subtle and its illumination is unimpeded, yet it does not say of itself, "I illuminate extensively."

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: from the jewel of his mind, he brings forth the light of wisdom from his mouth, which universally illumines the trichiliocosm; yet he does not say of himself, "My light of wisdom can now illuminate anything."

Why is this? It is because these bodhisattvas do not act for their own sake, but rather desire to lead sentient beings to the gate of liberation, sealing them with the sacred seal of the Buddha. They purify buddha-fields for the sake of all beings and provide protection for them, remaining free from all discursive thoughts. Their eye of wisdom illuminates everything without exception, clearly discerning the root of birth and death, as well as the eight factors of the past, future, and present, and the merit of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*). Through the supernormal power of the exhaustion of outflows, they realize the cessation of perception and feeling, which cannot be fully understood even by arhats and pratyekabuddhas.

The Bodhisattva awakens to the nature of phenomena as that which is realized: they are like illusions and transformations, like mirages in the heat, like plantain trees and wild horses, like echoes, like reflections in a mirror and the moon in water, like bubbles and dreams; all are unreal. These five aggregates of clinging are suffering, empty, and not-self, being merely a composite of the four great elements.

Furthermore, one should contemplate the six elements—earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness—which reside within the three realms: the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm. These constitute the realm of death; the Dharma-body of Nirvana is the true realm. To understand the realm of birth-and-death and the Dharma of Nirvana as one and not two, and without any distinction, is likewise true of the four great elements and the self.

If the self is empty, then all dharmas are also empty; if all dharmas are empty, then the six objects of mindfulness are likewise so. One does not fall into inverted views nor dwell in birth and death, yet one does not even conceive of realizing the Middle Way as a proof. This is called the Bodhisattva’s profound understanding of the essential principles of the Dharma; thus, those saved are not in vain, and receiving sustenance is not false. Abiding securely on the Path, there is no fruitlessness.

Furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who, employing the four immeasurable minds, deeply investigate the bottomless source of birth and death; they rescue beings with wealth and comfort them by encouraging them toward the Way. These Greatly Compassionate Bodhisattvas perceive everything they behold as treasure; mountains, rivers, rocks, cliffs, trees, stems, and branches all become the seven precious jewels, which they then use extensively for giving so that beings may attain the realization of the Way.

At that time, the Bodhisattva observes sentient beings who are attached to suffering; for their sake, he explains that the five aggregates are suffering, are old age, and lack true reality. He teaches that by practicing [the cessation of] attachment to form and suffering, one achieves the Way through the extinction of such practice. The meanings of suffering are manifold, yet attachment is its root; when these two matters are exhausted, it is called the Way.
Chapter 14: On Valor At that time, the Bodhisattva Most Victorious (Vijayin) came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How is it that the initial resolve and practice of a bodhisattva cannot be interrupted?"
"How is it that a bodhisattva’s mental consciousness is secure and cannot be abandoned?
At that time, the World-Honored One told Most Excellent: "A bodhisattva who has first resolved on awakening should study what is to be studied;

they do not linger in birth and death nor do they fear a self. Although they dwell in the past, future, and present, they remain without dread. They are thus able to courageously destroy false views. Upon first hearing the flavor of the Dharma, their faculty of faith is perfected. Their minds are constantly fixed upon the state of cessation, always remaining detached from worldly affairs. They aspire only to the unsurpassed, right, and true path; they consult and praise the scriptures, listening to them without weariness. Even when encountering suffering or pleasure, they do not become weary."

The reason for this is that their minds are firm and immovable; after passing through one, two, or three lifetimes, they shall, at the appropriate time, attain the Tathāgata’s samādhi of right reception and meditative concentration.

Furthermore, he attains the Samādhi of Faithful Reception Without Deception, and further attains the Samādhi of Conceptual Retention and Receiving Prediction; gradually, he reaches the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas from nowhere. For this reason, it is said that the internal practice of a Bodhisattva who has resolved his mind cannot be interrupted by anyone.

The Bodhisattva focuses his mind exclusively on non-attachment to the marks of form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*). He does not contemplate whether things are permanent or impermanent, suffering or pleasure, beautiful or ugly, distant or near. Furthermore, he does not contemplate phenomena of the past, future, or present. Nor does he think, "I shall attain Buddhahood and preside over a trichiliocosm. He does not contemplate the notion of existence, nor does he contemplate the notions of birth, attachment, defilement, fetters, or mental volition. Through immeasurable gateways, he receives the wondrous Dharma; yet he neither returns nor perceives returning, neither feels aversion nor perceives aversion, neither feels insufficiency nor perceives insufficiency, neither abandons nor perceives abandoning. There is no relinquishing and no destruction; there is no seeing and no having seen; there is no increase and no decrease, no difference and no change; it is not a spontaneous activity, yet it is not a lack of activity.
The reason for this is that what is called "spontaneity" (svabhāva) is encompassed by the dharma-realm of empty space.

Thus, the Bodhisattva spontaneously accomplishes an infinite and immeasurable mind of great vows; without weariness or distress, and without ever regressing, they resolve to deliver all sentient beings.

The reason for this is that the Bodhisattva, desiring to deliver all sentient beings and lead them to parinirvāṇa, remains for seventeen kalpas without abandoning or forsaking them, discerning that all dharmas of the three periods of time are empty and quiescent—namely, that all dharmas are empty and all dharmas are without self.
Why is this? Because they desire to go from here to there.
A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, using the divine eye to observe as far as the realm of space, considers: "Are there more sentient beings dwelling upon the earth element?"
"Are the sentient beings in the realm of empty space many?
Indeed, when one observes the sentient beings in empty space, they cannot be calculated and have no limits.
The Bodhisattva with the divine eye further reflected:
"What I have now observed is exceedingly profound and far-reaching: would there be more formless sentient beings within the empty space that encircles the four continents and Mount Sumeru?"
"Are those with form more numerous?
The Buddha told Most Victorious:
"Even a Bodhisattva with the divine eye cannot know the number of those without form."

The reason for this is that such is not their realm. Now I shall provide an analogy to further clarify this meaning; those with clear vision should understand this parable. Suppose there were a square space of eight cubits, equal in height and breadth, without any vacant gaps;

if one were to calculate the number of formless beings within it, they would be equal in number to the beings of the four continents. To know their count, one would count from one up to a hundred million (*koṭi*), treating each hundred million as a single unit; then, starting again from one up to a hundred million, one would treat each subsequent hundred million as a single unit. Counting in this manner up to seven times, such is the limit of the number of formless beings in empty space.
He further addressed Varapuruṣa:

"When the Bodhisattva Divyacakṣus observes the formless sentient beings in space, it is like a person looking at a great square stone that is level from top to bottom, solid and without flaw; therefore, he cannot know their number."

When a Bodhisattva who has resolved upon enlightenment first begins their training and ascends to the stage of a Bodhisattva, if they are able to deliver that many sentient beings without their own minds wavering, you should know that they will not be disturbed by Māra. Wandering through the triple world, they rely upon spiritual friends; thus, the perils of fear and dread shall no longer arise. For any Bodhisattva who dwells in this state, it will not be long before they receive a sincere prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*). Practicing skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), they inspire and assist others, pointing the way to Nirvāṇa and declaring the certainty of liberation. Furthermore, they expound the Four Noble Truths as the seal of the Tathāgata, distinguishing each one clearly to reveal the path.

If there are sentient beings who are unwilling to awaken, he employs countless skillful means to act as their guide. Those who are deluded by habitual ignorance and thereby brought to various sufferings can sever their craving and desire; thus, being in accord with non-attachment, they immediately attain transcendence and perfect enlightenment. All the sages and worthies remain silent, for this is liberation.

That which is called "liberation" refers to liberation from birth, old age, sickness, and death; yet that [liberation] neither dies nor undergoes death, and it is neither liberated nor is it an act of liberating.
What, then, is liberated?

Without attachment, without bondage, without cessation, and without arising; without anything to be accomplished, without anything to be performed, and without anything to be attained—this is what accords with the Right Path.

Sentient beings are deluded and obstructed, not being liberated from time to time; out of compassion for them, the Tathāgata appears in the world. Wherever he travels, he manifests as a Guide. Those sentient beings who hear the Dharma reach the stage of non-retrogression. If there are those who joyfully receive and uphold the True Dharma, they shall attain the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

The Bodhisattva who has resolved upon enlightenment constantly contemplates and reflects: from what do the six decays (ṣaḍāyatana)—eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—arise, and into what do they cease?

Phenomena arise from phenomena themselves, and phenomena cease from phenomena themselves. One perceives neither the deviant nor the correct; one neither constructs nor acts, and does not perceive "this is mine" or "this is not mine. One does not rely on internal nature for self-observation, nor should one rely on external things for discernment.
Furthermore, one should reflect: form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not transcend past form;

past form is not found within, nor without, nor in between the two. Past feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness do not transcend past feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;
past feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not found within, nor without, nor in between the two. They do not transcend the past.
Form abides; it is not past form that abides, nor does it exist at the limit, nor is it here.
It does not transcend the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, and dharmas; nor is it found in past eye, ear, nose, mouth, body, or mind-dharmas.
It is neither internal, nor external, nor obtainable in between the two. It does not transcend the conceptualization and cognition of cessation, nor does it abide therein.

It is not found within, nor without, nor in between the two; it is likewise for the future, present, and past forms, feelings, perceptions, mental formations, and consciousness, as well as for the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, and their respective cognitions and cessations.
"Furthermore, Most Victorious One!

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva cultivates the unimpeded path through supernormal wisdom, even if one were to calculate all the meritorious wisdom-activities of all Buddhas together, multiplying them tenfold, a hundredfold, a thousandfold, or ten-thousandfold, it would not equal the merit of a Bodhisattva who, having resolved their mind, establishes a single sentient being in the unsurpassed resolve for enlightenment, enabling them to achieve all-knowledge and fulfill all the dharmas of the Buddhas. Such a person has severed delusive thoughts and no longer harbors doubt; there are no gods or worldlings who do not revere and prostrate before them. They realize that all phenomena are illusory transformations and not real, and as all embodied beings advance toward the Path, they immediately attain the power of the Tathāgata’s spiritual feet."

At that time, the assembly of fourteen billion beings on the seat thirsted for the Tathāgata’s virtue of supernatural power (*ṛddhi*), longing to behold the Tathāgata manifest his majestic transformations.
Knowing the thoughts in the minds of the gathered assembly, the Buddha immediately emitted a great radiance from his seat;
light also issued from all the pores of his body, with hundreds of thousands of billions of rays of light emanating from each and every pore. One by one...
The radiance contains hundreds of billions of luminous night-shining divine jewels, intricately carved and inlaid with various precious gems;

it is covered above by a profusion of flowers and diverse fragrances. At each of the four corners of the jewels hang four fragrant necklaces, and upon each jewel there are hundreds of billions of canopies;
within each jeweled canopy are hundreds of billions of spontaneously appearing lotus flowers.
Upon each of the lion thrones were hundreds of thousands of billions of diverse colors;
within each color were hundreds of thousands of billions of mani-jewels atop lotus flowers;
upon each flower was further a hundred thousand billion canopies made of various extraordinary jewels; and beneath each canopy were hundreds of thousands...
There are billions of Tathāgatas preaching the Dharma; each Tathāgata possesses hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddha-fields,
and in each field there are hundreds of thousands of billions of natural bathing pools, and in each bathing pool there are hundreds of thousands of billions of wild ducks,
geese, and mandarin ducks sporting naturally.

At that time, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas upon the Jewel-Interlaced Platforms again emitted hundreds of thousands of billions of rays of light. Within each ray of light there were further emanated Buddhas, and each emanated Buddha spoke of the merits practiced by bodhisattvas who have resolved their minds upon enlightenment; they taught the twelve links of dependent origination and the dharmas of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self as the gateway to Nirvāṇa. Within each gateway, they turned hundreds of thousands of billions of dharmas of non-retrogression—dharmas not turned since ancient times, which the Tathāgata now turns for them. They manifested the majestic deportment of Buddhas and transformations of spiritual power (*ṛddhi*) such as had never been seen or heard before, inconceivable and beyond calculation.
At that time, all those gathered in the assembly marveled at what they had never before experienced, exclaiming:

"How extraordinary! How marvelous! It is by our own merit that we are able to behold this miraculous transformation—this blazing of the Dharma, this kindling of the Dharma, this inexhaustible manifestation."
“The Tathāgata is like the *tathāgatagarbha*: he does not abide in abiding; he is without form or image and without root.
He is neither attained nor obtained, neither gained nor acquired. He is profoundly deep and remote, real and not false. His wisdom is vast and extensive;
he eliminates ignorance and delusion yet does not destroy them. He accomplishes the *dharmadhātu* and transcends the future.”
The teachings of all Buddhas of the past and present appear before them; they manifest the power of the Tathāgatas to augment the Buddha-fields;
they produce the Bodhisattva path through the seal of the Buddha-mind; within this present life, they become Dharma-kings with pure eyes;
their wisdom-eye is purified and their spiritual lineage is fully matured; and their unimpeded Buddha-eye perceives through the wisdom-eye.
Discerning the meanings of phrases to open the gates of the Dharma, accomplishing the bodhicitta with virtuous friends, not disparaging realms nor destroying the spiritual lineage,
acting as a protective shelter for all sentient beings, achieving success in the household life, remaining fearless when amidst the multitude,
and employing skillful means in all circumstances so that none remain untransformed— this is called [the perfection of wisdom].
Their virtue is pure and free from further longing; their gestation in the womb is perfectly regulated. They increase the karmic activity of superior wisdom, raising clouds that are without cover;
the fierce fire of their wisdom burns away the masses of doubt and fetters. They proclaim the correct teaching, shaking it throughout the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*);

they possess the four immeasurables of compassion, the dhāraṇīs, and profound discernment. With the nine contemplations and six karmas, they possess courageous strength and fearlessness, and are endowed with faith and mindfulness.

The practice of wisdom and concentration is inexhaustible; entering samādhi by contemplating the ten directions, prostrating, revering, and making offerings to all Buddhas—this is called the supreme Bodhisattva Mahāsattva’s mind that cannot be discouraged or destroyed.
It is just as the nature of a bodhisattva is empty by its very essence; one who possesses eyes knows this to be emptiness, yet emptiness does not know of itself, saying, "I am empty.

The fundamental practice of a bodhisattva is likewise so: though they deliver beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and even more than that, and reach the buddha-fields where various Buddhas dwell to deliver sentient beings beyond all calculation, the bodhisattva does not think to themselves, "I have now delivered so many beings and caused them to reach the tranquil, unconditioned state of nirvana";
nor do they say, "By virtue of this karmic fruit, I shall attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path."

The Bodhisattva who has resolved his mind maintains a firm resolve; from the first setting forth until reaching the site of enlightenment, sitting beneath the King of Trees and subduing the hosts of Māra, all the merit, blessings, and virtuous deeds performed therein are dedicated entirely for the sake of sentient beings and not for himself. This is like empty space, which universally covers everything without exception, yet does not know itself, nor say, "I am empty."

The Tathāgata’s divine virtue and the light of his wisdom embrace all common people, causing them to achieve the Dharma-eye. Being neither detached nor attached, all dharmas are indestructible. Without a person or a self, he uses the bright sword of skillful means through wisdom—the correct teaching employed by all Buddhas—to eliminate the net of doubt with immeasurable merit.

This is the practice cultivated by Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas; it is the Bodhisattva’s conduct that purifies the three Brahma-abodes. Therein, there is neither emptiness nor non-emptiness; emptiness is neither produced nor does it exist as anything. It is without person, without self, without life-span, and without vital principle. One neither perceives birth nor perceives death; one walks alone without companion, beyond the reach of thought. One does not destroy the objective realm; it is without conceptualization and is empty. It is neither produced, nor is production perceived, nor is emergence perceived. There is no going and no coming, no action and no creation. The Dharma-realm is immeasurable, forming the activity of the site of enlightenment; the realm of space is boundless, free from all fetters and attachments, yet for the sake of sentient beings, it establishes a dwelling place.

When the notions of "mine" and "not mine" give rise to the conceit of a self, the bodhisattva maintains his resolve and, relying on the roots of goodness and immeasurable wisdom, purifies that path; he removes the defilements of the mind through the intellect and eliminates them with wisdom.
"O Most Victorious One!

When a Bodhisattva enters the Samādhi of Pure Contemplation, they observe the sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions, discerning: who should practice according to the Dharma, who should practice according to wisdom, and who should correspond with pure conduct?"
If there are sentient beings who should receive the Dharma, one shall then preach the twenty-five dharmas to them.
What are these twenty-five? They are:
the signlessness of all dharmas, the formlessness of all dharmas, the patience regarding all dharmas, the perception of all dharmas, and all dharmas...
Rootless; the sphere of all phenomena is unattainable; all phenomena are without anything to be grasped; the entrance into the non-duality of all phenomena;
all phenomena are beyond measure; all phenomena cannot be severed; all phenomena are so profound they cannot be pursued;
all phenomena are the awakening of that which is not awakened; the power of all phenomena is indestructible; all phenomena...
Regarding "accomplishment and non-accomplishment": all phenomena are indestructible yet are destroyed; all phenomena are impermanent yet transcend permanence;
all phenomena are undefiled; all phenomena practice purity; all phenomena are the contemplation of nature; all phenomena are untainted;
all phenomena have already relinquished the past; all phenomena uproot doubt and remove the net; and all phenomena give rise to wisdom from no source.

Receiving the prediction [of enlightenment], wherein all dharmas are fundamentally non-existent and lack even the name of "suffering"—this is called the Bodhisattva’s pure cultivation of the twenty-five dharmas.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva practices the wisdom of the three types of patience: the wisdom of transgression, the wisdom beyond transgression, and the wisdom that is neither beyond nor not beyond transgression.
What is the bodhisattva’s practice of transcending wisdom?
The indestructible body of the dharma-realm is primordially non-existent; it is that which the Tathāgata practices, not that which is cultivated by pratyekabuddhas or arhats.
Non-transgression wisdom is the superior clarity of wisdom practiced by the noble ones and *pratyekabuddhas*; it is not the practice of Buddhas or *arhats*.
Furthermore, that which is neither non-transgression wisdom nor not non-transgression wisdom is the practice of *arhats*, not the practice of Buddhas or *pratyekabuddhas*.
What is transcendent wisdom? This is the domain of the Buddhas, not that of Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas.

In this regard, in the mere snap of a finger, a Bodhisattva, through the mindfulness of wisdom, thinks: "I shall extensively deliver sentient beings who are bottomless; my wisdom-karma of boundless and shoreless conditioned thoughts and the adamantine samādhi shall never regress. This heart of great resolve surpasses that of Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas; this is called transcendent wisdom, which is not the practice of Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas.
Why is it also called "non-transcending wisdom"?
It is that which is practiced by the noble Pratyekabuddhas;

herein, the Bodhisattva resolves his mind and undertakes training, desiring to purify the Dharma-realm and guide sentient beings, proclaiming the Buddha-dharma and expounding the nectar-like wisdom, seeking the site of enlightenment for the sake of the Unsurpassed Way.

If there are sentient beings who go directly from a single path to where a bodhisattva dwells, and bestow upon beggars whatever they cherish—whether their head, eyes, marrow, brain, kingdom, city, wife, children, or other beloved things—and do so except for their parents and teachers, seeking no reward for the fruits of such giving; this is the second path.

In this way, from one lifetime to a hundred lifetimes, and from one kalpa to a hundred kalpas, although he bestowed wealth and gifts, he did not perceive the objects themselves. He did not see to whom the objects belonged, from where they arose, where they originally came from, or where they went when they ceased. Understanding that objects have no fundamental basis, he did not perceive any dwelling place or house for them.
At that time, this bodhisattva, observing with the wisdom of emptiness, perceives neither body nor objects, neither person, nor even where the gift is bestowed.

However, this bodhisattva has accumulated practices for a very long time, and his mind and intentions are swift; desiring to realize the unsurpassed, right, and true path, he aspires to deliver sentient beings and purify the Buddha-land.

However, this bodhisattva delights in solitude and tranquility, constantly dwelling among mountain crags. With a mind focused on stillness and mindfulness fixed before him, he reflects within himself:

"The manifold virtues I have previously practiced are fully perfected; I shall surely attain the unsurpassed, true, and correct path of supreme enlightenment. Yet, when a Buddha appears in the world, his body is adorned with the various marks, and he extensively delivers sentient beings to the shore of the unconditioned. It is essential that the Great Sage first enters parinirvāṇa in the realm of no-remainder; only then shall I advance to achieve the Buddha-way."

The Buddha told Most Victorious (Jiǎngshèng): “The thoughts and practices of that bodhisattva’s vows were not in error. When the Tathāgata had finished his teaching while in the world and entered parinirvāṇa in the nirvana without remainder, and when the True Dharma had been extinguished such that there was no longer a Buddha in the world for one kalpa, two kalpas, or even up to a hundred kalpas, the bodhisattva in the mountains and marshes would reproach himself, saying: ‘Alas! My efforts have been in vain. A long time has passed since the Buddha left the world, and the Semblance Dharma has been extinguished; sentient beings with whom I shared past affinities are all dwelling in their respective places, their minds filled with afflictions. Wandering restlessly, he went beneath a tree and scraped the bark with the nail of his right index finger. Striking exactly upon a hollow spot, it made a sharp *huó* sound. His mind suddenly awakened, and he immediately attained the unsurpassed, true, and perfect Way.”

Looking around to left and right, he saw no attendants; his form was concealed and his marks hidden as he did not turn the wheel of Dharma, appearing like an ordinary person. Having transcended the human realm, this is called the practice of a wise and holy Pratyekabuddha who possesses non-surpassing wisdom, yet is neither a Buddha nor an Arhat.
What is meant by "neither surpassing wisdom nor not surpassing wisdom"?
It refers to that which is cultivated by Arhats, but not by Buddhas or Pratyekabuddhas.
In this regard, since time immemorial, the Bodhisattva has accumulated practices through diligent effort, desiring to attain unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment.
The Way of the Most Perfectly Awakened One consists of practicing giving, patience, diligence, meditation, and wisdom;
or giving away one’s head, eyes, kingdom, wealth, wife, children, servants, and attendants;

never refusing those who come with requests, even if it means piercing one’s own body to shed blood exceeding the waters of the four seas, or offering one’s own bones as alms throughout the four continents.
However, within that state they do not attain realization; gradually regressing, they fall back into the conduct of ordinary worldlings.
With a mind weary of birth and death that does not advance vigorously, they secretly regret their past actions in their hearts.

Seeking only to liberate themselves while abandoning sentient beings, they eventually employ skillful means to seek out a teacher from whom to receive instruction; by upholding the Dharma of the Śrāvakas, they finally attain it.
Upon awakening, one reflects upon former meritorious efforts and perceives that they cannot be attained;
this is called both non-transcendent wisdom and not non-transcendent wisdom—the practice of an Arhat, and not that of a Buddha or a Pratyekabuddha.
What is the bodhisattva’s correspondence with pure conduct?
This is that which is practiced by Buddhas, arhats, and pratyekabuddhas.

That which is called pure conduct consists of purifying the three spheres, purifying the three eyes, and purifying the three aggregates; it is the purity of ethical discipline, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the vision and knowledge of liberation. From the three wholesome dharmas up to the eighteen dharmas free from outflows, all wholesome dharmas—both mundane and supramundane—are entirely purified.

Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Arhats cultivate this pure conduct; upon reaching the attainment of the Way, they do not undergo intermediate rebirth. No manifold perceptions arise, nor can they be perceived; there is neither arising nor ceasing, nor is there any cessation of consciousness. Where there is an end and a beginning, there is a dwelling place; but for one who realizes there is no end and no beginning, how could there be any location?
At that time, the Bodhisattva Most Victorious again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

How is it that the mind of a bodhisattva who has detached from desire neither increases nor decreases, and furthermore does not conceive thoughts of this as suffering or pleasure, or this as beautiful or ugly?”
"Furthermore, do you not also refrain from thinking of the beginning, middle, or end?
Regarding the dhyāna, śamatha, and samādhi of the past, future, and present, do you not likewise refrain from thinking to yourself, 'I am free from desire'?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Most Victorious (Jinvarāja), saying:

"The desireless Bodhisattva dwells within the realm of desire, traveling everywhere to preach the Dharma and provide instruction. Although his mind is unstained—like one standing amidst hot ashes or in a bottomless pit of fire—he takes pity on those sentient beings who are bound by the four torrents and submerged in the twelve seas. Seeking an escape, they do not know the way to proceed; yet the Bodhisattva’s inner mind endures this without finding it difficult. He discerns the five aggregates—the phenomena of their arising and decaying: form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—and contemplates the four great elements and all that is born and extinguished as being like bubbles on water, mirages in the wild, or plantains and illusions: empty and unreal, and lacking any solidity."

Why is this? Because the most profound Dharma is difficult to exhaustively fathom. The profound nature of form (*rūpa*) is such that the Path is likewise; the profound nature of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) is such that worldly phenomena (*loka-dharma*) are likewise; the profound nature of worldly phenomena is such that the realm of empty space (*ākāśa-dhātu*) is likewise. To skillfully examine the realm of empty space and the realm of phenomena (*dharma-dhātu*), one finds therein no perception of consciousness, self (*ātman*), person (*pudgala*), or life-span (*jīva*). To calculate these things is truly like an illusion or a transformation. Contemplating the eight worldly conditions of the mundane world, one sees they are turbid, defiled, and obstruct the person’s progress toward the Path; yet through pure contemplation, one realizes they have no fixed location whatsoever.

Why is this so? Because it is the nature of phenomena that they are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self. A person with eyes who can penetrate this is called a Bodhisattva whose mind neither increases nor decreases, who perceives neither suffering nor pleasure, neither good nor evil, neither beauty nor ugliness, and who is entirely free from attachment to the dependent origination of the three periods of time.

The element of earth is solid, its sphere being naturally so; the nature of water is moisture, its nature being naturally supple; the nature of fire is blazing, its nature being naturally hot; the nature of wind is drifting and wavering, moving and turning without staying still. When observing the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the four great elements are quiescent and non-existent. From what do earth, water, fire, and wind arise, and into what do they cease?

If a bodhisattva discriminates within the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), should the earth element increase, the natures of water, fire, and wind will each become discordant; consciousness will naturally sink and gradually become disassociated, for the earth is heavy while consciousness is light, and each desires to separate from the other.
If the water element increases, the realms of earth, fire, and wind will successively weaken, and consciousness will suddenly wish to depart, finding no peace in its abode.
It is like a person staying in a quiet room who intends to go out to another village; first he steps his right foot outside the threshold—this is called the increase of the earth element;
next he extends his right hand outside the door—this is called the increase of the water element;
then he steps his left foot outside the threshold—this is called the increase of the fire element.
Furthermore, extending the left hand outside the gate may be called the increase of the nature of wind (*vāyu*).
Advancing forward toward the path is what is meant by "the spirit departs";
arriving at the village signifies proceeding toward the five destinies (*pañcagati*). One who understands this thoroughly comprehends the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
It is neither hard nor soft, neither hot nor light; yet hardness is where it resides, softness is where it reaches, heat is where it tends, and lightness is where it moves.

In this way, the Bodhisattva discerns the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); though he observes each aspect individually, there is no fixed location. He contemplates that the nature of the dharma-realm is inherently diverse: the cultivation of the spirit and the growth of the body each differ from one another.
