Among the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), fire is the most potent poison, while the other three elements are naturally harmonious with one another.
The reason for this is that a bodhisattva should observe that the four great elements within and without are likewise so.
The four great elements of sentient beings in the three realms are not the same; yet, if one seeks their origin, no location can be known.
Furthermore, one should contemplate the destination of the six sense-faculties: the eye is empty and eye-consciousness is also empty; one who understands emptiness is the Dharma-realm.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should further contemplate and understand the six decays (*ṣadāyatana*): when the eye perceives form, the form does not exist, nor does the preceding object that enters as form exist; the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are likewise so.

Furthermore, a bodhisattva should study the characteristics of truth and the characteristics that are not truth, the characteristics of the path and the characteristics that are not the path, and the characteristics of emptiness and the characteristics that are not emptiness.
"How does a bodhisattva study the characteristics of truth and the characteristics that are not truth?"

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva thoroughly understands that all things are fundamentally non-existent (*mūla-abhāva*); this fundamental non-existence is one and without duality. He also knows the realization of the Way, yet there is no realization; he neither perceives the acceptance of realization nor the non-acceptance of realization, nor does he perceive what is appropriate nor what is inappropriate. To fully comprehend what is appropriate and what is inappropriate—this is called the characteristic of truth (*satya-lakṣaṇa*).
The mark of truth for a bodhisattva is that it is true in emptiness and true even when far from emptiness; it neither exists nor does not exist—this is called the mark of truth.
Through the adamantine right concentration, one relies on emptiness, abandons the habitual grasping of the root, and attains its exhaustion.
To understand these three matters is also the characteristic of truth (*satyalakṣaṇa*).

The characteristic of truth for a bodhisattva is to realize that there is no reality within and to know that there is no entry without; not seeing what is pleasant or not seeing what is unpleasant; not seeing what is possible or impossible—this too is the characteristic of truth. Within, they do not sever right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*);

without, they manifest such that, as if dwelling in seclusion, their mind is always tranquil. Even if the external world is tumultuous, they know that the abiding in suffering and so forth is equal to whatever they encounter.

As for the characteristics of the Truths (*satya-lakṣaṇa*): the realization of the Path verifies that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are empty and that the five aggregates have no master; that which arises through conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is likewise empty; one does not abide in nor perceive abiding in wisdom, exhausting all conceptualization (*saṃjñā*); one does not abide in doubt or fetters, nor does one abide in them; one does not dwell upon the five matters, nor follow the ten wholesome or ten unwholesome paths, nor the beginning and end of the world. This is called the characteristic of the Truths.
When a bodhisattva practices in this way regarding the characteristics of truth, they do not regress.

That which is not a characteristic of truth is the ultimate reality (paramārtha) of the realm of empty space; knowing it as quiescent, conditioned by liberation, and without bondage—this is called the bodhisattva’s non-characteristic of truth.
"What is the mark of the path and the mark of what is not the path for a bodhisattva?

To harbor hesitation, fetters, and doubt; to be stained by what is unlovely in the world; to be self-opinionated, perverse, harmful, violent, and fallen into suffering—this is called the mark of the path."

To perform an action in the present life and receive its retribution in a future life, without relying on a teacher or turning toward a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra), is also a characteristic of the path.
What, then, is that which is not a characteristic of the path for a bodhisattva?

That which is not the mark of the Way consists of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, which are the entryway into conditioned and unconditioned dharmas; it does not abide in duality, nor is it distant from duality; it does not follow conditions, nor is it separate from conditions; it does not dwell in conditions, nor does it pursue conditions; it is neither transcending nor non-transcending; it is neither fruition nor non-fruition; it is not one, two, three, four, or even ten, yet it is not non-ten; it is neither produced nor unproduced; it is neither extinction nor non-extinction; it is neither arising-and-ceasing nor non-arising-and-ceasing; it is neither verbal teaching nor non-verbal teaching; it is neither understanding emptiness nor non-understanding of emptiness; it is neither cessation through reflection nor non-cessation through reflection.

If a bodhisattva examines these twenty-four matters and, through contemplation, realizes that the beginning and the end are distinguished within the mind, they will not dwell in birth and death and remain free from bondage and attachment. Possessing neither a competitive mind nor arrogance, they neither exalt themselves nor disparage others; they should then enter the Samādhi of Shattered Body and Wandering Dispersion. Among the ten billion concentrations, this is the foremost; it is the most honored and noble, with nothing surpassing it. This is not the realm of Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas.

At that time, the World-Honored One entered meditative absorption while seated upon his throne; this samādhi is named "Single-Minded Fearlessness. He caused the fourfold assembly to become unified from top to bottom, such that each was free from extraneous thoughts and devoid of distracted imaginings.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Varaprabha, saying:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon this well!
I shall now analyze the samādhi for you, so that all who have gathered here may be free from doubt."
The Most Excellent One replied:
“So be it, World-Honored One!
I wish and desire to hear it; may those who seek joy obtain peace and security.”
The Buddha told Most Victorious:

"There is a samādhi called 'Dispelling All Knots,' which causes sentient beings with form in infinite and immeasurable lands to eliminate suffering and pain, so that they no longer have any afflictions.
Furthermore, there is a samādhi called 'Brave Compassionate Radiance,' which causes all sentient beings to be free from enmity."
Furthermore, there is a samādhi named "Abundant Virtue"; when the Tathāgata enters this samādhi, he causes all classes of sentient beings to be free from thoughts of hunger and thirst.
Furthermore, there is a samādhi named "Purity"; when the Tathāgata enters this samādhi, he causes all sentient beings to attain the purity of the Dharma-eye.
Furthermore, there is a samādhi named "Purity of the Auditory Faculty"; when the Tathāgata enters this samādhi, he causes all classes of sentient beings to obtain the divine ear for hearing.

Furthermore, there is the Samādhi of Mental Quiescence; when the Tathāgata enters this samādhi, he causes the various classes of sentient beings to turn away from the heterodox and proceed toward the orthodox.
Furthermore, there is the Samādhi of Eliminating Evil; when the Tathāgata enters this samādhi, he causes the various classes of sentient beings to cultivate the ten paths of wholesome action.
Furthermore, there is a samādhi named Solitary Pacing; when the Tathāgata enters this samādhi, he causes the various classes of sentient beings to abandon false views and receive the true path.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi called Pathway to the Goal; when the Tathāgata enters this samādhi, he causes sentient beings to proceed toward the Way without confusion.
Furthermore, there is a samādhi named Accomplishment; when the Tathāgata enters this samādhi, he causes sentient beings to abandon evil precepts and take up pure precepts.
Furthermore, there is a samādhi named Joy of Shame and Remorse; when the Tathāgata enters this samādhi, he causes sentient beings to uphold patience.

Furthermore, there is a samādhi called "Advancing in Virtue"; when the Tathāgata enters this samādhi, he causes those among the classes of sentient beings who are indolent and fallen to arouse a spirit of heroic vigor.

Furthermore, there is a samādhi called "Solitary Without Companion"; when the Tathāgata enters this samādhi, he causes sentient beings who delight in delusion to swiftly enter meditative concentration.
Furthermore, there is a samādhi called "Subduing"; it causes sentient beings who cling to folly to be adorned with wisdom of their own accord.
Furthermore, there is a samādhi named "Without Leakage," which causes sentient beings who lack faith to dwell securely in the faculty of faith;
furthermore, there is a samādhi named "Virtue of Retention," which, when the Tathāgata enters this samādhi, enables sentient beings who have heard little to attain great learning;

furthermore, there is a samādhi named "Regulation of Dignified Conduct," which, when the Tathāgata enters this samādhi, causes all classes of sentient beings to maintain a composed appearance and not lose their sense of propriety.
Furthermore, there is a samādhi named Bestowing Grace; when the Tathāgata enters this samādhi, he causes sentient beings attached to desire to be forever free from craving.
Furthermore, there is a samādhi named Deliverance; when the Tathāgata enters this samādhi, he causes sentient beings who are prone to anger to sever their resentment and hatred.
Furthermore, there is a samādhi named Non-delusion; when the Tathāgata enters this samādhi, he causes sentient beings who are ignorant and deluded to cultivate the practice of wisdom.

Furthermore, there is the Samādhi of Universal Pervasion; when the Tathāgata enters this samādhi, he causes all classes of sentient beings not to be attached to the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*).

Again, there is a samādhi named "All Bodies and Physical Forms"; when the Tathāgata enters this samādhi, he causes all sentient beings in the lands of the ten directions to manifest hundreds of thousands of billions of physical forms, yet those sentient beings do not know one another.
O Most Victorious One! To state the essentials briefly:

even if the Tathāgata were to speak for eon after eon, up to a hundred eons, regarding the samādhis entered by the Tathāgata, they could never be fully exhausted; only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is able to expound them thoroughly.
At that time, Varaprabha came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How extraordinary and marvelous! The transformations produced by the physical marks of the Tathāgata’s body are inconceivable and beyond measure; he adorns himself with formless skillful means."

Regarding the samādhis spoken of and entered by the Tathāgata, which were never before seen or heard: if there is a bodhisattva who, upon hearing the name of this samādhi, fixes their mind upon it and recites it, they will always attain mastery wherever they travel. Furthermore, if one encourages others and rejoices on their behalf, having thereby made offerings to all the Buddhas’ teachings, this becomes a realm beyond that of the śrāvakas and is likewise unattainable for those of the pratyekabuddha vehicle.

If there are those who slander this samādhi of concentration, they will dwell perpetually in darkness and never attain clear understanding; even if they subsequently obtain a human body, they will enter the prison of no rescue, yet their transgression will still be slight and insufficient to mention.

If one harbors hatred or envy toward the samādhi of meditative concentration, the measure of their transgression is difficult to fathom, lasting for many kalpas; they will be deaf, blind, and mute, never hearing the Dharma. Even if they obtain human form, they will constantly suffer much pain, being double-tongued and deceitful, yet unable to speak.

Were it not for a bodhisattva who is vast in learning and widely erudite, they would be unable to believe in this samādhi of right concentration. If there is one who encourages others to recite and practice this samādhi, they shall immediately behold the Buddhas of the ten directions. Furthermore, as I now expound the intent of this concentration, if one’s resolve remains unchanging, they will correspond to right concentration.
At that time, Jyotiṣprabha, empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"Today, all those who have gathered in this assembly—the bodhisattvas, the fourfold assembly, devas, nāgas, spirits, and ghosts—all desire to behold the concentration of the Tathāgata and the wonders it can stir; they may thus receive much nourishment and achieve great accomplishment."

I only pray that the World-Honored One will look upon us with compassion and pity, emitting a great radiance that illuminates the Buddha-fields of the Buddhas throughout the ten directions, so that the pure and virtuous beings therein may receive this light, be transformed, and all attain liberation.

At that time, the World-Honored One approved what had been said. Immediately upon his seat, he entered meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in accordance with its form; this samādhi was named "The Concentrated Mind of the Wheel of the Right Toe. He emitted a great radiance, and after that radiance had illuminated this Sahā world-system, it further illuminated the *Gaṅgā*-sands of lands belonging to the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Bodhisattvas from the lands of the ten directions, numbering in the hundreds of billions, followed that light and arrived in this Sahā world-system.

To the east of here, beyond as many Buddha-fields as there are grains of sand in ninety-six Ganges Rivers, there is a land named Sāgararatna. There dwells a Buddha named Ratnaviśuddha Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttarapuruṣa, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān, who currently resides and teaches the Dharma. In that place, there was a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva named Pratibhānamati-avaivartika; seeing this light, he went to the presence of the Tathāgata Ratnaviśuddha, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and stood to one side.
At that time, the Tathāgata Ratnaviśuddha addressed the Bodhisattva Prajñāmati, saying:

"When you arrive in that land, maintain your dignified deportment without failing in propriety. Why is this? Because the dispositions of those in that land are stubborn and their conduct is impetuous; do not be affected by their suffering or pleasure. The sentient beings of that land mostly harbor arrogance and do not comply with the True Dharma; if you see any shortcomings in them, be careful not to be startled or afraid. If you can act in this manner, you should know that now is the right time."
The many bodhisattvas in that buddha-field addressed their Buddha, saying:
"We have truly gained great benefit and merit; we congratulate ourselves on not having been born in the Land of Endurance."

At that time, the Bodhisattva Pratibhānakūṭa, surrounded by ten thousand bodhisattvas in front and behind, arrived at this Sahā world in the time it takes a strong man to bend and extend his arm, and stood before the Buddha Śākyamuni.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing [the answer], addressed Most Victorious, saying:
"Do you see the Bodhisattva Discerning Wisdom and the other bodhisattvas? He replied:
“Yes, I have seen it,” [he replied]. The Buddha told Most Victorious:

“This bodhisattva possesses the foremost analytical eloquence regarding meaning, along with kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. His speech is gentle, his aspirations and conduct are lofty and far-reaching; he smiles before speaking and maintains a serene and pleasant countenance. When questioned, he does not repeat himself, and his explanations are concise. He guides and delivers sentient beings just as a Buddha does, attaining non-retrogression and establishing himself in the path of a bodhisattva.”

At that time, the Bodhisattva Biancong and ten thousand bodhisattvas prostrated at the feet of the World-Honored One, circumambulated him three times to the right, and with palms joined toward the Buddha, praised him in verse:
“His voice resounds throughout the ten directions; His merit, fame, and teachings are renowned.
In whatever direction the Honored One among Men goes, There are none who do not receive his deliverance.”
The Buddha-field is pure, where even the names of the five realms of existence are unheard;
having forsaken that for this, his compassion is beyond compare.
What the World-Honored One now manifests is truly rare among men.
Though one’s accumulated virtue be like Mount Sumeru, One should cast oneself beneath the feet [of the Buddha].
Even if one practices diligence for one kalpa up to a hundred kalpas,
It is not equal to practicing a heart of compassion within the Sahā world for even a brief moment.
When the Buddhas appear in the world, they first select a pure land;
yet you, O Benevolent Honored One, alone are able to endure within this world of five turbidities.
How marvelous, how exceedingly rare! You protect and deliver beings with impartiality.
The flowing teachings and the Three Vehicles purify one's body, speech, and mind;
having already perfected the path of a Bodhisattva, they possess no regressive thought.
Their resolve is redoubled in vigor; for this reason, I now bow my head in prostration.
Severing all knots of doubt, Swiftly practicing the ten virtuous deeds,
Fully endowed with the qualities of all Buddhas, The ocean of wisdom they proclaim is profound.
Whether remaining in their own lands, Or as guides for hundreds of millions of eons,
It is not as good as remaining here in this land to save a single person during a kalpa;
nor is it like traveling through immeasurable lands, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges,
where one never hears of suffering or the eight states of no leisure.
This person was mostly stubborn and fierce, with a body formed by manifold defilements;
the Four Truths are like pure water, which cleanses both the internal and external through bathing.
Our faith has reached its ultimate point, and thus we have come from afar to take refuge.
"I wish to hear the Dharma for the concentration of the mind; I pray that you will expound it at this time.
Having praised the Buddha with these verses, the Bodhisattva Biancong then came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is meant by a bodhisattva whose resolve is firm and steadfast, capable of receiving the concentration of the mind, and who never tires of the instructions they hear?"
"What is meant by a bodhisattva whose words and deeds correspond and whose inner nature is supple?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Biancong, saying:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon this well!"
"I shall analyze its meaning for you. He replied, "So be it."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha told Bodhisattva Biancong:

“If one cultivates the mind of meditative concentration and accomplishes four dharmas, it will cause the bodhisattva’s resolve to become firm and capable of receiving concentration, such that they never grow weary of the instructions they hear.”
What are the four dharmas? They are:

practicing the four immeasurable minds of loving-kindness and compassion without indolence; regarding the people one delivers as being like illusions or transformations; and knowing that the Buddha’s wisdom has no equal. These, O Bodhisattva Biancong, are called the four.
“By accomplishing four dharmas, one’s resolve becomes firm and steadfast, enabling one to endure and receive meditative concentration.
“In what way does a bodhisattva direct their mind with single-minded intent so that their speech is free from confusion?
The Buddha told Biancong:
"In this regard, a bodhisattva must further accomplish four dharmas. What are these four?

A bodhisattva exclusively teaches the emptiness of sentient beings and teaches the emptiness of all phenomena; they are entirely without attachment to any sense-bases (*āyatana*); they praise the meritorious deeds performed by bodhisattvas; and they discern the dharmas of good and evil, the conditioned and the unconditioned, while contemplating and practicing skillful means (*upāya*). These are called the four dharmas."
“How does a bodhisattva increase their roots of goodness so that they become ever more abundant and never diminish?
The Buddha told Biancong:
“Furthermore, there are four dharmas that increase the roots of goodness.”

What are the four? First is faith, second is learning, third is giving, and fourth is the essential departure [from suffering]. These are called the four dharmas by which a bodhisattva increases their roots of goodness.
“How is it that a bodhisattva’s mind is neither distracted nor confused, and is free from doubt?
The Buddha told Biancong:
“Furthermore, one should contemplate four dharmas so that the mind remains focused and undistracted.”
What are the four dharmas? They are:

keeping the mind constantly focused; maintaining restraint and propriety; not hoping for gain or offerings; and not seeking fame or reputation. These are called the four dharmas by which the mind remains undisturbed.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas that increase one's roots of goodness.

What are these four? They are: teaching others to establish faith; not expecting a reward after having given; being a protector of the Dharma; and not contradicting the instructions and teachings of the Bodhisattvas. These are called the practices of the four dharmas.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas that a bodhisattva should contemplate and reflect upon, by which they may proceed from one stage to another, whether regressing or advancing.
What are these four dharmas?

To teach sentient beings to cultivate their roots of goodness, to distance themselves from all evils, to refrain from ignorance and delusion, and to never abandon their great vows with a mind free from cowardice—these are called the four dharmas practiced by Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas that a bodhisattva should uphold.

What are these four? They are: transforming sentient beings through skillful means; establishing ordinary people on the stage of faith; ensuring that what is delivered is not in vain; and manifesting the majestic marks of a Buddha to receive sentient beings. These are the four dharmas that a bodhisattva should uphold.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas that a bodhisattva should contemplate and reflect upon.

What are these four? They are: acting with appropriate timing in advancing or halting; not being attached to clothing or ornaments; acting in accordance with the requirements of the time; and constantly enduring both suffering and pleasure. These are called the practices of the four dharmas.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas.
What are these four dharmas? They are:

subduing one's own mental nature, constantly generating the aspiration for enlightenment, not departing from skillful means, and single-mindedly recollecting the Buddha. These are called the four dharmas.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas that a bodhisattva should contemplate and reflect upon. What are these four?

In this regard, a bodhisattva should contemplate dwelling in solitude, distancing himself from the mind of a śrāvaka and the intent of a pratyekabuddha, seeking the Dharma without satiety, and extensively explaining the sublime Dharma he has heard to others. These are called the four dharmas.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas that a bodhisattva should contemplate and reflect upon. What are these four?

Seeking treasures to provide for the destitute, administering medicine to treat the sick, seeking the meaning [of the Dharma] without weariness, and enduring all suffering—these are called the four dharmas.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas that a bodhisattva should contemplate and reflect upon.
What are these four? They are:

practicing the patience of non-arising, the patience of transcending cessation, contemplating the fundamental twelve links of dependent origination, and neither clinging to patience nor being attached to patience, remaining detached from each. These are called the four dharmas.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas that a bodhisattva should contemplate and reflect upon.
What are these four? They are:

contemplating the meditation on foulness and impurity, counting the inhalations and exhalations of the breath, practicing pure and wholesome dharmas, and maintaining self-humility. These are called the four dharmas.
Furthermore, there are four dharmas that a bodhisattva should contemplate and reflect upon. What are these four?

One should observe sentient beings who are responsive to the Dharma before administering the medicine; one should always maintain mindfulness of reverence and never become self-exalting; if among a great assembly, one should not be attached to gain and offerings; and one should practice skillful means so as to be unhindered in all circumstances. These are called the four dharmas.
Furthermore, there are five dharmas that a bodhisattva should contemplate and reflect upon.

What are these five? Receiving the dharma of equality without omission; contemplating one’s own body and the bodies of others as equal and without distinction; attending to and serving virtuous friends; and forever severing the fetters and latent tendencies so that none remain. These are called the five.
Furthermore, there are five dharmas that a bodhisattva should contemplate and reflect upon.

What are these five? They are: examining one's own faults without seeing the shortcomings of others; maintaining a mind of loving-kindness even when among those of evil disposition; kindling all dharmas to eliminate attachment to their conditions; ensuring that the resolve for the Way is firm and never forgotten; and also causing other people to practice the intent of the Way. These are called the five.
Furthermore, there are five matters that a bodhisattva should contemplate.

What are these five? First, giving always precedes; second, teaching others to practice generosity; third, when giving with a focused mind, not discriminating between the faults or virtues of sentient beings; fourth, realizing that all dharmas are profoundly deep and attaining liberation; and fifth, proceeding until one becomes a Buddha and adorns the tree of enlightenment. These are called the five dharmas.
Furthermore, there are five dharmas that a bodhisattva should contemplate and reflect upon.
What are these five? They are:

knowing the arising and ceasing of conditioned phenomena; not abandoning sentient beings regarding the powers and fearlessnesses; discerning the various types of knowledge; knowing superior knowledge; and not being in contradiction with one another. These are called the five dharmas.
Furthermore, there are five dharmas that a bodhisattva should contemplate and reflect upon.

What are these five? To transcend the five destinies forever; to make offerings to, serve, and revere all Buddhas; to enter the samādhi of loving-kindness for one’s own delight; to have the immeasurable wisdom of the Buddha manifest before one’s eyes; and to have no doubt or difficulty regarding immeasurable samādhis. These are called the five.
Furthermore, there are five dharmas that a bodhisattva should contemplate and reflect upon.

What are these five? To give rise to the mind of great vows and never regret them midway; to act in accordance with one’s words and not speak recklessly; to rely on dhyāna without being attached to dhyāna; to maintain mindfulness without attachment; and to dwell in various places without finding pleasure therein—these are called the five dharmas.
“Discerning and Wise Bodhisattva!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva cultivates this meditative concentration as their fundamental practice, they shall attain the Tathāgata’s right reception (samādhi).

At that time, when the World-Honored One preached this Dharma, two hundred million devas and worldlings conceived the aspiration for supreme, perfect, and true enlightenment. Furthermore, five thousand sons of gods attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti). At that moment, the bodhisattvas from various Buddha-fields each brought flowers and incense to present as offerings; the flowers reached up to their knees.
The Scripture on the Ten Abodes and the Severing of Bonds, Scroll Five.
The Scripture on the Ten Abodes and the Severing of Bonds, Scroll Six.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Chapter Fifteen: The Chapter on the Shattered Body.
The Buddha addressed Ajita:
“When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva enters the Samādhi of the Shattered Body, he causes the Bodhisattva to enter this samādhi and become fully endowed with ten kinds of abidings.”

What are these ten? All worlds abide in suchness; all directions abide in suchness; all kalpas abide in suchness; all sentient beings abide in suchness; all dharmas abide in suchness; all bodhisattva practices abide in suchness; all bodhisattva vows abide in suchness; all meditative concentrations abide in suchness; all Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, abide in suchness; and the entire realm of earth abides in suchness.
If a bodhisattva attains this "shattering-body" samādhi, they shall obtain these ten abidings in suchness.
“How does a bodhisattva enter the samādhi of the pulverized body?
In this regard, O Most Excellent One!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva enters the pulverized body, he first enters meditative concentration within the body and then arises from outside the body.”
Entering meditative concentration externally from within the body; entering concentration in one body from another body;
entering concentration in another body from one body; entering human-body concentration from the body of a yakṣa;
entering yakṣa-body concentration from the body of a nāga; entering nāga-body concentration from the body of an asura; entering [asura-body concentration]...
The concentration of the asura body arises from the concentration of the deva body; the concentration of the deva body arises from the concentration of the brahmā body;

the concentration of the brahmā body arises from the concentration of the body in the desire realm; the concentration of the body in the heavenly realms arises from the concentration of the body in hell;

the concentration of the body in hell arises from the concentration of the body in the human realm; and the concentration of the body in the human realm arises [from the concentration of the body in the heavenly realms].

Emerging from other states, one enters the concentration of a thousand bodies and emerges from the concentration of a single body; one enters the concentration of a single body and emerges from the concentration of a thousand bodies;

one enters the concentration of a hundred million bodies and emerges from the concentration of a single body; one enters the concentration of a single body and emerges from the concentration of a hundred million bodies;
one enters the concentration of sentient beings with form on the continent of Jambudvīpa and [emerges] from the concentration of sentient beings with form on the continent of Aparagoyānī.
Rising from the concentration on sentient beings with form in Aparagoyānī, he enters the concentration on sentient beings with form in Uttarakuru;
rising from the concentration on sentient beings with form in Uttarakuru, he enters the concentration on sentient beings with form in Pūrvavideha;

rising from the concentration on sentient beings with form in Pūrvavideha, he enters the concentration on sentient beings with form in the eastern direction, and then rises from the concentrations on sentient beings with form in the other three directions.
Entering the concentration on sentient beings with form in the three directions, he arises from the concentration on sentient beings with form in the four directions;
entering the concentration on sentient beings with form in the four directions, he arises from the concentration on all living beings with form in the various oceans;

entering the concentration on all living beings with form in the various oceans, he arises from the concentration on the bodies of ocean deities; entering the concentration on the bodies of ocean deities, he arises from the ocean...
Emerging from the water-element concentration, one enters the sea-water-element concentration; emerging from the sea-water-element concentration, one enters the sea-earth-element concentration;
emerging from the sea-earth-element concentration, one enters the sea-fire-element concentration; emerging from the sea-fire-element concentration, one enters the sea-wind-element concentration;

emerging from the sea-wind-element concentration, one enters the concentration of the four great elements; and emerging from the concentration of the four great elements, one enters the concentration of non-existence.

Emerging from the concentration on non-existence, he enters the concentration on Mount Sumeru; emerging from the concentration on Mount Sumeru, he enters the concentration on the mountains of the seven precious jewels;
emerging from the concentration on the mountains of the seven precious jewels, he enters the concentration on the hundred grasses, trees, mountains, rivers, crags, and cliffs;
emerging from the concentration on the hundred grasses, trees, mountains, rivers, crags, and cliffs, he enters the concentration on pure and fragrant flowers.
Emerging from the Samādhi of All Precious Vessels, he enters the Samādhi of Pure and Fragrant Flowers in All Precious Vessels;
emerging from the Samādhi of All Precious Vessels, he enters the Samādhi of the Vehicles, Garments, and Food of All Sentient Beings from the Four Directions, the Upper, and the Lower Regions;

emerging from the Samādhi of the Vehicles, Garments, and Food of All Sentient Beings from the Four Directions, the Upper, and the Lower Regions, he enters [the Samādhi] of the Three Thousandfold World System.
Entering the concentration on the embodied beings of the Sahā world-system, he arises from the concentration on the embodied beings of the Sahā world-system;
entering the concentration on the embodied beings of a thousand-world system, he arises from the concentration on the embodied beings of a three-thousandfold great thousand-world system;

entering the concentration on the embodied beings of a three-thousandfold great thousand-world system, he arises from the concentration on the embodied beings of hundreds of thousands of millions and three-thousandfold great thousand-world systems.

Entering the meditative absorption of sentient beings with form in hundreds of thousands of millions and trichiliocosm world-systems, he arises from the meditative absorption of sentient beings with form in infinite world-systems;
entering the meditative absorption of sentient beings with form in infinite world-systems, he arises from the meditative absorption of sentient beings with form in incalculable world-systems;
entering the meditative absorption of sentient beings with form in incalculable world-systems...
He emerges from the meditative absorption on sentient beings with form in immeasurable buddha-fields and enters the meditative absorption on sentient beings with form in immeasurable buddha-fields;
he emerges from the meditative absorption on sentient beings with form in boundless buddha-fields and enters the meditative absorption on sentient beings with form in boundless buddha-fields;
he emerges from the meditative absorption on sentient beings with form in incalculable buddha-fields.
Entering the concentration of sentient beings with form in the Buddha-lands of the Nameless, one arises from the concentration of sentient beings with form in the inconceivable Buddha-lands;
entering the concentration of sentient beings with form in the inconceivable Buddha-lands, one enters the concentration of sentient beings with form in infinite,
immeasurable, and inconceivable Buddha-lands, and from that infinite, immeasurable, and inconceivable...

He enters the concentration on sentient beings with form from the concentration on sentient beings with form; he emerges from the concentration on sentient beings with form and enters the concentration on extremely distant sentient beings, and emerges from the concentration on extremely distant sentient beings and enters the concentration on extremely near sentient beings;
he enters the concentration on the eye-base from the concentration on the eye-base, and enters the concentration on the ear-base from the concentration on the ear-base.

Entering the concentration of the eye-sphere, he arises from the concentration of the nose-sphere; entering the concentration of the tongue-sphere, he arises from the concentration of the nose-sphere;
entering the concentration of the body-sphere, he arises from the concentration of the mind-sphere; entering his own concentration, he arises from his own concentration;
entering another’s concentration, he arises from another’s concentration; entering his own concentration... [and so forth].
From the meditative absorption of all sentient beings with form, they emerge from the meditative absorption of incalculable lands,
as well as infinite, immeasurable, and inexpressible lands; they enter the meditative absorption of incalculable lands, as well as infinite, immeasurable, and inexpressible lands,
and emerge from the meditative absorption of all sentient beings with form, entering the state of a śrāvaka.
Emerging from the concentration of a pratyekabuddha, one enters the concentration of a pratyekabuddha; emerging from the concentration of a śrāvaka, one enters the concentration of oneself;
emerging from the concentration of one's own body, one enters the concentration of the Buddha-body; emerging from the concentration of the Buddha-body, one enters the concentration of one's own body;

emerging from the concentration of a single thought-moment, one enters the concentration of ten billion kalpas; and emerging from the concentration of ten billion kalpas, one enters the concentration of a single thought-moment.
Entering the present concentration and arising from the present concentration; entering the past concentration and arising from the past concentration;

entering the future concentration and further entering the concentration of the three periods of time—thus, according to whichever concentration the bodhisattva enters and whichever they arise from, if they enter the concentration of the realm of empty space, they arise from the realm of empty space.
"O Most Excellent One, you should know this:

it is just as when a person is possessed by a spirit; wherever that spirit leads the body, the person does not realize it for themselves, yet the spirit relies upon that human body without manifesting its own form."

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: he enters internal concentration and arises from external concentration; he enters external concentration and arises from internal concentration. It is just as when a person dies and the spirit departs, having no place to rely upon and remaining unmoving; the body does not know where the spirit is, and the spirit, having taken on a new form, does not know where its former body now resides.

O Most Victorious One, you should know that it is likewise for the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: first they enter the meditative concentration of discerning the existence of phenomena through equal contemplation; subsequently, they enter the concentration of emptiness and never again perceive existence, such that what arises before and ceases after are mutually unaware of one another.

The Bodhisattva should further contemplate that it is like a person who has attained mastery over the mind through the perfection of psychic power (*citta-vaśitā-pāramitā*): they can transform a single body into many bodies, and those many bodies may again merge back into one. Yet, consciousness does not perish from the single body to immediately arise in the many bodies; nor is it obtained that consciousness perishes from the many bodies to arise within a single body. It does not proceed from one to many, nor does it proceed from many to one.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: entering a single-body concentration and arising from a manifold-concentration, or entering a manifold-concentration and arising from a single-body concentration.

It is like the realm of earth, which is moistened with water as its basis; the myriad things that arise are each different, yet both the human realm and the ghost realm are equally moistened by it. The myriad things do not know of themselves, "I am that which has been produced," nor does the water know, "I am that which has moistened."

The bodhisattva mahāsattva is also like this: having attained this samādhi, one becomes the countless, and the countless become one; yet the countless do not know why they have become one, nor does the one know why it has become countless!
"O Most Victorious One!
This is called the 'Samādhi of Crushing the Bodies of All Sentient Beings,' which is the practice cultivated by the eighth-stage Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.
One who dwells in this samādhi shall obtain the ten titles of a Buddha and be praised for being endowed with ten additional merits."
What are these ten? They are:
being called the Tathāgata, because he cultivates suchness according to suchness;
being called a Buddha, for a Buddha is one who has fully awakened to all phenomena, having gone from this shore to the other shore.
He is named Most Victorious, because he is honored by sentient beings and they offer him worship;
he is named All-Knowledge, because he is fully endowed with all the virtues of omniscience;
he is named Inexhaustible, because he acts as a protective shelter for all sentient beings.
He is named the Guide, for he shows the correct path to all classes of sentient beings;
he is named Peerless, for he is fully endowed with the dharma-realm of all sentient beings and all forms of wisdom;
he is named Wondrous Light, for all sentient beings are graced by his illumination.
He is titled "The Ten Powers" because his vows are fulfilled and he possesses discerning knowledge of phenomena that is unattached and cannot be defiled;
he is titled "Manifest in All" because he causes all dharmas to be unified within the single sovereignty of the *pāramitā*.
"O Most Victorious One!
That a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva attains the ten titles of a Buddha and the ten meritorious qualities of praise is entirely due to the grace of the majestic spiritual power of this samādhi."
"When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva abides in this samādhi, they obtain ten radiances that illuminate them of their own accord.
What are these ten? They are:

the radiance of all Buddhas that illuminates them of its own accord; the radiance of the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*)—the vehicle upon which there is no one who does not ride—that envelops them throughout all worlds; and the fragrance of the light of instruction for all sentient beings."

The immeasurable radiance of the four fearlessnesses; the radiance of the dharma-realm in all its locations; the light of the essential departure that is entirely free from desire and removes craving; the radiance that transforms and moves all sentient beings; the light of the Buddhas that is non-reliant and unstained; the radiance of skillful reflection; the radiance of the perfection of equal and right awakening; the radiance of the suchness of the nature of all dharmas and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); and the unsurpassed light that proclaims the removal of the afflictions of the fetters.
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva abides in this samādhi, they will obtain these ten radiances that illuminate themselves.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva should skillfully train in the ten practices of tracelessness.

What are the ten? They are: the mind’s reflections leave no trace in body, no trace in speech, and no trace in mind; dwelling in emptiness while establishing a place of abiding; desiring to accomplish practice through non-practice; not engaging in conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) nor destroying phenomena; not disparaging the work of wisdom; practicing the wisdom of non-arising; training in the dharmas of both the learner and the non-learner; responding with wisdom and eloquence; and the purity of the meaning and flavor of formless wisdom.

This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva abiding in this samādhi, possessing various distinctive powers to sever attachment to objects; entering from one into various kinds of concentrations, whether arising or contemplating the "equal parts" (sabhāga), or both the equal and unequal parts; proceeding from small to large and from large to small, from narrow to broad and from broad to narrow; contracting what is extended and extending what is contracted; making the bodiless have a body and making that which has a body bodiless; whether arising or in concentration, or in concentration or arising; making the defiled free from defilement and making the undefiled defiled.

One who awakens to this samādhi is able to destroy all objective realms, just as a person breaks a broken jar. It is like the efficacy of a great mantra’s protective power: various kinds of forms and various kinds of sounds may be restrained by the mantra, or compelled by illusory sounds. The practitioner of the mantra employs spirits, while the illusionist employs external forms. Those who see illusory forms are apprehended by the visual consciousness; those who hear illusory sounds are apprehended by the auditory consciousness; those who smell illusory fragrances are apprehended by the olfactory consciousness; the flavors produced by illusion are apprehended by the gustatory consciousness; and the various physical forms produced by illusion are apprehended by the tactile consciousness. There are illusions and great illusions that turn the high into the low and the low into the high; their workings and pursuits are inconceivable, and they are apprehended by the mental consciousness.
Thus, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva abides in this samādhi, they manifest various transformations, whether dispersing or gathering them.
"O Most Victorious One, you should know!
I shall now provide an analogy; it is only those with eyes who can comprehend this."

It was as when the devas and the asuras fought together, and the devas were victorious while the asuras were defeated. At that time, the asuras, knowing themselves to be inferior, devised a stratagem and manifested a bathing pool from which various lotuses sprang forth. The asuras, whose bodies were seven thousand yojanas in height, concealed their forms along with their armies and retreated to hide within the fibers and nodes of the lotus stalks. The devas sought them but could not find them; this is what is meant by the asuras being skilled in the art of illusion.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: having accomplished the illusion of all-encompassing wisdom, they proceed from one stage to the next with their wisdom undiminished. Those who are called "Bodhisattvas," each attracting others by their own characteristics, are all gathered through the illusory method of wisdom. In this way, the Bodhisattva enters the meditative absorption of the whole body and manifests the meditative absorption of the dispersed body.

For example, suppose there is a person, whether in the human realm or in the realm of hungry ghosts, who plants a seed in the earth and irrigates it at the proper times so that it grows large. The seed enters the earth while the fruit emerges above; the former seed is not the latter fruit, and the latter fruit is not the former seed, yet the former seed does not depart from the latter fruit, nor does the latter fruit depart from the former seed.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: alone experiencing form while abiding in this samādhi, he is able to leave existence behind and does not dwell within existence. It is like the union of a man and a woman; the male is pure and the female is turbid, and consciousness dwells between them. Within the mother’s womb, it gradually passes through ten months. Due to the purity of past conduct and the pursuit of meritorious vows, the limbs and joints of the body become increasingly complete. The six sense faculties are perfected and their natures are balanced and correct. Consciousness and the six sense faculties have distinct origins; the six sense faculties are the marks of receiving existence. Following the good or evil of one's past actions, one comes to receive a physical form, yet upon seeking its original source, it is like an illusion or a transformation.

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is also like this: taking the mind of supreme liberation as his father and mother, he dwells in and undergoes birth through the consciousness of wisdom; entering the concentration of non-existence and arising from the concentration of existence, or entering the concentration of existence and dwelling in the ground of non-existence, he is then able to ride upon clouds in the void amidst thunder and lightning, raining down at the appropriate time to provide abundant moisture and nourishment.

However, that dragon palace does not exist in the void, nor is it the actual dwelling place of the dragons; rather, they manifest various transformations within the void—sometimes brilliant, sometimes subtle—so that all classes of sentient beings may look up and behold them. While the palace rests upon the earth, rain falls from above; how marvelous is this principle of transformation!

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is also like this: dwelling in this samādhi and the dharma of illusory transformation, he enters the concentration of signlessness and arises from signs; he enters the concentration of signs and arises from signlessness.
"Most excellent indeed!
When a bodhisattva dwells in this samādhi, there is no difficulty whatsoever in making space into earth or making earth into space.
It is just as if, in the heavens, there were a palace of crystal light composed of various jewels, or like that Great Lord Brahmā..."
When the deva ascended this hall, he raised his eyes and beheld a thousand worlds,
ten thousand worlds, a hundred thousand worlds, and a trichiliocosm; within them were all the celestial palaces and dragon palaces,
as well as those of the yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas.

Śūlika, from humans and non-humans down to the three evil realms; from Mount Sumeru, the Iron Ring Mountains, and the Great Iron Ring Mountains, to the Black Mountains, the Great Black Mountains, and the mountains of the seven treasures; from rivers, oceans, and their sources, to cities, towns, and villages;
from mountains, valleys, trees, medicinal herbs, flowers, and fruits—whether beautiful or ugly, pure or turbid—throughout the trichiliocosm.
All physical forms, down to the most subtle forms within the realm of empty space, Brahmā perceives from afar within his palace;
they shine upon one another without the slightest obscuration.
Just as garments are displayed on racks here among humans, or as one sees the reflection of one's own face in a bright mirror, so too is it with those celestial palaces:
sitting, rising, coming and going, eating, drinking, and sleeping—all are present before one’s eyes like a jewel held in the palm of the hand.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: dwelling in the samādhi of the pulverized body of all sentient beings, he attains mastery over all samādhis—mastery over the Buddha-samādhi, mastery over the samādhi of transforming sentient beings, mastery over the samādhi of roaming through all dharmas, mastery over the samādhi of accomplishing practice, mastery over the samādhi of the supreme liberation, mastery over the samādhi of all correct attainments (*samāpatti*), mastery over the samādhi of entering, emerging, sitting, and rising, mastery over the samādhi of all wisdoms, and mastery over the samādhi that makes the snapping of a finger last for one kalpa.
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwelling in this samādhi, delighting in the ten masteries of the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
There are ten matters by which the bodhisattva-mahāsattva manifests majestic power and fearlessness.
What are the ten? They are:
manifesting the Buddha’s majestic radiance that transcends the realm of empty space; unbreakable vigor that attains the *pāramitā* of liberation amidst all phenomena subject to destruction;
manifesting the bodhisattva practice of vast vows and fearlessness; and sporting in the Tathāgata’s play through the *pāramitā* of the gate of speech.
It manifests the purity of worlds; it manifests the purification of defilements and illuminates the world;
it manifests its presence among sentient beings to demonstrate the inconceivable;
and it manifests the uninterrupted transmission of the sutras and Dharma by all bodhisattvas.
It reveals the arrival at the Buddha-lands to offer worship and perform services;
it reveals that the fundamental activity of wisdom is inconceivable;
and it reveals the discernment of samādhi without fear.
Manifesting entry into subtle meditative concentration, they know the direction of their progress and deliver beings through the means of a bodhisattva;
manifesting the purification of buddha-fields, they do not sever the dharma of bodhisattva vows, but illuminate themselves and remain without fear.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas dwell among the laity, they manifest the form and image of a Buddha and are free from fear; they manifest the turning of the wheel of Dharma for the sake of those to be transformed, revealing the root of the roots of goodness of all Tathāgatas, establishing them in the Buddha-vehicle so that all may achieve fulfillment, and manifesting the perfection of the power of their resolve.

Furthermore, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva contemplates the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), thoroughly comprehending that the dharmas practiced throughout countless, limitless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas all appear before him, manifesting the majestic brilliance of the Dharma and kindling the radiant light of the Path.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is able to calculate and know all days and nights, months and years, seasons, and ages.
By employing the wisdom of equality used for as brief a moment as a finger-snap, the bodhisattva knows the affairs of the three periods of time without the slightest error, manifesting fearlessness.

This is called the most supreme state of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who, dwelling in this samādhi, is able to illuminate all the pāramitās and attain the ten fearlessnesses. Amidst the great assembly, he enters meditative absorption and, through skillful means, shatters his body into dust; this is the practice cultivated by the eighth-stage Bodhisattva.
Chapter 16: The Entrance of the Body (Kāyāyatana) At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ajita:

"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva again contemplates his own body—the body as a support and the entrance of the body—and is able to discern and understand it entirely as being without a fixed location."

At that time, the Bodhisattva enters the meditative absorption of the "Entry into the Body and the Sustenance of Dharmas" (kāya-dharmadhāraṇī-samādhi), attaining supreme mastery among all concentrations.
Within every single pore of his body, he enters the samādhi of the "meditative absorption of the entry into the dharmadhātu," attaining mastery therein.
He manifests illusory phenomena within the various dharmadhātus, knowing the distinctions between past and future lives.
Regarding worldly phenomena, they thoroughly understand hundreds of thousands of millions of matters within the world;
throughout countless, limitless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) eons, they are able to fully comprehend all that is good and evil within the Buddha-worlds.

They observe the accomplishment of the retinues of the Samyaksaṃbuddhas, remaining entirely equanimous toward both the pure and the impure, never severing wholesome dharmas, and never diminishing the Mahāyāna.
With the mind firm and unwavering, throughout one eon, a hundred eons, a hundred thousand eons, ten billion eons, a hundred thousand billion eons—
limitless, immeasurable, asaṃkhyeya, incalculable, beyond the reach of counting sticks or the scope of thought—
for such numbers of eons, he enters meditative absorption (*samādhi*) within the worlds of the Buddhas.
Emerging from that state of meditative absorption, they again arise from within it to enter this intermediate concentration;
arising from that intermediate state, they travel to those worlds and are thus able to bring the practices of those sentient beings to maturity.

Without losing the true Dharma of the essence of the *dharmadhātu*, they come and go through the three periods of time without obstruction, preaching the Dharma to transform and teach those who are limited, causing them to know where to turn for refuge.

With the eye of wisdom, they shatter and enter into the Dharma, attaining mastery over all dharma-realms. They are fully endowed with the perfection of concentration that destroys the ear, remaining without obstruction.
Entering the concentration of the nose-faculty, their mental resolve does not diminish their skillful means;

they skillfully enter the concentration of the tongue-faculty and liberate themselves from attachment to flavors. They achieve the concentration that shatters the body, coming and going without hindrance, and enter...
Shattering mental concentration to accord with wisdom-consciousness,
that bodhisattva-mahāsattva practices such contemplation and attains such knowledge; dwelling within this body while entering meditative absorption,
he immediately acquires ten thousand koṭis of bodhisattva dhāraṇīs, and turns the wheel of Dharma in the world in accordance with worldly conventions.
Upon entering, he further attained ten trillion treasuries of conduct that are pure and unstained;
he further attained ten trillion sense-faculties that transcend all-knowledge; he further attained ten trillion supernormal powers that wander without obstruction;
he further attained ten trillion concentrations that surpass all other concentrations; and he further attained ten trillion bases of spiritual power for wandering.
Reaching the realm of infinite space, he further attained ten trillion powers that gradually increased across all modes of practice;
he further attained ten trillion ways to forever sever longing and all conceptualizations;

he further attained ten trillion states of cessation wherein nothing whatsoever appears; and he further attained ten trillion manifestations of majestic spiritual transformations that appeared before him.
"O Most Victorious One! This is called the attainment by a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva of these ten thousand koṭis of practices without any deficiency."
"Furthermore, a bodhisattva should mindfully practice the adornment of ten trillion limbs and joints to wrap themselves therewith.
Furthermore, they should practice the ten trillion means for delivering sentient beings."
Furthermore, one should practice ten trillion vehicles so that all classes of sentient beings may ride these vehicles to reach the other shore.
Furthermore, one should practice ten trillion *jvālā-samādhi* concentrations so as to illuminate the world, leaving no place in darkness.
Furthermore, he attained ten trillion forms of analytical eloquence regarding meaning, which were neither inappropriate nor improper;
he attained ten trillion great vows, such that the minds of those who came to observe him did not waver;
and he attained ten trillion aspirations of faith, free from perverse or inverted views.
Furthermore, he attained ten trillion correct paths, purifying the tracks where Bodhisattvas come and go and travel about.
Moreover, ten trillion rays of light issued forth from his face.
Furthermore, he obtained ten trillion scriptures that manifest the virtues of bodhisattvas;
he also obtained ten trillion roots of purity to purify the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).

This is called the supreme Bodhisattva Mahāsattva being entwined by immeasurable merits, adorning the tree of enlightenment without losing the ultimate limit (*koṭi*); all these are the requisites for the Bodhisattva’s progression toward the Way.

If a bodhisattva accomplishes these requisites, they will ascend to the stage of a bodhisattva and receive renown; perfumed by the fragrance of virtue, they will be honored by others; wherever they go among the multitude, they will immediately obtain offerings and sustenance; and their meritorious deeds in the present life will be inexhaustible.
"If there is a bodhisattva who dwells in this Samādhi of the Sovereignty of Mind within the Dharma-Realm,
they will be born into a noble family and not dwell in a lowly or base station; with a multitude of bodhisattvas as their retinue, once established in this samādhi,
they will see from afar ten billion *asaṃkhyeya* Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas in the eastern direction."
The names, surnames, and titles, as well as the dimensions of the lands, are all clearly discerned;

throughout the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below, one is able to recognize each and every name and title of ten billion *asaṃkhyeya* Buddha-fields and their respective Tathāgatas.
One establishes the bodhisattva practices and points out the gates of the Way, causing those bodhisattvas to become pure.

In the Buddha-field, the Tathāgata’s body emits immeasurable radiance; the Tathāgata’s eye manifests inconceivably; the Tathāgata’s supernormal power of hearing is beyond measure; the Tathāgata’s supernormal power of smelling is manifold and incalculable;
the Tathāgata’s supernormal power of the tongue is vast and boundless; the Tathāgata’s supernormal power of the mind is not a perception of formlessness; [the Tathāgata’s] divine...
The supreme Dharma of the Tathāgata’s feet delivers infinite beings; because the path of the Tathāgata is fully accomplished without superior, middle, or inferior;
because the fame of the Tathāgata spreads far and wide; because the Wheel of the Dharma of the Tathāgata is constantly turning—turning in the present world;
because the Tathāgata’s followers currently consult and receive his teachings; and because the True Dharma of the Tathāgata is immeasurable.
Because it cannot be interrupted; because the roots of goodness of the Tathāgata are currently praised; because the universal discourse of the Tathāgata’s conduct is beyond being surpassed;
because the lineage of the Tathāgata is accomplished and there is nothing in the three periods of time that it does not subdue;
because the birth of the Tathāgata proclaims all dharmas to the ignorant; and because the locus of the Tathāgata’s Dharma is manifested.
Because of the clarity of wisdom. "O Most Victorious One!

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva establishes a locus by manifesting the purity of the realms. Through the Buddha’s heavy rain of the Dharma-nectar, he displays the verbal teachings of all Buddhas’ spheres and manifests all Buddha-dharmas. Understanding that illusory forms are not real, he realizes the nature of all dharmas; because he gives rise to spontaneity that is unmoving and unchanging, he discerns the principles of the images of all dharmas. Thus, the Tathāgata’s immeasurable merits are fully perfected and inexhaustible."
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva dwelling in this samādhi, such that in whatever direction they travel, there is no obstruction.

Furthermore, when the bodhisattva dwells in this samādhi, they travel through the aggregates (skandhas), bases (āyatanas), and elements (dhātus) without any hindrance; their mind treats all phenomena as illusions, knowing dharmas that are immeasurable, limitless, and boundless, and they bring all bodhisattvas to a state of peaceful abiding.

Upon entering this Samādhi of Sovereignty over Mental Concentration, one is able to know the names, surnames, and individual appellations of all the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, and Perfectly Awakened Ones—from each single name up to ten thousand billion *asaṃkhyeya* Buddhas, Tathāgatas, and Perfectly Awakened Ones. One reaches as far as hundreds of thousands of billions of Buddha-fields, dwelling there within the bodies of Bodhisattvas who abide peacefully therein. With immeasurable and limitless mental conceptions and intentions, one further establishes places of residence through the skillful means of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Because all phenomena are never forgotten, they attain the knowledge and vision of liberation; because they constantly draw near to the ocean of wisdom, they aspire to manifest that wisdom; because they abide in a state of having no location while manifesting that all phenomena have no place of origin; because they establish the station of Buddhahood by manifesting that all phenomena are universally pervasive and without before or after; because they manifest the unimpeded wisdom of the sense-gates, skillfully employing the sharp Dharma through the discernment of wisdom; because they do not violate dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*) so as to establish the realms of existence as being without coming or going; because they manifest the pure station of insight through unimpeded wisdom; because they manifest the attainment of perfect enlightenment; and because they illuminate the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) as being without increase or decrease.
This is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva who, dwelling within this samādhi, is able to set out upon the path of the Mahāyāna.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should practice the ten gates to the ocean of destinies without ever becoming weary or satisfied.

What are these ten? They are: the ocean of Buddhas appearing without weariness; the ocean of sentient beings being transformed through movement and stillness without weariness; the ocean of the Dharma increasing wisdom without weariness; the ocean of the field of merit producing [beings] without weariness; the ocean of the spiritual power of abiding in the dharma-less and non-contemplative, which has no fixed location and is without weariness; the ocean of the illumination of wisdom, because of grasping wisdom without distraction; the ocean of the sense-gates, because of the wisdom that proceeds from one stage to the next without confusion or error; the ocean of mind and thought, because of being able to fully perceive the various kinds of minds and thoughts of all sentient beings, knowing that immeasurable minds have increases and decreases; the ocean of practice, because of fulfilling all vows; and the ocean of great vows, because of the essential accomplishment of the ultimate, pure path of liberation.

This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva abiding in this samādhi, whereby they are able to attain these ten oceans of gateways to the realms of existence without ever feeling weary or satisfied; such is the practice cultivated by the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.
“Furthermore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should contemplate ten foremost non-arisings (*anutpāda*).
What are the ten? They are as follows:
first, contemplating the categories of sentient beings is the foremost non-arising;”
First, the non-arising of the supreme among those who observe the heavens;
second, the non-arising of the supreme among the highest Brahmā deities;
third, the non-arising of the supreme among those whose world-protecting minds are indestructible.
First, the contemplation of being peerless and solitary among sentient beings, which is the foremost, is the first non-arising;
second, the contemplation of subduing the hosts of Māra with a mind fixed and undisturbed, which is the foremost, is the second non-arising;
third, the contemplation of the five destinies as formless, which is the foremost, is the third non-arising.
The first non-arising is the contemplation that all sentient beings are also without defilement;

the second non-arising is the contemplation of the supreme qualities of the Buddhas; the third non-arising is the contemplation of the sovereign, essential path of liberation and its radiant manifestation. The tenth non-arising is [the contemplation of] the supreme [state].
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s contemplation and reflection upon these ten foremost non-arising [realities].
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva should contemplate that there are ten matters concerning the destinies and births within the realm of sentient beings.
What are the ten? They are:
the power of firm renunciation to transform all sentient beings; the power of diligence to establish them in non-retrogressive practice;
the power of purity and non-attachment, because all phenomena are empty and free from defilement; and the power of rest to bring all [virtues] to fulfillment.
Because of mastery over the Dharma, they achieve the power of discerning and deliberating upon the turning and non-turning of the mind;

because they are endowed with the spontaneous power of the Dharma, they achieve great wisdom; because they accomplish the power of non-obstruction through preaching the Dharma, they achieve the power of fearlessness by establishing the foundations of the Dharma; and they achieve the power of resolute intention regarding both the unknown and the already known.
Because wisdom accomplishes the power of non-duality and is without arising or ceasing, it is called the most supreme. When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates these ten powers—
the greatest power, the incomparable power, the power that is neither high nor low, the immeasurable power,
the nurturing power, the immovable power, the power of rebirth in auspicious realms, and the power free from anger— [he attains this realization].
The power of strength, the power of blazing wisdom, and the power of the accumulation of diligent and arduous practice— these are called the ten powers that one should mindfully cultivate.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva should skillfully contemplate these ten powers.
What are the ten? They are:

the power of skillfully entering emptiness, the power of skillful purification, the power of skillful subtlety, the power of the skillful Dharma-body, the power of skillful worldly dharmas, the power of skillfully kindling the Dharma, the power of the skillful quiescence of roots, the power of skillful unprecedentedness, the power of skillful awakening, and the power of skillful transcendence.
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva abiding in these ten powers and being able to maintain a concentrated mind.
Furthermore, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva should contemplate twenty powers to attain the gateway to concentration.
What are these twenty? They are: the power of a great being;
the power of associating with virtuous friends (*kalyāṇamitra*); the power of the ultimate realization of perfect enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*);
the power of attaining proximity through the cultivation of roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) in the past; the power of being perfumed by immeasurable roots of goodness; and the attainment of...
The Tathāgata’s power to deliver or not deliver; the power of subduing the defilements of the mind so that they are neither arising nor ceasing;

the power to increase the bodhisattvas’ mindfulness so that it is uninterrupted; the power to adorn the bodhisattvas so that they attain joy; the power to assist the bodhisattvas so that their wholesome dharmas are uninterrupted;
the power to remove the bodhisattvas’ minds from unconditioned attachment; and the power to fulfill the bodhisattvas’ vows so that there is nothing sought.
...the power of the bodhisattva’s concentration through mental reflection; the power of the bodhisattva’s faculties being free from confusion;
the power of the Dharma King; the power of the immeasurable body free from attachment; the power of wisdom through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*);
the power of fearlessness regarding all phenomena; the power of establishing sentient beings so that they are never lost or diminished; and regarding...

That all sentient beings walk alone without disturbing one another is called the power of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who dwells in this samādhi; it is the power of non-existence that surpasses all Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas, and only through this can one enter the power of the Bodhisattva’s meditative concentration.
Chapter Seventeen: On Eloquence (Pratibhāna) At that time, the Bodhisattva Most Victorious (Varasena) came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How does a bodhisattva, being fully endowed with all virtues, cut off the expectations of sentient beings, filling them all so that none harbor resentment?”
The Buddha told Ajita:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well!
I shall now provide you with a thorough analysis of it."

From the first generation of the resolve for enlightenment until the attainment of Buddhahood, a bodhisattva must adorn and purify the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), emitting great radiance that illuminates those realms; even the most obscure places receive its light. Those who behold this light harbor no fear and have nothing to dread; their minds become fervent and redoubled with joy, increasing their merit without departing from pure conduct. They purify their own practice and cultivate the unsurpassed path, such that their karmic merit becomes inexhaustible and their wisdom has no boundaries.

The practice of the Bodhisattva’s Dharma is likewise boundless; the vehicle of the Bodhisattva has no bottom; and the realm of the Bodhisattva is inconceivable, beyond the capacity of Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas to fathom.
The beings saved by the Bodhisattva are again boundless; the multitude of virtues he accomplishes is likewise without limit.

The purity achieved by the Bodhisattva does not abandon his great vows; the Bodhisattva provides the essential means of liberation and points toward the gateway of the Way. Yet, if one wishes to discuss the initial threads of all the Bodhisattva’s dharmas, they cannot be grasped.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain the status of a bodhisattva only after incalculable kalpas, and only thereafter do they fulfill the path of a bodhisattva.

When there are those who come to draw near and serve them, they further encourage and inspire these people to achieve the virtues of a bodhisattva, and their fame spreads far and wide. All who hear their names come to attend upon, guard, and make offerings to them, desiring to have them as a field of merit for their own future welfare and benefit.

If there are sentient beings who see the Bodhisattva, he immediately expounds for them the unsurpassed wisdom of the Dharma; those who hear the Dharma before him never feel satiety, as he widely disseminates the light of wisdom without destroying the nature of phenomena.

The reason for this is that sentient beings who hear the Dharma receive the authentic teaching, thereby doubling their intellectual cultivation, and they proclaim the correct instructions without exhaustion.
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells within this samādhi, they are able to widely disseminate all virtuous merits;
with an infinite, immeasurable, incalculable, and vast intention, the Bodhisattva directs each and every thought toward giving.
Following his previous conditions, he entered into samādhi; then, arising from that concentration, he contemplated the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) through self-reflection.
By means of this samādhi, he came to know the sphere of samādhi, discerning countless types of samādhi:
the samādhi of concentrated mental observation, the samādhi of universal observation, the samādhi of desireless observation, and the samādhi of observing characteristics.
The samādhi of what is presently observed, the samādhi of observing deportment, the samādhi of observing tranquility,
the samādhi of observing mindfulness, the samādhi of observing waiting, the samādhi of observing joy, the samādhi of observing security, the samādhi of observing protection,
and the samādhi of observing the way of escape— having abandoned what has already arisen, they abandon all that has not yet arisen.
One should delight in dhyāna and fix the mind in samādhi; though one dwells within samādhi, one remains unstained by it.

"O Most Victorious One, you should know that it is like the palace of the great Nāga King Anavatapta, which is composed entirely of the seven treasures. From the spring of Anavatapta, the four great rivers flow; they issue from the four gates in full abundance yet do not harm the sprouting crops, and the water is so clear and transparent that its color is like that of space."
At that time, four rivers issued from the four gates and flowed toward the four directions, all returning to the ocean.
As for those four rivers: the first is named Gaṅgā, which issues from the elephant’s mouth;
the second is named Sītā, which issues from the lion’s mouth.
The third is named Sītā, which issues from the mouth of the ox;
the fourth is named Vakṣu, which issues from the mouth of the horse.
These four great rivers flow from these four mouths toward the four directions and converge into the four oceans.
As for the great river Gaṅgā, its water flows from the bodies of elephants made of the genuine treasure of musāragalva;
as for the great river Sītā, its water flows from the bodies of lions made of the genuine treasure of vajra;
as for the great river Sindhu, its water flows from the bodies of oxen made of the treasure of agate.
As for the great river Vakṣu, its waters flow from the bodies of horses made of blue lapis lazuli.
These four types of jewels are all celestial treasures, not treasures of the human world.

When these four great rivers first emerge, each is one *yojana* wide; as they flow, they move with measured grace, silent and without sound. Each great river circles the divine spring seven times to the right before entering the ocean. At intervals of one *yojana* between each of these seven circuits, various kinds of lotuses grow—*utpala*, *padma*, *saugandhika*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka*—as well as many precious jewels, all of which grow therein.

Furthermore, there are various subtle and exquisite incenses, their colors and fragrances beautiful; various kinds of gems illuminate one another, such that those who behold them never tire of gazing. These rare and extraordinary treasures allow one to see through the surface to the interior; within the span of one *yojana*, the jewels reflect one another like *maṇi* pearls, shining everywhere.
Within those seven layers dwell various species of birds, singing in mournful harmony as they enjoy one another’s company;
furthermore, there are a hundred kinds of divine trees and medicinal herbs, whose fragrant breezes spread afar, reaching even unto the realm of that śramaṇa.
Now, that palace of the dragon Anavatapta measures fifty *yojanas* in each of the four directions—east, west, south, and north—and is purely adorned with the seven treasures.
