Furthermore, various kinds of multicolored *maṇi* jewels are interspersed throughout it.

Moreover, *maṇi* jewels are suspended in the air, serving as the sun, moon, and stars arrayed across the firmament. Bull-head sandalwood is used for fuel in the kitchen, and within the palace, three times each day, a rain of various fragrant flowers falls: *utpala*, *kumuda*, *puṇḍarīka*, *sugandhika*, and *manojñāgandhika* lotuses.

Various kinds of jewels formed the palaces, their radiance illuminating one another in continuous succession, just as the Anavatapta Spring gives rise to the four great rivers, flowing from its four mouths toward the four oceans.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: having attained the unimpeded river of the four analytical eloquences (*pratisaṃvid*), he discerns the four paths and returns them to the ocean of wisdom.
Just as that Gaṅgā River is composed of the true jewel musāragalva, with water flowing from the mouth of an elephant to reach the sea.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: from the mouth of the blue-and-white dharmas, he brings forth immeasurable meanings; all are the caskets of the Tathāgata’s secret treasury that expound and clarify the profound meaning. He causes all dharmas to each obtain their names, manifests the flavor of the Dharma, and kindles the light of wisdom, leading them all to cast themselves into the boundless ocean of wisdom.
It is like that great river Sītā, whose body is composed of true vajra-jewels, flowing from the mouth of a lion to the ocean.

So too it is with the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva: he brings forth the eloquence of Dharma, wielding the Buddha-vajra to protect all living beings and cause them to attain illumination; grasping the wisdom-vajra, he casts it into the ocean of non-obstruction.
Just as that great river Sītā, composed of agate jewels, flows from the mouth of an ox and reaches the ocean, so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:

he produces appropriate eloquence such that those who have doubts or obstructions are forever free of hesitation, and he causes sentient beings to be without contention. According to their respective capacities and karmic responses, he discerns the meanings and purposes, causing the various classes of sentient beings to bring their practices to maturity, leading them all to return to the ocean of non-conditioned non-attachment.
Just as the great river Vācālī, composed of blue lapis lazuli, flows from the Horse’s Mouth and pours entirely into the ocean;

so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, who attains inexhaustible eloquence in contemplating all dharmas, manifesting within them for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas without end. He skillfully nurtures and protects the wholesome dharmas, leading them toward the auspicious path, and causes all those who observe the precepts to return to the ocean of the Buddha, where they become of one single flavor.

Just as those four great rivers wind seven times to the right around the Anavatapta Spring before flowing toward the four directions and returning to the four oceans, so too it is with the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva:

his bodily conduct is perfected and never deviates to the left; his verbal conduct is perfected and never deviates to the left; and his mental conduct is perfected and never deviates to the left. With wisdom as the foremost of the qualities he cultivates in his will, just as those four rivers flow toward the four directions and return to the sea, so too it is with the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, who rides upon the eloquence of the four wisdoms and proceeds toward the four directions.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva should contemplate the directions in which all Buddhas abide, serving and paying them homage without losing dignified deportment;
furthermore, he should manifest the radiant light of the Dharma of all Buddhas, upholding the dhāraṇī teachings so as not to forget or lose them;
furthermore, he should manifest the various perfections of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), fully perfecting the root of the Bodhisattva’s manifold practices.
Furthermore, manifesting great compassion, he dwells among sentient beings and manifests the turning of the wheel of Dharma.

Just as those four rivers encircle Lake Anavatapta seven times, within which there are various kinds of lotuses—blue utpala, red kumuda, white puṇḍarīka, sugandhika, and pūrṇabhadrika—and various fragrant flowers that perfume the four directions.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: from the first generation of the resolve until the attainment of Buddhahood, throughout that interval, he transforms and guides sentient beings who have not yet been trained, exhorting them and preaching the Dharma until they reach the stage of non-retrogression. He expounds upon right meditative absorption (*samādhi*) for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas without ever becoming weary; he does not abandon even a single person until they are saved. He purifies Buddha-lands, adorns and prepares the stages of realization, enters the Lion’s Gait Samādhi of focused intent, and advances toward the Tree of Enlightenment with a mind as indestructible as a diamond, free from any difficulty.
Just as within the sevenfold enclosures of that Lake Anavatapta, trees of the seven treasures grow to adorn it, with fruits and fragrant flowers beyond measure, so too is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:

he adorns the pure land of a Buddha-field, producing the flowers of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and through contemplation and reflection, he contemplates the true Dharma with the mind of the Path.
Just as that palace of Anavatapta is fifty yojanas in length and breadth, pure and free from blemish, and likewise devoid of wind-blown dust or filth;

so too is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva: his mind of the Way is pure and without blemish, inwardly harboring various roots of goodness and merit, and fully possessing immeasurable dhyāna-concentration dharmaparyāyas.
Just as the Anavatapta Spring is surrounded by walls made of ox-head sandalwood and various miscellaneous jewels, so too is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva;

he is encompassed by the vision of ten billion hundred thousand wisdoms arising from the thoughts of the path-mind. Without deficiency in his original vows and without the need for supernormal powers, he accomplishes the practice of the mind and achieves the karma of wisdom, such that all roots of goodness are entirely purified.
Just as within the palace of Lake Anavatapta, the ground is entirely inlaid with pearls and amber, emitting various kinds of light that illuminate everything without exception;

so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva. Entering the inconceivable scope of the wisdom of the subtlest atom, they lead and protect sentient beings to the marshland of sorrowlessness. Adorned with various kinds of precious jewels and necklaces, they do not destroy the essential nature of the Dharma-realm. Dwelling in the unconditioned abode of all Tathāgatas, their mental inclinations never regress.

Just as that Dragon King Anavatapta provides protection for all the minor dragons, causing those who feel fear to be without dread; and while the divine dragons on his left and right possess majestic virtue, all the minor dragon kings of the great ocean come to pay their respects and offer congratulations.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is likewise in this way: for the sake of all sentient beings who possess form and harbor fear, he acts as their protection and refuge; according to the time, he nurtures them so that they are free from resentment. Whether within his own realm or beyond it, his mind is equal like space; though dwelling in the world, he spreads the light of wisdom, protecting and guarding all living beings no differently than his own body.

Just as the springs of Lake Anavatapta give rise to the four great rivers that spread throughout Jambudvīpa, winding and turning through various enclosures before returning to the ocean, and moistening and nourishing all the lands they pass through; so too is it with this.

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is also like this: riding upon the ocean of the four wisdoms, they carry all devas, humans, Māras, Mārakāyikas, Śakras, Brahmās, and other celestial and non-human beings, causing them all to proceed toward the ocean of great wisdom and to resolve upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path—endowed with the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the eighteen unique qualities—and reaching the foot of the Bodhi tree, they never again regress.

What are called the four rivers of wisdom are as follows: First is the river of the wisdom of vows (*praṇidhijñāna*), which constantly makes vows to deliver sentient beings, yet does not rely upon the internal body and remains without attachment.

Second is the river of the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) that is boundless and fully endowed, which purifies the bodhisattva path and encompasses all realms; it moves to and fro and circulates everywhere without attachment, its hearing is inexhaustible and never-ending, and it brings forth the wisdom of the three periods of time to expound the meaning of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self.

Third is the ocean of wisdom of the bodhisattva’s meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which adorns itself with innumerable concentrations; it travels to the Buddha-fields of the ten directions to pay homage, serve, and make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, and brings forth the sourceless ocean of all Buddhas.

The fourth is named the River of Great Compassion; it causes all classes of sentient beings to dwell securely in compassion and establish themselves in non-retrogression. It uproots all suffering so that there is no more feverish affliction, and further employs countless skillful means to lead them forward without lingering attachment. This ocean of the Ten Powers accumulates a vast store of precious jewels, so that those with the karmic affinity to cling to them may know where to turn for refuge.
Just as the four great rivers flow from the Anavatapta Spring and all return to the ocean—being inexhaustible, endless, and inconceivable—so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.

Having attained superior and vast vows and accomplished the wisdom of their aspirations, they cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva; their observation of phenomena through wisdom is likewise inexhaustible. They realize the unsurpassed path without hesitation or obstruction, and they also know the concentrated minds of the Buddhas gathered together, delighting in that which the Buddhas enjoy.

Just as the Anavatapta Spring gives rise to four great rivers, and each river branches into five hundred tributaries, all of which eventually flow into the ocean without disturbing sentient beings or causing them any harm.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: relying upon the wisdom of his vast vows, his resolve remains unshakable; he cultivates the practice of universal salvation, extending compassion to all beings; he perceives both the conditioned and the unconditioned, awakening to all dharmas; he practices unimpeded wisdom, never severing the root of the Dharma, and instructs others in the essential path of liberation so that they may dwell in the stage of non-obstruction.

It is like the Anavatapta Spring, where within its sevenfold tiers grow various kinds of rare and wondrous treasures; their radiance illuminates one another with a brilliance equal to the light of the sun. Wherever it shines, all are benefited by that light a hundredfold and a thousandfold. Those with eyes behold the five colors—azure, yellow, and the rest—within the palace of Anavatapta; just as when the sun is in the sky, there is none who does not rely upon it, each form and substance possessing its own radiance without crowding one another. These jewels press against one another, producing various sounds that are exceedingly soft and gentle, such that one never tires of listening.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: dwelling in this Samādhi of Sovereignty over the Dharma-realm, they observe within each and every pore countless, immeasurable billions of hundreds of thousands of Tathāgatas, as well as the various assemblies of Buddha-fields—Bodhisattvas and disciples—listening to and hearing the flavor of the Dharma. They uphold it without forgetting, reciting it day and night, as if rescuing someone drowning in a deep abyss. Manifesting the body of a Tathāgata throughout all worlds, it is inconceivable and immeasurable; furthermore, they go to visit and draw near to the worlds of various Buddhas, paying homage, serving, and making offerings while presently hearing the flavor of the Dharma. Within the state of meditative concentration entered during hundreds of thousands of kalpas, they perceive neither length nor brevity, neither greatness nor smallness.

The Bodhisattva perceives within each and every pore the lands and cities of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas, the number of their disciples and retinues, the various types of forms and differing modes of speech, and how they move about and interact according to their own inclinations, each enjoying themselves in accordance with their respective vows; yet he perceives neither congestion nor spaciousness.

Why is this so? Because when a bodhisattva enters the state of mind fixed in the Dharma-realm, the mind is subtle and difficult to perceive, possessing no form or substance. Its traces of activity are extremely fine and beyond all analogy; it perishes of its own accord in every moment of arising, yet remains unaware of this. The realm of samādhi is inconceivable; the realms traversed through contemplation and meditative practice cannot be fathomed by thought. Even the abodes of the Buddhas have no fixed location. The manifestation of the Buddha’s majestic demeanor is inexhaustible, being difficult to achieve and difficult to practice, yet one never abandons or loses the bodhisattva path midway.

Transcending all realms of Māra, those who are not firmly attached abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and attain pure virtues. Possessing the essential ten powers (*daśabala*) of the Tathāgata, they seek the unsurpassed and limitless activity and practice the profound and subtle meaning of the True Dharma without regarding it as difficult.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: according to his mental intention, in the space of a single thought-moment, he arises from samādhi and knows the affairs of the three periods of time;

he is immediately able to discern the destinies of good and evil, attains mastery over all dharma-realms, and neither relies upon the internal nor relies upon the external, investigating the beginning and the end without [finding them].
Seeing the initial signs, they find no location and perceive no conceptualization; by transcending all thoughts, they exercise the analytical discernment of all meanings.
They travel through the Buddha-fields to pay homage, serve, and make offerings without ever feeling weary or satisfied.

Entering the realms of all phenomena, they contemplate and analyze them to exhaust their very source; they do not abide in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) nor fall into extremes, cultivating everything.
Wisdom does not cling to wisdom; though there is coming and going, no circling is perceived. One contemplates wisdom as a transformation, yet in reality there is no transformation.
The shared nature of sentient beings is likewise so; when one seeks its root, it can neither be measured nor limited.
One purifies all worlds without perceiving any purification, and proclaims to sentient beings: "For what purpose do you give rise to suffering?"
From what does it arise? Suffering, emptiness, non-self, and the absence of person, life, or soul—all these are utterly non-existent.
It manifests various transformations of impermanence; it dwells neither in birth-and-death nor is it attached to nirvana.
It transcends all kalpas and crosses over the realms of death, observing all appearances without the mind becoming deluded.
However, that bodhisattva, through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), thoroughly fulfills all wisdoms; remaining ultimately pure with an unshakable resolve,
they contemplate all worlds and all sentient beings— those who transmigrate and those who do not— and cause them all to attain liberation,
ensuring that the wisdom of all sentient beings within the entire world-system and the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) never diminishes.
Regarding majestic deportment, one next attains the Dharma through the Dharma without losing its proper sequence;

observing the Buddha’s accumulated practices without ever feeling weary or satisfied, one relies upon the treasury of all Buddhas to bring forth great treasures. Within all samādhis, one manifests expediently and without obstruction;
suchness is naturally maintained without stagnation, and the profound meanings of the Dharma phrases that expound the Way and its teachings are inexhaustible.
With great wisdom and eloquence, they discern the forms of characters and bring forth the *dhāraṇīs*, elucidating the various secret treasuries of all Buddhas;
having themselves departed from lust, they also cause sentient beings to be free from lust, anger, and delusion.

“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice skillful means throughout incalculable kalpas, manifesting various kinds of paths according to the capacities of beings to transform them and enable their liberation.”

All dharmas are naturally liberated, yet one does not perceive this naturalness; because there is neither liberation nor non-liberation, one establishes great compassion. Toward all sentient beings, one does not even perceive the notion of "sentient being. One counts the inhalations and exhalations; when breath issues forth and when breath enters, one realizes that the nature of all worlds is fundamentally natural and that dharmas abide eternally of themselves. Those who previously practiced and gave rise to consciousness are said to be "undetermined"; seeing no movement or shifting, one speaks of the dharma-flowing. Though transforming sentient beings, one does not perceive any act of transformation. One purifies the three fields of precepts and enters the Tathāgata’s chamber; giving rise to the perception of all dharmas, the mind attains fearlessness. Preaching the dharma with purity, one turns the wheel of the dharma which is indestructible; the aspiration for the Way flourishes, and ultimately there is never the intent of an Arhat or Pratyekabuddha.
This is called the most supreme!

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva attains this Samādhi of Sovereign Control over the Dharma-Dhātu, they greatly increase their merit and advance to the higher stages of Bodhisattvahood, never again toiling in vain.
Chapter 18: On Expedient Wisdom and Insight Furthermore, O Most Victorious One!
A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should further contemplate the tenth samādhi of expedient wisdom, insight, and concentration, and should mindfully practice it.

What is the Bodhisattva’s practice of the tenth samādhi of skillful means, wisdom, and concentration? In this regard, Most Victorious One! There is a samādhi of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva named "Infinite Intent.

When a Bodhisattva dwells in this samādhi, they observe and know infinite physical actions; they observe and know infinite verbal actions; they observe and know infinite mental actions; they observe and know infinite Buddha-fields to which they go to adorn them; they observe and know infinite sentient beings whom they go to subdue; they observe and know the accomplishment of the karmic wisdom of infinite sentient beings who are to be transformed; they observe and know the emission of infinite great radiances to receive those not yet liberated; and they observe and know the emission of infinite lights of the marks of a Great Man that illuminate everything without exception.

He observes and knows that he alone is able to turn the immeasurable wheel of the true Dharma—which neither gods, nor worldlings, nor Māras, nor Māra-heavens, nor Brahmā, Śakra, or the Four Heavenly Kings can turn—and he observes and knows that immeasurable Bodhisattvas travel through the Buddha-fields, acting as leaders for all sentient beings. Although they have attained the power of a Buddha, they do not rely on that power; though they release their bodies and minds, it is as if there were nothing released. They attain the wisdom of a Buddha yet do not cling to that wisdom; they initiate it by means of the Buddha’s arising. They traverse immeasurable realms by means of the Buddha’s supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*); they purify all practices by means of the Buddha’s purity; they transcend all practices by means of the Buddha’s conduct; they surpass all measures by means of the Buddha’s measure; and through the Buddha’s courageous concentration (*vikrīḍita-samādhi*), they harbor no timidity, attaining the purity of a Buddha to perform the works of a Buddha.
Once the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has dwelled in this samādhi, he universally contemplates all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
Having contemplated all-knowledge, he further contemplates the activity of all-knowledge; having contemplated the activity of knowledge, he is immediately able to cultivate knowledge.
Being able to cultivate knowledge, he receives the instruction of knowledge; having received the instruction of knowledge, he contemplates wondrous knowledge. Having contemplated the wondrous...
Wisdom then seeks the conditions for wisdom; having been provided with the conditions for wisdom, one attains the wisdom of liberation.

Having attained liberation, one attains liberation without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*). Having attained that which is without remainder, one accords with the unsurpassed essential rectitude of the Dharma and Vinaya.

One lengthens the bodhisattva practice and accomplishes the bodhisattva deeds, advancing the bodhisattva’s resolve and enduring the bodhisattva’s sufferings, yet withdrawing from [worldly attachments].
The Bodhisattva enters the Bodhisattva-piṭaka with skill; he grasps the Bodhisattva’s illumination and dispels the Bodhisattva’s darkness;
he abides on the Bodhisattva stages and manifests the marks of a Bodhisattva; he removes the deafness of Bodhisattvas and purifies the voice of a Bodhisattva.

Upon hearing this, the bodhisattva remains unmoved and does not turn back; he harbors no fear nor does he regress. His mind feels neither weariness nor aversion, and he does not dwell on personal gain. He neither abandons nor becomes suspicious, neither interrupts nor relies upon what he has heard and seen as a bodhisattva.

The reason for this is that Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas enter among all sentient beings according to their respective types; they observe the principles of the Dharma to form a heart of great vows, acting as a model for those beings, riding upon the Great Dharma Vehicle to enter the ocean-river of the Buddhas, proceeding directly toward their destination without ever losing their thorough penetration.
“A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should always contemplate the three great vows; upholding the mind of these great vows, they lead sentient beings from this shore to the other shore.”
What are called the three great vows?
The first is named the superior great vow; the second is named the middling superior great vow; and the third is named the inferior superior great vow.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva has three great vows.
What are these three? They are:
first, the superior-middle; second, the middle-middle; and third, the inferior-middle. These are called the three great vows.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva has three great vows.
What are these three? They are:
first, the lower-high; second, the lower-middle; and third, the lower-lower. These are called the three great vows.
“O Most Victorious One, you should know!

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva attains this tenth samādhi of skillful means, wisdom, and concentration, they are then able to reach this foremost, supreme, and great mind of the vow, nurturing sentient beings and purifying Buddha-lands. He held—
Through skillful means and wisdom, they are free from the bonds of craving and desire; having learned well, they penetrate deeply into the single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*) of the bodhisattva.
They understand that all characteristics are themselves without characteristics, and they thoroughly comprehend the illusory and transformative nature of the bodhisattva.
They establish the intentions of sentient beings in steadfastness, dedicating their minds and wills entirely for the sake of all living beings throughout the future, the past, and the present.
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, practices great compassion that universally covers all beings;
for those lacking wisdom, he manifests the light of insight; for those who are blind and sightless, he acts as their eyes;
for those without protection, he provides shelter; he fulfills all the dharmas of the Buddhas, bringing hope to sentient beings.
One eliminates the perception of dharmas.

Why is this so? It is like a householder who has accumulated ten billion treasures—gold, silver, precious gems, musaragalva, agate, pearls, and amber—within his storehouses; furthermore, there is within them a wish-fulfilling moon-jewel, which, wherever it is placed, illuminates everything without exception, its color and form being supreme because the very nature and substance of that jewel are inherently luminous.

The Bodhisattva is also like this: having obtained the wish-fulfilling jewel of the mind, he opens the gate of wisdom; with the radiance of wisdom, he universally illuminates all things, penetrating the comings and goings without obstruction. Entering this meditative state is likewise free from hindrance. Just as the light of that bright jewel shines forth, his own aspirations and abilities manifest spontaneously according to their inherent nature; no one can restrain or compel him to act otherwise.

Why is this? Because its essential nature is spontaneous and there is nothing that can cause it not to be so; yet it is not so, and it is also not not-so. One does not perceive sentient beings as being so, nor does one perceive sentient beings as not being so.
“O Most Excellent One, you should know that sentient beings also arise from both the ‘thus’ and the ‘not thus.
How do sentient beings arise from both the ‘thus’ and the ‘not thus’?

As for the statement that "sentient beings arise from *tathatā* (suchness)": the limitations of the five destinies flow on without interruption; whether as one body, a hundred bodies, or a thousand million bodies; across one eon, a hundred eons, or a thousand million eons; they discard one body and receive another, accomplishing the four great elements and nurturing the five aggregates—this is called sentient beings arising from *tathatā*.
How do sentient beings emerge from non-existence? In this regard, the essential nature of sentient beings is fundamentally empty;

emptiness itself has no consciousness and is devoid of conceptualization. At that time, four winds arise from the four directions: first, the wind of earth-essence blows into space; second, the wind of water-essence blows into space; third, the wind of fire-essence blows into space; fourth, the wind of wind-essence, which is the very wind of space itself. When the spirit meets with obstructed consciousness and they suddenly encounter one another, these five factors converge to form a physical body. Encountering the conditions of heaven, one becomes a deva; encountering the conditions of humanity, one becomes a human. According to what the form is stained by, its specific body is thereby constituted.

If there were the element of earth but lacked water, fire, and wind, it could not be established; if there were the element of water but lacked earth, fire, and wind, it could not be established; if there were the element of fire but lacked earth, water, and wind, it could not be established; if there were the element of wind but lacked earth, water, and fire, it could not be established; and if there were consciousness that relies upon space and governs itself independently, lacking earth, water, fire, and wind, it too could not be established.

A bodhisattva should contemplate that consciousness is subsumed within the emptiness of the dharma-realm; when consciousness is associated with the four great elements and the five dharmas, it forms a body of the five aggregates that is vigorous, sharp, and swift. Thereupon, within the realm of emptiness, consciousness itself perceives coldness, coarseness, roughness, hardness, and rigidity. Immediately recognizing this as being detached from emptiness, one focuses the mind in contemplation; the mental recollection of the perception of emptiness becomes tranquil and unconditioned. Thus, one awakens to oneself within the void space as not coming into this world, entering the unconditioned realm of nirvana without remainder and attaining parinirvāṇa.
If that consciousness-spirit is dull and unsharp, clouded and dazed, lacking faith in the departure from emptiness, it will claim that its own body is identical to empty space.
Consequently, it undergoes sensory opposition through form and enters the gateway of rebirth; meeting with good it becomes good, meeting with evil it becomes evil.
When it encounters virtuous beings, it believes in the existence of good and evil, and comes to know the present life and future lives as venerable.
Disregarding elders and juniors, wearying of worldly suffering yet practicing virtue without ceasing, one may eventually attain the Way;
yet encountering evil spirits, the consciousness becomes forever estranged from the good. Willingly indulging in evil, one wanders through birth and death, traversing the sufferings of hell;
the conscious spirit undergoes affliction without a moment’s rest, only then awakening to realize that its past conduct did not accord with the prohibitions and precepts.
Gradually reforming oneself through self-reproach, abandoning evil and embracing good, one proceeds from the initial aspiration through the passage of kalpas, accumulating merit and virtue;
only by fulfilling all practices does one attain the Way. This is what is meant by saying that sentient beings also emerge from "not so."
“A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should always contemplate with single-minded observation what is appropriate and what is inappropriate.
How does a Bodhisattva observe what is appropriate and what is inappropriate?
That which is ‘appropriate’ refers to worldly dharmas; that which is ‘inappropriate’ refers to the Path.”
To affirm is to be burdened; not to affirm is to be without attachment.
To affirm is to exist; not to affirm is emptiness.
To affirm is to possess consciousness; not to affirm is already to be free from it.
Thus, there is name, birth, aging, illness, and death; otherwise, there is no birth and no phenomena of arising and ceasing, nor is there any wandering or rushing through the five destinies.

A bodhisattva should reflect thus: "Abandoning what exists, one cultivates the practice of non-existence; the light of universal knowledge is without obstruction. Abandoning and extinguishing one's own dharmas, they naturally do not arise, nor does one perceive their extinction. One purifies all worlds throughout the ten directions, delivering those who have not yet been delivered. Though there is intimacy, one perceives no intimacy; one exerts oneself for the sake of others without calculating suffering. Bearing heavy burdens, one always acts as a leader, ushering others into the ocean of Dharma and seeking undisturbed concentration. One gathers infinite and immeasurable precious treasures—the fivefold dharma-nature, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, meditative concentration, liberation, the marks and signs of excellence, and the supernormal powers—regarding these as treasures, the mind harbors no fear nor dread."

"Furthermore, there is a samādhi called the Unconditioned Concentration (*asaṃskṛta-samādhi*). When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells in this samādhi, they manifest radiant meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) to purify the traces of sentient beings without ever becoming weary. They expound the emptiness of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-śūnyatā*) to all sentient beings; those who understand emptiness then attain timely awakening, turn their minds toward the Path, and never regress."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ajita:

"Just as I today abide in this samādhi of sovereign mastery over the dharma-realm, I observe with my divine eye the expanse of space above; within the realms where sentient beings dwell, in the mere twinkling of an eye, there are hundreds of thousands of millions of incalculable sentient beings who are about to receive form and approach the gate of birth."

At that time, the countless Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the ten directions, all manifested transformation bodies dwelling within the realm of empty space. They expounded the Dharma of emptiness and non-substantiality to the consciousnesses of those four elements, teaching: "To be appropriate with emptiness and yet further detached from emptiness, and likewise to create detachment from consciousness—this is to forever leave behind the empty calculation of 'self'."

If one who relies on emptiness contemplates the form of consciousness through the meditation on emptiness, they will immediately relinquish the substantial form of consciousness within the realm of emptiness, enter the state of no-remainder, and attain parinirvāṇa, never again returning to this world to receive the form of the five aggregates or undergo various sufferings and afflictions.

The Tathāgata’s provisional wisdom is formless; he delivers consciousness into the realm of empty space, manifesting extraordinary spiritual transformations and virtuous edification. At times he manifests the pure lands of all Buddhas; at times he remains standing in the silent composure of the worthy and holy ones; and at times he walks in meditation or recites scriptures without weariness.
Although consciousness does not perceive them, the majestic deportment and ritual etiquette of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones,

are never neglected. A Bodhisattva should contemplate that while the infinite lands covered by space have no such thought as "I am now covering so many lands," nor does space itself think of its own great merit.

Why is this? That which is covered by emptiness is such by its very nature; phenomena do not change or alter, but abide naturally and eternally. Phenomena do not move or shift, nor are they manifold; they are neither born nor extinguished, and furthermore, they do not undergo transformation.
The reason for this is that the nature of the dharma-realm of empty space is spontaneous.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva should contemplate the consciousness of the spirit of empty space; this consciousness has three characteristics.
What are the three? First, one-pointedness;
second, remorse; third, neither one-pointedness nor remorse.
What is the one-pointed consciousness of the space-deity?

What is called "a single destination" refers to the tendency toward the gates of birth to nurture the seeds of the aggregates (*skandha*); according to their respective types, the defiled consciousness (*vijñāna*) assumes its form.

Bodhisattvas should know that the consciousness of the spirit in empty space also has a state of intermediate dwelling. When consciousness unites with the four vital energies (*dhātu*), it comes to this intermediate dwelling; having dwelt there, it receives a form. This may last for half a month, or a full month, or for two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, eleven, or twelve months. Then, from this intermediate dwelling in empty space, it proceeds toward the five destinies (*gati*); once it dwells within these five destinies, they immediately manifest before it.

Having entered the cessation within the five destinies, one may remain for one, two, three, four, or up to twelve months; even when transformed as a deva, there is no fixed period of days, months, or years. There is likewise a state of cessation within the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals, each of which differs from the others.
Within the sphere of space and consciousness, it abides serenely, formless and invisible; only the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones of the Avīci realm, are able to see it.
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s dwelling in the midst of empty space while tending toward the gate of birth.
What are the two regrets of the consciousness of the space-deity?

These two regrets are as follows: when the four elements combine and consciousness dwells within them, one regrets having received this form; yet, with a mind contemplating emptiness, one remains serene and non-active, without calculating or clinging to perceptions.

Furthermore, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, abide in the teaching through the nature of the transformation Buddha, awakening beings at that very moment, and then enter parinirvāṇa within the realm of nirvana without remainder.
Most Excellent One, you should know this!

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, throughout the three periods of time, have instructed and exhorted sentient beings, leading countless numbers of them to reach that shore of the unconditioned. For the sake of a single sentient being, they traverse the three periods of time, undergoing toil and hardship, employing innumerable skillful means to transform and deliver them; though they dwell amidst suffering and affliction, they do not regard it as labor, nor do they harbor any heart of weariness or exhaustion.

When the Tathāgata appears in the world, he manifests the bodies of all Buddhas, dwelling within the consciousnesses in the realm of empty space, and for their sake he expounds the unsurpassed Dharma of the ultimate atom. He causes the consciousnesses of his parents to awaken; having received these transformative words of the Dharma, they immediately enter the realm of *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* at that very spot and pass into *parinirvāṇa*. These instances are incalculable and exceed in number the sentient beings saved by all the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, throughout the ten directions—there is nothing with which to compare them.

This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva abiding in this Samādhi of the Sovereignty of Mind within the Dharma-Realm; being able to grasp skillful means and exercise wisdom, they cultivate immeasurable dharmas and thereby ascend to the stage of a Bodhisattva.
What is meant by the third state, where the consciousness of the space-deity neither has a destination nor has regret?

That which is called "neither having a destination nor having regret" means that the dharma-nature of the realm of space contains consciousness within it; its abiding form is like a shadow or a light. It is extremely subtle and minute, contemplating emptiness with mental consciousness; it does not reach the realm of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), yet in retreating, it does not fall back to the existence of the human world.
"This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva who neither has a destination nor has regret.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Most Victorious (Varasena) came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

Thus it was said by the World-Honored One: "The consciousness of the space-deity abides within space, its form like a shadow or a reflection; only the Bodhisattva Aviyana and the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are able to see it."

If it were the case that the divine consciousness and the cessation within the four elements, as well as in space, merely involve coming and going, then in the realm of Nirvana and in the ultimate truth (paramārtha) as well, there would likewise have to be a divine consciousness and there would likewise have to be a cessation.
If there were consciousness that abides in cessation, what difference would there be between that realm of *nirvāṇa* and empty space, or consciousness abiding in the void?

If there were no difference, then *nirvāṇa* would not exist. Because *nirvāṇa* would not exist, there would be no fruits of the path nor the teachings of the Three Vehicles. The realm of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) and the realm of *nirvāṇa* would then be no different; *nirvāṇa* would be birth and death, and birth and death would be *nirvāṇa*.
“World-Honored One!
According to what I have heard from the Buddha regarding the consciousness of the space-deity and its abiding within the void, my doubts have increased all the more.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Sujaya:

“In that realm of Nirvāṇa and the ultimate truth (paramārtha), there is both consciousness (vijñāna) and an intermediate state (antarābhava). The consciousness of Nirvāṇa and its intermediate state are each distinct from the dharma-nature (dharmatā) of the consciousness and the intermediate state of emptiness.”

In *nirvāṇa*, the consciousness is serene and unmoving; it neither shifts nor changes, nor is there any gateway for its arising. Regarding its destination, there is likewise no birth, aging, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, or affliction. To say that consciousness is eternally extinguished is not the case of eternal extinction; to say that consciousness arises again is likewise not the case of arising.
"For that which abides in the interim, it takes eternal quiescence as its abiding.
The Buddha told Most Excellent:

"When a Tathāgata appears in the world, all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present—numerous as the sands of the Ganges—neither grasp at nirvāṇa nor undergo ultimate extinction."
“If the Buddha, the World-Honored One, were to enter *nirvāṇa*, he would not be the Perfectly Awakened One, nor would he be one who possesses the great vows.
The Buddha told Most Victorious:
“Since the time that the names of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones of the three periods of time have existed, I have never seen any of them enter *nirvāṇa*.”
Even if all future Buddhas were to appear within the Dharma-realm and dwell throughout the realm of *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, they would not enter the state of *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
Most Victorious One, you should know this!

The consciousness of the Tathāgata and the consciousness of nirvāṇa are not different; however, the consciousness of nirvāṇa is formless, shadowless, and devoid of luminous characteristics—it is unmoving and cannot be shifted.
As for the consciousness of the Tathāgata, it possesses movement and can be shifted.
That consciousness and this consciousness are one and not different; there is difference only in terms of movement and non-movement.
A bodhisattva should contemplate emptiness: where there is emptiness, there is consciousness and cessation; where there is existence, there is consciousness and cessation.
If there were further dharmas existing outside of nirvāṇa that possessed consciousness and a place of rest, that would be called "supreme"!
The divine consciousness of space rests within space; the divine consciousness of nirvāṇa rests within nirvāṇa—this is what is meant by their respective distinctions.
*The Scripture on the Ten Abodes and the Severing of Bonds*, Fascicle Six.
*The Scripture on the Ten Abodes and the Severing of Bonds*, Fascicle Seven.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Chapter Nineteen: Transforming Sentient Beings At that time, the Bodhisattva Most Victorious addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva traverse birth and death, undertaking diligent and ascetic practices, proceeding from one buddha-field to another, nurturing sentient beings and adorning the site of enlightenment? Although they transform sentient beings, they do not perceive those being transformed, nor do they perceive sentient beings, nor do they perceive themselves as having anyone to transform.
"The reason for this is that one contemplates the dharma-nature as void, quiescent, and non-existent.
The Buddha told Most Excellent:
"So it is, so it is! It is just as you have said!"

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, upholding a great and boundless resolve of universal vows, nurtures sentient beings and purifies Buddha-lands; yet, while transforming sentient beings, he perceives neither the act of transformation nor the sentient beings themselves.

The reason for this is that, through the contemplation of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), one observes that all things are void, quiescent, and utterly non-existent; they are entirely empty and still, formless and signless, and thus cannot be seen.
All dharmas are empty of themselves; sentient beings are empty of themselves; lands are empty of themselves; nirvana is empty of itself; and bodhisattvas are empty of themselves.
"O Most Excellent One!

A bodhisattva should contemplate in this way: deeply entering the essential core of the Dharma, they understand that all phenomena have a single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*) which is suchness (*tathatā*).
All phenomena are empty and quiescent through manifold wisdoms, unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and free from any defilement or attachment; the bodhisattva-mahāsattva is likewise so."

Your resolute intention for the Way is difficult to thwart; you shall certainly reach the unsurpassed, true, and correct Way to become a Most Perfectly Awakened One. Your will is like a diamond, never turning back. Adorning the Way-tree with the unconditioned Dharma, from the initial generation of the aspiration until sitting beneath the King of Trees at the site of enlightenment—whether those who have already been subdued, those currently being subdued, or those yet to be subdued—you do not give rise to pride during this interval. You harbor no pride of thinking "I am superior and they are inferior," no pride of thinking "I am equal to them," nor the pride of thinking "They are superior and I am inferior. There is no pride of superiority, pride of mediocrity, or pride of inferiority; no pride of mediocrity over superiority, pride of mediocrity over mediocrity, or pride of mediocrity over inferiority; and no pride of inferiority over superiority, pride of inferiority over mediocrity, or pride of inferiority over inferiority.
In this way, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should reflect upon and eliminate these various forms of pride, nor should they harbor envy or a conceited mind.

When the bodhisattva enters meditative concentration to observe which sentient beings are ready for deliverance and which are not, they employ skillful means to enter the five realms of existence and the eight states of no-leisure. If there are sentient beings who should be transformed, the bodhisattva becomes their friend or acquaintance, or acts as their parent, brother, or relative; or they appear as a great wealthy man, a noble, or an elder. According to the needs of those beings, they provide for their poverty and deprivation, producing immeasurable stores of gold, silver, precious gems, lapis lazuli, agate, pearls, amber, fine moon-pearls, and wish-fulfilling jewels. Or they provide food, drink, bedding, seats, and medicinal treatments for the sick and emaciated, giving all these things away without any stinginess or regret.

Furthermore, if someone should come to the Bodhisattva and earnestly beg for his head, eyes, hands, feet, kingdom, wealth, wife, children, or the seven kinds of precious objects, he is able to bestow them all as gifts, yet remains free from the notion of giving.

At that time, the Bodhisattva entered the samādhi of the sovereign concentration of the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu-vaśitā-samādhi-samāpatti). Through skillful means (upāya-kauśalya), he taught the dharma of emptiness to those sentient beings, saying:

"You should know that dharmas are unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) and have no agent. The six sense-faculties (ṣaḍ-indriya) are entirely without a master. When the eye sees forms, the form likewise has no counterpart; yet sentient beings, deluded by ignorance, give rise to consciousness within this, and through conceptualization and reflection, they find that the visual consciousness has no master."

If the ear hears sounds, the nose smells odors, the tongue perceives tastes, the body perceives tactile sensations, and the mind discriminates dharmas, the Bodhisattva observes that none of these exist at all.

When dharmas arise, they arise according to their respective conditions; when dharmas cease, they cease according to their respective conditions. One does not know the arising of arising, nor does one know the cessation of cessation; the twelve links of dependent origination and the eighteen fundamental bases are likewise thus.

At times, the Bodhisattva enters the Lion’s Vigorous Display Samādhi (*siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi*) and further manifests various kinds of transformations. Within these, he proclaims with pure and resonant voices; he manifests lands adorned with myriad jewels, fragrant with incense and flowers in five colors—azure, yellow, and the rest—while his majestic deportment remains pure and white, and his will is as firm as Mount Sumeru, unshakable and immovable.

Furthermore, he manifested immeasurable dharma-gates of meditative concentration, those which the Tathāgata constantly enjoys; all dharmas and the fundamental nature of sentient beings appeared before him.

At that time, the Bodhisattva again, by means of his supernormal power, entered immeasurable meditative concentrations and manifested himself: seated cross-legged upon a single lotus flower, he displayed his physical body with the merits of all dharmas throughout infinite and immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas; he purified the traces of sentient beings' attachments and conceptualizations, guided Bodhisattvas onto the path of essential liberation, and relying on omniscience, he expounded the nectar-like Dharma, radiating the light of wisdom to manifest the Buddha-wisdom free from all defilement and attachment.

Or they may erect stupas made of the seven precious gems, filling one world-system, or two, or three, or four, extending even to the Brahma-heaven or up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven, remaining for kalpas without entering parinirvāṇa.

At times, the Bodhisattva, through skillful means, enters the tranquil concentration of the unconditioned and perfects all roots of goodness; without abandoning the Tathāgata’s possession of all-knowledge, he instructs and transforms sentient beings by the power of samādhi.

There may be sentient beings who are to be delivered by hearing the teaching of sound; there may be sentient beings who are to be delivered by hearing the teaching of fragrance; there may be sentient beings who are to be delivered by knowing the meaning of taste; there may be sentient beings who are to be delivered by their bodies attaining suppleness; and there may be sentient beings who are to be delivered by realizing the Dharma through the mind.
At that time, the Bodhisattva further thought:

"Sentient beings who hear my voice must desire to hear the meaning of my purity; I shall now manifest the eight tones of a Tathāgata, and through these eight tones, I shall expound the eight phrases: the tone of suffering, the tone of its origin, the tone of its cessation, and the tone of the path; the vision of suffering leading toward suffering, the vision of its origin leading toward its origin, the vision of its cessation leading toward its cessation, and the vision of the path leading toward the path."
At that time, when the sentient beings heard such a sound, their minds were not yet awakened, and they desired to behold the light and his body.

The Bodhisattva entered meditative concentration and, through the contemplation of equality, transformed the earth element—the mountains, rivers, stone walls, trees, flowers, and fruits—so that they all became the seven treasures. Musaragalva, agate, crystal, lapis lazuli, coral, and amber all emitted radiance; these lights shone upon one another, eclipsing the light of the sun and moon.

At that time, the minds of the sentient beings were not yet awakened, and they further desired to behold the light of the sun and moon. The Bodhisattva, observing and knowing their mental intentions, immediately entered the Samādhi of Unobstructed Mental Intention and emitted light from countless thousands of billions of pores.

Within each ray of light was a lotus flower made of the seven treasures; within each lotus flower was a pedestal made of the seven treasures; upon each pedestal was a canopy made of the seven treasures; beneath each canopy was a throne made of the seven treasures; and upon each throne sat a Tathāgata, who preached to those sentient beings the root of suffering: "The arising of suffering without suffering is the Truth of the Absence of Suffering; the arising of accumulation without accumulation is the Truth of the Absence of Accumulation; the arising of cessation without cessation is the Truth of the Absence of Cessation; the arising of the path without a path is the Truth of the Absence of the Path."

Those sentient beings who heard the sound and those who saw the light, upon hearing the resonance of suffering, conceived within their minds a sense of weary detachment; they each gave rise to the perception of suffering, emptiness, and non-self, as well as the perception of neither arising nor ceasing, and thereupon, while sitting, they exhausted the very source of suffering and responded with pure resonance.
At that time, the sentient beings seated there who had smelled the fragrance, their minds not yet awakened, again gave rise to this thought:
"We desired the most exquisite fragrance, yet now the Great Sage speaks only through vocal teachings."

The Bodhisattva, knowing the thoughts in the minds of those sentient beings, entered the samādhi of meditative absorption known as the "Extremely Subtle Fragrance. He then transformed the earth element—including mountains, rivers, stone walls, trees, flowers, and fruits—so that they were all permeated with fragrance. There were *gośīrṣa-candana*, *kakkola*, *ainara*, *bhadraśrī*, *māndārava*, *pārijātaka*, *pūrṇamāndārava*, and blue lotus flowers; such various flowers, numbering in the thousands and hundreds, pervaded the four directions so that there was nowhere one did not smell their fragrance.
At that time, although the sentient beings heard this fragrance, their minds were not awakened; [the Bodhisattva] wished to cause the Way and its teachings to emerge from within the fragrance.
Then, the Bodhisattva, knowing what was being thought in the hearts of those sentient beings, immediately preached the Dharma of the six grave precepts from within the fragrance.

At that time, the sentient beings who smelled the fragrance had their minds opened and their intentions awakened; having brought an end to the afflictions of this world, they would no longer be reborn, and reaching the limit of suffering, they immediately attained the fruit of the Way.
At that moment, the sentient beings on the seats who were attached to flavors did not have their minds opened or awakened, and they thought:
"Our minds are set upon delighting in and clinging to exquisite flavors, yet now the Great Sage teaches the doctrine of fragrance; this is truly not what our hearts desire."

The Bodhisattva, knowing the thoughts of those sentient beings, entered the samādhi of meditative absorption on the extremely subtle and pure flavor. He then transformed the earth element, mountains, rivers, stone walls, trees, flowers, and fruits so that they all became nectar and natural food and drink, their fragrance wafting and their sweetness immeasurable.

At that time, although the sentient beings obtained this flavor, their minds were not awakened; they desired to crave what was before them and naturally presented it, and upon seeing its form, they finally fulfilled their wish.

The Bodhisattva, knowing the thoughts in the minds of those sentient beings, immediately enters the samādhi of swift and unimpeded movement. He then transforms the earth element—mountains, rivers, stone walls, trees, flowers, and fruits—entirely into sentient beings. Each and every sentient being holds various kinds of natural ambrosia (*amṛta*).

From within this ambrosial food, these voices emerge: "The sweet flavor exists externally and the tongue-consciousness tastes it; when these two factors meet, afflictions (*kleśa*) arise. I shall now practice self-restraint and contentment as supreme, seeking merely to sustain the physical form so that pain does not arise, just as a cart requires grease to carry a heavy load, or as a wound requires medicine to alleviate its agony."

"All such teachings as these arise from the 'flavor' [of the Dharma]; when sentient beings hear them, their minds open and their intellects awaken. Having brought an end to the afflictions of this life, they will not come to birth again; exhausting the limits of suffering, they shall immediately realize the fruit of the Path."
At that time, among the various classes of beings seated there, those whose minds were attached to fine and smooth textures did not attain awakening; they thought to themselves:
"My mind is currently intent upon attachment to fine and smooth textures, yet this Great Sage now speaks of exquisite flavors—this is truly not what my heart desires."

The Bodhisattva, knowing the thoughts in the minds of those sentient beings, entered the samādhi of meditative absorption known as the "Extremely Subtle and Gentle Compliance of Desire. He then transformed the earth element—mountains, rivers, stone walls, trees, flowers, and fruits—entirely for the sake of the sentient beings; each and every being was clothed in a natural *kalpavṛkṣa* garment, with celestial silks and celestial brocades wrapped around them.

When sentient beings see it and reach out their hands to touch it, they realize for themselves that it is soft and cannot be grasped; they think of a hundred sets of robes, and they arrive spontaneously. Only when the sentient beings' minds awaken do they reproach themselves:
"Alas! Why did I cling so greedily to these robes?"
"Is it not that I have fallen of my own accord into the dust and toil of the world, becoming a withered skeleton bound by flesh and blood?
Then he heard a voice from the air speaking these words:

"Man, you should know that the five pleasures of the human realm are neither true nor real. When the mind becomes attached to subtle and smooth sensations, they gradually give rise to entanglements; therefore, reproach yourself and abandon this greedy craving."

At that time, when the sentient beings heard the voice from mid-air, they finally attained awakening; having exhausted the suffering of this life, they would not be reborn again, and reaching the end of suffering, they immediately realized the fruit of the Path.
At that time, among the various classes of beings seated there, those who craved the Dharma but whose minds were not yet awakened thought to themselves:
"Our minds are now set upon the subtle and wondrous Dharma; yet today the Great Sage speaks only of fine textures and smoothness—this is truly not what our hearts have longed for."

The Bodhisattva, knowing the thoughts of those sentient beings, immediately entered the samādhi of the concentration of mind on the immeasurable dharma-realm. He then transformed the elements of earth, mountains, rivers, stone walls, trees, flowers, and fruits so that they all became for the sake of sentient beings; for each and every sentient being, he preached the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, meditative concentration (dhyāna), and liberation, as well as the conditioned and the unconditioned, the out-flowing and the non-out-flowing, and how birth, cessation, attachment, and severance are all non-existent.

At times, the Bodhisattva observes the inclinations of the minds and intentions of sentient beings, and then employs skillful means to manifest physical forms and characteristics, appearing and disappearing at will; he soars into the void and performs the eighteen transformations, coming and going from the sky without any obstruction.

Alternatively, they may manifest cities and palaces within various lands to expound the Buddha-dharma, enabling all classes of sentient beings to attain the inconceivable essential samādhis of the Buddhas.

At that time, in the cities manifested by the Bodhisattva, the inhabitants move about together in infinite numbers, treating one another with mutual respect and hospitality as if they were father, mother, elder brother, or younger brother; they are humble and modest, always being the first to offer their reverence.

At that time, the Bodhisattva further entered the Incomparable Radiance, causing all the Bodhisattvas to enter this radiance and sit in the full lotus posture; some sat upon high thrones and others upon lotus flowers, filling the entire world without any empty space remaining.

In some instances, he manifests as the body of a Buddha seated upon a precious lotus flower, expounding for all the Buddhas' six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, meditative concentration (dhyāna), and liberation; furthermore, through the Tathāgata’s eighteen unique qualities (āveṇika-dharma) and four fearlessnesses (vaiśāradya), he bestows grace upon sentient beings so that each may receive salvation.

At that time, the Bodhisattva again, by the power of his supernormal faculties, emitted a great radiance, manifesting hundreds of thousands of millions of Buddha-worlds. Each ray of light individually drew in hundreds of thousands of millions of sentient beings; riding upon the light, they arrived here, heard the Dharma, and attained deliverance.

Within each and every pore there are ten billion rays of light; within each ray of light there are ten billion lands. At that time, these manifested lands possess naturally awakening *maṇi* jewels, interspersed with various kinds of rare treasures. These *maṇi* jewels hang in the void ten fathoms above the ground; the radiance of the pearls penetrates everywhere, such that there is nowhere it does not illuminate.

Furthermore, there were extraordinary maṇi jewels serving as adornments; upon each jewel were ten billion river-sand-like Buddha-lands, and within those ten billion hundreds of thousands of multi-storied pavilions and towers, each pavilion contained ten billion hundreds of thousands of precious lotus lion-thrones from Buddha-lands. Upon each precious lion-throne were ten billion hundreds of thousands of divine precious lotuses from those lands, and upon each flower sat ten billion hundreds of thousands of Tathāgatas on lion-thrones, with each Tathāgata emitting a great radiance that overspread ten billion hundreds of thousands of Buddha-lands.

In each and every Buddha-field, there are ten billion hundreds of thousands of Tathāgatas possessing the virtue of the fearless lion’s roar; in each instance of this fearless virtue, there are ten billion hundreds of thousands of dwelling places for sentient beings; for each sentient being, there are ten billion hundreds of thousands of manifested Buddha-lands; in each Buddha-land, there are ten billion hundreds of thousands of Dharma phrases, meanings, and flavors, as well as the various teachings of the Buddhas; within each of these Dharma phrases, meanings, and flavors, there are ten billion hundreds of thousands of arising sutra-teachings that blaze forth amidst the dust of afflictions—even so it is with the various gates of the Dharma; from within each of these Dharma-gates, there are produced immeasurable manifestations of manifold wisdoms and the Dharma of non-retrogression, wherein the meanings and flavors of these various kinds of wisdom differ.

Within each and every turning of the wheel of Dharma, ten billion hundred thousand sentient beings were delivered and brought to matured practice. Within the buddha-fields of each and every such being, there were further ten billion hundred thousand buddha-lands, wherein each transformed their own realm to lead beings toward the wholesome destination, causing all classes of sentient beings to reach the path of Buddhahood.

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva enters this samādhi, they personally manifest immeasurable transformations of majestic spiritual power. The realm of this samādhi is such as has never existed before and has never been seen; its manifestations exhaust all variety, transcending what can be measured by the mind or conceived by the intellect. Whether internally, externally, or in between, no location is perceived; neither the time of coming nor the time of going is seen.
Why is this so? It is because the essence of all dharmas is spontaneous (*svabhāva*).

Although one may practice for a hundred kalpas desiring to exhaust all defilements, and though one acts according to the Tathāgata’s vow to bestow grace upon sentient beings, yet throughout immeasurable and infinite kalpas, one remains unattached, non-abiding, and unstained; nor can a name be established for such a state. Seeking its root, it is found to have no location whatsoever.

If there were someone who, wishing to employ expedient means and stratagems to investigate the form and characteristics of this meditative concentration and its transformative power, would find that its meaning is extremely profound and inconceivable; it is a dharma to be practiced by the Buddhas alone, and is not something cultivated by Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas.
“O Most Excellent One!
You should further contemplate this principle:

the Bodhisattva undergoes hardships and dwells among those in the eight difficult conditions, observing whether the minds of sentient beings possess desire or are free from desire, and he fully knows whether such desires are many or few.”
He fully knows whether there is a mind of hatred or a mind free from hatred, and whether it is great or small;
he also fully knows whether there is a mind of delusion or a mind free from delusion, and whether it is great or small.

If those sentient beings possess a mind of craving and lust, becoming excessively attached to female beauty—calculating it as being fine, plump, and fair—and their minds find pleasure therein such that they cannot part from it, at that time the Bodhisattva again manifests skillful means and devises extensive stratagems.

He immediately manifests for them the contemplation of the impurity of the foul body (*aśubha-saṃjñā*). Before the eyes of the assembly, he manifests his own impermanence: the four elements disperse and fall in different places; after one day, two days, or even up to seven days, the physical form becomes bloated, its odors foul and impure; or at times, the corpse’s flesh and blood have completely decayed, leaving only the tendons and bones connected together.

He further manifests various other transformations of form: sometimes manifesting a skull, or the thigh bone, arm, and elbow each in a separate location; over a long period, these change until they resemble the color of a white pigeon, and as the months and years pass, they become identical to excrement and soil.

Having thus observed sentient beings, the Bodhisattva awakens to himself and realizes that their false desires are the conduct of ordinary worldlings leading to rebirth in the evil realms; not returning to the Right Path, they feel self-repentance, and seeing that the past cannot be recovered, they turn to the Great Sage. They follow and cultivate the Brahma-faring, entering the pure abyss, washing away the defilement of lustful desire, refining the spirit, and casting off fetters. Thereby they attain unsurpassed, perfect, and true enlightenment, purifying their own land and nurturing sentient beings. This is called the Bodhisattva observing the mind of craving and desire, then preaching the Dharma for them so that they may attain the fruit of the Way.
Bodhisattvas should know that there may be sentient beings who lack a mind of desire yet whose minds are restricted to the minor and do not reach the Great Way;

the Bodhisattva encourages and brings them to fulfillment through the path of equal and perfect enlightenment. Using the non-dual Dharma of the treasury of wisdom, he guides and instructs them to know the correct path, establishing them in the Mahāyāna so they do not take the minor path. Having accumulated merit, established virtue, and practiced goodness for incalculable eons without weariness, their minds were once deluded and confused, unable to distinguish the true from the false, such that they only now realize for themselves that they had not reached the ultimate goal.
What is the non-dual path of the bodhisattva?

When a bodhisattva practices the non-dual path, the bodhisattva is constantly pure yet does not abide in purity; while sporting in purity, they transform sentient beings externally—this is the non-dual path.
The bodhisattva is constantly quiescent yet externally manifests as if distracted; while sporting in quiescence, they transform sentient beings—this is the non-dual path.
When a bodhisattva enters meditative concentration, there is never any error; arising from that state of mind to transform sentient beings externally is the Way of Non-duality.

When a bodhisattva’s mind of giving never harbors regret, maintaining a firm resolve regarding the retribution of non-conceptualization to transform sentient beings externally and cause them to eliminate the three perceptions, this is the Way of Non-duality.

When a bodhisattva is fully endowed with precepts without ever having a deficiency, further using the prohibitions and disciplines to transform sentient beings externally, this is the Way of Non-duality.
The Bodhisattva’s profound wisdom and far-reaching discernment do not lead him to boast of his own accomplishments; internally he is always single-minded and unstained—this is the Way of Non-duality.

Grasping wisdom to transform all things, he truly knows there are no boundaries; therein he examines his mind to prevent it from scattering, and uses this very Dharma to instruct and transform sentient beings, leading them across the wilderness to the sorrowless marsh—this is the Way of Non-duality.

"The Bodhisattva cultivates the samādhi of patience and right concentration; manifesting his body in places of diligent suffering such as mountains, marshes, and uninhabited regions, or appearing near villages and settlements to practice begging for alms, he may remain there for one year up to a hundred thousand years, or for one kalpa up to a hundred thousand kalpas, manifesting within that time the endurance of immeasurable suffering."

At that time, humans and non-humans dwelling in the mountains—including rākṣasas and ghosts with two feet, four feet, or countless feet—each brought swords and staves to assault the Bodhisattva; some used sharp blades to cut off his nose, yet his nose immediately grew back again like a jambu fruit.
"O Most Victorious One, you should know this:

as for the jambu fruit, taking one produces two; taking two produces four; taking four produces eight; taking eight produces sixteen; and taking sixteen produces thirty-two. In this manner, as it continues to multiply, the tree becomes entirely fruit until no more of the tree's form remains, nor can its branches, leaves, stalks, or nodes be seen."

When a bodhisattva practices patience while entering meditative concentration in this way, if someone were to come and cut off the bodhisattva’s nose—taking one piece and producing two, taking two and producing four, taking four and producing eight, taking eight and producing sixteen, and taking sixteen and producing thirty-two—and thus continue multiplying until the body is entirely transformed into noses with no physical form remaining, such that even hands, feet, head, or eyes can no longer be seen; [the bodhisattva remains unmoved].

Sentient beings saw only that his nose was infinite in measure; immediately, they gave rise to a thought of regret for having taken it, and they yearned with longing to behold the Bodhisattva’s original body.

At that time, the Bodhisattva emerged from samādhi; his mind was calm and composed as he arose from concentration. He restored his form to be no different than before, gradually moving to manifest inhalation and exhalation, and then opened his eyes as if about to speak.
Upon seeing this, all sentient beings threw themselves upon the ground, prostrating with their five limbs to take refuge, vowing to serve as attendants by the Bodhisattva’s side.

At that time, the Bodhisattva observed the thoughts within the minds of sentient beings and delivered them according to their needs at each moment; thereafter, the Bodhisattva again entered meditative absorption (*samādhi*), his inner mind tranquil and free from any other discursive thoughts.

Furthermore, there may be sentient beings who come to where the Bodhisattva is, surrounding him on all sides and gouging out his eyes; yet his eyes immediately regenerate, becoming like polished, translucent lapis lazuli.

Suppose someone were to take molten lapis lazuli, as large as a *vīra* fruit, and scatter it upon the ground; though it would disperse like mustard seeds beyond recovery, each piece would still clearly reflect one another with its own brilliant luster.

Sentient beings see only the physical form of the Bodhisattva as their eyes and no longer perceive his original form or appearance; immediately they give rise to thoughts of repentance for their past deeds, reproaching themselves and aspiring to behold the Bodhisattva’s true essence.

At that time, the Bodhisattva immediately relinquished his samādhi; with a mind calm and composed, he arose from concentration and manifested his physical form as it was before, without any difference. He gradually moved his limbs to demonstrate inhalation and exhalation, appearing as if he were speaking.
Upon seeing this, all sentient beings threw themselves upon the ground, prostrating with their five limbs to take refuge, vowing to serve as attendants by the Bodhisattva’s side.
At that time, the Bodhisattva observed the thoughts within the minds of the sentient beings and delivered them according to their needs and circumstances.
At that time, the Bodhisattva again entered meditative concentration; his inner mind was tranquil and free from any other distracting thoughts.

Furthermore, there were sentient beings who came to the Bodhisattva’s presence and, grasping sharp knives in their hands, struck his head and feet; yet his head and feet grew back just like the *kūṭaja* tree.

As for the *gotara* tree, if someone comes to cut down its branches, leaves, trunk, or joints, and these various segments are each placed in a different location, in the mere twinkling of an eye they will immediately regenerate from the energy of the earth as they were before, with branches, leaves, trunks, and joints each forming a complete tree.

At that time, the Bodhisattva was likewise so: his body and limbs were entirely transformed into heads and feet, with no trace of his original form remaining. Sentient beings saw only the Bodhisattva’s body consisting entirely of heads and feet, no longer perceiving his original appearance; they immediately gave rise to thoughts of repentance for their past actions, reproached themselves, and yearned to behold the Bodhisattva’s true original body.

Having sought and relinquished samādhi, his mind became tranquil and composed as he arose from concentration; he manifested his physical form once more, appearing no different than before, gradually moving his limbs to demonstrate inhalation and exhalation, and finally opening his eyes as if about to speak.
Having seen this, all sentient beings threw themselves upon the ground, prostrating with their five limbs and vowing to serve as attendants by the Bodhisattva’s side.
At that time, the Bodhisattva observed the thoughts within the minds of the sentient beings and delivered them according to their needs and circumstances.

This is called the Bodhisattva’s knowledge of whether there is a mind with desire or a mind without desire, and whether it is much or little; yet he does not think to himself, "I am in the midst of worldly toil and my efforts are in vain," nor does he think, "These sentient beings are easy to lead and inspire. In the practice performed by the Bodhisattva, no practice is seen, nor is anyone seen who receives the teaching. Both the act of practicing and the act of teaching are entirely empty and quiescent. He sees neither "one" nor "not one"; since "one" itself is without oneness, how much more so for those who speak of "oneness" or "one dharma"—these too are merely provisional designations.

Regarding what is called "the eye," the eye is but a provisional designation; the same applies to the ear, nose, tongue, body, mind, and their respective objects—forms, sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and mental phenomena.
The reason a bodhisattva speaks of "a single dharma" is that they wish to open the gateway of dharmas to manifest immeasurable gateways, leading beings to the state of non-dharmas to instruct them.
At that time, Jyotiṣka again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“How does one come to know whether sentient beings possess a mind of anger or a mind free from anger, and whether such states are many or few?”
The Buddha told Ajita:

"When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva travels through and enters immeasurable Buddha-lands of the world-systems, he observes each and every class of sentient beings—those that fly, those that crawl, those that move, and those that breathe, down even to the smallest ants—and distinguishes whether they possess a mind of anger or lack a mind of anger, whether it is great or small; having discerned each one individually, he administers the appropriate medicine."

If there are sentient beings who abound in anger and hatred, they will immediately encounter the transformations of suffering, emptiness, and impermanence: some will be devoured by insects and beasts; some will be harmed by thieves and the blades of weapons; and some will be unexpectedly burned or boiled by water and fire—such manifold transformations are beyond calculation.
If those sentient beings attain awakening of mind, they will follow his instructions and receive his transformation, immediately attaining liberation at that very place.

If there are sentient beings who perceive impermanence and change yet their minds do not awaken, the Bodhisattva then employs expedient wisdom to enter the Samādhi of Patience; this samādhi is named "Contemplation of Impermanence.
Furthermore, there is another samādhi named "Compassionate Subjugation that Dispels Anger."
If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva enters this samādhi-samāpatti, they will be able to subdue and eliminate the mind of anger.

Should there be extremely wicked rākṣasas, ghosts, spirits, tigers, wolves, thieves, or bands of malevolent beings who come toward the bodhisattva with the intent to harm them, they shall turn back midway before they have even arrived.

The reason for this is that the power of the meditative concentration of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*) protects and covers all directions and realms; there is not a single billion-fold world-system (*koṭi-nayuta-kṣetra*) that does not receive its salvation.
For one who has attained entry into the samādhi of loving-kindness, there are ten matters of the Dharma; what are these ten?
