This refers to cultivating profound wisdom and performing immeasurable deeds; possessing total retention and a powerful memory such that the mind cannot be thwarted; being inherently immeasurable yet taking the Dharma-realm as one’s measure to enter into the infinite; that which has been practiced by all Buddhas of the future, past, and present; sealed with the supreme seal of the Dharma; relying on the power of the Tathāgata to augment the Buddha-lands; and constantly establishing one's resolve to purify the site of practice and establish the karma of a Bodhisattva.
A practitioner who acts in this way accords with the Dharma and Vinaya and accords with the state of non-arising. They attain the opening of the eyes and awaken with great clarity;
their eye of wisdom is pure and forever free from the obscuration of dust. They obtain the eye of the spiritual lineage and attain the Buddha’s pure eye.
The eye of wisdom has no exterior; the analytical eye is profound and far-reaching; the Dharma-eye is constantly settled; such is the true spiritual friend.
Taking the eye as one's protection, one attains the profound eye of the Way and the eye of eloquence; with speech free from obstruction, one achieves the eye of non-doubt;
with a mind free of "self" or "other" and without hesitation, one enters the eye of the Dharma-gate to guide those who are blind;
by discerning the meanings and flavors, one reveals the Dharma-gates, draws near to true spiritual friends, and accomplishes the mind of the Way.
The realm they establish cannot be obstructed, nor can it be sought after by those who would disparage it;

this is called the Bodhisattva’s discernment of all eyes to accomplish the work of the Path. They act as virtuous and benevolent friends to all the world, pre-emptively understanding that which has not yet arisen and manifesting majestic signs. Established in roots of goodness, their transformations are unimpeded, and their merit—
Their virtue is pure and their aspirations are inevitably fulfilled; they enter the womb with integrity and encounter all forms of liberation, severing the web of doubt.
They spread the heavy clouds of wisdom throughout the realm of space, and through the Dharma of the noble ones, they dissolve the defilements of the mind.
Their established vows are ever present before them, and whatever they undertake is never met with hesitation or difficulty; their faculty of faith is firm.
His meritorious achievements are indeed inexhaustible; personally attending upon the various Buddhas, he eliminates thoughts of sorrow and joy.
His resolve for the Way grows ever deeper as he gathers the precious jewels of wisdom. He serves the sages of knowledge like exquisite incense and flowers;
when wafted by the wind, there is none who does not perceive them, and all that is foul and defiled is rendered pure.
"O Most Excellent One, you should know!

I am currently residing here within Jambudvīpa; the country where I dwell is named Vaiśālī. Observing the lands and realms of all directions with my physical eye, I see that there is no place where suffering and affliction exceed those found here, yet even so, beings here emerge from the lineage of the Tathāgata."

Now, the foul stench of these sentient beings reaches upward through ten thousand *yojanas* into the void; yet among humans, the gods are the "seed of heaven," and the gods themselves know by observing their past lives that all the merit they have accumulated stems from the human body. Were it not for humans planting the roots of manifold virtues, they would not receive such blessings and joy.

"O Most Victorious One, you should know that at that time, the various devas, each leading their retinues, desired to come to the world and all arrived in the air. Upon reaching the boundary of the foul-smelling heavy clouds of the human realm, they smelled the rank and impure odors of the world; they immediately returned to their own abodes and did not enter the human realm."
The reason for this is that because of its fragrance and purity, it is unfit for habitation.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice great compassion, they do not select among the lands they transform whether they are good or ugly, pure or impure; nor do they think in their hearts, "I now wish to joyfully teach and transform this place, but am unable to do so in that place."

Just as I now dwell in this Sahā world-system, having completed my work of transforming sentient beings without exception, all the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the ten directions offer their praise from afar. Each, within their own land, addresses the fourfold assembly, saying: "In such-and-such a direction, there is one named so-and-so who bears the name and title of Śākyamuni Tathāgata. Amidst the five boiling cauldrons, the five iron thorns, the five swords, the five blazing fires, the five states of chaos, the five states of no refuge, and the five difficult debts of this Sahā world-system, he is able to dwell therein and instruct sentient beings—this is most marvelous and extraordinary! He distinguishes the various stages of the worthy and the sage, and the perfections (pāramitās)."

The bodies of the various devas are pure and free from defilement; having reached the edge of the stinking clouds, they immediately return to the heavens. Upon arriving at their palaces, they go out to the rear gardens and enter the Aśoka Pond for seven days and seven nights to bathe themselves. They do so because they still fear that the foul odor of the human realm might cling to them, and their hearts take no pleasure in wandering within the human world.

At that time, the fragrant winds of the devas spread far and wide, reaching down to the realm of space for eighteen thousand yojanas; furthermore, beyond this distance, there is the Anuvāta wind, whose fragrance descends through the realm of the Vāyu-gandha wind for two thousand yojanas.
Although the various devas possess the fragrance of manifold virtues, it still does not equal the fragrance of the precepts maintained by those free from desire.

A bodhisattva should observe that while the devas consume blessings they deem eternal, when celestial messengers appear before them, they regret their lack of preparation; thus, one should aspire to cultivate meritorious deeds among human beings. At such a time, how could the mind be concerned with the distinction between fragrant and foul odors?

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is likewise: although dwelling amidst the five scorching flames of suffering and affliction, his mind does not grow weary or despondent, nor does he turn back in regret; his intention is always fixed on the liberation of sentient beings.

If there is a person of noble and holy power who, by means of their supernormal abilities, takes an ordinary person up to the realm of Fragrant Incense in the highest void and then brings them back down to this world, the body will remain perfumed for three times seven days before the fragrance finally ceases.
For one who is free from desire and fully endowed with the precepts, the fragrance of their virtuous discipline will never be severed, even as kalpas pass and kalpas go by.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva dwells within the world and grows amidst the world; moreover, they act as a great torch of light for the world. Though they undergo diligent toil, they do not regard it as suffering; their aspiration for the Way flourishes and their mind never falters. This is called the Bodhisattva observing sentient beings—whether they possess a mind of anger or a mind free from anger, whether such states are many or few—and knowing them all completely.
At that time, Ajita again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

How does a bodhisattva, with single-minded contemplation, observe sentient beings and fully know whether they possess a mind of delusion or a mind free from delusion, and whether such minds are many or few?"

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva entered the Samādhi of Clear Wisdom and Right Reception, universally observing the worlds as far as the limits of space. Regarding all classes of sentient beings therein—from those with one foot or two feet to those with countless feet, including devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans—he understood their origins, discerning and investigating each one to ascertain their true nature.
If there are sentient beings who possess much ignorance, I shall calculate for them and expound the twelve fundamental links of dependent origination:

ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form; name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging; clinging conditions existence; existence conditions birth; and birth conditions aging, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair.

Possessing minds free from impure and distracted thoughts, he expounded with fluency and in both direct and reverse order the inexhaustible wisdom: "With the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease; with the cessation of volitional formations, consciousness ceases;

with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, aging and death cease. With the cessation of aging and death, there is no longer any sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, or impure conduct. Leaks (āsrava) are a great affliction; Nirvāṇa is sublime."
In this way, the Bodhisattva contemplates all appearances and expounds them to exhaustively reach their fundamental source.

If there are sentient beings whose deluded minds are firmly entrenched and whose consciousness is not clear or bright, he gradually guides and leads them to a place of stillness. There, he further explains for them the Dharma of original non-existence—the Dharma of neither arising nor ceasing, the Dharma of neither attachment nor cessation—and analyzes the signs of rise and fall throughout the three periods of time. He shows that although deluded actions pass away, consciousness cannot be extinguished; he extensively illuminates the Dharma-gate to manifest wondrous wisdom, giving rise to the Buddha-way with all virtues complete. Without abandoning the Bodhisattva’s practice as a spiritual friend, they constantly roam in the tranquil halls of Bodhisattvas and enter the profound and essential contemplations of all Tathāgatas.
"Furthermore, one should contemplate the ten essential and firm dharmas.
How does one contemplate the ten essential and firm dharmas?
One contemplates the characteristics of the Buddha-treasury and the Dharma-body; one reflects upon the inconceivable and gathers it back into oneness; one understands emptiness."

Without thought and without multiplicity, arising and ceasing of their own accord without a master or substance, past actions leave no trace and cannot be guarded or maintained as they give rise to various realms; the dharma-realm and the realm of space are likewise inexhaustible.
Bondage and liberation are self-liberated, removing the attachments of sentient beings; relying upon roots of goodness, one accomplishes all-knowledge and transcends—
They have fully accomplished the realm of immeasurable wisdom and all swift intelligence; they satisfy the aspirations of bodhisattvas,
purify the conduct expressed through the traces of bodhisattva speech, never lose sight of the meaning of the Tathāgata’s path,
do not abandon the characteristics of the nature of all phenomena, and their minds are unerring as they enter into the most subtle [realities].
If the mind is like a vajra, its power cannot be destroyed; it is that which all Buddhas bestow as a prophecy (vyākaraṇa).
Since there are no sentient beings whatsoever who ought to be delivered, what is taught is non-dual and irreversible.
These are called the ten essential dharmas of firmness for a bodhisattva; by advancing toward the fruit of the Way, attaining the Way will not be difficult.
"This is called the most supreme, sublime, and inexhaustible Dharma of the Bodhisattvas; you should mindfully practice it.
Chapter Twenty: The Extinction of the Three Paths. At that time, the Bodhisattva Most Victorious rose from his seat, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Indeed, World-Honored One!"

The Tathāgata, the Arhat, possesses boundless virtue and wisdom; he does not rely on the gates of the Way to seek liberation, but through pure training, he diligently cultivates and aspires to reach it, his Vajra-samādhi being immeasurable.
Now I have heard the Tathāgata say that extinction is pure, that the three paths return to one, and that there are no longer two names nor any attachment to duality.
If this is indeed so, why seek the unsurpassed, most true path?
"So be it, World-Honored One!
We pray that you will expound [the Dharma] so that those on the path of seekers may forever forget the delusions of consciousness.

At that time, the World-Honored One turned his golden body to look toward the four directions at all those gathered in the assembly; they were tranquil and nameless, each free from discursive thoughts. He cast a subtle glance upon the Most Excellent One and addressed him, saying:
"How excellent is this question!
It is truly difficult to hear.
The Tathāgata shall explain it to you one by one, so that future students may forever be free from doubt."
Jināgra addressed the Buddha, saying,
“I wish and desire to hear it.
The Buddha said to Jināgra:

“The root of the path of purity does not give rise to defiled branches; because its essential nature is pure, all phenomena are pure, and furthermore, the dharma-nature itself is entirely pure. One should gradually distinguish between the finite and the infinite: through the purity of the infinite, one attains the purity of the three periods of time, and by realizing the emptiness of the three periods, one contemplates the three realms.”
This is called the Samādhi of Subtle Purity.

Most Excellent One, you should know that the three paths to extinction differ in their categories and vary in their orientations. The body is the root of defilement; thought is the pool of defilement; perception is the drifting dust; and consciousness is the head of bondage. If three are extinguished while one remains, purity is not attained; if two are extinguished while two remain, purity is likewise not attained; if three are extinguished while one remains, purity is likewise not attained. Only when four are extinguished and emptiness alone remains does one reach purity; the same applies to the purity of all-knowledge.

From the initial stage of the path up to the state of non-attachment, and further from the first dwelling through to the tenth dwelling, one extinguishes the four returns, the four returns-to, and the four obstructions. What are these four?

As for what are called the four: the body is the root of defilement, fully possessed by ordinary beings; mindfulness is a pool of defilement where the four currents run wild; perception is drifting dust that gives rise to eighty thousand cravings; and consciousness is the head of bondage, tethered to the three realms of existence.

Therefore, the Great Sage manifests three paths with appearances that seem superior or inferior; yet in reality, their *nirvāṇa* is without any distinction. The Path resides in *nirvāṇa*, which is not separate from emptiness and stillness.

The *nirvāṇa* of a Bodhisattva is named for the deliverance of sentient beings; the *nirvāṇa* of a Pratyekabuddha is named for the manifestation of supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*); and the *nirvāṇa* of a Śrāvaka is named for the manifestation of narrowness and inferiority.
Furthermore, Most Excellent One!

A bodhisattva, through the four immeasurables of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, nurtures and sustains sentient beings. Should they guide even a single person into the path of restraint, their faculties will be filled with boundless serenity, delight, and joy.

At that time, consciousness is clear, still, and unconditioned; devoid of thoughts of the mundane or the supramundane, all emotions are entirely purified, as pure as *nirvāṇa*. Therein, everything is forever exhausted and nothing exists; this is called "non-thought" (*amanasikāra*). One should not have anything to think of, nor perceive thought-moments, for even thought itself is non-thought. For the learner of non-thought, there is learning yet no learning. Form is neither form nor non-form, and one does not perceive form. Mental consciousness and its perceptions likewise lack the perception of consciousness. From the body of the five aggregates up to the formless, the essence of phenomena is pure; one does not perceive the existence of thought, yet there is nothing to be thought of.
"O Most Excellent One, you should know this!
As for what is called Nirvāṇa—if that Nirvāṇa were something distant, would it not be so?
Do not hold such a view."

The reason for this is that the essence of the dharma of non-thought is formless; when one contemplates this essence, it is nirvana. The essential nature of nirvana is the contemplation of the dharma; these two are one and not two, and there is no distinction between them. Nirvana is nameless and invisible, and there is nothing capable of establishing a name or designation for nirvana.
"Thus it is, Most Victorious One!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva who trains in this pure path of nirvāṇa should accord with the path by maintaining non-mindfulness.
Most Victorious One!
Furthermore, one should distinguish this: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva wishes to practice and fully realize this pure path, the essence of *nirvāṇa*, they should cultivate pure conduct.
How does a bodhisattva cultivate such pure conduct?
One should constantly ensure that body, speech, and mind are pure and free from blemish.
What is meant by the body being pure and without blemish?

In this regard, the Bodhisattva’s own body is already pure; understanding all external bodies to be likewise pure, he realizes his own body is empty and tranquil, understands all bodies to be empty, knows his own body is quiescent and understands all bodies to be quiescent, and realizes his own body is liberated, as are all bodies.

The Bodhisattva should further contemplate the observation of dharmas, clearly understanding that there is neither indolence nor pride; since his own body is without pride, how could the Way have pride?
Therefore, the Bodhisattva realizes that the body is without pride.

The Bodhisattva gives rise to the thought of contemplating the world as impure and foul; seeing that the body is like a shadow or a reflection, he perceives no notion of purity. Reaching the realization that purity itself is non-conceptual, he then accords with Nirvana.
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s path to pure Nirvana, which is without distinction.
The Bodhisattva Most Victorious addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"How is it that a bodhisattva is pure in essence and free from desire, yet possesses desire while being without desire?
The Buddha told Most Victorious:

“The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva circulates through the five destinies and transmigrates within birth and death; through skillful means and provisional manifestations, he adapts his teachings to the needs of the time. For some, he speaks of the purity of the body and thus discourses on non-arising; for those who perceive birth and death, he shows that there is no birth and death. Understanding non-arising, he realizes that birth and death are one and not different, nor do they possess various distinct names.”

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva should discern the activities of the body; having realized their non-arising, he understands that these births and deaths are the activities of the body, thereby penetrating both internal and external phenomena.
What are called the activities of the body?
The rise and fall of the three periods of time—past, future, and present—are such that the past leaves no trace, the present leaves no record, and the future has no designation.
Furthermore, O Most Victorious One!
That which has gone is forever exhausted; that which comes is inexhaustible; and the present is ever-shifting.
One should also contemplate the dharmas of exhaustion and non-exhaustion.
How does one contemplate the dharmas of exhaustion and non-exhaustion?

In this regard, the bodhisattva discriminates and thoroughly understands the pure perception of space; that which is inexhaustible is serene, unconditioned, and free from conceptualization. Those who possess conceptualization have a great deficiency regarding the noble precepts and discipline.
The Buddha told Ajita:

"In the past, when I attained Buddhahood and sat beneath the Bodhi tree, for seven days and seven nights I gazed at the tree without blinking. I reflected in my mind upon the Buddhas of the past, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, considering by what means they attained self-awakening and what dharmas they first mastered."
At that time, O Most Victorious One!

I again had this thought: "The Buddhas of the past, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, who attained supreme perfect enlightenment by means of the body-dharma, did so through the convergence of causes and conditions, possessing consciousness and perception. Those who understand these conditions realize they are empty, without perception, and free from all defilement; furthermore, they perceive neither arising nor ceasing, neither attachment nor cessation."
Thus it is, O Most Victorious One!
To observe in this manner is called the purity of the body; indeed, one whose body is pure returns entirely to the ocean of wisdom.
O Most Victorious One, you should know this!
The meaning of returning to the ocean has ten aspects. What are these ten? First, returning to the ocean of the Buddha is the contemplation of the formless nature of phenomena;

returning to the ocean of sentient beings is to transcend the perils of existence; returning to the ocean of the Dharma is because it gathers all wisdom; returning to the ocean of the field of merit is to establish the root that is fundamentally non-existent; returning to the ocean of the five aggregates is to manifest defiled phenomena; returning to the ocean of wisdom is to discern the various directions of instruction and admonition; returning to the ocean of the meaning of the roots is to increase the roots of goodness; returning to the ocean of the abiding mind is to thoroughly know the immeasurable thoughts and intentions of sentient beings, understanding them with unimpeded liberation; returning to the ocean of practice is not to violate one's vows; and returning to the ocean of great vows is to investigate the origin of birth and death.
This, O Most Excellent One,
is called the meaning of the ten gates through which Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas return to the ocean;
one should mindfully practice so that all return to the Tathāgata’s untainted Dharma-body.

Furthermore, regarding the observation of the Tathāgata’s untainted body (*anāsrava-kāya*): it does not abide in fundamental non-existence (*mūla-abhāva*) nor does it fall within the three realms. One thoroughly understands that fundamental non-existence is the single Dharma-body. One observes the body as untainted, abiding in the manner of fundamental non-existence; abiding yet not seeing abiding, there is likewise no place of abiding. With this untainted body, one enters the ocean of birth and death, manifesting a form-body (*rūpa-kāya*) that is like a non-form-body—boundless, limitless, formless, and invisible to sight. Even when the form-body ceases, its cessation is not perceived; nor is the birth of the body perceived, for its fundamental non-existence is like the abiding in fundamental non-existence.

The body of the Tathāgata is pure and free from all blemish; it enters among the multitudes of sentient beings, manifesting in accordance with their preceding forms and appearances. He thoroughly understands the purity of the bodies of sentient beings, realizing that his own body is pure and the bodies of sentient beings are pure—unitary and non-dual, neither manifold nor diverse, fundamentally equal and non-existent [in essence].

Fundamentally there is no non-existence, nor does one perceive the existence of a path; likewise, there are no mundane dharmas, whether with outflows or without outflows, nor does one perceive the instructions of the three vehicles as being the path of Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, or Buddhas. Furthermore, one does not perceive the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, or the eighteen unique qualities; regarding all the dharmas of the paths of the worthy and holy ones, one is entirely without attachment.
This is called the bodhisattva’s practice that should be pure and should be without anything to which it should respond.
Furthermore, Most Victorious One!
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should reflect upon the purity of verbal expression. What is meant by verbal expression being pure?

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva entered the "Pure Samādhi of the Realm of Space" and universally observed all sentient beings within the trichiliocosm who possess form—whether wise or foolish, pure or impure, handsome or ugly—and saw that they all return to emptiness and are entirely pure.
The Bodhisattva should further contemplate and observe with equanimity; even within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), he perceives neither equality nor inequality. Why is this?

Because he observes through the mark of equality, he perceives neither the marks of equality nor inequality, nor the absence of marks (*animitta*). Furthermore, observing all phenomena through the mark of equality, he does not perceive the dharmas of the Path as having limits or boundaries, nor does he perceive worldly dharmas as having limits or boundaries. He does not perceive the noble ones as transcending the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātuka*), nor does he perceive the strength of ordinary beings as being superior or inferior.

O Most Victorious One, you should understand this! The Bodhisattva discerns pure sounds; there is no sentient being who harbors conceptual attachments in their mind. He skillfully examines vocal resonance and perceives it as being without resonance. He does not see sorrow or joy, nor permanence or impermanence. Regarding those who delight in inversion and those who do not, he realizes that all sentient beings are fundamentally pure, free from desire and defilement, and devoid of arising, ceasing, attachment, or severance. They possess no root of the three poisons: lust, anger, or delusion.

Furthermore, one should observe that the twelve links of dependent origination and the eighteen fundamental elements are entirely pure from ignorance through death. Ignorance does not know the volitional formations it produces, nor do the volitional formations know that they arise from ignorance. Phenomena arise spontaneously and phenomena perish spontaneously; since phenomena do not perceive phenomena, how could there be ignorance or volitional formations?
It is thus, O Most Excellent One!

Dharmas do not know one another; when dharmas arise, they simply arise, and when dharmas cease, they simply cease. A dharma does not itself know whether it arises or does not arise, nor whether it ceases or does not cease. Therefore, it is said that there is neither arising nor ceasing, neither attachment nor annihilation.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Most Victorious addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

The deluded activities of the three periods of time revolve around the body; when there is a body, these activities follow it, and when there is no body, these activities cease. This is likewise true for everything up to old age and death."
“I only pray, World-Honored One,
that you will expound upon these doubts, so that future sentient beings may forever be free from hesitation and obstruction.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Most Victorious, saying:

“Delusion does not defile the body, nor does the body defile delusion; delusion does not perceive that ‘I have a body,’ nor does the body perceive that ‘I have delusion. Each is pure and devoid of a self; what is called ‘self’ is entirely empty and quiescent. This is called the universal purity of a bodhisattva.”
Regarding what is called "purity of speech":
what is speech? What is not speech?

Speech does not abide within, nor does it abide without; one does not perceive speech as having emergence or entry. One should then fully realize the ten meanings of steadfastness and discern the destinies of the aggregates and elements of sentient beings.
What are the ten? In this regard, a bodhisattva first seeks the essential means of deliverance for the sake of transforming all sentient beings;
they manifest countless transformations because their diligence is free from attachment.
He manifests the power of non-obstruction because all phenomena are empty;
he manifests the power of the cessation of thought because he has attained mastery over all phenomena;
and he manifests the turning back of mind, intellect, and consciousness, both by means of their transformation and non-transformation, as well as through the discernment of meanings and flavors.
He manifests the power of the nature of reality, because wisdom is made manifest;
he manifests the power of mastery, because he teaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings;
he manifests the power of fearlessness, because he abides securely in the True Dharma.
He manifests eloquence, manifesting each instance of immeasurable wisdom;
he manifests non-dual power, for there is no peer to it.
Such is his supreme excellence!

When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva discerns the dispositions and destinies of sentient beings, they are neither internal, nor external, nor in between the two; yet one might wish to say, "This is a bodhisattva."
He replied: "No, World-Honored One."
“How could desire, lust, anger, and delusion be the bodhisattva? He replied, “No.”
“World-Honored One!
If it is not by means of desire, anger, and delusion that one is a bodhisattva, then is it by means of various defilements, fetters, and attachments that one is a bodhisattva? He replied:
"No, World-Honored One! The Buddha said to Ajita:

“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas do not cling to speech, nor do they cling to non-speech; all dharmas are without clinging or non-clinging. One does not perceive clinging or non-clinging even in the eyes, ears, nose, mouth, body, or mind. The sounds and resonances that are produced arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions, like the wind moving and sound emerging. Whether from the wise or the foolish, the beautiful or the ugly, there is no diversity in sound; it neither dwells within nor exists without, and when sought in the interval between them, it cannot be found.”
The Buddha told Ajita:

“When a bodhisattva mahāsattva dwells in the samādhi of primordial immovability, his contemplation, diligent mindfulness, and all his practices are equal to space—neither abiding nor non-abiding, and devoid of manifold conceptualizations.”
"Thus it is, Most Victorious One!
The speech and sounds of sentient beings, all vocal resonances, are entirely empty and not real; they are deceptive dharmas that cannot be relied upon.
At that time, Most Victorious addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If the Noble Truths of the Tathāgata constitute the fruits of the Path of the Sages, and expedient means are not the truth, how can they constitute the Most Perfect Enlightenment?
The Buddha told Most Victorious:
“The path and dharmas of the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, are profound, certain, and true; because he has attained the true dharma, he understands that all dharmas are neither real nor existent.”
Furthermore, O Most Victorious One!

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva circulates through the five realms of existence to instruct sentient beings, delivering and liberating them according to what is appropriate for each. He observes the names and sounds of sentient beings and turns the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma, causing them to understand retribution in accordance with the meaning of the Dharma-words. To those who delight in suffering, he explains the root of suffering; he understands that all dharmas and words are ultimately wordless.
What constitutes speech?
From where does speech arise?
One thoroughly understands that the speaker has no arising.

At that time, the Bodhisattva further explained to sentient beings who delight in habitual practice the root of such practice: that this habituation is birth, this is the cause, and this is the condition. He analyzed how causes and conditions are fundamentally without the continuity of habituation; he saw neither the existence of habituation nor the existence of words.
"O Most Victorious One! This is called the delight in practicing that all sounds of sentient beings are empty and not real.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva responds to preceding sentient beings with the teachings of the Way, causing those who hear the Dharma to act in accordance with it; yet they do not know the destination of their practice, nor the fruit of its retribution."
This is called the Bodhisattva practicing non-practice and realizing non-realization; suchness, the single characteristic, and the equal cessation of all suffering.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva should further contemplate the exhaustion of the suffering of sentient beings, thoroughly penetrating all dharmas as having no birth, and understanding that sounds and voices have no place of abiding. Whether sitting or walking, they are always as if with a single mind; though wandering amidst the clamor of the world, they are always as if in quietude. Even when among a great assembly, they remain silent like a sage; if they wish to speak, their speech ceases of its own accord. Tracing back the words spoken, they find neither attachment nor non-attachment, seeing neither exhaustion nor non-exhaustion. In all dharmas, they likewise see no exhaustion, nor do they see arising, ceasing, attachment, or severance. When sound issues from speech, it leaves no trace whatsoever.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva contemplates eight practices for the sake of sentient beings who delight in the Path: that these beings cultivate and advance toward Nirvana through right speech, right action, and so forth, up to right concentration. Whether they act in accordance with the Dharma or not, he regards them all equally as the single contemplation of emptiness—non-dual and without error.
This is called the purity of speech of a bodhisattva mahāsattva, being free from blemish or defilement.
Furthermore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should contemplate and reflect upon the purity of mental consciousness.
What is the purity of a bodhisattva’s mental consciousness?

In this regard, the bodhisattva’s mind is pure and free from defilement; it is fundamentally pure, yet one does not perceive a fundamental basis for that purity. This fundamental nature of the mind cannot be stained, and nothing can create obstacles for the mind.

Why is this? Because Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas realize that the mind is fundamentally pure and do not perceive any [separate] purity; yet many in the world are deluded and ignorant, becoming stained by attachment to it. Having attained realization of emptiness through contemplation, they have nothing to which they cling; they discern the ultimate while practicing skillful means within that which is inherently pure from the beginning.

Bodhisattvas should know that, moreover, the fundamental nature of the mind has no coming or going; it does not discriminate between high and low, noble and base, or honorable and humble. It does not perceive that what existed originally is now non-existent, nor does it perceive that what exists now was originally non-existent. It does not dwell upon the roots of virtue; for one who dwells upon the roots of virtue, this is called emptiness, this is called non-arising, and this is called Nirvana.
He asked: "Does that root of virtue fully comprehend the fundamental nature of the mind? He replied:
"No. [The Master asked,] "Is it that by understanding internal emptiness, one comprehends the external? He replied:
"No," Viśeṣa said to the Buddha, "If that is so, how can it be empty?"

The Buddha said: “The mind is fundamentally empty; it is neither fundamental nor non-fundamental, neither mind nor non-mind. For a bodhisattva who is fixed in the emptiness of the mind, one does not perceive the mind itself. One’s own mind is fundamentally non-existent externally and fundamentally non-existent internally; it is one and not two, devoid of any names for various distinctions. The mind is not my mind, and there is no mind within the mind;

my mind is not mind, and there is no self within the self. Form is not my form, and there is no form within form; I am not form-self, and there is no self within the self. My mind and my form are not my mind and my form; form, my mind, and my self are not form, my mind, and my self. This extends to sound, odor, taste, touch, and mental objects (*dharmas*): they are not my mind and my *dharmas*, nor are they my mind, my *dharmas*, and my self.”

Why is this? Because the mind is fundamentally empty and that which is external is also empty; by knowing that what is external is empty, one realizes that all dharmas are likewise empty—unitary and non-dual, without manifold characteristics or appearances.

All dharmas are likewise thus: one does not see that what originally existed now no longer exists, nor does one see that what currently exists originally did not exist. Non-existence is not non-existent, and existence is not existent; as for existence, one does not know why it exists, and as for non-existence, one does not know why it is non-existent. Non-existence is eternally non-existent of itself, and existence is eternally existent of itself. Existence does not emerge from existence, and non-existence does not emerge from non-existence. Non-existence is not non-existent by its own nature, and existence is not existent by its own nature. Existence does not know non-existence, and non-existence does not know existence. All sounds are empty and not real; this is called the purity of the Bodhisattva’s mind.
As for that which is pure of mind, it cannot be defiled by the thirty-six turbidities; the mind is fundamentally free from dust and grime, with nothing to which it can ever become attached.
Furthermore, through skillful means and expedient wisdom, one realizes that the source is inherently pure, yet one does not give rise to conceptual attachments regarding this purity.

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, through the samādhi of mastery over the concentration of purity and emptiness that understands the beginning and the end, is able to voluntarily enter and emerge from the cycle of birth and death, traveling back and forth through the five destinies to plant the roots of all virtues;
as for those roots of virtue, they know that mind, consciousness, and cognition are devoid of mind, consciousness, and cognition.

Furthermore, with one's original mind, one takes pity upon all beings; one realizes that sentient beings are empty and non-existent, and that the self, persons, and life-span are pure from beginning to end.

Moreover, by extending the roots of virtue to all, one causes the various classes of sentient beings to advance and cultivate the Path. To contemplate that sentient beings and the Path are equal and non-dual in this way is what is called "purity from beginning to end."

Furthermore, by means of this purity, lust, anger, and delusion are equal to the Path; the Path is then lust, anger, and delusion, and delusion is then the Path. The purity of the Path and the purity of delusion are one and the same; they are neither two nor many.
"The Bodhisattva contemplates the beginning and the end as inherently pure, remaining unattached to any defilements.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Most Victorious (Jiasheng), saying:

"When bodily conduct is pure and one commits no evil; when verbal expression is pure and always returns to ultimate sincerity; and when mental intention is pure and extends compassion to all—when these various practices are fully perfected, one is called a Bodhisattva."

At that time, when the World-Honored One spoke this "Chapter on Original Non-existence and Purity," five thousand bodhisattvas all attained the stage of being born only once more before buddhahood (ekajātipratibaddha), and countless thousands of people all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, impartial path of enlightenment.
Chapter Twenty-one: The Vehicle of Signlessness. Most Excellent addressed the Buddha, saying:

"From the first production of the thought of enlightenment until the attainment of Buddhahood, how does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva thoroughly comprehend the single characteristic as being without characteristics, and furthermore, by means of signlessness, differentiate the single characteristic?"
"How does a bodhisattva dwell amidst sensual desires with a pure mind, and how does he emerge from those sensual desires back to purity?
The Buddha told Bhishmagarjitasvararāja:

"A bodhisattva who practices skillful means rides upon the vehicle of signless purity of mind; he circulates through the five destinies and the worlds of the ten directions, whether taking birth in the realm of desire, the realm of form, or the formless realm. Although he dwells within these realms, he is not defiled by them. Together with good men and good women, he delights them with the joy of the Dharma."

Furthermore, he traveled through the realm of form, dwelling in palaces together with various devas; or, in the Brahma Heaven, he expounded the subtle vehicle of the signless Dharma to the Brahma Kings. Amidst the assembly of Brahmas, he would sometimes pace back and forth and at other times remain in the noble silence of a sage, standing alone as the most honored one, beyond compare.
Furthermore, O Most Victorious One!

The Bodhisattva manifests the teachings of the Way subtly therein, gradually subduing the various devas so that they may practice the True Truth (*satya*). He removes the minds of the various Brahmās who reckon [existence] as pure, dwelling in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) for a hundred kalpas or even up to a hundred thousand kalpas. Then, descending from the realm of form to be born in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), he constantly delights in stillness within, dwelling alone in mountain forests; though he dwells among men, his mind remains perpetually in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).

At times, the Bodhisattva may manifest as having a household with a wife and children following him, and he dwells together with sentient beings in their worldly occupations. Whether occupying a high station while appearing humble, or in a lowly position while appearing noble, he observes the minds of sentient beings in their movements, sitting, rising, speaking, coming, going, advancing, and halting; yet he neither gives rise to arrogance nor does he disparage himself.
The reason for this is that they have thoroughly realized the purity of both the fundamental and the derivative.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva again dwells in hundreds of thousands of meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*) and samādhis; by the majestic power of these samādhis, he again contemplates the trichiliocosm, manifesting physical marks, signs, radiance, and supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*). With the mastery of expedient means (*upāya-kauśalya*), he wanders and transforms beings with ease; when the mind accords with purity, it is called "signlessness" (*animitta*).

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva abides in this samādhi, they are able to seek the signless path of the vehicle. They do not perceive signs arising, nor do they perceive non-signs arising; because they practice the path through non-arising, they do not even conceptualize it. Regarding the signless nature of the noble path, they neither seek signs nor seek non-signs. Having thoroughly realized that the characteristics of the path are signless, when [the path] arises, it arises immediately, and when it ceases, it ceases immediately. There is the cessation of the practice of signs within the signs of the path toward existence, and the cessation of the practice of signs within the signs of existence. This is called the Bodhisattva’s characteristic of the path.
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva likewise does not seek signs as the sign of the Way.
Why is this? The Way itself is signless; one does not seek signlessness as the sign of the Way.
One does not perceive the union or dispersal of phenomena as the mark of the Way;
nor does one perceive the twelve links of dependent origination—such as self, person, life, or lifespan—as the mark of the Way arising from ignorance and volitional formations;
nor again does one perceive the absence of self, person, life, or lifespan as the mark of the Way arising from ignorance and volitional formations.

Why is this? Because the Way itself is without marks and does not perceive marks; one does not look toward what is produced nor hope for the marks of the Way. One thoroughly understands that the four great elements are neither body nor non-body, neither permanent nor impermanent, neither empty nor non-empty, neither self nor non-self, and that grasping and abandoning, combining and dispersing, are all not real. This is what is meant by a bodhisattva mahāsattva acting as they ought and being as they ought to be.
They are neither different nor not-different; one neither perceives difference nor perceives non-difference. This accords with the mark of the Path, which is markless.

Whether it be a wholesome body or an unwholesome body, a determinate body or an indeterminate body, a tainted body or an untainted body, a conditioned body or an unconditioned body, a body that succeeds or a body that fails, whether combining or dispersing, taking up or discarding—all such distinctions of marks and the mark of the Path are entirely empty and non-existent, like a dream, a shadow, an echo, or a mirage in the heat.

Furthermore, it is neither that the body is empty nor that the body is not empty; neither that the body has perception nor that the body is without perception; neither that the body has aspiration nor that the body is without aspiration. The body is neither associated with non-desire nor dissociated from it; the body is neither associated with the twelve links of dependent origination nor dissociated from them, and the twelve links of dependent origination are likewise neither associated with nor dissociated from it. This remains the case up to the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).
The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is such that it neither corresponds with the characteristics of the Path nor does it not correspond;
the craving born from ignorance is likewise neither corresponding with the characteristics of the Path nor is it non-corresponding;
all phenomena—name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*)—neither correspond with the characteristics of the Path nor do they not correspond.

“Furthermore, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva should enter the samādhi of the immovable mind within the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti). Next, they contemplate the characteristics of the Path as being neither associated with nor dissociated from the eighteen fundamental bases (āyatana);
the dharma-nature as being neither associated with nor dissociated from the twelve links of dependent origination;
and the limitless, immeasurable, and inconceivable defilements of affliction as being neither associated with nor dissociated from the characteristics of the Path.”
Even unto the various sensory faculties of the dharma-nature, they neither correspond with the twelve links of dependent origination nor do they not correspond;

even unto old age and death, which are devoid of the dharmas of lust, anger, and delusion, they neither correspond with the marks of the Path nor do they not correspond, yet they are not non-corresponding;
whether numbered or unnumbered, they neither correspond with the marks of the Path nor do they not correspond, yet they are not non-corresponding.
The characteristics of the Way are non-dual; they neither correspond with the numbered nor the unnumbered, nor do they not correspond.

Regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), whether there is the conventional or the non-conventional, the outflowing or the outflow-free, the conditioned or the unconditioned, the determinate or the indeterminate, wholesome dharmas or unwholesome dharmas, or whether things are beautiful or ugly—through the practice of non-duality and the practice that is not non-duality, one seeks the characteristics of the Way with an undisturbed mind.

Regarding the characteristics of seeking the Way: it does not correspond with, nor is it non-correspondent to, the ultimate truth (paramārtha), the conventional (saṃvṛti) or the non-conventional, the outflowing (sāsrava) or the non-outflowing, the conditioned (saṃskṛta) or the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), the determinate (vyākṛta) or the indeterminate (avyākṛta), nor to wholesome dharmas or unwholesome dharmas, whether beautiful or ugly. It is neither corresponding nor non-corresponding to them.

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva regards the markless nature of all phenomena, he neither perceives a mark nor does he perceive it as being without mark; this path is markless, and yet he does not perceive a mark therein—this is called the path corresponding to the markless.
The dharma of the markless mark is inherently empty and quiescent; like space, it is markless yet not without marks. One should respond to this mark by having nothing to which to respond.
Thus, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains this samādhi of the mark of the path, they attain complete mastery over all dharma-realms.

Having entered this samādhi, he discerned each and every pore of his own body; therein, infinite, immeasurable, and inconceivable Buddha-worlds all appeared before him. Once these worlds had appeared, the attendant disciples also appeared, who, thirsting for the Dharma, listened without ever being satiated. He caused that great assembly to see everywhere throughout the trichiliocosm the Tathāgata’s golden body emitting immeasurable light. From each and every ray of light, countless and immeasurable Buddha-fields appeared, wherein the physical forms of Buddhas manifested within those lands. Standing amidst those assemblies, they proclaimed the Great Dharma, so that those who heard it became firm and did not abandon the *vajrasamādhi* concentration.

Furthermore, throughout hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas in that realm, he circulates and teaches, manifesting expedient wisdom; yet were it not for expedient wisdom, he would not perceive those who could be transformed by such expedient wisdom.

Though dwelling in that realm, the mind is like a reflection; even amidst fierce flames or mirror-like forms, the mind harbors no such thoughts. Though kalpas may be vast and long, seeking their origin, none can be found; yet within this interval, one might give rise to thoughts of indolence and pride.

Furthermore, he does not think that sentient beings are easy to transform, nor does he think: "In a single day and night, my teaching and transformation have reached throughout worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges for billions of koṭis of kalpas; my transformative work is particularly superior to that of all other Buddhas."

In this way, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva enters the signless concentration of the nature of the path, they distinguish each and every pore of their body and travel about to teach and transform others without weariness; even if there are none to be transformed, they do not become overly indignant toward lust, anger, and delusion.
They purify those worlds and attend the great assemblies of those Tathāgatas, seeing neither the long nor the short, and giving rise to no impure thoughts.

Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva wanders through the immeasurable Dharma-realm, subduing the mind and its faculties; he endures all afflictions through practices never before performed; and because he establishes the practice of vigor by fully discerning all things, he abides in inconceivable concentration, the concentration on the signless path, and the concentration on the mark of the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*). These are one and not two, and are without differentiation. He causes those sentient beings to discern the signs of the path—whether mundane or supramundane, with outflows or without outflows, conditioned or unconditioned, determinate or indeterminate, with desire or without desire—and yet he does not perceive them as being associated with the signs of the path, nor as being dissociated from them.

The signs of the path are neither associated with the mundane or supramundane, with outflows or without outflows, determinate or indeterminate, or with desire or without desire, nor are they dissociated from them.
The characteristics of the Path are neither associated with the twelve links of dependent origination nor dissociated from them;

they are likewise neither associated with nor dissociated from ignorance, craving, birth, old age, sickness, and death. The twelve links of dependent origination are neither associated with the Path nor dissociated from it; and ignorance, craving, birth, old age, sickness, and death are neither associated with the Path nor dissociated from it.

"Most excellent! When a bodhisattva mahāsattva attains this concentration on the marks of the path (mārga-lakṣaṇa-samādhi), they perceive neither correspondence nor non-correspondence. This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s state of being 'correspondent yet without anything to correspond to' within the concentration on the marks of the path; likewise, within the concentration on the signless (animitta-samādhi), they perceive neither correspondence nor non-correspondence. This is called being correspondent yet without anything to correspond to—a state that cannot be fathomed or known by arhats or pratyekabuddhas."
Why is this? Because it is not within their domain.

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, are inconceivable; they universally enter all worlds of the ten directions, manifesting various marks and signs, majestic deportment, and the eighteen transformations, the lion’s leap, and the samādhi of fearlessness.
"At that time, Most Victorious One!

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, being fully endowed with the Tathāgata’s concentration of the marks of the Way, does not abandon the concentration of the adamantine vow. He transcends all Buddhas and there is nothing further to be crossed; yet he neither perceives one who crosses nor perceives one who does not cross."

In a single thought-moment, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva arises from samādhi; yet, without abandoning sentient beings suffering in distress throughout the ten directions, he immediately proceeds to provide them with the four requisites of offering—robes, food and drink, elephants and horses, and the seven treasures—as well as bedding, cushions, and medicines for the sick. With skillful means and wisdom, he guides and governs all, doing so entirely for the sake of sentient beings and not for himself. Traveling from one Buddha-land to another, he teaches and transforms beings, circulating everywhere to proclaim the True Dharma without ever feeling weary or satisfied.

Entering the lands of all Buddhas, they cause all sentient beings therein to receive transformation; yet there is no one who perceives it. They flourish the Buddha-work and manifest all-knowledge; wherever their minds reach, they arrive instantly upon thought.

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva enters this samādhi of the characteristics of the path, they universally enter the mind, consciousness, and awareness of all classes of sentient beings within the Buddha-worlds of the ten directions—worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—and observe their thoughts and discern their past actions: which are headed for hell, which for the realm of hungry ghosts, which for the animal realm, which for the heavenly realms, and which for the human realm.
In this way, in the mere twinkling of an eye, a bodhisattva mahāsattva is able to discern the destinies of all sentient beings.

Whether there are sentient beings practicing the path of goodness who are established in the concentration on the signs of the path, he also knows whether those sentient beings possess the mind of a śrāvaka, the mind of a pratyekabuddha, or the mind of a bodhisattva.

In this way, the bodhisattva mahāsattva travels throughout all buddha-worlds, paying homage to and serving the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; he purifies all buddha-lands and fulfills all that sentient beings desire.

Or, in various Buddha-fields, seeing beings who are stingy and greedy, he immediately manifests himself as practicing great giving; in those fields, he raises the banner of great giving and addresses everyone with a pure Brahma-voice, saying:
"Virtuous ones, you should know that my name is 'The All-Giver Who Seeks No Reward'."

"If there is a lack of clothing, food, medicine for the sick and emaciated, bedding, or the like; or if there is national wealth, wife and children, elephants, horses, or the seven treasures—the Bodhisattva practices giving from the first moment of generating the aspiration until the attainment of Buddhahood, bestowing everything except for the three things that are not to be given."
What are the three? First, one's father;
second, one's mother; and third, one's teachers and elders. These are called the established roots through which a bodhisattva practices giving within the buddha-fields.

"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), again travels to the lands of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Seeing sentient beings there who are indolent and arrogant, he manifests himself as one who upholds the precepts and practices the eighteen dharmas; or he dwells beneath trees, in wildernesses, among burial mounds, on high mountains, in deep precipices, or in secluded forest caves, earnestly honoring the precepts and not transgressing any of the various laws."

Wandering among humans, he maintains dignified deportment and ritual propriety; whether entering or leaving, advancing or halting, walking or sitting, his mind is always earnest and compassionate, never departing from the precepts.

He thoroughly understands that the prohibitive precepts are fundamentally non-existent, that all who are born must perish and all things are impermanent, and that his own body and those others are one and no different, ultimately pure.

From stage to stage up to the tenth stage, one does not perceive the tenth stage as an obstruction or the transcending of the tenth stage as non-obstruction; it is just like a bird flying through space, leaving no tracks behind.
He understands that all phenomena are empty like space; things are not things, and even non-things are not things.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is likewise: wandering through immeasurable worlds of the Buddhas, he does not abandon his firm and resolute mind of great vows, but gathers in those indolent sentient beings, establishing them securely in the samādhi of the marks of the Path.

"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, wielding the wisdom of skillful means, travels again through the lands of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Seeing sentient beings therein who are indolent, constantly harboring anger, and never having experienced joy, the Bodhisattva manifests before them and practices patience.

If someone reviles him, he remains silent and does not retaliate; even if someone were to cut off his hands and feet or mutilate his body, his mind would not waver. He does not give rise to resentment, maintaining a mind like the earth. He penetrates the realization that this body is a composite of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*); when the spirit departs, it disperses—what is there to value? The wise, through discernment, find not a single thing therein worth craving. It is like a butcher’s house where an ox is divided into four parts; once the beginning and end are understood, one realizes that nothing at all exists."
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is also like this: he understands that the body has no master and nothing that belongs to it. What is this body?
To whom does the body belong?
Names, marks, titles, and characters are all entirely unreal.

There may be a bodhisattva who, through the practice of meditative concentration and patience, sits upright at the foot of a tree in a desolate wilderness where no people dwell, contemplating with single-minded focus.
Travelers and cowherds passed by his side, carrying firewood and grass; some pricked his nose with branches or pierced his earlobes with them.
The Bodhisattva immediately became aware of this, yet having observed it thoroughly, he closed his eyes again and remained serene in mind, his thoughts undisturbed and free from other perceptions.
Or if he encounters passersby who strike and pelt him with tiles and stones, wounding his head and eyes and maiming his body,
the Bodhisattva’s consciousness remains unshaken and undergoes no change, nor does he give rise to distracted thoughts.
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s practice of patience through the cultivation of dhyāna, by which they rescue and deliver sentient beings beyond measure or record.

Furthermore, by means of inconceivable power, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva travels to buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions; seeing sentient beings there who constantly harbor indolence and arrogance, the bodhisattva manifests before them in a state of diligence, gathering in those beings and establishing them in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

At that time, for the sake of a single sentient being, the Bodhisattva passes through hundreds of thousands of kalpas with a mind that is neither indolent nor weary, nor does he feel exhausted or despondent. Why is this?

Because he has thoroughly realized that the dharma-realm is empty and non-existent; he delivers beings by means of the Way of the Tathāgata, yet while delivering sentient beings, he perceives no one delivered, nor does he perceive anyone not delivered. This is called the diligent vigor of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, whose mind remains unchanging and free from other thoughts.

During that interval, they undergo various sufferings and afflictions: sometimes encountering world-systems where the fires of the kalpa’s conflagration arise with flames reaching as far as the Brahma Heaven; sometimes encountering the emergence of waters that likewise reach the Brahma Heaven; or sometimes encountering the movement of winds that blow through the world-systems, shattering them like dust and mist. Yet the Bodhisattva, dwelling therein, gathers all sentient beings and establishes them in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), ensuring they are not disturbed. This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s unflagging diligence as he travels through world-systems as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, through the skillful means of expedient wisdom (*upāya-kauśalya*), travels to the lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges throughout the ten directions. Seeing that the minds of those sentient beings there are distracted and unstable, the Bodhisattva manifests the practice of seated meditation (*dhyāna*) for them—whether sitting in villages, among trees, or within deep mountain caves—and remains thus for hundreds of thousands of kalpas without any other thought, thereby drawing in sentient beings and causing their minds to become undistracted."

At that time, the Bodhisattva entered meditative absorption by the side of the road; the name of this samādhi is the "Formless Contemplation Samādhi. One who enters this concentration may remain for one kalpa or even up to a hundred thousand kalpas; though heaven and earth may melt away, mountains and rivers, trees and forests may all be scattered, and the oceans, springs, and swift currents of the great rivers may all dry up, the Bodhisattva remaining in absorption sits in meditation therein, his mind neither shifting nor decaying.

Or cowherds passing by, carrying firewood or grass, might prick his nose with wooden branches or pierce his earlobes; some might pull back his eyes to look at them, or open his mouth to examine his teeth; others might reach forward to seize him by the crown of his head but fail to catch him, or attempt to cut the Bodhisattva’s nails with sharp knives but likewise fail.

Why is this? Because the power of meditative concentration and spiritual majesty of these bodhisattvas is indestructible; furthermore, the Buddhas of the ten directions augment their spiritual majesty so that these bodhisattvas do not encounter suffering or affliction.

This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva who wanders through the lands of the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; upon seeing those with distracted minds, he immediately enters meditative concentration, proceeding from kalpa to kalpa without weariness.

"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, by means of skillful expedient means (*upāya-kauśalya*), travels to *koṭis* of Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. There, observing sentient beings who possess ignorance and delusion, the Bodhisattva manifests wisdom to them and analyzes the meaning and principles for those beings. He contemplates the events of the three periods of time—the past, present, and future—and transcends the successive stages (*bhūmi*). From stage to the stageless, and from the stageless to the stage, he is like a flying bird, encountering no obstruction."

The Bodhisattva is also like this: that which is not an image is taken as an image, and that which is an image is taken as not an image; that which is not a thing is taken as a thing, and that which is a thing is taken as not a thing.
Why is it that what is not an image is taken as an image, and what is an image is taken as not an image?

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva entered the meditative absorption of the "Limit of Space" (ākāśakoṭi-samādhi) and contemplated the worlds of other directions; he saw that medicinal herbs, fruit trees, mountains, rivers, rocks, and cliffs were all empty like space, and even emptiness itself was empty and non-existent.

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is also like this: all worlds are equal to space; this is called the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva regarding that which is not an image as an image, and regarding an image as not an image;
regarding that which is not a thing as a thing is likewise so.

Furthermore, he enters the meditative concentration of mastery over manifold wisdoms, manifesting to sentient beings the removal of deluded and ignorant perceptions, establishing them all securely so that they reach the other shore. This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva roaming through immeasurable worlds in the ten directions, observing those sentient beings with deluded and ignorant perceptions, and manifesting for them the light of wisdom so that there is forever no more darkness.
*The Scripture on the Severing of Bonds in the Ten Abodes*, Scroll Seven.
*The Scripture on the Severing of Bonds in the Ten Abodes*, Scroll Eight.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty.
22. Chapter on Equal Compassion (Samatā-maitrī-parivarta), the Twenty-second.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Most Victorious (Varasūra) came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

“How does a bodhisattva enter the samādhi of equal compassion and universally observe the three-thousandfold great thousandfold world system—the realms of humans, the aggregates of form (rūpa-skandha), the aggregates of spirit (nāma-skandha), and the various realms of dragons and ghosts—manifesting one body, two bodies, up to hundreds of thousands of bodies?”
"How does a bodhisattva, by means of the power of the spiritual bases (*ṛddhipāda*), travel from one Buddha-field to another, just as a person wanders through space without any obstruction?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Most Victorious (*Jinvarāja*):
"Excellent indeed is this question; it is most marvelous and extraordinary. I shall now expound its meaning for you; listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well!"
All dharmas are empty, quiescent, and without origin; even the manifold wisdoms attained through the realization of the Way leave no trace.

When a Bodhisattva enters the samādhi of right reception and contemplates the trichiliocosm, observing all sentient beings among its myriad forms—those who possess the five aggregates—he examines those bodies that arise and those that perish: from what do they arise, and into what do they perish?

Furthermore, one enters into the elements of space, earth, water, fire, and wind, discerning each one individually as being utterly non-existent; when phenomena arise, they arise, and when phenomena cease, they cease.
Most Victorious One, you should know this!

In the distant past, while practicing the Bodhisattva path for a long time, I maintained one-pointed concentration in meditative absorption with an undistracted mind. Entering the Immovable Samādhi, I contemplated sentient beings within the void—limitless, immeasurable, and beyond calculation—and I taught and transformed them according to their various forms and natures.

Among those sentient beings, there are those with lust, anger, and ignorance, and those without lust, anger, and ignorance; those with desires and intentions, and those without desires and intentions; those with minds of malice, and those without minds of malice. The Bodhisattva, through skillful wisdom, enters among them according to their types; his form accords with theirs to suit all, while his mind remains in meditative concentration without ever becoming distracted or erring. In the space of a finger-snap, he enters hundreds of thousands of Buddha-fields, sometimes teaching by observing through the wisdom of the Dharma-nature, or leading them with the True Dharma through the teachings of emptiness, suffering, impermanence, and non-self. The beings transformed by the Bodhisattva are likewise boundless, as he instructs them in the practice of the ten virtuous actions.

What are these ten? First, purifying the buddha-field without calculating its merit; second, expounding wisdom with unimpeded knowledge; third, sitting beneath the tree of enlightenment with a mind free from fear or weakness; fourth, subduing demonic adversaries and causing them to realize their own erroneous paths; fifth, traversing various realms to deliver immeasurable beings; sixth, having a mind like the element of earth—enduring all things without wavering; seventh, discerning the characteristics of ease or difficulty regarding the gates of the faculties; eighth, exercising judgment in all matters of pure and mature conduct; ninth, individually analyzing the aggregates (*skandhas*), bases (*āyatanas*), and elements (*dhātus*), as well as form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; and tenth, contemplating the six internal sense organs to eliminate the six external objects, such that when the eye sees forms, no visual consciousness arises, and one fully realizes that both external forms and internal consciousness are empty and non-existent: "Of what is this form? Where does this visual consciousness reside?"

If the ear hears a sound but does not give rise to ear-consciousness, then both the external sound and the internal consciousness are understood to be entirely void and non-existent; as for this sound, whose is it, and where does the ear-consciousness abide?

If the nose smells an odor but does not give rise to nose-consciousness, then both the external odor and the internal consciousness are understood to be entirely void and non-existent; as for this odor, whose is it, and where does the nose-consciousness abide?

If the tongue perceives flavors but does not give rise to tongue-consciousness, then both external flavors and internal consciousness are entirely understood to be void and non-existent; for whom do these flavors exist, and where does tongue-consciousness abide?

If the body perceives smoothness and softness but does not give rise to the conceptualization of consciousness, then both external contact and internal consciousness are entirely understood to be void and non-existent; for whom does this smoothness and softness exist, and where does body-consciousness abide?
"O Most Victorious One,

you should know that when a bodhisattva enters meditative concentration, they discern each category individually to teach and transform beings accordingly— whether by verbal instruction, by supernormal powers, or by skillful wisdom— entering each class of being without any hindrance."
"At that time, the Bodhisattva further transforms and instructs sentient beings through ten dharmas.

What are these ten? First, being fully endowed with the faculty of wisdom, his concentration is undisturbed. Second, his awakening-mind is firm, and he expounds wisdom without obstruction. Third, he extensively elucidates the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*), being complete in their meaning and purpose. Fourth, he understands that signs are profoundly quiescent, and his various marks of excellence are without deficiency. Fifth, he understands the path and the non-path, realizing they are empty and non-existent. Sixth, his mind honors the Wheel of Dharma, teaching without weariness. Seventh, while practicing the Bodhisattva path, he does not perceive a self-body. Eighth, although he delivers sentient beings, he does not perceive anyone who is delivered. Ninth, he understands that internal and external emptiness are one and not two. Tenth, when analyzing the body, he does not perceive any transformation."

This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva who, being endowed with these ten dharmas, is able to travel throughout all buddha-fields, proceeding from one buddha-land to another, never being separated from the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
“A bodhisattva should mindfully cultivate the various gates of dhāraṇī.
What is meant by ‘dhāraṇī’?
It is the dhāraṇī of the seal of all dharmas. When a bodhisattva attains this dhāraṇī, they eliminate all false conceptualizations regarding all dharmas.”
Furthermore, there is the *samādhi-dhāraṇī* of Universal Radiance; a bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī treats all beings with equal compassion and harbors no inverted views.
Furthermore, there is the *dhāraṇī* of Wisdom-Light; a bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī causes impure buddha-fields to become pure.
Furthermore, there is the *dhāraṇī* of Radiant Illumination; when a bodhisattva attains this *dhāraṇī*, they are entirely free from the dust and obscurations of all distracted thoughts.
Furthermore, there is the *dhāraṇī* of Eloquence in Meaning; when a bodhisattva attains this *dhāraṇī*, they practice contemplating all phenomena and enter meditative absorption without wavering.
Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī of the eloquence of Dharma; the bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī distinguishes the meanings of phrases without losing their proper sequence.
Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī of the eloquence of resonance; the bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī observes sounds and voices to deliver beings according to their respective types.
Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī of appropriate discernment; a bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī is able to adapt appropriately to all things and bring all practices to fulfillment.
Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī of the foundations of mindfulness; a bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī causes the fetters of affliction to cease forever and never arise again.
Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī of the abandonment of mental formations; when a bodhisattva attains this dhāraṇī, they minutely examine all phenomena without any hesitation.
Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī of the divine feet; when a bodhisattva attains this dhāraṇī, they remain in the world for a lifespan lasting hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
Furthermore, there is the Fundamental Dhāraṇī; a bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī distinguishes the gates of the faculties and their arising and ceasing without change.
Furthermore, there is the Power-and-Influence Dhāraṇī; a bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī cultivates the adamantine body that cannot be obstructed or destroyed.
Furthermore, there is the *bodhyanga-dhāraṇī*; the bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī expounds all dharmas and brings enlightenment to all beings.
Furthermore, there is the *mārgānga-dhāraṇī*; the bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī contemplates and realizes the fundamental nature of the causal conditions of the three periods of time.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi-dhāraṇī; the bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī, because they embrace the Way amidst all distracted thoughts.
Furthermore, there is the upāya-prajñā dhāraṇī; the bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī acts appropriately and without fixed direction, yet remains without a sense of self-awakening.
Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī of giving; when a bodhisattva attains this dhāraṇī, they understand that these three things are entirely non-existent.
Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī of ethical discipline; when a bodhisattva attains this dhāraṇī, they perceive neither one who cultivates discipline nor one who violates it.
Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī of patience; when a bodhisattva attains this dhāraṇī, they perceive neither anger nor patience, nor do they perceive distracted thoughts.
Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī of diligence; when a bodhisattva attains this dhāraṇī, they perceive neither the practice of diligence nor laziness.
Furthermore, there is the *samādhi-dhāraṇī*; a bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī remains unperturbed even when ten thousand sounds roar like thunder, such that his hair does not stand on end.
Furthermore, there is the *prajñā-śūnyatā-dhāraṇī*; a bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī encompasses all knowledge within consciousness and expounds it fluently and without obstruction.
Furthermore, there is the unimpeded dhāraṇī; the bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī encounters no obstruction regarding any supernormal wisdom.
Furthermore, there is the vast and remote dhāraṇī; the bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī, though possessing hundreds of thousands of bodies, can merge them back into one.
Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī of Instruction; when a bodhisattva attains this dhāraṇī, they teach with the True Dharma such that their words are neither redundant nor cumbersome.
Furthermore, there is the inconceivable dhāraṇī; when a bodhisattva attains this dhāraṇī, it is not something that can be reached by arhats or pratyekabuddhas.
