Furthermore, there is the Bodhi-tree dhāraṇī; the bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī adorns buddha-fields and never departs from the presence of the Buddhas.
Furthermore, there is the subduing Māras dhāraṇī; the bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī maintains a firm resolve and a mind that does not waver.
Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī of the marks of physical presence; when a bodhisattva attains this dhāraṇī, each and every mark brings forth hundreds of thousands of merits.
Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī of the secondary signs; when a bodhisattva attains this dhāraṇī, they do not perceive the marks and signs as being like necklaces adorning the body.
Furthermore, there is the *dhāraṇī* of Radiant Splendor; a bodhisattva who attains this *dhāraṇī* perceives the manifestation of immeasurable forms within hundreds of thousands of lights.
Furthermore, there is the *dhāraṇī* of Delivering Beings; a bodhisattva who attains this *dhāraṇī*, though delivering sentient beings, yet there is no one who delivers.
Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī of Vast Wisdom; when a bodhisattva attains this dhāraṇī, their mind is like space, free from partiality or narrowness.
Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī of the Path-Mind; when a bodhisattva attains this dhāraṇī, they do not conceive of nirvāṇa, nor do they cling to existence.
Furthermore, there is the *dhāraṇī* of Extinction; a bodhisattva who attains this *dhāraṇī* perceives neither extinction nor birth.
Furthermore, there is the *dhāraṇī* of Purity; a bodhisattva who attains this *dhāraṇī* purifies all defilements so that they are inexhaustible yet not exhausted.

Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī of "Sufferinglessness. When a bodhisattva attains this dhāraṇī, they understand that suffering is without suffering; this is called the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).

Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī of "Origination and Accumulation. When a bodhisattva attains this dhāraṍī, they fully comprehend that the intentional conditions of accumulation are fundamentally empty and non-existent.
Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī of extinction; when a bodhisattva attains this dhāraṇī, they extinguish the habitual afflictions and will never again create them.
Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī of the noble path; when a bodhisattva attains this dhāraṇī, they dwell securely in the unconditioned and the eternal tranquility of nirvāṇa.

Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī of the synthesis of śamatha and vipaśyanā; when a bodhisattva attains this dhāraṇī, they contemplate and fully understand the rise and fall and the destinies of the sublime Dharma.
Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī of the treasury of emptiness; when a bodhisattva attains this dhāraṇī, they encounter no obstruction regarding the profound essentials of the Dharma.
Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī of the Contemplation of Dharmas; a bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī contemplates and realizes that all dharmas are entirely without a master.
Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī of Pure Sound; a bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī has speech that is soft and gentle, like the voice of Brahmā.
Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī called "Appropriate"; when a bodhisattva attains this dhāraṇī, whatever they say to others accords with their minds and intentions.
Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī called "Equanimous Mind"; when a bodhisattva attains this dhāraṇī, their speech is warm, supple, and fluent, without any obstruction.
Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī of "Wandering Abodes. When a bodhisattva attains this dhāraṇī, whatever instructions or admonitions they give will never cause harm or injury.
Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī of "Majestic Radiance. When a bodhisattva attains this dhāraṇī, they shall feel no timidity or weakness even when amidst a great assembly.
Furthermore, there is the *dhāraṇī* of Vigorous Display; when a bodhisattva attains this *dhāraṇī*, they roar the lion’s roar, causing those that fly, fall, run, or crawl to submit.
Furthermore, there is the *dhāraṇī* of the Precepts; when a bodhisattva attains this *dhāraṇī*, they subdue all sentient beings who are difficult to awaken.
Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī of the Path of Entering; a bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī understands that nirvāṇa is free from the notions of arising and ceasing.
Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī of the Dharma-nature; a bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī causes all those who are deceitful and flattering to see the true path.
Furthermore, there is the *samādhi-dhāraṇī* that pacifies the mind; a bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī does not give rise to arrogance or conceit toward others.
Furthermore, there is the *dhāraṇī* of thorough penetration; a bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī hears the sublime wisdom of others and does not lose the teachings of the Dharma.
Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī of Arousing Reverence; a bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī immediately abandons arrogance and serves all Buddhas.
Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī of the Sphere of Space; a bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī gradually enters the fundamentally pure and quiescent dharma-realm.
Furthermore, there is the unimpeded dhāraṇī; the bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī masters the ritual procedures and understands the fundamental nature of all phenomena.
Furthermore, there is the immeasurable dhāraṇī; the bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī finds that the teachings spoken in the past are likewise inexhaustible.
Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī of powerful memory; the bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī distinguishes written characters and knows the directionality of the Dharma.
Furthermore, there is the ultimate dhāraṇī; the bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī understands that the fundamental nature of persons and the dharma-realm are likewise pure.

Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī of the "Difficult to Extinguish. A bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī understands that sentient beings purify the internal and external, which are empty and quiescent.

Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī of the "Boundless. A bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī realizes and knows that the fundamental is non-existent, and that even this non-existence is itself non-existent.
Furthermore, there is the *mālā-dhāraṇī*; the bodhisattva who attains this *dhāraṇī* will have no impediments whatsoever in the sūtras and dharmas they preach.
Furthermore, there is the *sūkṣma-ārya-dhāraṇī*; the bodhisattva who attains this *dhāraṇī* will perceive neither exhaustion nor non-exhaustion even within that which is exhausted.
Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī of differentiation; when a bodhisattva attains this dhāraṇī, it is not something that can be deliberated upon by those of the two vehicles.
Furthermore, there is the Tathāgata-dhāraṇī; when a bodhisattva attains this dhāraṇī, they awaken sentient beings to the path of quiescence.
Furthermore, there is the *dhāraṇī* of the ten stages; the bodhisattva who attains this *dhāraṇī* constantly speaks of non-abiding and does not perceive abiding.

Furthermore, there is the *dhāraṇī* of the aggregates and elements; the bodhisattva who attains this *dhāraṇī* discerns the fundamental nature of the body and does not give rise to defiled attachment.
Furthermore, there is the *dhāraṇī* of Solitude; when a bodhisattva attains this *dhāraṇī*, it is like a call that produces no sound.
Furthermore, there is the *dhāraṇī* of the Nature of Cognition; when a bodhisattva attains this *dhāraṇī*, they are able to contemplate all things without becoming attached to words and letters.
Furthermore, there is the *dhāraṇī* of realizing the source; when a bodhisattva attains this *dhāraṇī*, there is no speech, no discourse, and no instruction or precept.
Furthermore, there is the *dhāraṇī* of letters; when a bodhisattva attains this *dhāraṇī*, they personally recognize their past lives and know whence they have come.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-wheel dhāraṇī; the bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī is without intention, without thought, and without consciousness.
Furthermore, there is the ambrosia dhāraṇī; the bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī is without obstruction when lecturing, reciting, or preaching the Dharma.
Furthermore, there is the profound dhāraṇī of universal entry; a bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī can analytically distinguish each of the four propositions and their combined meanings.

Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī of the Dharma-banner; a bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī thoroughly understands the underlying principles and clearly discerns the fundamental nature of all phenomena.
Furthermore, there is the inexhaustible dhāraṇī; the bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī thoroughly elucidates the ultimate limit [of reality] without being separated from his retinue.
Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī of equal awakening; the bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī constantly expounds the immeasurable and unattached True Dharma.
Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī of all phenomena; the bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī studies and practices all phenomena without losing their proper sequence.
Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī of great vows; the bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī understands that wisdom is entirely free from both opposition and conformity.
Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī of skillful means; the bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī adapts their transformation to the various types of beings without harboring any timidity.
Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī of the wisdom of the path; the bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī discerns the stage of the summit and cultivates the pāramitās.
Furthermore, there is the *māyā-nirmāṇa-dhāraṇī*; a bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī discerns that the dharma-realm has no nature of internal or external.
Furthermore, there is the *antarābhava-dhāraṇī*; a bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī [discerns] the dwelling places and caves where the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, reside.
Furthermore, there is the Bodhimanda Dhāraṇī; when a bodhisattva attains this dhāraṇī, the lands of the ten directions become brilliantly radiant with golden light.
Furthermore, there is the Subduing Māras Dhāraṇī; when a bodhisattva attains this dhāraṇī, no heterodox practitioners remain unsubdued.
Furthermore, there is the *dhāraṇī* of self-guarding; when a bodhisattva attains this *dhāraṇī*, they protect body, speech, and mind without perceiving any protection.
Furthermore, there is the *dhāraṇī* of preaching the Dharma; when a bodhisattva attains this *dhāraṇī*, they are fully endowed with the root of the Dharma, without any deficiency or omission.
Furthermore, there is the *dhāraṇī* of Self-Reliance; a bodhisattva who attains this *dhāraṇī* observes the mentalities of immeasurable sentient beings.
Furthermore, there is the *dhāraṇī* of Earnestness; a bodhisattva who attains this *dhāraṇī* employs skillful means in their teaching to cause others to enter the restraints of the Path.
Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī of transformative flow; a bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī distinguishes all forms of wisdom without being attached to past or present.
Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī of pliancy and compliance; a bodhisattva who attains this dhāraṇī receives the Dharma without weariness and remains free from anger or delusion.
Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī of advancing virtue; when a bodhisattva attains this dhāraṇī, they realize that all phenomena are fundamentally non-existent.
Furthermore, there is the dhāraṇī of physical forms; when a bodhisattva attains this dhāraṇī, they never forget or abandon those who behold their form.
Furthermore, there is the *dhāraṇī* of the Śrāvakas; a Bodhisattva who attains this *dhāraṇī* calculates all phenomena as being immeasurable and unattached.
Furthermore, there is the *dhāraṇī* of Accordance with Suffering; a Bodhisattva who attains this *dhāraṇī* listens to and gathers the flavor of the Dharma, which is equal and non-dual.

At that time, when the World-Honored One was expounding this Dharma-gate of the dhāraṇī, twelve billion nayutas of people all attained the patient endurance of the non-arising of phenomena through ultimate faith; furthermore, immeasurable sentient beings all resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ajita:

"The conduct of a bodhisattva is inconceivable; it is not something known by arhats or pratyekabuddhas. It is through the movement of the majestic power of the samādhi of universal compassion and the meditative absorption of right reception that such things are possible. For this reason, I preach the Mahāyāna Vinaya, guiding them with correct transformation and restraining them with the dharma-robe."
At that time, Ajita came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!

It is well said that all dharmas are practiced without beginning or end; one understands that the nature of phenomena is empty, non-existent, and tranquil. Each and every distinction is both void and still. That which is expounded by the Mahāyāna extends widely to all, and those who hear of the Bodhisattva practices shall, after the end of their lives, all be reborn in the world-system of Vast Patience."
At that time, the entire assembly was filled with uncertainty, desiring to behold that buddha-field.

The Tathāgata, perceiving through his divine insight the thoughts in the minds of the sentient beings, immediately employed his supernormal power to emit light from the crown of his head, which universally illuminated the trichiliocosm as well as those immeasurable lands of the Vast Endurance.

The Buddha of Vast Patience is named Ananta; he possesses the power of dhāraṇī and a retentive memory that never forgets. Extraordinary teachings are always present before him. Having made offerings to all Buddhas throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, he has accumulated the methods of the Path and thereby attained this unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
The Buddha told Most Victorious:
“A bodhisattva should mindfully practice the ten stages of dwelling. What are these ten?

First, to discern the dharma-realm and realize its emptiness; second, to understand that the body is void and quiescent, with no master within or without; third, to awaken the mind regarding the four great elements so as not to rely on anything remaining; fourth, to see no nirvana in any phenomena; fifth, for the actions of body, speech, and mind to be tranquil and non-abiding; sixth, to guard the precepts such that there is neither "precept" nor "violation of precept"; seventh, to practice without negligence, taking the restraint of the mind as the foundation; eighth, to vow to achieve the Way without abandoning one's original resolve; ninth, to employ inconceivable dharmas to deliver those who are difficult to awaken; tenth, for all practices to be pure and the conduct performed to be without attachment. These are called the ten fundamental dharmas practiced by Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas.

"Furthermore, a bodhisattva should next practice ten dharmas. What are these ten? First, the complete purity of precepts and conduct free from negligence; second, bestowing the gift of learning without destroying the dharma-realm;

third, discerning the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) while knowing them to be empty and quiescent; fourth, knowing that the four types of impermanence all lead to extinction; fifth, understanding the eighteen difficult-to-comprehend afflictions of the aggregates, bases, and elements; sixth, being fully endowed with vows so that all Buddhas offer praise; seventh, establishing sentient beings who have not yet established their faculties in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); eighth, entering meditative concentration such that no one can disturb it; ninth, universally observing all internal and external conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*); and tenth, personally observing the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of one's own body."
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s practice of being mindful of the ten roots of the Dharma, by which he shall personally attain the realization of supreme perfect enlightenment.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva should also practice the meditative absorption of samādhi; that which is called samādhi is the samādhi of equal contemplation. When a Bodhisattva attains this samādhi, he establishes the vision of wisdom and does not become negligent.
Furthermore, there is a samādhi called "Gathering the Mind" (*cittasaṃgraha*); a bodhisattva who attains this samādhi is able to gather in all fetters so as not to allow them to bind or adhere.
Furthermore, there is the "Guarding the Precepts" (*śīlārakṣa*) samādhi; a bodhisattva who attains this samādhi guards body, speech, and mind so that worldly afflictions do not arise.
Furthermore, there is the Samādhi of Equality; when a bodhisattva attains this samādhi, their mind is like space, giving rise to no dualistic conceptions.
Furthermore, there is the Great Jewel Samādhi; when a bodhisattva attains this samādhi, they manifest the inexhaustible jewels of the seven factors of enlightenment.
Furthermore, there is the Samādhi of the Tree of the Path; when a Bodhisattva attains this samādhi, the flowers of the path bloom in full splendor, and all who behold them are filled with joy.
Furthermore, there is the Samādhi of the Ocean’s Capacity; when a Bodhisattva attains this samādhi, it cannot be measured or fathomed by those of the Two Vehicles.
Furthermore, there is the Samādhi of Entering the Chamber; when a Bodhisattva attains this samādhi, there is no profound and essential treasury of the Dharma that they do not examine and master.
Furthermore, there is the Moonlight Samādhi; when a Bodhisattva attains this samādhi, they travel everywhere among all Buddhas, coming and going and moving about in their presence.
Furthermore, there is the Moon-Brightness Samādhi; when a bodhisattva attains this samādhi, they universally illuminate all things such that none fail to receive its light.
Furthermore, there is the Profound-Inspection Samādhi; when a bodhisattva attains this samādhi, they understand that the dharmas of the three periods of time are without arising or ceasing.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi of neither hatred nor love; when a bodhisattva attains this samādhi, they regard enemies and foes with equanimity, as if they were their own infants.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi of great compassion; when a bodhisattva attains this samādhi, they regard all sentient beings as their own fathers and mothers.
Furthermore, there is the Samādhi of Compassion and Loving-kindness; when a bodhisattva attains this samādhi, they shed tears for all sentient beings.
Furthermore, there is the Samādhi of Pity and Sorrow; when a bodhisattva attains this samādhi, they are likewise devoid of the notions of self, person, or life-span.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi of non-conception; a bodhisattva who attains this samādhi is able to turn the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi of the suffering of conditioned existence; a bodhisattva who attains this samādhi does not let their efforts go to waste for incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
Furthermore, there is the samādhi of the power of wisdom and precepts; when a bodhisattva attains this samādhi, they do not perceive a self in their pure conduct.
Furthermore, there is the samādhi of detachment from the body; when a bodhisattva attains this samādhi, they distance themselves from all fetters yet do not violate the precepts.
There is the Samādhi of Self; when a bodhisattva attains this samādhi, they are free from attachment to either this shore or the other shore.
Furthermore, there is the Samādhi of Profound Penetration.
When a bodhisattva attains this samādhi, they speak of dharma-patience as being neither quiescent nor non-quiescent.
Furthermore, there is the Samādhi of Purity; when a bodhisattva attains this samādhi, they contemplate and discern pure conduct.
Furthermore, there is the Samādhi of Correspondence (*saṃprayukta-samādhi*). When a Bodhisattva attains this samādhi, they do not give rise to nor extinguish corresponding dharmas.

This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s Samādhi of Right Reception (*samyak-pratigraha*). Traveling to the Buddha-fields of other directions, they perform every kind of offering to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; yet they feel no fear and encounter no difficulties. Even if their body were to perish and their life end therein, with every joint dismembered, they observe their own body as being like grass, wood, walls, or fences, and they practice patience without giving rise to any defiled attachment.

When hearing harsh words, he does not feel distress; even when encountering joy, he does not feel celebration. He seeks the source of those teachings and finds no location; he understands what is said and finds it has neither beginning nor end. Since the mind that is fundamentally non-existent is itself devoid of reality in each instance, this is called the pure concentration of mind of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.

Although his mind may be distracted, his mind is free from fetters; it is neither here nor there, and regarding all internal and external phenomena, it is entirely pure. To contemplate in this manner constitutes patience (*kṣānti*); this is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s establishment of the patience of wisdom through the purity of body, speech, and mind.
"Furthermore, Most Excellent One!

A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should further practice the meditative concentration of diligence (*vīrya-samādhi*), so that all wholesome dharmas may increase without any loss. He should contemplate the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) as neither increasing nor decreasing, taking the outflow-free wisdom-contemplation (*anāsrava-prajñā-vipaśyanā*) as his guiding principle."

Furthermore, one should contemplate and observe the mundane dharmas (*loka-dharma*), seeing that among all phenomena there is neither accomplishment nor non-accomplishment; one sees neither the noble truths nor perversions; one neither follows nor abandons, and there is neither coming nor going. This is the inexhaustible treasury where the jewels of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas are accumulated. One does not see the dharmas of the past, future, or present; from where do they come, and to where do they go? They come from nowhere, and their departure leaves no trace.

The Noble Eightfold Path is the foremost of all dharmas; it distinguishes each of the four noble truths individually, removes conduct based on inverted and deluded conceptions, and preaches the Dharma for others without any obstruction.
One understands that sentient beings are empty and lack substantial reality, and upon investigating all phenomena (*dharma*), they too cannot be apprehended.

Why is this so? Because phenomena arise from one another and phenomena perish from one another; persons do not exist apart from phenomena, nor do phenomena exist apart from persons. Persons are themselves empty and quiescent, and phenomena are likewise empty and quiescent. As persons are spontaneous (*svabhāva*), so too are phenomena spontaneous. One who understands spontaneity accords with the practice of unsurpassed, true, and correct enlightenment, and thereby attains the inexhaustible practice of the Buddha-dharma.

If there is one who seeks the Dharma—whether as a seeker, as one currently seeking, or as one yet to seek—it is unattached and unstained throughout the three periods of time. When such a seeker has sought this, they neither gain anything nor lose anything; this is called "supreme."
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas establish the practice of diligence in sublime wisdom.
"O Most Victorious One, you should know!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should further contemplate the practice of meditative concentration and the samādhi of right reception; they do not violate the dharma-precepts, which are equal and non-dual, nor do they perceive duality; furthermore, they neither achieve [anything] nor fail to achieve it."

He enters meditative concentration through right attainment; in all concentrations, he does not give rise to distracted thoughts. Regarding all dharmas, there is neither conceptualization nor relinquishment. He understands that both the internal and external are entirely without a master. This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s single-minded right attainment and non-destruction of meditative concentration.

Furthermore, they do not perceive any conjunction; having relinquished all objective spheres, they neither depart nor remain. They practice non-attached dhyāna with a mind that proceeds without difficulty. This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva who neither establishes themselves in dharmas nor departs from dharmas.

Always with a single intention, one realizes that all phenomena are spontaneous; understanding that all phenomena are devoid of the conceptualization of arising and ceasing, they cannot be measured by body or mind. Contemplating with a concentrated mind that is equanimous and non-dual, the orientation of one's fundamental nature involves neither what is appropriate nor what is inappropriate, nor does one perceive anything as appropriate.

Discerning the root of the twelve links of dependent origination: conditioned by volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) there is ignorance (*avidyā*); conditioned by ignorance there is consciousness (*vijñāna*); conditioned by consciousness there is name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); conditioned by name-and-form there are the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*); conditioned by the six sense bases there is contact (*sparśa*); conditioned by contact there is existence (*bhava*); conditioned by existence there is craving (*tṛṣṇā*); conditioned by craving there is grasping (*upādāna*); conditioned by grasping there is becoming (*bhava*); conditioned by becoming there is birth (*jāti*); conditioned by birth there arise death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair, beyond all calculation. To state it briefly: this body of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*), a fragile form, cannot be maintained for long.

At that time, the bodhisattva practices the equality of original non-arising; they fully comprehend that form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are all empty and quiescent. Furthermore, through right concentration (*samādhi*), they have no defiled attachment even toward the originally pure dharmas. They do not perceive form, nor do they conceptualize form as being with or without form. Thus they transcend all inverted practices; this is called the single-minded meditative concentration of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, which is beyond the reach of arhats and pratyekabuddhas.

Although the non-Buddhists who possess the five supernatural powers may have immeasurable lifespans, because they lose their divine feet (*ṛddhipāda*), they do not reach the ultimate state. Those who practice dhyāna and samādhi can dwell for one kalpa or even exceed one kalpa without finding it difficult, because they have attained dhyāna-samādhi which surpasses wisdom [of the mundane kind], and having cast off worldly toil, they do not give rise to false views. This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s aspiration for the Path to transform and enlighten sentient beings.

Adapting to physical forms as required and administering medicine according to the illness, he further enters the Samādhi of Equal Compassion through the method of observing emptiness with wisdom. He surveys the trichiliocosm in its entirety and proceeds to Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, causing all sentient beings who are ready for deliverance to attain liberation; this is the Tathāgata’s meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), which brings all common folk to final nirvāṇa.
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s establishment of the samādhi of universal compassion, by which immeasurable beings are delivered beyond all calculation or limit.
Thus it is, O Most Victorious One!
Such is the sublime majesty of the Tathāgata’s divine virtue.
Now, one who wishes to contemplate the Dharma should do so with the eye of wisdom; it is neither with the physical eye, nor the divine eye, nor that which is beheld by Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas.

By contemplating all dharmas, one understands that all dharmas are quiescent, understands that all dharmas are pure, understands that all dharmas are empty, and understands that all dharmas are fixed. This is called the boundless and immeasurable mind of great vows of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva.

There is no practice, no location, and no entry; all phenomena are quiescent. This is what is cultivated by those in meditative concentration, not the conduct of the distracted. To universally observe all phenomena as being entirely thus—such observation is the contemplation of phenomena (dharmānupaśyanā).

The Bodhisattva Dharmadarśana does not perceive any destination to which all phenomena tend. Those who contemplate phenomena yet do not discern such categories as these lack the site of enlightenment and fail to reach the ultimate; they do not achieve a concentrated mind through the True Dharma.

A bodhisattva should mindfully eliminate false views, seeking nothing and grasping at nothing; nor should they trade for or seek to receive heavy blessings. Knowing that all internal and external phenomena are entirely empty and quiescent—this is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva entering the samādhi of universal compassion. To contemplate and realize that all phenomena are utterly non-existent, and to see phenomena through this non-existence, is what is called "seeing the Dharma."

Now, one who perceives the Dharma perceives no self, no person, no life-span, and no soul; these are all provisional designations and not true dharmas. Conditioned phenomena are not the realm of the unconditioned, and the realm of the unconditioned is not conditioned phenomena.

The Bodhisattva understands that conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, outflows and the absence of outflows, the permanent and the impermanent, as well as the self, persons, and life-span are all non-existent; this is the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s discernment of the concentrated mind regarding the dharma of non-arising and non-ceasing.

If a bodhisattva contemplates the characteristics of all phenomena and understands that these manifold characteristics are empty, quiescent, and non-dual, and does not perceive duality; by understanding that duality is non-duality, one then accords with the concentrated mind.
Regarding inverted dharmas, he understands them to be non-existent; he does not see anyone correctly proceeding toward the Path, nor does he see anyone erring by falling into various views.

Thus, regarding the immeasurable wisdom of sentient beings, he gives rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). He purifies the Buddha-spheres and purifies the Buddha-lands, traveling from one Buddha-field to another to serve and make offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones. Furthermore, with the contemplation of supernormal powers and clear wisdom, he universally examines the trichiliocosm to see if there are any sentient beings whose faculties are pure and mature, yet who have not encountered sages and worthies and have consequently fallen into the three miserable realms.

At that time, the Bodhisattva must abide in the rescue [of beings] so that they do not wither or fall away; or again, at that time, the Bodhisattva, the Sage, on account of ordinary sentient beings, further creates conditions, moving back and forth without his efforts being in vain, and in the space of a finger-snap, he dwells in hundreds of thousands of samādhis and meditative states, establishing wisdom-insight and cultivating all merits.

When practicing giving, one reckons that among gods and humans there is fundamentally no giver; understanding that these three factors are all non-existent—this is called the bodhisattva’s proper engagement in giving.

Furthermore, if a bodhisattva instructs others through the Vinaya, they understand that both the transgression of precepts and the prohibitive rules themselves are non-existent; being neither possessed of precepts nor devoid of them, this is what constitutes true adherence to the precepts.

Furthermore, a bodhisattva constantly practices patience; seeing others practicing patience, he rejoices on their behalf. Even if he encounters anger and rage, he harbors no grief or distress. His patient endurance is entirely devoid of [self-referential] existence; it is neither one nor two, nor even up to a hundred thousand. Understanding that there is both patience and the absence of patience—this is what truly accords with patience.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva constantly practices diligence; seeing those who are diligent, he rejoices on their behalf; even if he encounters laziness, he does not harbor resentment. He understands that laziness and diligence are one and not two, nor are they dualistic; there is neither progress nor indolence. Only by understanding that progress and indolence are empty and quiescent does one truly accord with diligence.

Furthermore, whether walking or sitting, the bodhisattva is always single-minded; his meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) and right absorption (*samāpatti*) are never impaired. Even when the thunder of heaven and earthquakes produce ten thousand sounds all at once, he focuses his mind with one intent, such that nothing can shift or move the bodhisattva’s mind. He understands that both concentration and distraction are ultimately non-existent; by understanding that concentration is itself non-concentration, he accords with the true meaning of concentration.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva’s wisdom moistens and nourishes the masses; it encompasses and discerns the myriad affairs of state, responding appropriately without fixed method. He expounds and explains with thorough mastery, never violating the Buddha’s teachings. With the observation of equal wisdom, he perceives neither the worthy nor the foolish. He understands that both wisdom and ignorance, as well as folly and delusion, are entirely non-existent. He perceives neither existence nor non-existence; existence and non-existence are both empty, quiescent, and non-dual. This is called the Bodhisattva’s correspondence with wisdom.

Such is the characteristic of all dharmas in their purity: one neither perceives a characteristic nor does one perceive that there is no characteristic; by understanding that characteristics are non-characteristics, one thereby accomplishes the primary and secondary marks, delivering sentient beings to the shore of the unconditioned.

"Furthermore, the bodhisattva again enters the concentration of emptiness and dwells within the realm of space, discerning each and every sentient being within that realm. Whether by means of verbal instruction, supernormal powers, radiant signs, or ascetic practices, he teaches and transforms them, leading sentient beings to enter the discipline of the Path."

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva practices the dharma of non-conceptualization, eliminating conceptual attachments and inverted conduct; he then travels to the Buddha-fields of other directions, constantly using the unchanging dharma of non-conceptualization to instruct and transform sentient beings until they universally reach the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva practices the wishless (*apraṇihita*), they do not seek the retribution of existence within the three realms; they do not rely upon persons nor cling to the marks of physical excellence (*lakṣaṇa*). They discern the formation and disintegration of the five aggregates (*skandha*)—both internal and external—and distinguish each of the elements of form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, as well as the external objects and internal sense bases, as being empty and unreal.
"So it is, Most Excellent One!

When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva makes the great, universal vow to deliver the multitudes of sentient beings, he does not perceive any who are delivered; if there are no sentient beings at all, how much less could there be those who deliver them?"
"This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva establishing the meditative state of universal loving-kindness, causing all sentient beings everywhere to attain the faculty of wisdom.

At that time, when the World-Honored One preached this Chapter on Universal Loving-Kindness, fourteen *nayutas* of people all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path, and eight thousand bodhisattvas immediately attained the Samādhi of Universal Loving-Kindness while remaining in their seats.

Chapter Twenty-Three: The Dharma-Dhātu At that time, the World-Honored One emitted light from the mark of his tongue, which universally illumined the trichiliocosm. It further shone upon the Buddha-lands of the ten directions; throughout the four intermediate points, above, and below, there was nowhere it did not reach. It also illuminated eighty-four *koṭi* of worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the eastern direction—worlds of profound stillness where all Buddhas assemble, where no followers of the two vehicles exist, where they constantly preach the extraordinary practices of Bodhisattvas, and where the various worlds are distinguished according to their respective orders.
"I too have come from that world to this Sahā world.
The reason for this is that I made a vow and drew the lot without error.
The Buddha told Ajita:

"I now recall that among the assembly of that Buddha, one hundred million Buddhas simultaneously took up the counting-sticks (*śalākā*). I was the leader, destined for this world-system, along with Maitreya, Yuangji, Siṃha, Yonghui, Deputu, Guangwen, Jinyan, Xuanji, Baoxiong, Changbei, Xianjie, and Hongshi—these and other such Buddhas, one hundred million Tathāgatas, simultaneously received the counting-sticks and came to this Sahā world."
The Buddha addressed Sujaya and those assembled:

"The worlds of the Buddhas are inconceivable; they transform their forms and manifest through skillful means in infinite ways. How could you know that Maitreya Bodhisattva is only now beginning to practice the bodhisattva path?"
Do not form such a view. Why is this?

Maitreya has accumulated practices for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; he first attained equal and perfect enlightenment through his vows, while I have only recently begun my practice and am thus his follower. Whether manifesting asceticism, or manifesting radiant signs, or appearing as a bodhisattva, a youth, or a disciple, I preach the Dharma according to the fundamental conduct of each person.
As the Bodhisattva Maitreya sat upon that throne, the Buddha said to Maitreya,
"Reveal how many manifestations of the Buddha’s radiant forms and their retinues there are.
At that time, Maitreya concealed his bodhisattva body and manifested the form of a Buddha, along with its buddha-fields, kingdoms, and inconceivable disciples and bodhisattvas.

The assembly, seeing this, marveled at such an unprecedented marvel: formlessness is spontaneous, physical appearance is spontaneous, all phenomena are spontaneous, and likewise, all Buddhas are spontaneous.

At that time, the great assembly again beheld eighty-four billion worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges in the eastern direction—worlds of profound stillness—where the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, were expounding upon the extraordinary conduct of bodhisattvas through eighteen hundred subtle and wondrous Dharma-gates.
What are the eighteen hundred subtle and wondrous Dharma-gates?
When a bodhisattva practices the Dharma-gate of primordial purity, one who attains this Dharma-gate does not realize its fruition within the limits of the past.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of the Teaching Beyond Words; a Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate wanders through the realm of empty space such that none can perceive or know it.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Non-Attainment; a Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate, though they deliver sentient beings, does not perceive anyone being delivered.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Non-Apprehension; a Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate understands that all things are fundamentally pure, being without a master within or without.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Designations; a Bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate realizes that all dharmas are empty and lack substantial reality.
Furthermore, there is a dharma-gate of accomplishment; a bodhisattva who attains this dharma-gate, though dwelling within the conditioned, does not cling to the notion of existence.
Furthermore, there is a dharma-gate of transforming consciousness; a bodhisattva who attains this dharma-gate enters the formless realm and performs teaching and transformation through formlessness.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Manifesting Forms; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate manifests countless forms to teach and transform sentient beings.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Causes and Conditions; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate creates causes and conditions for those sentient beings.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of the Sound of Phenomena; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate hears only the resonance of sound but does not see its form.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Transcending Existence; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate does not perceive phenomena of arising and ceasing, or of attachment and annihilation.
Furthermore, there is a dharma-gate of liberation; a bodhisattva who attains this dharma-gate does not perceive nirvana as a realm of extinction.
Furthermore, there is a profound and abstruse dharma-gate; a bodhisattva who attains this dharma-gate discerns the secret and essential scriptures of the Tathāgata.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Formless Images; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate enters the formless concentrations to transform sentient beings.
Furthermore, there is the Dharma-gate of Non-contemplative Practice; a bodhisattva who attains this Dharma-gate realizes that the Buddha-dharma has neither instruction nor location.
Furthermore, there is the dharma-gate of counting the breaths. A bodhisattva who attains this dharma-gate understands that all dharmas are non-numerous and that cessation is non-cessation.
"Thus it is, Most Victorious One!"
"Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas obtain such eighteen hundred subtle and wondrous Dharma-gates.

At that time, when the entire assembly heard those Buddhas expound these subtle and wondrous Dharma-gates, they all attained the *kṣānti* of the dharma of ultimate conviction while remaining in their seats. Countless sentient beings who were inclined toward the Lesser Vehicle all resolved to attain the unsurpassed mind of equality on the Path.

At that time, the World-Honored One and Maitreya withdrew their radiance, which entered back through the openings of their faces. The Tathāgata’s great compassion is as lofty and majestic as this; he transforms and enlightens sentient beings beyond measure, leading each to their respective destinations and establishing them in firm resolve.
At that time, the assembly again had this thought:

"Just now we all together universally beheld the world of tranquility, yet now it has suddenly vanished entirely; could this not be an illusion, a mirage, or a reflection in water? Or is it not rather a dream, a mirror-image, or a fleeting hallucination?"
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the assembly, addressed Śāriputra, saying:
"What do you think, Śāriputra?
Have you ever heard the Tathāgata speak to you of the practices of a śrāvaka as being conditioned phenomena or unconditioned phenomena?"
Are these phenomena with outflows or phenomena without outflows?
Are they real phenomena or unreal phenomena?
Are they manifest phenomena or non-manifest phenomena?
Are these the dharmas of affliction or the dharmas free from affliction?
Are these dharmas with numerical measure or dharmas without numerical measure?
Are these dharmas with attachment or dharmas without attachment?
Are these phenomena subject to cultivation, or are they not subject to cultivation?
Are these phenomena characterized by hatred, or are they free from hatred?
Are these phenomena to be relinquished, or are they not to be relinquished?
Are these the dharmas of ordinary persons, or are they not the dharmas of ordinary persons?
Are these the dharmas of the noble ones, or are they not the dharmas of the noble ones?
Are these the dharmas of the foundations of mindfulness and the bases of psychic power, or are they not the dharmas of the foundations of mindfulness and the bases of psychic power?
Are these the factors of the faculties, powers, enlightenment, and the path, or are they not the factors of the faculties, powers, enlightenment, and the path?
Are these the factors of training, or are they not the factors of training?
Are these the factors of the disciples, or are they not the factors of the disciples?
Is this the Dharma of the Pratyekabuddhas, or is it not the Dharma of the Pratyekabuddhas?
Is this the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas, or is it not the Dharma of the Bodhisattvas?
Is this the Dharma of the Buddhas, or is it not the Dharma of the Buddhas?
"What do you think, Śāriputra?
Have you ever heard the Tathāgata speak these words of instruction? Śāriputra replied:
"No, World-Honored One! The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"I am still among the assembly of śrāvakas; I do not say that there is a conceptual attachment regarding the severance of outflows, much less would I preach a teaching that possesses a fixed abode? This is not so."

When one speaks of the Wheel of Dharma, it is entirely without location; there is no speech, no teaching, and no conception of a dharma. Since the dharma arises like an echo, how could there be any dharma?
What do you think, Śāriputra?
I shall now provide an analogy, for the wise understand through analogies.

It is like a man of great courage who perceives the realm of space as entirely formless; yet that man intends to plan a city and desires to paint upon the void with various colors, depicting either the forms of devas, or the forms of humans, or the forms of nāgas, ghosts, spirits, or caṇḍālas, or even the forms of crawling and flying insects and animals.
"What do you think, Śāriputra?
Would that person’s intention to give not be possible? Śāriputra replied:
"No, World-Honored One!
It is most difficult, most difficult, and truly unprecedented."
The Buddha told Śāriputra:
"The skillful transformations of the Tathāgata are inconceivable; it is even more difficult than that to establish verbal teachings. Why is this so?"

All modes of practice—conditioned and unconditioned phenomena, tainted and untainted phenomena, mundane and supramundane phenomena; the twelve links of dependent origination and the six groups of consciousness; the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path; as well as all Buddhas of the past, future, and present—are formless and imageless, beyond being seen. They are without grasping or rejecting, without gathering or dispersing; they cannot be carried away and cannot be attained. They are the realm of empty space, tranquil and still, non-dual.

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, travel through all realms and expound their teachings for the sake of all sentient beings; yet, while there is truly no name, they provisionally establish names, and while there is truly no written word, they provisionally establish words, and while there is truly no nature of phenomena, they speak of the nature of phenomena.
Furthermore, Śāriputra,
it is exceedingly difficult for a bodhisattva mahāsattva to employ skillful means to adapt to sentient beings according to their fundamental dispositions.

If there are bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās who have profound faith in such empty and quiescent dharmas and are fully endowed with all practices, they will be able to accomplish the marks and signs of a Tathāgata; they will travel from one buddha-field to another, serving and making offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.

Furthermore, from that Buddha, he attained powerful memory and dhāraṇī, and likewise received this profound and subtle meaning, which he further propagated and disseminated so that all might hear and know it.
A bodhisattva mahāsattva should mindfully cultivate the seven dharmas of non-attachment.
What are these seven? They are:

understanding that all existence is entirely non-existent; being unstained by existence and not perceiving existence; manifesting forms while lacking any marks of form; for if even a Buddha does not exist, how much less could there be marks of form?
All worlds likewise have no beginning; how much less could they have a root from which one might infer their origin?
The fundamental nature of sentient beings is infinite and bottomless; who could conceive of it or measure their conduct?

Phenomena arise naturally and phenomena cease naturally; yet one does not perceive any arising or ceasing. All phenomena are like transformations and all phenomena are like illusions; yet one does not perceive these illusions, transformations, or mirages. All phenomena are natural and all phenomena are unborn; yet one does not perceive arising, ceasing, attachment, or annihilation.

"Śāriputra, it is said that a bodhisattva mahāsattva who accomplishes these seven dharmas of non-attachment is able to fulfill all practices and gradually attain the rank of a bodhisattva. Seated beneath the Bodhi tree, they subdue the hosts of Māra; their manifold virtues accumulate, and they are fully endowed with the marks and signs of radiance. From the first stage through to the tenth stage, they never regress in the interim. They are constantly seen and protected by all Buddhas, and are honored with flowers, incense, songs, music, garments, banners, and streamers by devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas. Their merit and spiritual power increase further, and they advance toward the unsurpassed, supreme path of the Truly Real."
The Buddha again addressed Śāriputra:

"Reflecting upon myself in the past when I was practicing the bodhisattva path—whether as a youth (Kumāra), or as a Brahmā-body, or at times leaving home to cultivate the discipline of a śramaṇa—I made offerings to Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Whether by means of my head, eyes, kingdom, wealth, wife, or children; or by means of medicine and the four requisites of service; I merely heard these Buddhas discourse upon the meaning of suffering, the meaning of emptiness, and the meaning of non-self. Or they spoke of the six perfections: emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; or they spoke of the dharmas for training in the precepts and the Way; or they spoke of the teachings on patience, gentleness, and harmony."

"Sometimes they remain in seclusion for kalpas without arising; sometimes they enter meditative absorption such that their bodies and spirits are unmoving. All this is because the internal dharmas have not yet been perfected.
The Buddha further addressed Śāriputra:

"When I first received this profound and wondrous Dharma from the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, in the world of Quiescence, all the Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas who had gathered there immediately attained the patient acceptance of accordance with the Dharma (anulomikī-kṣānti)."
At that time, twenty-four thousand beings among those present in the assembly immediately attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
All Buddhas of the past, future, and present collectively proclaim and expound this profound Dharma, which is entirely without location and wherein one perceives neither self, person, nor life-span.

He observes that the fundamental nature of sentient beings is pure and wholesome; for those who possess conceptualization, he teaches non-conceptualization; for those who possess discursive thought, he instructs them in non-discursiveness; and for those who possess obstructions, he demonstrates non-obstruction.

If there are good sons or good daughters who recite and skillfully uphold this profound Dharma, and furthermore propagate it by explaining it to others, their merit and virtue will be beyond measure or limit.

If there are practitioners who cultivate the bodhisattva path, exercising loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity while taking pity on all beings, and who desire to achieve the rank of a bodhisattva, they should constantly practice and uphold the profound treasury of the Dharma.

If a son or daughter of good family were to fill the three thousandfold world-system, upholding the five precepts, practicing the ten wholesome actions throughout, and attaining the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, and the four formless absorptions, it would not equal hearing this profound and subtle Dharma even once.

If one cannot contemplate for many days, seven days will suffice; if not for seven days, then six, five, four, three, or even one day; if not for one day, it may be done for the duration of a finger-snap.
"What do you think, Śāriputra?

Even if the number of śrāvakas like yourself were to fill the worlds of the ten directions, and one were to provide them with the four requisites—robes, food and drink, bedding and seating, and medicine for the sick—for billions upon billions of kalpas, it would not equal the merit of hearing once this profound and essential Dharma."

Why is this so? Because the Bodhisattva is a treasury of the Dharma and a collection of precious jewels; if he were to further expound the meaning of even a single phrase—the meaning of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and non-self—the three gates of liberation, the four types of clear wisdom, the practice of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and the practice of non-arising, non-origination, and non-extinction—then such a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva would possess immeasurable peaceful virtues, and his merit would be limitless and beyond all comparison.

If there are bodhisattvas who, with limited and obstructed bodies, cultivate conditioned dharmas to teach and transform sentient beings so that their aspirations are fulfilled, yet such individuals have never heard of the path of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), it is impossible for them to tread upon the profound and subtle Dharma of a bodhisattva.

If there is a bodhisattva who, through meditative concentration and right reception, draws from immeasurable dharmas, expounding and disseminating profound scriptural canons and hearing the unconditioned dharma—wherein all dharmas are empty and entirely non-existent—this is the profound meaning that none can equal.

Therefore, if a bodhisattva wishes to fulfill the aspirations of sentient beings, wishes to explain their meaning to others, further wishes to proclaim the secret and essential teachings of the Tathāgatas and bodhisattvas, and wishes to cause sentient beings to realize the four fruits of the path, they should always mindfully study this profound and essential Dharma.
The Buddha again addressed Śāriputra:

"In the past, when I was traveling and studying as a bodhisattva practicing the path, I constantly cultivated the six perfections and the four immeasurables. With great compassion, I bestowed my grace upon sentient beings by expounding the flavor of the ambrosia; sometimes through verbal teachings, sometimes through the noble silence of the sages, sometimes by manifesting supernormal powers, sometimes through skillful means and expedients, sometimes through the five paths of supernatural penetration, sometimes by wandering through the single path, sometimes by the pratyekabuddhas flying their alms bowls through the void, sometimes by the śrāvakas receiving verbal instructions, and sometimes by manifesting as a youth appearing to be ignorant."

Śāriputra, you should know that the skillful manifestations of a bodhisattva’s teaching are boundless and inexhaustible. Adapting to worldly customs and entering among various classes of beings, they may enter into earth, enter into water, enter into fire, and enter into wind. The bodhisattva discerns that the four great elements are fundamentally devoid of a master; he discerns that the realm of earth, both internally and externally, is empty and tranquil, and the realms of water, fire, and wind are likewise so.

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva discerns all beings: those with lust, anger, and ignorance, and those without lust, anger, and ignorance; those with hearts of craving and desire, and those without hearts of craving and desire; those with arrogant minds, and those without arrogant minds; those with concentrated minds, and those without concentrated minds; and those with distracted minds, and those without distracted minds. The Bodhisattva discerns them all.

Some he taught by means of *ānāpāna-smṛti* (mindfulness of breathing), some by means of the contemplation of the impurity of the foul secretions, some by means of the dharma of *nirvāṇa* and cessation, some by means of conditioned and unconditioned dharmas, some by means of tainted and untainted dharmas, some by means of worldly dharmas or supramundane dharmas, and some by means of the path of supernatural powers and the exhaustion of outflows (*āsrava-kṣaya*).

I once traveled to the world of Universal Wisdom, where for twelve intermediate kalpas I entered a state of meditative concentration for the sake of a single sentient being; with body and spirit unmoving, I did not shrink from toil as I waited to transform and guide them.
Could this sentient being be anyone else?
Do not entertain such a thought.
If you wish to know who he is, it is none other than the Bodhisattva Most Victorious (Jinsheng) here present.

The Bodhisattva Most Victorious was born into a noble family in the world of Universal Wisdom; because of the merit accumulated in past lives, he was never born into a poor, destitute, or impoverished household. From one birth, two births, up to hundreds of thousands of births, and even throughout twelve intermediate kalpas of receiving physical form, he always remained in noble and honorable circumstances, never dwelling in lowliness or meanness.

I shall also enter meditative concentration and, from a place not far from him, observe his mental state. Although he has failed to understand a single profound dharma throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas, he will later be able to awaken on his own; his mind will suddenly open, and he will come to take refuge in my person, desiring to hear the profound, wondrous, and immeasurable scriptural collections. For him, I shall preach the inexhaustible treasury of the Dharma.

What is called the "Inexhaustible Treasury" is the discernment of sounds and resonances; it may fill the trichiliocosm with a single sound, or adapt a single phrase to suit the mentalities of all sentient beings, such that the teachings it utters surpass even the Brahma-voice.

Furthermore, there is the inexhaustible treasury of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), by which one travels to the worlds of the Buddhas throughout the ten directions to serve and make offerings to the Tathāgatas, World-Honored Ones, and to receive the profound, wondrous, and rare Dharma. Regarding all ascetic practices, they surpass those of diligence, observance of precepts, patience, vigor, single-mindedness, wisdom, and skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*).

Furthermore, there is an inexhaustible treasury that brings about the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*). These four foundations of mindfulness are the practice of the untainted dharmas (*anāsravadharma*). The foundation of mindfulness on phenomena (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*) is the path to *nirvāṇa*, while the others are what ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) cultivate.

The four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path—since their retributive fruits and realizations are entirely non-existent and are not even perceived to exist, this is called the Bodhisattva’s inexhaustible treasury.

What can be brought to an end? The luminous radiance of equanimity that skillfully expounds the fundamental nature can be brought to an end; the cultivation of the characteristics of the dharma-nature can be brought to an end; that which the mind contemplates can be brought to an end; the contemplation of the five aggregates can be brought to an end; the clear understanding of the twelve links of dependent origination can be brought to an end; and the knowledge of the internal and external four great elements can be brought to an end.
Śāriputra replied, “No, World-Honored One.”
"It is not something that even a Tathāgata can fully exhaust.
The Buddha again addressed Śāriputra:
"Furthermore, there are four dharmas of the inexhaustible teaching that serve as gateways to eloquence."

What are the four? First, the discernment of inexhaustible wisdom; second, the illumination of inexhaustible wisdom; third, contemplation, powerful memory, and dhāraṇī; fourth, the discernment of eloquence that is unsurpassed.
"Śāriputra, these are called the four inexhaustible treasuries that a bodhisattva should practice.
Furthermore, there are four other inexhaustible treasuries that cannot be carried away."

What are the four? First, their nature is difficult to guide because they dwell in negligence; second, the mind for the Path is difficult to guide because its fundamental nature is profoundly deep; third, they enter into the ultimate limits of all things and practice that which has neither beginning nor end; fourth, they enter into the minds of sentient beings and thoroughly understand the non-existence of phenomena.
"This is called the inexhaustible treasury of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
The Buddha again addressed Śāriputra:
"Furthermore, there are four firm and inexhaustible treasuries that constitute the dharma-gate of eloquence for a bodhisattva."

What are the four? First, their vows are firm and steadfast, and they do not cling to heterodox factions. Second, their fundamental conduct is pure, and they do not give rise to worldly afflictions. Third, following the teachings of the ancient Buddhas, they establish patience and remain free from anger. Fourth, they act in accordance with conditions without losing their original vow.

This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s inexhaustible treasury of eloquence, the Dharma-gate by which one subdues the hosts of Māra and their enmity beneath the Tree of Enlightenment with a mind free from fear or weakness.
Furthermore, there are four further inexhaustible treasuries of the Dharma-gates of the Wheel-turning Kings.

What are the four? First, that which is spoken is sincere and does not disparage others; second, thoroughly investigating dependent origination to know from whence things arise; third, instructing and admonishing sentient beings without ever becoming weary; and fourth, discerning with clear wisdom to ascend to the stage of a Bodhisattva.
"This is called the inexhaustible treasury of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s non-defiling dharma-precepts, which is the constant practice of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
The Buddha further addressed Śāriputra:
"Furthermore, there are four inexhaustible treasuries through which the bodhisattva-mahāsattva accomplishes the dharma-realm."
What are the four? First, illuminating the dharma-realm to achieve mastery over coming and going.
Second, illuminating the dharma-nature to realize that nothing exists.
Third, there is the differentiation of the fleshly eye, the heavenly eye, the wisdom eye, the Dharma eye, and the Buddha eye.
What is the fleshly eye? It is that which perceives forms and images, wherein visual consciousness is not absent.
What is the divine eye? That which is called the divine eye perceives the physical forms of celestial beings without seeing [their] karmic retribution;
the wisdom-eye discerns without seeing defilements; the dharma-eye is pure and fully endowed with the six perfections; and the Buddha-eye is clear and bright, observing both marks and the markless.
"Fourth, illuminating retribution and response without being attached to the three realms.
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s inexhaustible treasury that accomplishes the dharma-realm.
The Buddha again addressed Śāriputra:
“Furthermore, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have four inexhaustible treasuries. What are the four? First is the treasury of diligence and non-conceptual concentration.

Whether there is a mind seeking wisdom or a mind not seeking wisdom; whether there is a mind that is finite or a mind that is infinite; whether there is a mind that has attained realization or a mind that has not—discrimination between internal and external is entirely non-existent.”

Therefore, Śāriputra, wherever a bodhisattva who practices skillful means may be, his circulation and teaching take diligence as supreme; he takes the diligent application of the prohibitions and precepts as the foundation; he seeks the accumulation of merit from all World-Honored Ones; hearing the Dharma, he rejoices and gathers together clear wisdom; he proclaims the Way of the Teachings yet remains without verbal instruction; and regarding all dharmas of the future, past, and present, his wise contemplation is firm—this alone constitutes the true teaching.

That which the Tathāgata speaks is not by means of letters; since the letters are pure, the teaching of the Dharma is also pure. This constitutes the accumulation of the merit of wisdom, the establishment of firm patience, and the establishment of non-retrogression.
This is what is meant, Śāriputra:
it is not by means of craving for form nor by relying on form; it is not that there is no form, yet one understands form as being without form. Therefore, it is called the *dharmatā*.

Even if the three thousand great thousandfold world systems were filled with fragrant incense, soft silks, banners, and canopies, and those who came to make offerings did not inspire joy in him; even if he remained far removed from indolence and harbored no cowardice, avoiding greedy and distracted thoughts and eliminating the mind of anger—only by thus attaining equal and perfect enlightenment and expounding the secret essentials could he achieve Buddhahood.

Having renounced one’s own physical well-being, one establishes a heart of great vows, taking upon oneself the suffering and afflictions of those sentient beings. With diligence and a love for the Dharma, one strives to lead sentient beings into the chamber of the Dharma until they reach the state of a practitioner on the path. The devas bear witness as gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans all come to offer worship. Good sons and good daughters provide support and encouragement to bring others to Buddhahood; their resolve is firm so that they never retreat from the realization of wisdom. They deliver those who, through various causes and conditions, have fallen into the three miserable realms—those who are ignorant, unconscious, and without ultimate understanding.

"Śāriputra, it is said that when a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivates the dharma of non-conceptualization and the dharma of wordless teaching, they are then able to accomplish the holy teaching of the Tathāgata."
At that time, all those gathered in the assembly who heard this profound Dharma gave rise to the resolve for supreme, non-retrogressive enlightenment.
Then Śāriputra came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"As for these people whom we have just heard of, how long will it be before they attain Buddhahood?"
The Buddha told Śāriputra:

"These individuals shall all become Buddhas after two hundred incalculable kalpas; they shall all share the same title: Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Perfect in Knowledge and Conduct, Sugata, Knower of the World, Unsurpassed One, Tamer of Men, Teacher of Gods and Humans, Buddha, World-Honored One. Their world shall be called Pure, and the kalpa shall be named Difficult to Traverse."
That Buddha-world is exclusively of the One Vehicle; there are no names for śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas, and it constantly discusses the immeasurable virtues and conduct of bodhisattvas.

The land is level and even, devoid of mountains, rivers, mounds, valleys, streams, or gullies of various kinds; it is like celestial silk. It is not illuminated by the light of the sun or moon, but is instead mutually illumined by the radiance of its own manifold marks and signs. Its myriad virtues are vast and universal, corresponding to the myriad thoughts and conceptions of sentient beings.
The reason for this is that the dharma-realm is without differentiation or contradiction.
In those Buddha-worlds, food consists of natural nectar, and they wear garments of karpāsa silk, dwelling in a manner similar to the blissful abodes of the sixth heaven.
The land was fertile and the five grains were abundant and inexpensive; it was replete with the seven treasures: gold, silver, precious gems, musaragalva, agate, pearls, and amber.
There was a Wheel-Turning Sage King named Varṣapuṣpa, who was escorted by the seven treasures.

As for what are called the seven treasures: the first is the wheel treasure (*cakraratna*). Regarding this wheel treasure, it is fourteen cubits in length and breadth, composed entirely of the seven precious substances; the wheel has a thousand spokes, each of which bears auspicious marks. When the king intends to go east, the wheel immediately proceeds as a guide.

The second is the elephant-treasure. As for what is called the elephant-treasure: its color is like white snow, and it has six tusks in its mouth; each tusk possesses auspicious marks. When the king wishes to mount the elephant to travel and observe the world, he can traverse the world in the mere twinkling of an eye without any difficulty.

Third is the Horse Treasure (*aśvaratna*). As for what is called the Horse Treasure: its body is a deep azure-blue with vermilion manes and tail; it travels through the void without its hooves touching the ground. When the horse lets out a roar, it shakes the world, and there is no one who does not hear it. If the King wishes to travel to the east, west, south, or north, he can reach them all in the mere snap of a finger.

The fourth is the Jewel of the Woman (Strī-ratna). As for this Jewel of the Woman: her body emits the fragrance of the *utpala* lotus, and her mouth the fragrance of gośīrṣa sandalwood; she is purely flesh with no visible bones, possessing a most upright human form—neither fat nor thin, neither tall nor short, neither too pale nor too dark—and she is endowed with the sixty-four feminine graces. Whenever the King desires to take her as his consort, she immediately appears before him.

Fifth is the jewel-treasure. As for this jewel-treasure, it is three fathoms square and seven fathoms high. When the king wishes to test that jewel-treasure, he assembles his fourfold army of troops and horses during the night, at a time when humans are not abroad. He then takes the jewel-treasure out at night and places it atop a ten-thousand-fathom terrace; it illuminates the entire world so that none fail to receive its light. The jewel comes and goes according to the king's thoughts.

Sixth is the treasure of the treasury official. Regarding this treasure of the treasury official: at that time, when the Wheel-Turning Sage King desired to travel through various regions and worlds, his route led through the bottomless source of the great ocean. The King, wishing to test the verification of the treasury official, immediately commanded his charioteer:
"Stop here at this sea; I wish to rest."
He then issued an order to the treasurer of treasures:
"I now require gold, silver, precious gems, musaragalva, agate, coral, amber, crystal, and lapis lazuli; are you able to obtain these for me?"
At that time, the Treasure of the Treasury-Keeper knelt in the water and scooped up water with a vessel; then, according to his thoughts, the seven treasures appeared spontaneously.

The seventh is the Treasure of the Military Commander. As for this Treasure of the Military Commander, when the King intends to assemble the fourfold army, he addresses the Treasure of the Military Commander, saying:
"I wish to inspect the fourfold army; can you manage to have it ready without losing a moment?"
That Jewel of the Military Commander addressed the King again, saying:
"I do not know, O Holy King, how many troops you require? The King told him:
"I require ten thousand chariots each for the front, the rear, the left, and the right.
At that time, the Jewel of the Military Commander followed the King's command and immediately assembled the fourfold army exactly as he had spoken.

The so-called fourfold army consists of elephant troops, cavalry, chariot troops, and infantry; for each of these divisions, there are ten commanders and attendants, and it is the same for each of the four types of troops.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the most eminent members of the assembled multitude:
"As for that Universal Monarch of that time, could he have been anyone else?
Do not harbor such a thought."

The reason for this is that the body of the Bodhisattva Most Victorious (Jiǎngshèng) is precisely such a one. Wherever he manifests transformations, his speech and voice are gentle and supple; all classes of people receive his Dharma-sound.

He preaches with profound stillness and tranquility the boundless teachings of deliverance—the four debts of gratitude, the four immeasurables, and the six perfections. Through skillful means and expedient wisdom, he enters the samādhi of cessation; free from desire and untainted, he teaches the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, and non-action; the dharma of no-arising and no-ceasing, and the dharma without beginning or end. For all sentient beings, devas, and worldlings who dwell within his sphere, he distinguishes their noble wisdom and the roots of the path free from outflows. Sometimes he manifests sounds and voices to point toward and instruct them in the luminous Dharma, leading them into the discipline of the Law through urgent and piercing teachings; at other times, he uses spiritual powers, transformations, and radiance to instruct them, desiring to lead sentient beings gradually toward ultimate realization.

The Buddha told Śāriputra: "All sentient beings are without the marks of self or person; all dharmas are fundamentally pure; all dharmas are formless, unattached, and subject to cessation; all dharmas are indestructible; and when one contemplates and realizes the Buddha-lands, they are found to be entirely non-existent."
Furthermore, Śāriputra!

The twelve links of dependent origination, the five aggregates, and the six sense-bases are entirely devoid of form or image. The eightfold voice of the Tathāgata is neither male nor female; it is neither harsh nor soft; it is neither clear nor turbid; it is neither masculine nor feminine. This arises from having received the realization of the true fruit through the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), understanding and knowing purity as it illuminates the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), such that with a single sound it pervades the three thousand worlds of the ten directions.

I once traveled to the Wild Horse World (*Yemama*), located seventy-two billion *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (Ganges-sand) buddha-fields away from here. While I was there, I circulated and emitted a great sound that filled those buddha-fields; upon hearing this sound, ten billion sentient beings immediately attained the stage of non-retrogression and all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path.

At that time, my disciple named Maudgalyāyana, foremost in supernormal powers, ascended one Mount Sumeru and then another Mount Sumeru; in this manner, passing through kalpas after kalpas, his feet never trod upon the ground.

At that time, Maudgalyāyana was in the World of Wild Horses (*Yemashie*). He emitted a great sound that pervaded the three thousandfold world-systems of the ten directions, and through that sound he proclaimed this teaching: "The Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma is a practice never before seen; yet one does not perceive a practice, nor is there no practice. Because one understands practice as non-practice, it is called 'purity. All dharmas are without form and without resonance. Furthermore, he speaks of the Four Truths according to the nature of reality (*dharmatā*): understanding suffering as being without suffering and not abiding in suffering—because one enters such wisdom, it is called 'knowledge of suffering' (*duḥkha-jñāna*).

Because the cause of origination (*samudaya*) is thoroughly understood from its root, one understands origination as non-origination; because one does not perceive the existence of origination, it is called 'knowledge of origination' (*samudaya-jñāna*).

Knowing the locus of cessation (*nirodha*), arising from cessation and ceasing by means of cessation, and not even perceiving cessation itself—this is called 'knowledge of cessation' (*nirodha-jñāna*)."

The unconditioned Way has no nest or lair; it is that which the Buddhas of the past, future, and present praise. Even the Way spoken of by the present Buddha does not exist as a [substantial] way, and what was spoken by those of the past and future is likewise so. The Way has no form or image and cannot be seen; because one understands that the Way is non-Way, it is called "knowledge of the Way."
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s discernment of the discourse on the Path.
At that time, all classes of sentient beings in that world of Gāndhārī heard his voice but did not see his form.
At that time, the great assembly was struck with astonishment and wonder, thinking: "Who is this person?
He utters a vast sound that shakes the world, while simultaneously expounding upon profound and subtle doctrines."
At that time, the Tathāgata, knowing what was in the minds of the sentient beings, addressed Maudgalyāyana, saying:
"Set aside your supernormal powers and manifest your form within this assembly."
Then Maudgalyāyana, manifesting himself in that very form, suddenly arrived amidst the great assembly.

Those bodhisattvas were eighty-four thousand yojanas in height, while the Buddha’s body was one hundred and sixty-eight thousand yojanas tall. When the assembly saw Maudgalyāyana with his physical form, robes, and alms bowl, appearing like a śramaṇa, they were all struck with amazement and marveled at this unprecedented occurrence:
"What kind of being is this? Is it a beast or is it a human?"
At that time, the Buddha, knowing what was in the minds of the assembly, addressed them, saying: "Do not harbor such thoughts. For this reason:

seventy-two billion *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (Ganges-sand) numbers of Buddha-worlds away from here, there is a Buddha-world named Sahā. Therein dwells a Buddha named Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles.
