He has appeared in the world during an age of five turbidities, constantly teaching sentient beings through written words. The human lifespan is but a hundred years, and those who exceed this are few. By means of the four truths, the ultimate reality, he analyzes and explains the goal; his discourse on wisdom is non-abiding and unattached."
"This bhikṣu Maudgalyāyana is the foremost disciple among those with supernormal powers.
That Buddha then said to Maudgalyāyana, "Display your supernormal powers;
the great assembly here wishes to see them with eager anticipation."

At that time, Maudgalyāyana, having received the Buddha’s instruction, rose from his seat, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and suddenly vanished as he entered the meditative concentration of the Unobstructed Samādhi. He took up all the buddha-fields of the ten directions and placed them upon his right palm; with his left hand, he held those buddha-fields suspended in mid-air. Everyone beheld Maudgalyāyana’s supernormal power, yet though they sought to see his actual form, they were unable to do so.
Then that bodhisattva immediately took refuge in that Buddha, the World-Honored One, saying:
"I humbly beseech you, O Teacher of Gods, to grant me deliverance.
The Buddha said:
"There is no suffering, and in the end there shall be no harm.
At that time, that Buddha said to Maudgalyāyana:
"Stop, stop, Maudgalyāyana!"
"Relinquish your supernormal powers so that this bodhisattva may roughly discern the traces of your path.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana, receiving the Buddha’s instruction, immediately relinquished his supernormal powers and sat down as before.
Then that bodhisattva came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In that land of Kṣānti, by what means does Śākyamuni Buddha teach and transform beings?
How does he preach the Dharma?"
"Furthermore, by what path do you instruct and transform sentient beings?
By what skillful means and wisdom do you circulate and come and go?
The Buddha told the bodhisattvas:

"The sentient beings of that land are stubborn and difficult to transform; they contend with one another over right and wrong, each claiming themselves to be superior. For this reason, the Tathāgata employs a teaching of urgent exhortation to lead them into the discipline of the Path."

It is just as when dragon-elephants and various fierce beasts are unruly and untamed; one must apply the whip and staff to make them aware of suffering, and only then will they become well-trained and fit for the king to ride.

The sentient beings of that land are likewise; they are delivered and liberated through various verbal teachings—some by means of sounds of suffering to explain the resonance of suffering, and similarly by means of the sounds of the origin, cessation, and path.
At that time, the Bodhisattva marveled at what he had never before experienced, exclaiming:
"Excellent, excellent, World-Honored One!

That Buddha-Tathāgata’s undertaking of diligent practice is truly rare; he is able to teach and transform sentient beings and propagate the Great Way amidst a world boiling with the five defilements, until they reach tranquil extinction and return to the unconditioned."
*The Scripture on the Ten Abodes and the Severing of Bonds*, Scroll 8.
*The Scripture on the Ten Abodes and the Severing of Bonds*, Scroll 9.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Zhu Fonian of Liangzhou during the Yao Qin dynasty.
Chapter Twenty-Four: On the Knowledge of the Path.

At that time, ten billion sentient beings in the assembly, as well as the great multitude of Bodhisattvas, Śakra Devānām Indra, Brahmā Devarāja, and the gods of Tuṣita, Yāma, Nirmāṇarati, Paranirmita-vaśavartin, up to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, each harbored doubts and desired to hear the exposition of the essentials of the Ultimate Path.
“The Way is signless and invisible; how can the Tathāgata say that there is a Way?
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of those assembled, immediately addressed the Bodhisattva Most Victorious:
“Do you wish to proclaim the essentials of the subtle and ultimate Way?”
He replied: “So be it, World-Honored One!
I wish and desire to hear it.”
The Buddha addressed Ajita, the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, asuras, gandharvas, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans:

"Understand that the Way is traceless, quiescent, and nameless. If, Ajita, the Way had a location, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva would not attain supreme perfect enlightenment within the dharma of equality;
because the fruit of the Way has no location, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva attains equal and perfect enlightenment."
The Buddha again addressed Ajita:
"There are ten concentrations of the bodhisattva’s path-knowledge. What are the ten?

They do not engage in physical actions and have no attachments; they do not engage in verbal actions and have no attachments; they do not engage in mental actions and have no attachments. They roam within the realm of the Buddha without giving rise to the concept of a "Buddha. They transform and guide sentient beings until they attain unimpeded wisdom, causing all classes of beings to understand both the path and the non-path. Furthermore, they cause these beings to achieve supreme perfect enlightenment. They emit great radiance that shines everywhere, and from each ray of light emerge immeasurable transformation Buddhas. Each transformation Buddha expounds the most profound *ṣaḍpāramitā* (six perfections), constantly turning the wheel of Dharma and inspiring the Bodhicitta. They understand self and non-self, as well as the absence of a life-span; when body and mind are spontaneous and natural, this is called the Way.

That which is natural is the realization that the Way has neither ignorance nor wisdom; it is the realization that there is nothing to be realized and that one perceives no realization at all. To say "I am this Way" is not to see the "I," and to say "I am this Way" is not to see the "self. It is the same for the self, the person, the life-span, and the vital principle; all manifold wisdoms likewise have no form or image.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Most Victorious (Varasena) came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If the Way is formless and invisible, yet now the Wheel of Dharma is turned and the realization of the four fruits of the path is expounded—speaking of the Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, Arhat, Pratyekabuddha, Bodhisattva, and Buddha—why then do you speak of the five aggregates, omniscience (sarvajñatā), the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path?"

For what reason is it said that one purifies buddha-fields and transforms sentient beings, traveling from one buddha-field to another, while discerning clear wisdom and the pleasures of the six consciousnesses?
"Why, then, do you speak of the names of the Way—the four immeasurables, the six perfections, true suchness, and the dharma-nature?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Varaprabha:

"Regarding what you have asked, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva understands the Buddha-wisdom and the fivefold Dharma-body. He possesses skillful means (upāya) and does not perceive any movement or fluctuation; he who perceives movement or fluctuation does not participate in the discourse on the Way. He remains far removed from all attachments and dwellings; when one investigates the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), even the dharma-realm is not found."
The reason for this is that both are fundamentally non-existent.

Since there is no attachment to wisdom and it is as pure as the original state, the turning of the Wheel of Dharma is established to bring about the understanding that all phenomena are without attachment.
Therefore, Most Victorious One!

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are equal toward all things and are entirely without attachment; they neither perceive arising nor perceive cessation. The Buddha-fields are pure and sentient beings are also pure, as they manifest immeasurable radiance of wisdom.

Therefore, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should practice total retention (*dhāraṇī*), establish themselves in non-retrogression, and ascend to the rank of a bodhisattva; or, entering into meditative concentration and the correct reception of samādhi, they should transform sentient beings and purify buddha-fields. Because there is no manifoldness of paths, forbearances, or single practices, and because there is no verbalized dharma-knowledge, one forcibly establishes this wisdom.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice with mindfulness, transforming all who have not yet awakened so that they are free from all perceptions of consciousness.
This, O Most Victorious One, is called entering a single state of concentration—the pure path of wisdom entirely free from dust.

One who disciplines the undisciplined does not calculate suffering or pleasure, permanence or impermanence, beauty or ugliness; such a wise one is entirely free from conceptual attachment and distraction.

Seeking the Buddha-treasury, they are endowed with the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, and the four analytical knowledges, as well as great loving-kindness, great compassion, and the *dharmatā* of *tathatā*. All these are non-existent, being entirely empty and quiescent. Through the wisdom of the path of sincerity regarding the discernment of karmic retribution, because there is neither arising nor ceasing, they are called emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and are likewise without anything produced.
Therefore, Most Victorious One!
The essential core of the supreme path of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva—that which is discussed as the "path"—is precisely the realm of empty space.
Why is this so? Because the path is emptiness and emptiness is the path; they are one and not two, nor are there any distinctions between them.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Most Victorious came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent, excellent! How well you have expounded this Dharma!”
At that time, among the assembled multitude—gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans—the thought arose in their minds:

“Today the Tathāgata, for the sake of this great assembly, has expounded the incomparable Dharma of the wisdom of the Path, fulfilling the aspirations of sentient beings according to their respective inclinations.”
"When will this most excellent Bodhisattva attain the supreme path of perfect enlightenment?
Knowing the thoughts in the minds of the devas, nāgas, and spirits, the Buddha immediately addressed the fourfold assembly:

"This most excellent Bodhisattva, after an incalculable number of three hundred and thirty *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, shall become a Buddha, titled Minghui (Wisdom of Light) the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. His world shall be named Wuliang (Immeasurable), the kalpa shall be named Qingjing (Pure), and that Buddha-Tathāgata’s retinue of disciples shall number nine thousand nine hundred and ninety-two billion, with a lifespan of one hundred and twenty small kalpas."
At that time, the assembly, having heard the Buddha’s bestowal of predictions, each made a vow, desiring to be born in that buddha-world.
The Buddha then told them:
"As you have vowed, you shall certainly be born there; do not doubt it."
The Buddha again addressed Varapuruṣa:

"In this great assembly, there are many who have fought between the Śakra-devendra of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and the Asuras. At times the devas were victorious and the Asuras were defeated; at other times the Asuras were victorious and the devas were defeated. Each fought the other, harboring knots of resentment, and each possessed poisonous hatred that they could not relinquish."

"I humbly contemplate the World-Honored One, who, through skillful means, has expounded the Dharma of the voidness of the Way and wisdom, causing all devas, humans, and asuras to each harmonize and give rise to a heart of compassion."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed those gathered: "The Way is formless and invisible;

the roots of the three poisons are eternally without beginning or end. To cultivate the Way while in the world, faith alone is the most powerful. When a person practices kindness and goodness, benevolent deities provide protection, and the Buddhas of the ten directions all join in praise. In this life and in future lives, their accumulated merit shall be immeasurable."

All sentient beings within this Jambudvīpa—whether crawling, flying, or moving—who possess form, must all return to the law of extinction. Life is like a flash of lightning, like a mirage, like an image in a mirror, or like a bubble floating on water; where there is meeting, there is separation, and those who are born must inevitably die. You who have received these forms cannot escape this affliction; even if you enjoy the longevity of the heavens, you remain subject to the three miserable realms. You should be diligent and seek liberation from this path; listen attentively and receive my instructions.
At that time, the fourfold assembly was filled with universal joy and each gave rise to reverence, desiring to hear the teachings of the Tathāgata’s Dharma.
Then the World-Honored One addressed the fourfold assembly:
“Listen attentively, and reflect upon this well.”
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should mindfully practice the dharma-gate of the eight liberations. What are these eight?

If a son or daughter of good family observes the precepts without deficiency, guarding their body, speech, and mind; practices the four immeasurable minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity; constantly maintains mindfulness to draw near to and follow virtuous friends while causing the Three Jewels to blaze brightly; constantly maintains the resolve to seek the unsurpassed path of the Buddha; expounds the True Dharma they have heard for others; and in teaching the Way, does not speak of the Lesser Vehicle but encourages sentient beings to practice the Great Vehicle.

At times, the Bodhisattva expounds the Mahāyāna, wherein all things are equal and non-dual, and no recipient of the teaching is perceived; it is like space, formless and imageless. That which the Buddha has established is inconceivable, encompassing all practices and pervading every dharma. At times he speaks of the practice of emptiness, non-existence, and the stillness of space; at times he speaks of the fivefold Dharma-body.

It is, for example, like a person who obtains a wish-fulfilling maṇi jewel; in the midst of a great assembly, he wishes to cause the jewel’s majestic power to appear blue, yellow, white, or black, and he also causes all the people to take on its same color and form.

The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is likewise: according to what is contemplated in the minds and intentions of sentient beings, he immediately expounds the inexhaustible Dharma of the wisdom of the Path, causing each to rejoice and resolve to revere the Buddha-way. He exhaustively guides and shows them the gateways of wisdom and Dharma, benefiting sentient beings and inspiring them toward the Great Way.
In this way, the Bodhisattva gives rise to the mind of great vows to deliver sentient beings, yet he does not perceive any who are delivered; it is like space, coming and going without obstruction.
The Bodhisattva’s resolve to deliver people is thus, and he likewise does not perceive any sentient beings who have attained deliverance.
The Buddha told Jiǔshèng (Jiùshèng):

“You shall perform the offering of the śarīra through your parinirvāṇa for twelve intermediate kalpas (*antara-kalpa*). All sentient beings shall serve you; for those without causes and conditions, you shall create causes and conditions; for those without protection, you shall provide protection; and for those without shelter, you shall provide shelter.”

At that time, all classes of people shall offer incense, flowers, and music, bowing their heads in self-refuge; each and every relic shall emit radiance, and through its divine power and transformations, those who behold it shall rejoice—all of which results from the fulfillment of great vows and aspirations.

Just as the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power manifests extraordinary transformations—sublime, magnificent, and illuminating all—he radiates immeasurable light of wisdom; by means of this, they give rise to the aspiration for the unsurpassed Way.

Among those sentient beings, those who have set their minds on the wrong path may achieve the dharmas of a Pratyekabuddha or a Śrāvaka; others may be born in the heavens or attain human form. The śarīra relics shall be distributed throughout the eight directions, above and below, where devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans—all creatures with form that crawl, breathe, or draw breath—shall all make offerings and delight themselves with the five kinds of music.
The Buddha again addressed Most Victorious:

"When you become a Buddha, the ground shall be the color of yellow gold and be fully endowed with the seven treasures: gold, silver, precious gems, musāragalva, agate, coral, amber, crystal, and lapis lazuli."

If there are sentient beings who wish to obtain the bodily relics for veneration, they shall all have their wishes fulfilled according to their intent; tens of millions of billions of complete bodily relics will appear throughout the world, and the Dharma-scriptures shall circulate for seventeen intermediate kalpas.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Immeasurable Awakening Wisdom (Anantabuddhijñāna) who thought to himself:
"The bodily relics of the Most Victorious Great Being are distributed throughout the world to inspire the aspiration for the Way; how many people have been delivered by them?"
The Buddha, knowing the thoughts in his mind, addressed him, saying:

"Stop, stop, worthy sir! Do not speak such words; do not attempt to measure the Tathāgata’s unimpeded wisdom, samādhi, and meditative concentration with the limited and obstructed knowledge of your own person."

The radiance of the śarīra receives and delivers sentient beings; this is not something the mind can deliver, nor is it something the intellect can examine. Such is the Tathāgata’s divine virtue, wherein the Way and wisdom are sovereign.
Furthermore, the transformations manifested through the expedient means of all Buddhas are not within the reach of pratyekabuddhas or śrāvakas.

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas attain the Samādhi of Tranquil Concentration, they are entirely free from notions of proximity or distance regarding their meditative mindfulness. They travel everywhere throughout the ten directions—to kingdoms, states, counties, towns, celestial palaces, dragon palaces, the abodes of various honored deities, villages, human settlements, wildernesses, heavens, and wherever beings of the five destinies may go—manifesting bodily relics (*śarīra*) in each place. From each and every relic, light is emitted, which explains the incomparable Dharma of the Six Perfections, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, great kindness, and great compassion; it clarifies the four debts of gratitude, wisdom, and the discernment of the void and stillness. Thoroughly attaining mastery over the concentrated mind, they make offerings to these relics with equanimity and non-duality, their resolve for giving being firm, neither increasing nor decreasing.
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva entering the Samādhi of the Mind of Quiescent Intent, whereby he is able to discern the six internal and external sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
For what reason are they called the "six sense bases"?

Regarding what are called the six sense-faculties: if the eye sees a form but does not give rise to the perception of form, yet understands the form as an external object and gives rise to visual consciousness, then seventy-four afflictions of worldly dust will immediately arise.
What are the seventy-four?

There are fifteen consciousnesses of the desire realm, fifteen consciousnesses of the form realm, fifteen consciousnesses of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, fifteen consciousnesses of the aggregates of birth, and fourteen consciousnesses of the intermediate state.

The Buddha told the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas: "Within visual consciousness, when these afflictions arise, visual consciousness is produced. Furthermore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, suppose a son of good family or a daughter of good family hears sounds with the ear; if they do not give rise to the affliction of the ear, but instead understand that sounds are external objects and thereby give rise to auditory consciousness, then seventy-four afflictions arise: [The list of afflictions follows.]... Thus, there are seventy-four afflictions. Furthermore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, suppose a son of good family or a daughter of good family smells odors with the nose; if they do not give rise to the affliction of the nose, but instead understand that odors are external objects and thereby give rise to olfactory consciousness, then seventy-four afflictions arise: [The list of afflictions follows.]... Thus, there are seventy-four afflictions. Furthermore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, suppose a son of good family or a daughter of good family tastes flavors with the tongue; if they do not give rise to the affliction of the tongue, but instead understand that flavors are external objects and thereby give rise to gustatory consciousness, then seventy-four afflictions arise: [The list of afflictions follows.]... Thus, there are seventy-four afflictions. Furthermore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, suppose a son of good family or a daughter of good family touches tangibles with the body;

if they do not give rise to the affliction of the body, but instead understand that tangibles are external objects and thereby give rise to tactile consciousness, then seventy-four afflictions arise: [The list of afflictions follows.]... Thus, there are seventy-four afflictions. Furthermore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, suppose a son of good family or a daughter of good family cognizes dharmas with the mind; if they do not give rise to the affliction of the mind, but instead understand that dharmas are external objects and thereby give rise to mental consciousness, then seventy-four afflictions arise: [The list of afflictions follows.]... Thus, there are seventy-four afflictions. Furthermore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, suppose a son of good family or a daughter of good family hears sounds with the ear; if they do not give rise to the affliction of the ear, but instead understand that sounds are external objects and thereby give rise to auditory consciousness, then seventy-four afflictions arise: [The list of afflictions follows.]... Thus, there are seventy-four afflictions. Furthermore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, suppose a son of good family or a daughter of good family smells odors with the nose; if they do not give rise to the affliction of the nose, but instead understand that odors are external objects and thereby give rise to olfactory consciousness, then seventy-four afflictions arise: [The list of afflictions follows.]... Thus, there are seventy-four afflictions. Furthermore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, suppose a son of good family or a daughter of good family tastes flavors with the tongue; if they do not give rise to the affliction of the tongue, but instead understand that flavors are external objects and thereby give rise to gustatory consciousness, then seventy-four afflictions arise: [The list of afflictions follows.]... Thus, there are seventy-four afflictions. Furthermore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, suppose a son of good family or a daughter of good family touches tangibles with the body; if they do not give rise to the affliction of the body, but instead understand that tangibles are external objects and thereby give rise to tactile consciousness, then seventy-four afflictions arise: [The list of afflictions follows.]... Thus, there are seventy-four afflictions. Furthermore, bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, suppose a son of good family or a daughter of good family cognizes dharmas with the mind; if they do not give rise to the affliction of the mind, but instead understand that dharmas are external objects and thereby give rise to mental consciousness, then seventy-four afflictions arise: [The list of afflictions follows.]... Thus, there are seventy-four afflictions."

In the ear-consciousness of those in the desire realm there are fifteen; in the ear-consciousness of those in the form realm there are ten; in the ear-consciousness of those in the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception there are ten; and in the intermediate state and the state of having received a physical form, there are thirty-nine.
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:
"Within the ear-consciousness, when these defilements arise, the ear-consciousness is thereby produced."

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva smells an odor with the nose, if they do not give rise to nose-consciousness (*ghrāṇavijñāna*), yet give rise to nose-consciousness by conceptualizing external objects through the nose, then seventy-four afflictions (*kleśa*) arise:

fifteen in the nose-consciousness of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), fifteen in the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), and forty-four in the four concentrations of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).
The Buddha again addressed the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas:

"Suppose a son of good family or a daughter of good family, through the gustatory consciousness, perceives flavors and gives rise to afflictions of the tongue; therein, by discerning that all things are entirely without a master, one can, within desire and within consciousness, give rise to the seventy-four afflictions of the dusts."
What are the seventy-four?

There are fifteen in the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*), fifteen in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), forty-four in the realm of non-perception and non-non-perception up to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

Furthermore, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should contemplate the dharma of arising and ceasing: external contact and internal pleasure, coarse and subtle afflictions (*kleśa*). By discerning each one individually as being utterly non-existent, he then gives rise to body-consciousness through contact and pleasure; thus, the affliction of the seventy-four types of defilements arises.
What are the seventy-four?
Those so called seventy-four consist of fifteen [states] of desire, fifteen of form, forty-four from the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception down to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

Furthermore, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should contemplate the mental activity of dharmas: when a dharma arises, it arises; when a dharma ceases, it ceases. Yet, one neither perceives arising nor perceives cessation. Foolish and deluded people give rise to the conceptualization of mental consciousness within this process, whereby they immediately give rise to the afflictions of the seventy-four *kleśas*.
"What are the seventy-four afflictions?
There are fifteen of desire, fifteen of form, forty-four of the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception along with the intermediate state.
The Buddha further addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva:
"What is the knowledge of the path (mārgajñāna)?
For a bodhisattva, there are fifteen knowledges of the path within the desire realm.
As for these fifteen, they consist of observing seven aspects of existence in the world."
What are the seven? First, slandering the Path;

second, believing in [false] words; third, accepting [false] teachings; fourth, regressing while abiding in the Truths; fifth, being hesitant regarding the attainment of retribution; sixth, having progress in mind but obstruction in body; seventh, seeing with the eyes but not attaining [realization].
There are eight matters regarding the profound treasury of the Buddha; what are these eight? First, the Buddha-dharma is formless, yet it provides a dwelling place for those who seek it.

Second, it does not abide in the present, yet through mindfulness and calculation, one perceives its eternal existence. Third, the past is forever extinguished, yet by means of vows, one speaks as if it were still visible. Fourth, the future has not yet arrived, yet one speaks of it as being without birth or extinction. Fifth, suffering arises from conditions and brings about affliction, which one invites through the correspondence of causes and conditions. Sixth, though things are not yet exhausted, one speaks of their exhaustion through the practice of skillful means. Seventh, upon seeing the Path and relinquishing the Path, one begins from a single step forward. Eighth, the Buddha-dharma is non-dual, yet the mind dwells amidst diversity.
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s fifteen modes of affliction regarding the path-knowledge of the desire realm.
What are the fifteen modes of affliction regarding the form realm?

What are called the fifteen are: first, gracious moisture; second, an unshakable mind; third, attachment to celestial bliss; fourth, forgetting both sin and merit; fifth, being eternal; sixth, being free from pain and itching; seventh, abiding in the stage of correctness; eighth, practicing impartiality; ninth, patience that does not arise [from anger]; tenth, a path that is immutable; eleventh, the perfection of perception; twelfth, attachment to form; thirteenth, sovereignty; fourteenth, distant illumination; and fifteenth, *karmavācanā*.
This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s practice of approaching the Form Realm heavens while remaining mindful of distancing himself from fifteen types of afflictions.
How does the bodhisattva-mahāsattva, regarding the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception and the intermediate state, distance himself from forty-four types of afflictions?
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva entered the Samādhi of Formless Intent within the Supernormal Powers and went to that place to preach the forty-four practices of attachment to consciousness.
What are these forty-four?
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva explained the practice regarding consciousness: first, that consciousness has no fundamental self;
second, that it discards form and is without shape;
third, that there is sensation which receives retribution.
Fourth, conceptions are not firm;
fifth, the root and branches of conduct are severed;
sixth, one relies on emptiness without wisdom.
Seventh, quiescent cessation and concentration;
eighth, signlessness like extinction;
ninth, remaining undisturbed within consciousness.
Tenth, the intention is forgotten and is not an intention;
eleventh, one does not dwell upon the intention;
twelfth, consciousness does not abide in the Path.
Thirteenth, it does not abide in the mundane;
fourteenth, its nature is such that it is empty;
fifteenth, like an echo, it has no form.
Sixteenth is the mindfulness of the path as inexhaustible;
seventeenth is the realization that emptiness is without remainder;
eighteenth is the purity of nirvāṇa.
Nineteenth, awakening to and realizing the inclination toward tranquility;
twentieth, moistening the deluded mind with grace;
twenty-first, manifesting the transition into the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Twenty-second: seeing the intermediate state (antarābhava) assuming form;
twenty-third: interacting with those in the intermediate state who have assumed form;
twenty-fourth: knowing where one has come from.
Twenty-fifth, he sees those sentient beings in the intermediate state (antarābhava) coming and going;
twenty-sixth, he sees the forms of those in the intermediate state being born and passing away;
twenty-seventh, he sees himself receiving a form and receiving the intermediate state of hell.
Twenty-eighth, there are those who possess forms that undergo retribution for sins and those who possess forms that do not undergo retribution for sins;
twenty-ninth, seeing among those with celestial aggregates (deva-ātmabhāva) those who receive blessings and those who do not receive blessings;
thirtieth, seeing among those with human aggregates (manuṣya-ātmabhāva) those who receive blessings and those who do not receive blessings.
Thirty-first, he sees those receiving the intermediate state (antarābhava) of hungry ghosts, some of whom are high and some of whom are low;
thirty-second, he sees those receiving the intermediate state of animals, some of whom are heavy and some of whom are light;
thirty-third, some pass from a celestial intermediate state back into a celestial intermediate state, which occurs because their consciousness was not distracted at the time of death.
Thirty-fourth: some may take on human aggregates from celestial aggregates; this arises because their fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna), though powerful, lacks wisdom.
Thirty-fifth: some may receive the aggregates of an animal from celestial aggregates; this arises because their consciousness is shallow and their minds give rise to chaotic thoughts.
Thirty-sixth: some may receive the aggregates of a hungry ghost from celestial bodies; this arises because at the time of death, their minds were greedy and insatiable.
Thirty-seventh: some may receive the aggregates of hell from the body of a deva; this results from making a solemn oath to slander the worthy and the holy. Thirty-eighth:
some may receive the aggregates of a deva after the aggregates of a human; this results from the purity of the prohibitive precepts and the Dharma.
Thirty-ninth: some may receive the aggregates of an animal from the body of a human; this results from practicing with a fundamental intention that is not single-minded.
Fortieth: Or, from the human aggregate one receives the aggregate of a hungry ghost, because one alone cherished its excellence and did not share it widely.
Forty-first: Or, from the human aggregate one receives the aggregate of a hell-being, having first experienced its blessings and subsequently experiencing its calamities.
Forty-second: Or, from the aggregate of an animal one receives the aggregate of a deva or human, because one has exhausted previously created merit and does not create new.
Forty-third: Or, from the aggregates of an animal, one receives the aggregates of a hungry ghost or a hell-being; this is due to the eight states of no respite and the crimes that lack rescue.
Forty-fourth: When receiving aggregates, the consciousness does not err regarding the form of the aggregates.

"This is called the forty-four afflictions of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva regarding the realms of perception, non-perception, and the intermediate state (antarābhava) form. The Buddha again addressed Most Excellent: "The bodhisattva-mahāsattva should further contemplate the consciousness of the intermediate state of the space-deity.

Either consciousness arises from the consciousness of space; or one receives the aggregate of consciousness from the aggregate of consciousness; or one receives the aggregate of the sphere of nothingness from the aggregate of consciousness; or one receives the aggregate of the formless heavens from the aggregate of the sphere of nothingness; or one receives the aggregates of the six heavens from the aggregate of the formless heavens, up to the heaven of ultimate culmination."
From the Akaniṣṭha Heaven (the Ultimate Heaven), one further receives the aggregates (*skandha*) of the form and formless realms.
When a human receives the aggregates of a deva, the body is one and a half *zhū* in height; it departs immediately and does not linger.
When a human receives human aggregates, the body is three and a half cubits in height; at the slowest, it remains for seven days, or perhaps six, five, four, three, two, one, or even a single day.
When a human receives the *skandhas* of an animal, it takes at most three and a half days, or two and a half days;
when a human receives the *skandhas* of a hungry ghost (*preta*), it takes at most half the duration of a meal, or even as little as the snap of a finger;

when a human receives the *skandhas* of a hell-being, the form is three fathoms and a half high, though there are some exceptions; those who pass away do not wait ten days before they immediately arrive there.

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas all follow and transform beings by preaching the wondrous Way to them. Those whose minds awaken quickly do not undergo various forms [in the intermediate state] but attain the Way therein.
When an animal receives a human *āśraya* (physical basis), it is like two and a half cubits; at the very slowest, it passes through four days, three days, two days, or one day.

When an animal receives a celestial *āśraya*, its form is like three and a half fathoms; at the very slowest, it lasts for one and a half days, or one day, or half a day, or even for the duration of a finger-snap.

When an animal receives the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of a hungry ghost, its form is like seven *zhang* in height; some emerge [from the womb] after a maximum delay of five days, or four, three, two, or one day.
When an animal receives the intermediate state of a hell-being, its form is like one and a half *zhang*; the maximum delay is half a meal-time or even as brief as a finger-snap.
When hungry ghosts receive a celestial *āśraya*, their form is like half a fathom; at the slowest, they remain for one day or half a day, or during a mealtime, or for the duration of a finger-snap.
When hungry ghosts receive a human *āśraya*, their form is like two and a half cubits; at the slowest, they remain for four and a half days, or three, two, or one day.

When hungry ghosts receive an animal *āśraya*, their form is like four and a half fathoms; at the slowest, they remain for fifteen days, or fourteen, thirteen, twelve, eleven, ten, nine, eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, or one day.

When hungry ghosts receive the *āśraya* (physical basis) of hell, their forms are five and a half *zhang* tall; at the very longest, they remain for ninety days, though some may leave sooner—whether it be eighty, seventy, sixty, fifty, forty, thirty, twenty, ten, or even one day, it is likewise so.

"Furthermore, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should further observe in this way: when beings from the hells receive the intermediate state (antarābhava) of the devas, their form is four and a half *ṛtus* high; at the very slowest, they remain for five months, or four, three, two, or one month.
If those with the intermediate state of the hells receive the intermediate state of human beings, their form is two and a half *hastas* high;

at the very slowest, they remain for three months, or two, or one month. When those from the hells receive the intermediate state of animals, their form is eight and a half *hastas* high; at the very slowest, they remain for three and a half months, or two, or one month—the same applies here."
When those in the hells receive the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of a hungry ghost, their form is like nine *ren* in height, and they remain in this state for at least three days.

Sometimes, while in the intermediate state of a deva, one should receive the intermediate state of a human; yet before reaching it, one returns to receiving the intermediate state of a deva—such individuals possess sharp faculties and do not undergo suffering as described in the scriptures.

Sometimes, while in the intermediate state of a deva, one should receive the intermediate state of a human; yet suddenly, one enters the intermediate state of an animal—such types have exhausted their merit and are driven by their past conduct.

Sometimes, while in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of a deva, one who was destined to receive the intermediate state of an animal may suddenly find themselves born in the intermediate state of a human; such individuals have not violated the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*).

Sometimes, while in the intermediate state of a deva, one who was destined to receive the intermediate state of a hungry ghost (*preta*) may suddenly find themselves born in the intermediate state of an animal; such individuals have practiced and cultivated the "summit" stage of patience (*mūrdha-kṣānti*).

Sometimes, while in the intermediate state of a deva, one who was destined to receive the intermediate state of a hell-being may suddenly find themselves within the intermediate state of a hungry ghost; such individuals have ripened the fruit of their retribution by being born into the human realm.

There may be those who were about to receive the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of a hungry ghost, yet suddenly find themselves in the intermediate state of a deva; such individuals are so because their meditative concentration is undisturbed.

There may be those who were destined to receive the intermediate state of the three evil realms, yet suddenly receive the intermediate state of humans or devas; such individuals are so because they possess wisdom, supernatural penetrations, and a vast mind.

There may be those who were destined to receive the intermediate state of a single ultimate [rebirth], yet suddenly find themselves in the intermediate state of Ābhāsvara Heaven; such individuals are so because their minds are single-mindedly focused.

There may be those who are destined to receive the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of Universal Purity (*śubhakṛtsna*), yet suddenly find themselves in the intermediate state of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*); such individuals possess intelligence, but their minds fail to penetrate [the truth].
The Buddha told Most Victorious:

“When a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva sits beneath the tree of enlightenment, by means of the wisdom of all-knowledge, the unimpeded equalizing wisdom, the wisdom that grasps profound penetration, the wisdom of eloquence and insight, the wisdom that understands sounds and resonances, and the wisdom of non-retrogression, he surveys the trichiliocosm: who among those taking form do not take form; who among those in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) do not remain in the intermediate state; how many sentient beings are in the human realm, and how many sentient beings are in the human intermediate state?”
The Bodhisattva further observes the sentient beings within the human aggregates, perceiving all those who receive the forms of the four aggregates and knowing their quantities.
The Buddha told Most Victorious:

"The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva observes sentient beings in the heavenly realm within the intermediate state of heaven, and further observes sentient beings in the heavenly realm proceeding toward the four destinies, knowing all their quantities."

At times, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, by means of the six supernormal powers and the wisdom of non-retrogression, observes sentient beings who have taken form as animals; he knows exactly how many beings are undergoing the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of animals and how many are transitioning to undergo the intermediate states of the other four destinies.

The Bodhisattva further observes those sentient beings who undergo existence as hungry ghosts, knowing exactly how many beings are in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the hungry ghosts and destined for the four destinies.

At times, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva observes those sentient beings who undergo existence in the hells, knowing exactly how many beings are in the intermediate state of the hells and destined for the four destinies.
The Buddha told Ajita:

“By means of non-retrogressive wisdom, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva universally observes those within the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the five destinies who have received a physical form and those who have not.

There may be one who, while in the intermediate state of the human realm, suddenly finds themselves in the intermediate state of the heavenly realm; having attained parinirvāṇa within that heavenly intermediate state, they ultimately do not receive either a heavenly body or a human body.”

There may be those who, while in the intermediate state (antarābhava) of the heavens, suddenly find themselves in the intermediate state of humans and attain parinirvāṇa there, without receiving either a heavenly or a human body;

or there may be those who, while in the intermediate state of animals, suddenly find themselves in the intermediate state of humans and attain parinirvāṇa there, without receiving either an animal or a human form;

or there may be those who, while in the intermediate state of animals, suddenly find themselves in the intermediate state of the heavens and attain parinirvāṇa there, without receiving either an animal or a heavenly body.

There may be those who, while in the intermediate state (antarābhava) of a hungry ghost, suddenly find themselves in the intermediate state of a human; having entered the intermediate state of a human, they attain parinirvāṇa, never again receiving the body of a hungry ghost or a human body.

There may be those who, while in the intermediate state of a hungry ghost, suddenly find themselves in the intermediate state of a deva; having entered the intermediate state of a deva, they attain parinirvāṇa, never again receiving the body of a hungry ghost or a deva body.

There may be those who, while in the intermediate state of a hell-being, suddenly find themselves in the intermediate state of a human; having entered the intermediate state of a human, they attain parinirvāṇa, never again receiving the form of a hell-being or a human.

There may be those who, having been in the intermediate state (antarābhava) of hell, suddenly find themselves in the intermediate state of the heavens; they then attain parinirvāṇa within that celestial intermediate state, without receiving the physical form of either a hell-being or a deva.

This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s non-retrogressive wisdom, by which they universally observe the trichiliocosm and fully know all those who have received a physical form and those who have not, as well as all those with transgressions and those with merit.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Most Victorious (Jinsheng), along with eighteen thousand people, one hundred thousand devas, as well as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, immediately rose from their seats, joined their palms, knelt with their right knees on the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In diverse sounds yet with a single voice, we praise this unprecedented marvel: 'Excellent! Excellent!'"
World-Honored One!

It is wonderful that you have spoken of the formless dharma of the intermediate state (antarābhava), which is limitless, immeasurable, and inconceivable—a realm that cannot be traversed by arhats or pratyekabuddhas.
We earnestly desire to behold the physical form of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
We pray only that the World-Honored One will look with compassion upon us inferior beings, so that we may receive purification and forever remove the defilements of our minds.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed those in the assembly:
"Excellent, excellent! You have asked well about this meaning."
"I shall now manifest my supernormal powers for you, so that the assembly of the eight classes of beings may behold the physical forms of those in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).

At that time, the World-Honored One entered the Samādhi of Formless Contemplation and universally beheld the sentient beings in the intermediate states of the five destinies—those who had assumed form and those who had not, those with transgressions and those with merit—and he knew them all completely.

At that time, the sentient beings seated there also beheld the intermediate-state forms (*antarābhava*) within the five destinies. Furthermore, hearing the Tathāgata preach the teachings of the Way, they immediately attained the purity of the Dharma-eye regarding those forms, with all defilements exhausted. Some gave rise to the mind of the Mahāyāna; some spoke of the practices of profound resolve; and they taught according to the capacities of each type, remaining unstained by attachment.

Furthermore, they also see the physical forms of those in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), from the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the tenth stage; they see those who have attained the stage of being "born only once more" (*ekajātipratibaddha*), sitting beneath the King of Trees (*vṛkṣarāja*) and subduing countless hundreds of thousands of millions of Māras, their bodies golden in color and fully endowed with all the marks (*lakṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, various celestial lords—Śakra, Brahmā, and the Four Heavenly Kings—come to request that the Bodhisattva expound the resonance of the Dharma, so that it may be heard throughout the trichiliocosm.
They also behold the Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, in other directions, who dispatch emanated bodhisattvas to request the names, the distances and locations of their lands, and their pure practices.

Some were seen before him extolling the Dharma of the Tathāgata’s ten titles; some were establishing teachings and making offerings; and some were praising the virtues of the Tathāgata with various verses.
The sentient beings of this land, while in that intermediate state (*antarābhava*), behold various miraculous transformations of supernatural power (*ṛddhi-vikurvaṇa*) that are inconceivable.

Furthermore, they see the Tathāgata extend his tongue, from which radiates light; within each ray of light there are emanated Buddhas, surrounded before and behind by the eight classes of beings, who preach the Dharma of fearlessness and non-retrogression in wisdom, fully endowed with all the profound treasuries of the teachings.
Or he bestowed upon his disciples the prediction of their future enlightenment as Pratyekabuddhas, saying: "In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood, and your names shall be such-and-such.
At that time, eighteen thousand people and hundreds of thousands of devaputras, while still seated, all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
At that time, the World-Honored One withdrew his supernormal powers and sat as before, addressing the fourfold assembly:
"The divine virtues of the Tathāgata are inexhaustible; furthermore, there are four dharmas that are inconceivable."

What are the four? First, the Tathāgata’s secret intention is inconceivable; second, the fundamental nature of sentient beings is inconceivable; third, the Tathāgata’s wisdom of the path is inconceivable; and fourth, the Tathāgata’s resonance is inconceivable.
Furthermore, Most Excellent One!
There are again four matters that are inconceivable.
What are these four?

First, the Tathāgata’s majestic demeanor is inconceivable; second, the Tathāgata’s Dharma seat is inconceivable; third, the Tathāgata’s instructions and admonitions are inconceivable; fourth, the adamantine concentration of mind is inconceivable.
Furthermore, there are four matters that are inconceivable. What are these four?

That while beneath the tree of enlightenment, his mind is like space—this is inconceivable; that he perceives neither "is" nor "is not"—this is inconceivable; that he makes the small great and the great small—this is inconceivable; and that his words are invariably efficacious, yet he does not perceive any efficacy—this is inconceivable.

Furthermore, there are four matters regarding the dharmas that should be practiced, which must not be clung to with defilement: to speak of a self, yet neither perceive birth nor the existence of extinction; to be without creation or action, and likewise without attachment or cessation; for the fundamental nature of all sentient beings is pure.
"This is what is called, Most Victorious One!
the dharma that a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should practice, which is free from all attachment.
How so, Most Victorious One?"
“Does the World-Honored One have limits? He replied, “No.”
“World-Honored One!
He further addressed Varaprabha:
“All true dharmas arise from the dharma-realm; they are fundamentally without limit. Do they arise because there is existence?”
"Is it that there is neither non-existence nor existence? He replied,
"World-Honored One!"
"It does not arise from existence, nor does it arise from non-existence.
[The interlocutor asked: "O Most Victorious One!
Since all phenomena without limit do not arise from existence and do not arise from non-existence, how is perfect enlightenment attained?"
He replied, "World-Honored One!
There is no one who has attained perfect enlightenment."
The Buddha told Most Victorious:

“When the Tathāgata sat beneath the Bodhi tree, by means of the boundless Dharma, he taught that there is neither arising nor ceasing; all things are empty and quiescent. Naturally, there is neither wisdom nor the absence of wisdom. Since there is no wisdom, who is there to know?”

Therefore, O Most Victorious One! My teaching on the self is provisional and not ultimate; it neither perceives the Way nor does it perceive the Way as being perceived. It is without seeing, without hearing, without wisdom, and without attachment.

The understanding of the dharma-realm is likewise: one does not perceive arising or ceasing, nor does one establish a nest therein. For those who receive the teaching, there is likewise no perception of words, letters, or phrases.
"O Most Victorious One!
One understands that all phenomena are empty and formless; could there be any foolish person or one lacking wisdom who would dwell within emptiness?"
He replied, “No, World-Honored One.”
"All dharmas are such as their true nature (dharmatā); the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) is fundamentally non-existent and devoid of anything.

Now, it is said that there is a Way—namely, great kindness and great compassion, the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the six superior dharmas, and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—but one does not attain the realization of the Way by means of these dharmas."
The Way is formless and invisible; it is because of its formless nature that it is called the Way. The Way neither comes nor is it seen to go.
This is called the most supreme!
This is what is called the Way.

If the Tathāgata were to arise from the dharma-realm and cease within the dharma-realm, that would be the defiled practice of birth and death; because there is no arising or ceasing, it is called the Way.
The Buddha told Most Victorious:

“When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva enters the Samādhi of Contemplating Space, they practice untainted dhyāna within all realms. By means of this dhyāna-method, they travel to the unobstructed without confusion; being neither body nor mind, there is neither equality nor inequality. Contemplating the concentration of emptiness, they perceive neither hardness nor softness; their will is fixed in tranquility, with no response and no object. Even when responding, they do not see responding, nor do they see non-responding.”
This is called the most supreme!
The bodhisattva’s concentration on emptiness is infinite, immeasurable, and inconceivable; it is not something that can be attained by arhats or pratyekabuddhas.
For example, Most Supreme One!

When burning the mountains, wilds, thickets, forests, grasses, and trees, the fire is not the thickets and the thickets are not the fire; yet it is neither identical to the fire nor separate from the fire.

One should know that the fetters (*saṃyojana*) of a Bodhisattva are likewise: the fetters are not the Path and the Path is not the fetters; yet they are neither separate from the Path, for one understands emptiness through meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and the formless samādhi is also like this.

All phenomena are pure, equal, and fundamentally non-existent; by means of meditative absorption, one observes the limit of phenomena (*dharmaparyanta*) and thereby attains equanimity, free from defilement or pollution. The mind does not abide within, nor does it wander without; form has no place of abiding, nor is any abiding perceived. Thus, one transcends all those who are subject to inversion.

To establish that phenomena are formless is called the Way. Alternatively, by means of the five supernatural powers, the three types of penetration, and wondrous wisdom, one circulates throughout the four quarters desiring to transform sentient beings; yet in this transformation there is both the act of transforming and the absence of seeing any transformation—this is called the Way.

Transcending the five supernormal powers and departing from the meditative states of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas—without perceiving even the meditative states of the five supernormal powers or the pratyekabuddhas—this is called the Way.
Furthermore, by means of a concentrated mind and the samādhi of right reception, one observes the fundamental nature of phenomena: from what do phenomena arise, and into what do they cease?
To neither perceive arising nor perceive cessation is called the Way.
Regarding conditioned worldly phenomena and unconditioned phenomena of the Way, to neither perceive the worldly nor perceive the Way is called the Way.

The outflows (āsrava) are defilements, while the outflow-free (anāsrava) is pure; yet one neither perceives the outflows nor exists within them. The ten paths of wholesome action and the ten roots of unwholesome dharma—neither perceiving the good nor existing in evil. Gain, loss, defamation, praise, renown, insignificance, suffering, and pleasure—neither perceiving suffering nor perceiving pleasure. Not seeing the realization of the Way, nor remaining in the secular world; not seeing the preaching of the Dharma, but the silent composure of the noble ones (ārya).
"Thus it is said, Most Victorious One!
When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva enters the meditative absorption of emptiness, this is called the Path.
Furthermore, Most Victorious One!"

Furthermore, the bodhisattva-mahāsattva should contemplate the Ākāśagarbha-samādhi: not perceiving any remaining unconditioned state through which one dwells for kalpas, nor perceiving any remaining unconditioned state that is subject to change—this is what is called the Way.
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s establishment of the wisdom of emptiness and skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*).

From one Buddha-land to another Buddha-land, they make offerings to and serve the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones; they transform sentient beings and purify Buddha-lands. They do not perceive the marks of form while manifesting forms; the same applies to sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, and consciousness. They do not perceive anyone being delivered to *nirvāṇa*, nor do they perceive the process of transmigration within birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
If a son or daughter of good family recites, upholds, and cherishes this [teaching] without forgetting it, they shall immediately obtain eight merits of the present life.
What are these eight?

Contemplating all phenomena as empty, one has faith without hesitation; attaining the Buddha’s profound treasury, the mind is not timid or weak; the mind is pure and stainless, free from defilement; the mind is like a vajra, indestructible; one's conduct is authentic and true, remaining unattached to the realm of Māra; purifying buddha-fields and delivering those not yet delivered; the mind is set upon the Great Vehicle, taking no pleasure in inferior wisdom; associating with virtuous friends and not clinging to external things; seeking true contemplation, free from notions of self or person.
This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva attaining the eight merits.

Understanding that worldly dharmas are without self, without person, without life-span, and without vital principle, he accordingly enters right reception within the originally non-existent dharmas. Constantly abiding in meditative concentration until reaching Nirvāṇa, he transforms and enlightens sentient beings without weariness; this is what it means to see the Dharma and thus accord with the Way. Because he sees that all dharmas are quiescent, formless, without activity, and without location, he is called the Most Victorious!

For a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, emptiness is neither existent nor non-existent; that which is empty and yet not empty is quiescent and nameless. That names are neither existent nor non-existent—this is called the Way.

At times, when a bodhisattva dwells in the contemplation of all phenomena, they do not rely on the three bases nor cling to the three realms of existence. Thus, while a bodhisattva exists within the worlds of humans and devas, they give rise to the heart of great vows to extensively deliver all sentient beings, yet they do not perceive any sentient beings who are delivered. This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva establishing the wisdom of emptiness, forever remaining without attachment.

"O Most Victorious One, you should know! The Tathāgata circulates within and enters the formless meditative concentration (*arūpa-samādhi*), which cannot be understood by those of the two vehicles. Only a Buddha clearly knows the Buddha-wisdom—unimpeded, unattached, unstained, and undefiled; it is without attachment toward any objective realm. Even if one attains profound dharmas, one does not take joy in them; one does not cling to the eight worldly conditions or the eight states of no-leisure. Possessing the four unhindered analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), one is neither extinguished nor ignited, yet it is not that there is no ignition; one neither arises nor is born, yet it is not that there is no birth. The past is eternally extinguished and thus has no past; the present does not abide and thus has no abiding; the future has not yet arisen and no one is seen to be born. This is called a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, who is unattached and unimpeded, not clinging to the three bases and unstained by the three realms of existence."

At that time, ninety thousand sentient beings seated there, eleven nayutas of devas and humans, as well as various devas, nāgas, and spirits, immediately rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We, though lowly and base, have been permitted to participate in the pure Dharma; you have thus been able to proclaim the formless Dharma and the signless Dharma."
I only pray, World-Honored One!

That in future ages, those born within the intermediate state among humans or devas in the realm of the Buddha-land may, right there, receive the realization of the unconditioned, dwelling together in a single land on the same day and at the same time.

At that time, the World-Honored One smiled, and from his mouth issued forth light of five colors, which illuminated the trichiliocosm, circled his body three times, and returned to enter through his mouth.
Ānanda knelt with his hands joined in reverence and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Reflecting upon my own service to the Buddha for more than thirty years, I have never seen a radiance surpassing this.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound upon it for me, so that those who gather in the future may forever be free from the obscuration of dust."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying: "Do you now see these ninety thousand sentient beings and eleven nayutas of devas and humans?

Having ended their lives here, they shall all be reborn within the intermediate state (antarābhava) of the realm of empty space as numerous as motes of dust. Once born into the intermediate state, each shall successively attain Buddhahood, all bearing the same name: Arūpa Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat. They shall have only Bodhisattvas as their attendants; they shall dwell in that intermediate state for the duration of one kalpa, and after their parinirvāṇa, their bequeathed Dharma shall remain for another kalpa. Thus, they shall attain Buddhahood in succession without interruption."

At that time, when the World-Honored One had spoken this Dharma, the Bodhisattva Paryavadāta and countless sentient beings repented for having received human forms and those celestial bodies; they wept aloud in their seats, unable to restrain themselves.
The Buddha, knowing [the reason], asked: "Good son,
why do you weep for one never seen before?"
The Śuddhāvāsas deities said, “We also wish to be born in that land; it is because we are not yet prepared for it that we weep with grief.
The Buddha told the Śuddhāvāsas:
"Stop, stop! Do not speak such words.
Your original vow and resolute mind were of a different nature; why do you now wish to be born in another land?"
"The name of this Bhadrakalpa shall be 'Extinction. You shall succeed him and be known as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha named Viśuddha, fully endowed with the ten titles.
Chapter Twenty-five: Body, Speech, and Mind At that time, the Bodhisattva Most Victorious (Jinavarasūtra) came forward and addressed the Buddha:
"All dharmas are like illusions and transformations. How, within these illusory and transformative dharmas, does one teach and transform sentient beings and purify a Buddha-field?"
How does one purify and eliminate the three perceptions of self, person, and life-span?
How does one travel from one buddha-field to another, serving and making offerings to the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones?
The Buddha told Sujaya: "Excellent, excellent!
You are indeed able to let out a lion’s roar before the Tathāgata."
Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall expound its meaning for you.

Most Victorious One, you should know that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva constantly maintains mindfulness of the cultivation of the dharmas of body, speech, and mind, clearly observing all phenomena as being like illusions and transformations, without any attachment whatsoever to the past, future, or present.
At that time, there was a bodhisattva in the assembly named Ānanda who came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

Those sentient beings who delight in the profound root of the Dharma and further provide offerings, whose body, speech, and mind are purified and whose faculties are fully matured—this is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva.”
The Bodhisattva Adhika said:
"To understand that all phenomena are neither detached nor defiled, and to purify body, speech, and mind within these undefiled phenomena—this is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva."
The Bodhisattva Equal Compassion said:

“When one practices compassion toward all beings with universal pity, understands that all written characters are entirely without attachment, and does not perceive any phenomena enacted by body or speech—yet therein attains the pure Dharma—this is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva.”
The youth Sumati said:

"Regarding all dharmas, from the very beginning, it is taught that no teaching is seen; one does not perceive the notion of 'dharmas. To purify body, speech, and mind therein is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva."
The Bodhisattva Jyotirprabha said:

"The Buddha-dharma is non-dual, nor is duality perceived therein; it quiets all fetters and afflictions until they are exhausted, with neither arising nor ceasing. Within this state, one purifies body, speech, and mind—this is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva."
The Bodhisattva Padmabandhana said:

"To be able to travel throughout the worlds of the ten directions and, upon seeing pure worlds, not give rise to the notion of purity, while therein purifying one's body, speech, and mind—this is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva."
The Bodhisattva Prabhāsa said:
"All dharmas return to a state of no-return; within body, speech, and mind, there is neither arising nor ceasing. To purify body, speech, and mind therein is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva."
The Bodhisattva Dharmaviśuddhi said:

"All dharmas ultimately return to emptiness; within right meditative absorption, one gathers the mind so that it is not distracted, and therein purifies body, speech, and mind—this is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva."
The Bodhisattva Padmacāra said:

“To practice the inexhaustible conduct within the fundamental non-existence of dharmas, and to purify body, speech, and mind within the inexhaustibility of dharmas—this is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva.”
The Bodhisattva Right-Equivalence said:
"To know suffering and to know pleasure, yet to be without suffering or pleasure, and therein to purify body, speech, and mind—this is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva."
The Bodhisattva Aṅgana-parivarjita said:
"To understand that all dharmas are without the arising of anger, and to purify body, speech, and mind within this dharma of the non-arising of anger—this is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva."
The Bodhisattva Siṃhaketu said:

"To be fundamentally free from anger, lust, and delusion regarding the three dharmas, and not to perceive form as having arising or ceasing, while purifying body, speech, and mind therein—this is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva."
The Bodhisattva Bestower of Jewels said:

"The self, the person, and the life-span have arising and ceasing; yet, understanding that all phenomena are entirely without arising or ceasing, one purifies body, speech, and mind therein—this is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva."
The Bodhisattva Courageous Wisdom said:
"The dharma-gate of dhāraṇī perceives no destination; regarding this dharma that has no destination, this is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva Bhadrapāla said:

“Names and titles are empty and deceptive and cannot be maintained; yet foolish, ignorant worldlings take them to be real. To purify one’s body, speech, and mind therein is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva.”
The Bodhisattva Candraprabha said:

“To practice the pure conduct (brahmacarya) within the fundamental limit of suchness and thusness, yet not perceiving that suchness and thusness, and thereby purifying body, speech, and mind therein—this is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva.”
The Bodhisattva Welcome-Coming said:

"With the fragrance of the virtue of precepts, one universally perfumes the trichiliocosm; this fragrance is like the wind—neither the fragrance nor the wind is perceived. Within this, one purifies body, speech, and mind; this is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva."
The Bodhisattva Acintya said:

“The unconditioned is not separate from the conditioned, and the conditioned is not separate from the unconditioned. To understand that both the conditioned and the unconditioned are entirely non-existent, and thereby to purify one’s body, speech, and mind therein—this is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva.”
The Bodhisattva Viśuddha said:
“Those born in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens do not perceive the pure conduct that constitutes heavenly blessings; therein, one purifies body, speech, and mind—this is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva.”
The Bodhisattva Zhicheng said:

"One does not perceive that by being sincere one would commit the four transgressions, nor does one perceive that by being deceitful one would receive retribution in a future life. To purify body, speech, and mind therein is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva."
The Bodhisattva Sudarśana said:
“To perceive all perceptions of form as being without the perception of form, and therein to purify body, speech, and mind—this is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva.”
The Bodhisattva Ratnakaṇṭha said:

“To abide within the cycle of birth and death, observing that sentient beings experience both suffering and joy, and further observing that one’s own body experiences suffering and joy in the same way as theirs, thereby purifying body, speech, and mind therein—this is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva.”
The Bodhisattva Akṣayamūla said:
"To know that the root of all fetters (saṃyojana) is fundamentally pure, and thereby to purify body, speech, and mind therein—this is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva."
The Bodhisattva Constant Laughter said:
"To perceive neither a self within the dharmas of the sense faculties, nor an agent who creates a self, and therein to purify body, speech, and mind—this is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva."
The Bodhisattva Constant Compassion said:

"To practice the four immeasurable minds—loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—and to pervade the Buddha-fields with them, yet not perceive any sentient beings to be saved by these four immeasurables; therein purifying body, speech, and mind—this is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva."
The Bodhisattva Brahmacitta said:

“To establish sentient beings with wrong views in right view, yet within that right view not perceiving either the wrong or the right, and thereby purifying body, speech, and mind therein—this is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva.”
The Bodhisattva Puyan said:
"The mind of the great vow is firm and is not cowed by the Lesser Vehicle; therein one purifies body, speech, and mind—this is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva."
The Bodhisattva Vīra said:
"To uproot the lust of sentient beings so that they are not defiled by the three realms of existence, and to purify body, speech, and mind therein—this is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva."
The Bodhisattva Citta-viśeṣa said:
“To establish the patience of wisdom and constantly cultivate diligence, thereby purifying body, speech, and mind therein—this is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva.”
The Bodhisattva Thunder-Sound said:

“Regarding all roots of goodness, one contemplates the Dharma-realm as neither increasing nor decreasing; seeing that no phenomena possess a nest or dwelling place, one therein purifies body, speech, and mind—this is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva.”
The Bodhisattva Anikṣiptadhura said:

"If one were to take a *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (Ganges-sand) number of *kalpas* as a single day, fifteen days as a half-month, thirty days as a month, and twelve months as a year, and were to pass through hundreds of thousands of millions of such *kalpas* before a single Buddha appears to illuminate the world; and if, thereafter, one were to provide skillful offerings to *tathāgatas* as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, purify the Brahma-faring (*brahmacarya*), and only then receive the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), yet throughout this process never grow weary of the suffering of birth and death while purifying body, speech, and mind—this is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva."
The Bodhisattva Susthitāyus said:
"Constantly transforming the sixty-two views through supernormal power (*ṛddhi*), and purifying body, speech, and mind within those sixty-two views—this is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva."
The Bodhisattva Kṣepayitavya said:

“To contemplate that all dharmas are fundamentally empty and non-existent; that what arises arises of itself and what ceases ceases of itself; that dharmas give rise to one another and dharmas extinguish one another; and that arising does not know arising and ceasing does not know ceasing—to purify body, speech, and mind therein is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva.”
The Bodhisattva Viśālamati said:

“To discern each and every exhalation and inhalation that the mind contemplates without losing their sequence, yet neither perceiving an exit nor perceiving an entry, thereby purifying body, speech, and mind therein—this is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva.”
The Bodhisattva Śubhavijaya said:

"To discern the three periods of time—wherefrom they arise and whereunto they cease—and yet to perceive neither arising nor ceasing, thereby purifying body, speech, and mind therein: this is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva."
The Bodhisattva Upāli said:

"Not perceiving the observance of precepts nor their violation; not perceiving that one who violates precepts will enter hell, nor that one who observes precepts will receive the karmic reward of celestial bliss; therein purifying body, speech, and mind—this is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva."
The Bodhisattva Abhaya said:

“To cultivate the four bases of psychic power, to harbor no timidity regarding the four foundations of mindfulness, and to realize that the mind has no fundamental basis and thus not perceive a fundamental basis of the mind—therein purifying body, speech, and mind: this is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva.”
The Bodhisattva Immeasurable Compassion said:

"Those who have resolved their minds to feel compassion for all beings, traveling to the immeasurable Buddha-fields of other directions, seeking to deliver sentient beings without weariness, neither perceiving those delivered nor those not delivered, and therein purifying body, speech, and mind—this is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva."
The Bodhisattva Ratnadatta said:

“To promote the four debts of gratitude, to draw near to the Three Jewels, to practice giving, benevolence, and impartial benefit for others, and yet not perceive the merit of receiving retribution for these four debts of gratitude—purifying body, speech, and mind therein—is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva.”
The Bodhisattva Huigen said: “To regard all sentient beings as one’s own infant;

to wish to protect others just as one protects oneself; to bring sentient beings to peace and security to the shore of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); and not perceiving even those who have reached the other shore of nirvāṇa—purifying body, speech, and mind therein: this is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva.”
The Bodhisattva Śāntivīrya said:

“The Buddha’s inconceivable retribution is immeasurable; his faculties are tranquil and stilled, and he has faith that is free from greed and envy. To purify body, speech, and mind therein—this is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva.”
The Bodhisattva Guśarīra said:

“To accomplish the path of a Buddha so that one’s body attains the primary and secondary marks, and after entering *nirvāṇa*, for the relics to be distributed and fill the four quarters, the eight directions, above and below, such that devas, nāgas, and spirits all revere them; yet, while not perceiving any agent who teaches through these relics, to purify one’s body, speech, and mind therein—this is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva.”

The Bodhisattva Gandhaśrī said: “From each and every pore, immeasurable fragrances emerge; from each and every fragrance, immeasurable teachings emerge, delivering sentient beings without end. His supernormal powers and majestic spiritual authority are sublime and immeasurable, causing all sentient beings to give rise to the aspiration for the immeasurable Way. Among them, those sentient beings who are mistaken and should not follow the True and Right Way may instead achieve the path of a Pratyekabuddha or a Śrāvaka, or be reborn in the heavens and then return to human form. Yet he harbors no resentment toward them. The Great Way is noble, yet he does not feel shame for those he delivers through lesser paths. Within this, he purifies his body, speech, and mind; this is called the wisdom of a Bodhisattva.”
The Bodhisattva Mahāpraṇidhāna said:
“To be unstained by defilement, to give rise to no conceptual attachment toward the eight worldly dharmas, and therein to purify body, speech, and mind—this is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva.”
The Bodhisattva Karuṇāmṛta said:
"The Way is two and non-Way is one; yet neither one nor two is perceived. To purify body, speech, and mind therein—this is called the wisdom of a bodhisattva."
