First, to speak first and smile later so as not to wound another’s mind; second, to act in accordance with the Dharma as it has been taught, responding to what is correct and true; third, to understand that both the Way and non-Way are without a fixed abode; fourth, to know that whether there is expectation or no expectation, all returns to emptiness.
"This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practicing in accordance with emptiness, cultivating the unsurpassed path within all Buddha-dharmas.
When these four sets of four dharmas were spoken, twenty-two thousand devas and worldlings all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path;
furthermore, twelve thousand people immediately attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) while still on their seats.
Furthermore, there were countless sons of the gods from the ten directions who scattered flowers as an offering until they reached their knees.
29. Chapter Twenty-nine: The Three Poisons. At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”

Now I hear that the Tathāgata has taught the wisdom of the four dharma-gates, which is profoundly deep and subtle, establishing the faculties and attaining their powers; this is the practice of Bodhisattvas, not something that can be reached by Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas.

Now I ask the Tathāgata: regarding the future and the intermediate periods, when one contemplates the visualization of the impurity of foul substances during the first dhyāna, does one contemplate the impurity of one's own body, or does one contemplate the impurity of another's body?
The Buddha told the youth Mañjuśrī:

"There may be bodhisattvas who, before yet ascending to the stage of a bodhisattva, observe the impurities and foulness of their own bodies, thereby establishing the faculties and attaining power. Or they may observe their own bodies and the bodies of others, further employing skillful wisdom to manifest their bodies as putrid and filthy, with pus and blood overflowing. Within this state, they awaken countless sentient beings, causing them to abandon their attachment to purity and realize that all things are not real."
Furthermore, Mañjuśrī!
There may be bodhisattvas who, while in the stage of the future, cultivate the intermediate state above it before having yet clarified the first dhyāna;
there are also bodhisattvas who, having already transcended the future, abide in the intermediate state and further cultivate the first dhyāna through skillful wisdom.

There are some bodhisattvas who, having already transcended the intermediate pure stages of the future, next cultivate the first dhyāna, maintaining the root of the five practices, and subsequently ascend to the dharmas of the second dhyāna;

there are some bodhisattvas who, having relinquished the four higher dhyānas and the intermediate stage of the future, ascend in succession through the first and second dhyānas, while in the fundamental third dhyāna they maintain themselves through joy and tranquility;

furthermore, there are bodhisattvas who, having already departed from the third dhyāna, further relinquish the four mental formations to cultivate the fourth dhyāna, and within that fourth dhyāna contemplate the meditation on the impurity of foul secretions.

There are some bodhisattvas who have entered the samādhi of eternal quiescence and universally observe the world, seeing that there are no sentient beings, no self, no person, and no life-span; among those born or those passing away, nothing at all exists.

"O Most Victorious One, you should know that when a bodhisattva-mahāsattva universally contemplates all phenomena, they see neither that which arises nor that which ceases; furthermore, regarding all phenomena, they see neither the ultimate nor the non-ultimate. Furthermore, Most Victorious One!
When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates all fetters and attachments and seeks purity within them, he should ask what ought to be asked.

This dharma is eternally quiescent, secure, and immutable; it is pure throughout birth and death, and no defilement is seen therein. This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s discourse on non-arising.

one thoroughly knows that all fetters and attachments return to emptiness, and does not perceive anyone who undergoes birth and death or attains realization; who does not perceive a place of arising, ceasing, or birth; and who perceives neither emergence nor nirvāṇa—this is called the Bodhisattva’s discourse on non-arising.

The gathering and dispersing of causes and conditions, which are foul and impure, is called the Bodhisattva’s discourse on non-arising.

When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva realizes non-retrogression through the convergence and dispersal of causes and conditions, and through the unimpeded knowledge that severs [ignorance] and forever leaves the three realms of existence, this is called the Bodhisattva’s discourse on non-arising.

This is called the non-interruption of the roots of goodness of all dharmas; it is the knowledge that "this is wholesome, this is unwholesome; this is a worldly dharma, this is a supramundane dharma; this is an obstructive dharma, this is a non-obstructive dharma; this is a conditioned dharma, this is an unconditioned dharma; this is a dharma with outflows, this is a dharma without outflows. This is termed the discourse on non-arising of the bodhisattva-mahāsattva.
Furthermore, Most Victorious One!

One contemplates and discerns that the Buddha’s image is formless, and likewise discerns the manifold nature of the Dharma-nature; one contemplates the immeasurable merits of the Noble Assembly, and in succession contemplates that sentient beings are not uniform; furthermore, one should discern that the buddha-fields are diverse, and that the directions in which the mind tends are difficult to exhaustively fathom. This is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s discourse on non-arising.
Furthermore, Most Excellent One!
That all dharmas are entirely pure, and that all dharmas are entirely impure—this is called the Bodhisattva’s discourse on non-arising.
The Most Victorious One addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In what sense is it said that all dharmas are the discourse on non-arising?
Is it because all dharmas are impure that they are called the discourse on non-arising?"

“All dharmas are without consciousness and without the retribution of volitional formations; when there is the perception of consciousness that accords with dharmas, this is called ‘purity without purity.’”

The Most Victorious One asked again:

“Forever free from desire, one knows among hundreds of millions of dharmas which are determinate and which are indeterminate; that which is determinate is the Path, while that which is indeterminate is not the Path?

if there are sons or daughters of noble family who do not know whether the various dharma-realms are already determined, will be determined, or are not yet determined, then they have not understood, are not understanding, and will not understand those dharmas.

If there are sentient beings who harbor doubts regarding what is certain or uncertain, they will be unable to proceed from one stage to the next; because they do not transcend the successive dry grounds, they shall not leave birth and death to abide in the dharma of nirvāṇa.
"Why is this? Because the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not exhaust the root of birth and death until they reach Nirvāṇa.

"Therefore, son of good family, the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, do not speak of birth-and-death as inferior, nor do they speak of nirvana as superior. "Why is this? Because one does not perceive a place of wandering within birth and death, nor does one perceive Nirvana as something wherein extinction is attained.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Most Victorious rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Excellent, excellent!

That which the Tathāgata has spoken—speaking of the mark of nirvāṇa wherein there are no sentient beings—is a teaching of the Dharma and a teaching of its meaning that should truly be tranquil, seeing neither birth-and-death nor nirvāṇa.”

At that time, among the two thousand seven hundred bhikṣus seated there, those with outflows attained liberation of mind and realized the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Why was this?

Because when one understands birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), there is no birth-and-death; when one understands nirvāṇa (*nirvāṇa*), there is no nirvāṇa. Furthermore, they do not say there are sentient beings to be delivered, nor do they speak of the eternal stillness of nirvāṇa. Having understood the dharma of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), they realize there is neither birth-and-death nor nirvāṇa.
At that time, seven hundred bhikṣus sitting in the assembly rose secretly from their seats, gathered up their robes and bowls, and departed without a word.

Chapter 30: Inquiry into Nirvāṇa At that time, the Bodhisattva Most Victorious addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If there are sentient beings who wish to cause all dharmas to arise, there would be no path through which they could achieve equal and perfect enlightenment; how much less could they achieve the Way within nirvāṇa?”
This is not so. Nirvāṇa has no lineage and no name; how can one seek emptiness within emptiness?
Since Nirvāṇa does not possess even a single thing, how much less could one seek the numerical categories of all phenomena?
“World-Honored One!

These seven hundred bhikṣus, having shaved off their hair and beards and donned the three dharma-robes in the presence of the Tathāgata, hold alms-bowls in their hands and purely cultivate the Brahma-faring. Yet, through skillful means, they have regressed and remain on the level of ordinary worldlings, seeking only the dwelling-place of the lair of Nirvāṇa. It is like sesame oil, clarified butter, curd, and ghee: while the oil permeates everywhere, the ghee remains solid and settled.”
Birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are likewise so: in ultimate nirvāṇa there are no characteristics of dharmas, and the Great Way of nirvāṇa has neither shore nor bottom.

Beings deluded by various afflictions have long been attached to confusion, yet they falsely claim that nirvāṇa possesses birth and extinction, or attachment and cessation. Only those who practice the Way and maintain right view do not see any dharma arising or ceasing, and do not see any dharma being received or abandoned.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Most Victorious (Jiàishèng) came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

These seven hundred bhikṣus have each abandoned their practice and scattered upon merely hearing this Dharma teaching. How much more time must they pass before they can attain liberation, forever leaving birth and death behind and no longer remaining in wrong views?”
The Buddha told Most Excellent:
"If you wish to know, listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall dispel your doubts for you."
He replied: “So it is, World-Honored One.”
The Buddha said:

“Only after the passing of kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges does a single Buddha appear; even after experiencing seventy-two billion such kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, one still cannot attain deliverance.”

Why is this? A Buddha appears in the world only once in hundreds of millions of *kalpas*; it is extremely difficult to encounter a Buddha and even more difficult to hear his sutras. Today, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, is expounding the teachings of the Way amidst the great assembly, preaching the Dharma of Nirvāṇa, which is without birth or extinction.
To give rise to a mind of false views regarding this True Dharma means that wherever one is reborn, one will always remain in false views and never abide in the Right Path.

It is like a man who is courageous and possesses great strength; there is no skill or art he has not mastered, and he is fully equipped with the six arts. He has thoroughly penetrated all matters of celestial phenomena, geography, the stars, and portents.

However, this wrestler was constantly afraid of empty space; he devised a secret plan to run toward the four quarters and throw himself into a realm where there was no emptiness, yet wherever he went, he always saw empty space.
These bhikṣus are just like this: even if they were to pass through hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, attempting to establish the name "nirvāṇa" in empty space, this would be impossible.
If one does not realize emptiness (*śūnyatā*) wherever one goes, one will never achieve the fruit of the path despite seeking it.

It is like a person who wishes to seek emptiness: wherever they may be, emptiness is always before them. Furthermore, one does not proclaim that this emptiness or that emptiness has various characteristics, nor does one see anything coming from or going to emptiness that can be accomplished; this is the essential understanding of *nirvāṇa*.

Those bhikṣus have practiced heterodoxy since their previous lives and remain unawakened to this day; though they wish to seek the great path of nirvāṇa and the unconditioned, they do not yet even recognize its name or designation—how could they possibly discern the path to nirvāṇa?
To spend one’s entire life revolving in the cycle of existence seeking nirvāṇa is to labor in vain, for it cannot be attained. Why is this?

Nirvāṇa is a provisional designation, like an illusion or a magical transformation; it is empty and non-existent, merely designated as "emptiness. Such a provisional name is a deceptive fiction transmitted by the ignorant, not something praised within the Dharma and Vinaya of the noble ones.

At that time, there were also more than seven hundred bhikṣus who had established themselves in practice; while still upon their seats, they were cleansed of all defilements and attained the purity of the Dharma-eye. Possessing the three insights and the six supernormal powers without obstruction, they realized that the Buddha is unborn and neither arises nor ceases. They did not seek nirvāṇa through past dharmas; the teachings, admonitions, wisdom, and eloquence spoken by countless *saṃkhyeya* Ganges-sands of Buddhas of the past were entirely without variation. Why is this? Because all dharmas are entirely empty like space, and one does not perceive any nesting place from which the Buddhas emerge.

Śāriputra said, "All five hundred of you are individuals liberated from both sides; you are also fields of merit. The bhikṣus said:
“The noble wisdom of the Tathāgata is inherently pure; it is unstained by and unattached to any realm of phenomena.

"Furthermore, how many worthies are pure in their giving?
He replied, "Not receiving any dharmas is what is called purity."
He asked again:
"What is the field of merit for giving? He replied:
"To forget the dharmas of the Buddha-way is what is called a field of merit.
He asked again:
"Furthermore, how many sages among sentient beings act as good friends (kalyāṇamitra) to instruct others regarding good and evil?"
He replied, "Not abandoning any class of sentient beings— this is called a spiritual friend.
He asked again:
"How many sages in the world are able to repay the Buddha's kindness?
He replied, "Those who have attained the four fearlessnesses and do not sever the lineage of the Buddhas."
He asked again:
"How many virtuous people in the world are capable of making offerings to the Tathāgata? He replied:
"To practice for billions of kalpas therein without confusion—this is called making offerings.
He asked again:
"How many sages in the world are able to protect the Buddha-treasury?"
He replied, “I shall not violate the Buddha’s precepts for as long as my life lasts.
He asked again:
"Furthermore, how many worthies are able to give rise to reverence?
He replied, "Those who guard their faculties and are able to close off the six sense organs."
He asked again:
"What is that which is called a great treasure in the world? He replied:
"Regarding 'the one who has accomplished the seven treasures,'" he asked again:
"How does one understand the practice of contentment?"
He replied: "It is the cultivation of the meaning of the foremost, unsurpassed wisdom.
He spoke again:
"What is meant by having few desires regarding the world?
He replied, "It is not wishing for or seeking anything in the world."
He asked again:
"How does one understand non-attachment to the world? He replied:
"He has severed all fetters and is no longer subject to the five hindrances.
He asked again,
"Who in the world is happy and free from all suffering?"
He replied, “Because there is nothing to which one is attached, it is called happiness.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'having no attachments'?
He replied: "It is to understand that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and the eighteen fundamental bases (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*) are empty, quiescent, and unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)."
He asked again:
"Who has raised this objection? He replied:
"Externally abandon the six sense objects; internally abandon the six faculties.
He asked again:
"Who crosses from this shore to reach the other shore?"
He replied, "One who establishes the faculties, attains power, and realizes the Way.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'the bodhisattva’s mind of giving is uninterrupted'?
He replied: "It means eliminating the three perceptions so that afflictions do not arise."
He asked again:
"How does one maintain the precepts without deficiency or transgression? He replied:
"The mind of the Way is firm and steadfast, not abandoning the great vow.
How does one practice patience so as to face adversities without fear? He replied:
"Understanding that the mind is empty and quiescent, one does not give rise to the root of anger.
[The questioner asks: "How does a bodhisattva cultivate diligence? He replied:
"The thoughts of the mind have no beginning or end.
He asked again:
"How does one maintain meditative concentration so that the mind is not distracted or impaired?"
He replied: "The mind is settled in eternal stillness and does not receive external objects. [The questioner asked:
"How do the karmic activities of wisdom expound and clarify all dharmas?"
He replied, "To discern the meaning and intent without abandoning the mind of the Way.
He asked again:
“How does a bodhisattva practice a mind of loving-kindness without abandoning the roots of the path?
He replied: “It is not abandoning the view of sentient beings as those who are to be delivered.”
He asked again:
"How does a bodhisattva practice compassion? He replied:
“Contemplating all phenomena, one does not regress.
He asked again:
“How does a bodhisattva attain nirvana with an uninterrupted mind of joy?”
He replied, "I do not give rise to the notion of 'self' or calculate that there is a 'me'.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'the Bodhisattva guarding the mind so that it is not interrupted'? He replied:
"From the time one guards the roots of the Path until the attainment of Buddhahood, no other thoughts arise during that interval."
He asked again:
"How does a bodhisattva establish themselves in the faculty of faith? He replied:
"Transcending external dharmas, one does not associate with what is false.
He asked again:
"How does one understand emptiness without hesitation?"
He replied: “To understand that the Way is not the Way and that the Way has no root or source—
this is what is called the practice and conduct of a bodhisattva-mahāsattva.”
Chapter 31: The Four Brahma-Vihāras. At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī thought to himself:

"How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva cultivate the pure brahma-conduct of body, speech, and mind, traveling throughout the four quarters to deliver sentient beings, proceeding from one buddha-field to another, never abandoning them?"
"How does a bodhisattva advance toward the accomplishment of the work of buddhahood without losing the concentration practiced by bodhisattvas?
The Buddha, knowing his intention, immediately told him:
"So it is, so it is; it is just as you have said."
The fundamental practices of Bodhisattvas vary according to their types; I shall now expound their meanings for you.
Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon them well.
He replied, “So it is, World-Honored One!”
The Buddha told Rucideva:

"Physical conduct that is pure and does not commit any evils; verbal conduct that is sincere and does not lose the nature of reality (dharmatā); mental thought that is concentrated and remains unshaken by fear—this is called the foundation of a bodhisattva’s supernormal wisdom."

To cherish sentient beings with compassion while remaining unattached to sensual desires, to constantly cultivate the contemplation of impurity and the foulness of the body, and to steadfastly guard the mind so as not to dwell in the darkness of ignorance—this is called the foundation of a bodhisattva’s penetrating wisdom.

Amidst the multitude, he is like one in the wilderness, never losing his dignified deportment; whether advancing or halting, coming or going, his demeanor is always perfectly composed, and he has never transgressed the prohibitions and precepts of the Tathāgata—this is called the root of a bodhisattva’s supernormal wisdom.

Being fully liberated in all Buddha-dharmas, free from desire and unconditioned, and inconceivable; wherein the noble assembly practices such that the three vehicles are forever absent—this is called the foundation of the bodhisattva’s penetrating wisdom.

To clearly understand that liberation from desire is formless, and likewise for liberation from hatred and delusion as well as sloth, and to cultivate the nine successive stages of immovable dhyāna-awakening—this is called the root of a bodhisattva’s supernormal wisdom.

Not being attached to the desire realm in seeking the rank of a wheel-turning monarch, not dwelling in the form realm in hoping to achieve merit, and furthermore not contemplating the path of the formless realm—this is called the foundation of a bodhisattva’s supernormal wisdom.

Furthermore, regarding emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, there is no practice for exhausting out-flows that is not undertaken; one understands all phenomena to be like illusions and transformations—this is called the root of a bodhisattva’s supernormal wisdom.

There may be sentient beings who never lose their composure, such that from one state of abiding to another, their minds remain equanimous toward both love and hatred; this is called the root of a bodhisattva’s supernormal wisdom (*abhijñā*).

Not contradicting the root of all phenomena of the past, and likewise for the future and the present, they perceive neither defilement nor non-defilement and see no attachment therein; this is called the root of a bodhisattva’s supernormal wisdom.
Chapter 32: The Invitation by Brahmā. At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Most Victorious addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

His physical conduct is pure and he does not perform unwholesome deeds; his spoken teachings are never false; his mental intentions are pure and transcend the roots of the Path. The Four Immeasurables, the Hall of Brahma, which you now discuss—compassion, kindness, joy, and equanimity—are used to deliver sentient beings. He never forgets or abandons even a single person until they are delivered. By means of loving-kindness he removes lust, and by means of the contemplation of impurity he removes the notion of purity; observing that all marks are formless—this is called the foundation of the Bodhisattva’s penetrating wisdom.

They attain complete liberation from the root of all phenomena, and they attain complete liberation regarding the Three Jewels—whether conditioned or unconditioned, with outflows or without outflows; this is called the foundation of a bodhisattva’s penetrating wisdom.

Knowing that desire is non-existent, one does not give rise to further knowing; knowing that hatred has no root, one realizes all things are empty—this is called the foundation of a bodhisattva’s supernormal wisdom (*abhijñā*).

Practicing compassion without interruption, one does not cling to the desire realm, the form realm, or the formless realm; regarding the four dhyānas, one never gives rise to conceptualization—this is called the foundation of a bodhisattva’s supernormal wisdom.

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas constantly enter into emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, yet they do not seek out the characteristics of any phenomena. There may be bodhisattvas who give rise to a great vow, thinking: "Even if the sentient beings in my buddha-field when I have attained Buddhahood should lack even the names of the Three Vehicles, I shall today with utmost sincerity become a Buddha and attain equal and perfect enlightenment, extensively transforming sentient beings without ever becoming weary."
At that time, eight thousand devas and humans established themselves on the ground of faith, and the Māra king and his retinue immediately returned to their original abodes.
**Chapter Thirty-Three: Entrustment to Brahmā** The Buddha addressed the fearless Brahmā, the great assembly, and all the bodhisattvas:

"For incalculable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, I have accumulated merit and cultivated virtue until I attained Buddhahood of my own accord. I am untainted by the defilements of the eight worldly dharmas. Yet all sentient beings—including those that fly, crawl, and all forms of life—become stained by and attached to the five aggregates (skandhas), indulging in them without relinquishing them. Therefore, the worthy sages are not tainted by the eight dharmas; they understand that the five aggregates and the eighteen bases (āyatana) are empty and non-existent. They remain detached from the eight worldly concerns: gain and loss, defamation and praise, fame and insignificance, suffering and pleasure."
The Buddha again addressed the Brahmā:
"If there are good men or good women who recite, chant, receive, and uphold this sutra, neither Māra nor the gods of Māra will be able to obstruct or destroy them."
Why is this? Because it is protected by the majestic spiritual power of the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones.
If there are good men or good women who seek unexcelled, perfect, true, and complete enlightenment, they shall all attain the realization of its fruit through this scripture.
The Buddha again addressed Brahmā:
"Were there to be sentient beings filling the interval from one kalpa to a hundred thousand kalpas, even if they all together praised this sūtra, they could not exhaustively describe its merits."
Why is this? This sutra is titled "The Inexhaustible Treasury," which is beyond the reach of arhats and pratyekabuddhas;
it is also titled "The Questions of the Most Victorious Bodhisattva."
I now entrust this sutra to you; do not allow even a single word to be missing, ensuring that both the body of flavor and the body of phrases are all made complete.
Just as I have today attained the Buddha-way, with thirty-two marks and eighty secondary characteristics, my body golden in color and my halo seven feet wide, filling the entire trichiliocosm.

If there is a son or daughter of good family who, with utmost sincerity, seeks the Buddha-way and makes offerings to the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, it would not equal the merit of reciting this sūtra for even the duration of a finger-snap.

Why is this? It is because the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas have all attained the path to Buddhahood through this sutra; and the Srotāpannas, Sakṛdāgāmins, Anāgāmins, Arhats, and Pratyekabuddhas have all achieved their realization through this scripture.
At that time, the Brahmā Abhayadeva came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If there are good men or good women who seek the Buddha with utmost sincerity, reciting this sutra and holding it in mind without forgetting, we shall protect these good men and good women within a range of one hundred yojanas, so that Māras or celestial Māras shall find no opportunity to harm them.”
The Buddha told Brahmā:
"So it is, so it is; it is just as you have said.
All Buddhas of the past, future, and present recite this scripture, and they will certainly reach firmness and never regress."

If there are sons or daughters of good family who cultivate the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, the eightfold noble path, and emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, they shall all achieve worldly success through this scripture; thus there arise the four classes: bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās.

At that time, the youth Mañjuśrī, the Bodhisattva Varaprabha, the Venerable Śāriputra, and the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, and mahoragas, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, paid homage and departed.
